# THE SOCIAL ORGANIZATION AND THE SECRET SOCIETIES OF THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

## By FRANZ BOAS.

### PREFACE.

This paper describes and illustrates the collections of the U.S. National Museum regarding the social organization and secret societies of the Indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note> of the British Columbia coast. It is based on research conducted by the author over several years. Most of the facts presented here were observed and recorded by Mr. George Hunt of Fort Rupert, British Columbia. Mr. Hunt has a deep interest in everything related to the ethnology <term>ethnology</term> <note>The study of the characteristics of different peoples and the relationships between them.</note> of the Kwakwaka'wakw <note>The author uses "Kwakiutl," but "Kwakwaka'wakw" is the modern preferred name for this group of nations.</note> people, and I am deeply indebted to him. I am also grateful to him for explaining ceremonies I witnessed myself—the meanings of which were often difficult to grasp—and for finding individuals who could provide explanations on specific points.

I would like to thank Mr. C. O. Hastings of Victoria, British Columbia, who took the series of photographs reproduced in this report. Mr. John C. Fillmore and I transcribed a series of phonographic records of ceremonial songs. I also had the opportunity to verify many of these recordings by having the singers repeat the songs two years after the initial records were made.

I also wish to thank Professor A. Bastian, director of the Royal Ethnographical Museum in Berlin; Sir Augustus W. Franks, keeper of the ethnographical department at the British Museum; Mr. Franz Heger, director of the ethnographical department at the Imperial Royal Museum of Natural History in Vienna; and Professor F. W. Putnam, curator of the anthropology department at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. They all kindly permitted me to use specimens from their museum collections to illustrate this report.

| au | "ow" as in "how." |
| l | as in English. |

| L | the same as above, but short and forceful <note>original: "exploded"</note>; voiceless <term>surd</term>. |
| q | a "k" sound made at the back of the throat <term>velar k</term>. |
| g | a "g" sound made at the back of the throat <term>velar g</term>. |
| k | English "k." |
| k· | a "k" sound made further forward on the palate, almost like "ky." |
| g· | a "g" sound made further forward on the palate, almost like "gy." |
| x | like the "ch" in "brook" <note>original: "German *Bach*"</note>. |
| X | "x" pronounced at the back edge of the hard palate, between "x" and "x·." |

| h | as in English. |
| y | as in "year." |
| w<br/>m<br/>n | as in English. |
| , | a pause; when following a consonant, it is combined with increased force <note>original: "stress"</note> of articulation. |
| ' | accent mark. |

## I. THE INDIGENOUS <note>original: "Indian"</note> TRIBES OF THE NORTH PACIFIC COAST.

The Pacific Coast of America between Juan de Fuca Strait and Yakutat Bay is inhabited by many Indigenous tribes. While they are distinct in their physical characteristics and languages, they share a single culture. Their arts, industries, customs, and beliefs differ so much from those of all other Indigenous groups that they form one of the most clearly defined cultural groups on our continent.

While a quick glance at these people and a comparison with other tribes emphasizes the uniformity of their culture, a closer investigation reveals many unique traits within individual tribes. This proves that their culture has developed slowly and originated from several distinct centers, with each group contributing something to the culture we observe today.

The region inhabited by these people is a mountainous coast intersected by countless sounds and fjords <note>original: "fiords"</note> and dotted with islands, both large and small. <note>The following paragraph contains handwritten brackets and underlines in the original source.</note> Because of this, travel along the coast by canoe is very easy, while access to the inland is difficult due to the rugged hills and dense woods. A few fjords cut deep into the mainland, and the valleys opening into them provide access to the heart of the high mountain ranges that separate the coast from the interior highlands. These ranges form an effective barrier between the people of the interior and those of the coast. These fjords, along with their rivers and valleys, offer relatively easy access to the coast, and it is along these lines that cultural exchange has occurred.

Looking slightly beyond the territory defined above, the passes where cultural influences flowed most easily were the Columbia River in the south and the pass leading along the Salmon and Bella Coola rivers to Dean Inlet and Bentinck Arm. Of less importance are Chilcat Pass, the Stikine River, the Nass and Skeena rivers, and the Fraser River. Thus, there are only two major and four minor passes through which the coastal people came into contact with those of the interior. Consequently, they have occupied a rather isolated position and have been able to develop a unique culture without experiencing major invasions from other parts of America.

Since rainfall all along the coast is very high, the lower elevations are covered with dense forests that provide wood for building houses, canoes, tools, and utensils. Among these trees, the red cedar (*Thuya gigantea* <note>Now scientifically classified as *Thuja plicata*.</note>) is the most prominent, as it provides the locals with material for most of what they make. Its wood is used for building and carving, while its bark is used to make clothing and ropes. The yellow cedar, pine, fir, hemlock, spruce, yew, maple, and alder are also important to these Indigenous groups. The woods also abound with many kinds of berries, which...

<meta>This page continues the overview of the North Pacific Coast, transitioning from the description of the region's geography to a detailed account of the natural resources and the traditional diet and hunting practices of the Indigenous peoples.</meta>

REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

...are eagerly sought for. The kelp and seaweeds that grow abundantly all along the shore are also utilized.

In the woods, deer, elk, black and grizzly bears, wolves, and many other animals are found. The mountain goat lives on the higher ranges of the mainland. The beaver, otter, marten, mink, and fur seal provide valuable skins, which were formerly used to make blankets. The Indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note> keep dogs in their villages to assist the hunters.

However, the primary food source for the Indigenous people is provided by the sea. Seals, sea lions, and whales are found in considerable numbers; however, the people depend almost entirely upon various species of salmon, halibut, and the oulachon, or candlefish (North Pacific smelt <note>original: "Thaleichthys pacificus, Girard"</note>), which are caught in enormous quantities. Various types of cod and other sea fish also provide food. Herrings visit the coast early in the spring. In short, there is such an abundance of animal life in the sea that the people live almost solely upon it. Besides fish, they gather various kinds of shellfish, sea urchins <note>original: "sea eggs"</note>, and cuttlefish.

The people are, therefore, essentially fishers; all other pursuits are of secondary importance. Whales are hunted only by the tribes of the west coast of Vancouver Island. Other tribes are satisfied with the carcasses of dead whales that drift ashore. Sea lions and seals are harpooned, with the barbed harpoon point either attached to a float <note>original: "bladder"</note> or tied to the stern of the canoe. The harpoon lines are made of cedar bark and animal sinews. The meat of these sea animals is eaten, while their intestines are used for the manufacture of bowstrings and bags. Codfish and halibut are caught using hooks. These are attached to fishing lines made of kelp. The hook is equipped with a sinker, while the upper part is kept afloat by a float or a wooden buoy. Cuttlefish are used for bait. The fish are either roasted over or near the fire, or boiled in wooden containers <note>original: "kettles"</note> using red-hot stones to heat the water. Those intended for use in winter are split into strips and dried in the sun or over the fire. 

Salmon are caught in weirs <note>underwater fences or enclosures</note> and fish traps when swimming up the rivers, or by using nets dragged between two canoes. Later in the season, salmon are harpooned. For fishing in deeper water, a very long, double-pointed harpoon is used. Herring and oulachon are caught using a long rake. The oulachon are rendered <note>original: "tried"</note> in canoes or containers filled with water, which is heated by red-hot stones. The resulting oil is kept in bottles made of dried kelp. In winter, dried halibut and salmon dipped in oil is one of the principal dishes of the tribes living on the outer coast. Clams and mussels are collected by the women; they are eaten fresh, or strung on sticks or strips of cedar bark and dried for winter use. Cuttlefish are caught using long sticks; sea urchins are obtained with round bag nets. Fish roe, particularly that of herring, is collected in great quantities, dried, and eaten with oil.

Sea grass, berries, and roots are also gathered by the women. The sea grass is cut, formed into square cakes, and dried for winter use. The same is done with several kinds of berries, which, when used, are dissolved in water and eaten mixed with fish oil. Crab apples are boiled...

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of the North Pacific Coast tribes, specifically the Kwakiutl, detailing their traditional methods for food storage, hunting, clothing manufacture, and woodworking.</meta>

<page-num>319</page-num>

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

...and kept in their juice until late in the winter. They are also eaten with fish oil. The food is kept in large boxes made of bent cedar wood, with the bottoms sewn to the sides.

In winter, deer are hunted. Formerly, bows and arrows were used in their pursuit, but these have now been replaced by guns. The bow was made of yew wood or maple. The arrows had stone, bone, and copper points. Bows and arrows were carried in wooden quivers. Deer are also captured by being driven into large nets made of cedar bark, deer sinews, or nettles. Elk <note>original: "Elks"</note> are hunted in the same way. For smaller animals, traps are used. Deer and bears are also caught in large traps. Birds were shot with arrows equipped with thick, blunt points. Deerskins are worked into leather and used for various purposes—principally for ropes and, in the past, for clothing.

The Indigenous people <note>original: "natives"</note> of this region go barelegged. The principal part of their clothing is the blanket, and this was made of tanned skins or woven from mountain-goat wool, dog hair, feathers, or a mixture of these. The thread is spun on the bare leg using a spindle. Another kind of blanket is made of soft cedar bark, with the warp tied across the weft. These blankets are trimmed with fur. At the present time, woolen blankets are most extensively used. On festive occasions, "button blankets" are worn. Most of these are light blue blankets with a red border set with mother-of-pearl buttons. Many are also adorned with the crest of the owner, which is cut out of red cloth and sewn onto the blanket. Men wear a shirt under the blanket, while women wear a petticoat in addition. Before the introduction of woolen blankets, women used to wear an apron and a belt made of cedar bark. When canoeing or working on the beach, the women wear large, water-tight hats made of basketry. In rainy weather, a water-tight cape or poncho made of cedar bark is used.

The women dress their hair in two braids <note>original: "plaits"</note>, while the men wear it relatively short. The men keep it back from the face by means of a strap of fur or cloth tied around the head. Ear and nose ornaments are used extensively. They are made of bone and abalone shell. The women of the northernmost tribes (from about the Skeena River northward) wear labrets <note>lip ornaments</note>.

A great variety of baskets are used—large wicker baskets for carrying fish and clams, and cedar-bark baskets for storage purposes. Mats made of cedar bark—and in the south, those made of rushes—are used for bedding, packing, seats, dishes, box covers, and similar purposes.

In earlier times, woodworking was done using stone and bone implements. Trees were felled with stone axes and split by means of wooden or bone wedges. Boards were split out of cedar trees using these wedges. After the rough cutting was finished, the surface of the wood was planed with adzes; a considerable number of these were made of jade and serpentine boulders, which are materials found in several rivers. Carvings were executed with stone and shell knives.

<summary>This page describes the material culture and daily life of the Kwakiutl and neighboring tribes, including their hunting techniques, traditional clothing made from cedar and wool, and the tools used for woodworking.</summary>
<keywords>Kwakiutl, hunting, cedar bark, button blankets, woodworking, adzes, labrets, Skeena River, Indigenous technology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic overview of the North Pacific Coast tribes, transitioning from descriptions of clothing and tools to a detailed classification of linguistic groups and their geographic territories.</meta>

<page-num>320</page-num>

Stone mortars and pestles were used for mashing berries. Paint pots made of stone, brushes, and stencils made of cedar bark formed the kit of the Indigenous <note>original: "Indian"</note> painter. Pipes were made of slate, bone, or wood.

Canoes are made of cedar wood. The types of canoes vary somewhat among the different tribes of the coast, also depending largely upon whether the canoe is to be used for hunting, traveling, or fishing. The canoe is propelled and steered by paddles.

The houses are made of wood and reach considerable sizes. The details of construction vary significantly among the various tribes, but the general appearance is very similar from Comox to Alaska; farther south, however, the square northern house gives way to the longhouse of the Coast Salish. A detailed description of the house will be provided later on.

The tribes comprising the North Pacific group speak many different languages. From north to south, we find the following linguistic families, which are subdivided into numerous dialects as follows:

I. Tlingit, inhabiting southern Alaska.
II. Haida, inhabiting the Queen Charlotte Islands and part of the Prince of Wales Archipelago.
III. Tsimshian, inhabiting the Nass and Skeena rivers and the neighboring islands.
1. Nisqa', on the Nass River.
2. Gyitkca'n, on the upper Skeena River.
3. Ts'E'mcian, on the lower Skeena River and the neighboring islands.
IV. Wakashan, inhabiting the coast from Gardiner Channel to Cape Mudge, with the exception of the region around Dean Inlet; Vancouver Island, except its southeastern part from Comox to Sooke Inlet; and Cape Flattery.
A. Kwakiutl group.
1. Xa–îsla, on the Gardiner and Douglas channels.
2. Hē'iltsuq, from Gardiner Channel to Rivers Inlet.
3. Kwakiutl, from Rivers Inlet to Cape Mudge.
B. Nootka group, inhabiting the west coast of Vancouver Island and Cape Flattery.
V. Salishan, inhabiting the coast of the mainland and the eastern part of Vancouver Island south of Cape Mudge, the southern part of the interior as far east as the Selkirk Range, and the northern parts of Washington, Idaho, and Montana; also the region of Dean Inlet.
A. The Coast Salish.
1. Bî'lxula, on Dean Inlet and Bentinck Arm.
2. ÇaLō'ltx, at Comox and Toba Inlet, formerly north of Cape Mudge.
3. PE'nLatc, at Comox.
4. Sī'ciaL, on Jervis Inlet.
5. Sqxō'mic, on Howe Sound and Burrard Inlet.
6. Qau'etcin, on the Cowichan River and the lower Fraser River.

Among these languages, Tlingit and Haida on one hand, and Kwakiutl, Salishan, and Chemakum on the other, show certain similarities in form which lead me to consider these groups more closely related to each other than to the other languages.

The physical characteristics of the Indigenous <note>original: "Indians"</note> of this region also show that they are by no means a uniform people. As far as we currently know, we may distinguish four types on the coast of British Columbia: the northern type, including the Nisqa' and Tsimshian; the Kwakiutl type; the type from Harrison Lake; and the Salish of the interior, as represented by the Okanagan, Flathead, and Shuswap. <meta>This page continues the physical anthropometric descriptions of the Indigenous groups of British Columbia, specifically detailing the physiological distinctions between the northern tribes, the Kwakiutl, the Harrison Lake type, and the interior Salish, while introducing their social organizational structures.</meta>

REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

The types represented by these figures may be described as follows: The northern Indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note> are of medium stature. Their arms are relatively long, and their bodies are short. The head is very large, particularly in its transversal diameter. The same may be said of the face, the breadth of which is enormous, as it exceeds the average breadth of face of the North American Indigenous person <note>original: "Indian"</note> by 6 mm. The height of the face is moderate; therefore, its shape appears decidedly low. The nose is very low compared to the height of the face and is at the same time broad. Its elevation over the face is also only very slight. The bridge is generally concave and very flat between the eyes.

The Kwakiutl are somewhat shorter; the trunks of their bodies are relatively longer, and their arms and legs are shorter than those of the first group. The dimensions of the head are very nearly the same, but the face shows a remarkably different type, which distinguishes it fundamentally from the faces of all the other groups. The breadth of the face exceeds only slightly the average breadth of face of the Indigenous person <note>original: "Indian"</note>, but its height is enormous. The same may be said of the nose, which is very high and relatively narrow. Its elevation is also very great. The nasal bones are strongly developed and form a steep arch, with their lower end rising high above the face. This causes a very strongly hooked nose to be found frequently among the Kwakiutl; this type of nose is almost absent in all other parts of the Pacific Coast. This feature is so strongly marked that individuals of this group may be recognized with a considerable degree of certainty by the form of the face and of the nose alone.

The Harrison Lake type has a very short stature. The head is exceedingly short and broad, surpassing in this respect all other forms known to exist in North America. The face is not very wide but is very low, thus producing a <term>chamæprosopic</term> form, the proportions of which resemble those of the Nass River face, while its dimensions are much smaller. In this small face, we find a nose which is absolutely higher than that of the Nass River Indigenous person <note>original: "Indian"</note> with his huge face. It is, at the same time, rather narrow. The lower portion of the face appears very small, as may be seen by subtracting the height of the nose from that of the face, which gives an approximate measure of the distance from the septum to the chin.

The Salish of the interior have a stature of 168 cm. Their heads are shorter than those of the tribes of Northern British Columbia or of the Indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note> of the plains. Their faces have the average height of the Indigenous <note>original: "Indian"</note> face, being higher than that of the northern type of Indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note>, but lower than that of the Kwakiutl. The nose is high and wide, and has the characteristic Indigenous <note>original: "Indian"</note> form, which is rare in most parts of the coast.

The social organization of the tribes of the coast shows considerable variation. The tribes of the northern parts of the coast have a maternal organization, while those in the south are purely paternally organized. The central tribes, particularly the Kwakiutl, show a peculiar transitional stage.

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIGENOUS PEOPLE <note>original: "INDIANS"</note>.

The Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, and Hēiltsuq have animal totems. The first of these have two phratries: the raven ($Q'oa'la$) and the eagle ($G\cdot it\bar{e}na'$) among the Haida. The Tsimshian have four totems—raven ($Qanha'da$), eagle ($Laxskiyek$), wolf ($Laxk\cdot eb\bar{o}'$), and bear ($G\cdot ispawaduwE'da$); the Hēiltsuq have three—raven ($Q\bar{o}'ix\cdot t\bar{e}n\hat{o}x$), eagle ($W\bar{i}'k'oaqx\cdot t\bar{e}n\hat{o}x$), and killer whale ($Ha'lx'aix\cdot t\bar{e}n\hat{o}x$); the Xa-isla' have six—beaver, eagle, wolf, salmon, raven, and killer whale. Animal totems in the proper sense of this term are limited to these five groups or tribes. They are not found among the Kwakiutl, although they belong to the same linguistic family as the Xa-isla and Hēiltsuq. The clans of the northern tribes bear the names of their respective totems and are exogamous <note>marrying outside of a specific social group</note>.

However, it is important to understand that the native people do not consider themselves to be descendants of the totem. All my efforts to obtain information regarding the supposed origin of the relationship between humans and animals have always led to the telling of a myth. These myths state how a certain ancestor of the clan in question obtained his totem. The character of these legends is consistent among all the peoples of this region; this is true even farther south among the Kwakiutl and the northern tribes of the Coast Salish, who have no animal totem in the strict sense of the term. The ideas of the Kwakiutl regarding these matters will be described fully later on. As these legends reveal the fundamental views the native people hold regarding their totems, I shall provide abstracts of a few of them.

The following is a legend of the Tsimshian:

*The Bear Clan.*—An Indigenous man <note>original: "Indian"</note> went mountain-goat hunting. When he had reached a remote mountain range, he met a black bear who took him to his home and taught him how to catch salmon and how to build canoes. The man stayed with the bear for two years; then he returned to his own village. The people were afraid of him because he looked just like a bear. One man, however, caught him and took him home. He could not speak and could not eat anything but raw food. Then they rubbed him with magic herbs, and gradually he was transformed back into the shape of a man. After this, whenever he was in need, he called his friend the bear, who came to assist him. In winter, when the rivers were frozen, he alone was able to catch salmon. He built a house and painted the bear on the house front. His sister made a dancing blanket with a design representing a bear. Therefore, the descendants of his sisters use the bear as their crest.

It is clear that legends of this type correspond almost exactly to the tales of the acquisition of manitows <note>guardian spirits</note> among the Eastern Indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note>. They are evidence that the totem of this group of tribes is, essentially, the hereditary manitow of a family. This comparison becomes even clearer when we consider that every man among these tribes acquires a guardian spirit, but he can only acquire those that belong to his clan. Thus, a person may have the general crest of his clan and, additionally, use any guardian spirits he has personally acquired as his personal crest. This partly explains the great variety of crest combinations observed in the carvings of these people.

<summary>This page explains that animal totems among Northern Pacific Coast tribes are not viewed as ancestors but as hereditary guardian spirits acquired through ancestral encounters with animals. It details the specific totems of various tribes and provides a Tsimshian legend about the origin of the Bear Clan crest.</summary>

# REPORT OF THE NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

The more general the use of a crest is within the entire clan, the more remote the time to which the clan legend is attributed. In many cases, the incidents described are considered relatively recent and are therefore confined to the descendants of the specific person whom the legend concerns. The extreme case is the narrative of a single person acquiring one of the crests for the clan.

These ideas require that we find the clans or phratries subdivided and that a multiplicity of crests exists for each phratry. As an illustration of this phenomenon, I will provide a list of the crests and clans of the Stikine tribe of the Tlingit:

Crests of the raven phratry: Raven, frog, goose, sea lion, owl, salmon, beaver, codfish, skate.

Crests of the wolf phratry: Wolf, bear, eagle, killer whale, shark, auk, gull, sparrow hawk, thunder bird.

The phratries of the Stikine tribes are subdivided as follows:

The list is likely incomplete, but it shows the character of these subdivisions. Similar subdivisions, although less numerous, are found among the Tsimshian.

The crest is used to ornament objects belonging to a member of the clan; they are carved on columns intended to honor the memory of a deceased relative, painted on the house front, or carved on a column which is placed in front of the house, and are also displayed as masks during the festivals of the clan. It is impossible to draw a sharp line between a pure crest and figures or masks illustrating certain incidents in the legendary history of the clan. In order to illustrate this point, which is of great importance in the study of our subject, I will describe a few examples observed among the Nîsqa' Indians.

The <term>G·ispawaduwE'da</term>, the bear clan of the Nîsqa', use a headdress representing the owl (<term>māskutgunu'ks</term>) (Plate 1), surrounded by many small human heads called <term>gyad Em Laqs</term> <gloss>claw men</gloss>. This is worn during potlatches <note>ceremonial feasts involving the redistribution of wealth and status</note>, and commemorates the following tradition:

A chief at <term>T'Em lax'ā'mt</term> had a son who was crying all the time. His father became impatient and sent him out of the house, saying, "The

As an example of the use of the crest—namely, the clan legends used in the raising of memorial columns—I will provide the following: A man had the squid as his protector. After his death, his son held a festival, during the course of which the ground opened and a huge rock covered with kelp emerged. This was made of wood and bark. There was a cave under the rock, and a large squid came out of it. It was made of cedar bark, and its arms were fitted with hooks which caught and tore the blankets of the audience. The song of the squid was sung by women who were sitting on three platforms at the rear of the house:

When the G·itx·q'adô'q branch of the Qanha'da holds a festival, three masks make their appearance. One of these has a mustache and represents a young man named G·itgoô'yim (Plate 2, upper figure), while the other two are called *Cā'câ* (Plate 2, lower figures). They represent the following tradition:

While the people were staying at the fishing village Gulg·ē'uL, the boys, under the leadership of a young man named G·itgoô'yim, built a small house in the woods behind the town. They took a spring salmon with them and played with it until it was rotten. They caught small fish in the creek, then split and dried them. They made small drums and began to sing and dance. For four days they stayed there, dancing the entire time. Then they became supernatural beings. G·itgoô'yim's hair turned into crystal and copper. The people were about to move to another camp and went to fetch the boys, whom they heard singing:

After the squid and the rock had disappeared again, a man wearing the sun mask appeared in the doorway. When the people began to sing his song, a movable sun attached to the mask began to turn. The sun belongs to the G-ispawaduwE'da; the squid commemorates the misfortune of one of the ancestors of the deceased, who was captured by a huge animal while hunting squids at low tide. His friends tried to free him but were unable to do so. When the water began to rise, they pulled a bag made of sea-lion intestines over his head, hoping that the air inside might allow him to survive; however, when they looked for him at the next tide, they found him dead.

After the festival, a memorial column was erected. From the bottom upward, it represented first four men called Lōayō'qs, or "the commanders." These are a crest of the G-ispawaduwE'da. Tradition says that one night, several men dug a hole for a specific purpose behind a house near a grave tree. They saw an opening in the woods with a fire in the middle, around which ghosts were dancing. They sat there as if they were in a house, but the men saw only a pole where the door of the house would have been. Four men called Lōayō'qs were standing at the door and called to them, "nagwī't!" (to this side). Since that time, the G-ispawaduwE'da have used these figures.

On top of the four men was the sea bear (mEdī'ek Em ak·s) with three fins on its back. Each fin has a human face at its base. The tradition of the sea bear tells how four brothers went down the Skeena River and were taken to the bottom of the sea by Hagulâ'q, a sea monster over whose house they had anchored. His house had a number of platforms. Inside were the killer whales, who were Hagulâ'q's men. He had four kettles named Lukewarm, Warm, Hot, and Boiling, and a hat shaped like a sea monster with a number of rings on top. The name of his house was Helahā'idEq (near the Haida country). He gave the brothers the right to use all these objects along with their songs, which are sung at all the great ceremonies of the clan. The song of the house is as follows:

<image-desc>A musical score for a Kwakiutl song, featuring three staves of music in 3/4 time. A tempo marking indicates a quarter note equals 96. Phonetic lyrics are written beneath the notes on each staff.</image-desc>

->Qō......... milā yē ēq - dēs - ku nā dē<-

->qa - a - mila yē dēs - ku - nā dē hēla - hai - degi<-

->yē dēya gō ē nu - ēl wi hagu - lâq aya gō.<-

That is: My friend, walk close to the country of the Haida, the great Hagulâ'q.

## II. THE SOCIAL ORGANIZATION OF THE KWAKIUTL.

The Kwakiutl are divided into many tribes, which are themselves subdivided into septs and clans. Each clan of the Kwakiutl proper traces its origin back to a mythical ancestor who descended from heaven, rose from the underworld, or emerged from the ocean. Their crests and privileges, which will be discussed later, are based on the adventures of these ancestors from whom they claim descent.

First of all, I will provide a list of the tribes and their subdivisions:

1. Xa-isla'.

This list is not quite complete, but it is very nearly so. A number of the clans are subdivided into smaller groups, but it is very difficult to determine these subdivisions. For example, the **Naqô'mg·ilisala** includes a subdivision called **Mē'Emaqaua**, who are, however, not considered a separate clan. The **Lā'la-uiLEla** of the **La'Lasiqoala** are divided into two divisions—the **G·'ēg·'ō'tē**, the descendants of **G·'ō'tē**, and the **Hä'hēqolaL**, the descendants of **Hā'qolaL**. The **Lā'alax sEnt'aiō** of the **Kwakiutl** proper consist of three divisions: The **Lā'alax sEnt'aiō** proper, the **A'lk'unwēE** (= lower corner, speakers of the first division), and the **Hē'ha'mē'tawē**, the descendants of **Ha'mē'tawē**. The **Ts'E'nts'Enx·qaiō** of the **Wā'las Kwakiutl** are divided into two divisions—the **Ts'E'nq'am** and **Hai'māaxstō**. These divisions are given merely as examples, as I have not been able to find all the subdivisions of the different clans and tribes.

The recent history of these tribes and clans explains the development of this very complex social system. Historical tradition says that the **Guē'tEla** and the **Q'ō'moyuē**, both septs of the **Kwakiutl**, recently formed one tribe. At one time a quarrel arose between them, in which **Lā'qoag·ila**, the head chief of the **Guē'tEla**, was killed. Then they divided, and since that time they have formed two septs. There is a saying showing the close relationship between the two, to the effect that the **Guē'tEla** and the **Q'ō'moyuē** are twins—the former nursed at the mother's right breast, the latter at the left.

Still another tribe, which, however, I have not included in the above list because of its recent origin, has branched off from the **Kwakiutl**. These people call themselves **Mā'tilpē** (that is, the highest **Maa'mtag·ila**) and include the septs **Maa'mtag·ila**, **G·ē'xsEm**, and **Haai'lak·Emaē**, all of which are found among the **Guē'tEla** and **Q'ō'moyuē**.

While in these two cases new tribes were formed by a process of division, in at least one other case, a tribe has recently become a clan of another tribe. Specifically, the **Laa'luis** of the **Lē'kwiltôq** have joined the **Kuē'xa** of the same group and now form a fourth clan of the latter. This event happened during the great war with the southern **Salishan** tribes, which was fought in the middle of this century; the cause of the merging was the significant reduction of the tribe's population. The **Q'ō'm'ēnôx** have become entirely extinct. Another tribe that lived near the **Qō'sqēmox**, of which we have only traditional reports, the **Xoyā'les**, has been exterminated by the **Qō'sqēmox**.

These few authentic facts show that the numbers of tribes and clans have gone through significant changes during historical times. This conclusion is supported by the distribution of clans among various tribes and by the meaning of their names. We may distinguish three classes of tribal names and clan names, namely, those that are collective forms of the name of the ancestor, names taken from the

region inhabited by the tribe or clan, and names of honor. There is a decided tendency to substitute names of the latter class for others. Thus the name *Q’ō’moyuē* (the rich ones) is new. The *Xā’xamatsEs* took the name *Wā’litsum* (the great ones) only twenty-five or thirty years ago. I assume that the names *G·i’g·ilqam* (those who receive first), *G·ē’xsem* (chiefs), and *TE’mLTEMLELS* (those under whom the ground shakes), were adopted in a similar way. Other changes of names occur. Thus the Nimkish recently called themselves *Laō’koatx*, which is the name of one of the tribes of the west coast of Vancouver Island, and the *Lau’itsîs* are adopting the name *Ts’ā’mac*, which is the name of the Songish in the Comox dialect.

The geographical names are more suggestive. We find among the Nimkish a clan called *Nē’nêlk’·ēnôx*, the people from the head waters of Nimkish River. This would seem to indicate that the head waters of the river was their ancient home, and that they have joined the rest of the Nimkish. The same may be said of the *Ō’manits’ēnôx* clan of the *L’ā’sq’ēnôx*, the *Qoē’qoaaīnôx* of the *T’Ena’xtax*, and the *Nē’nêlpaē* of the *Qoē’xsōt’ēnôx*.

In all cases where the clan name or the tribal name is a collective form of the name of the ancestor, we may assume that the group formed at one time a single community. How this unit may be broken appears in the case of the *Mā’tilpē*. We observe that quite a number of such clan names are common to several tribes. Thus the *Sī’sīnLaē*, the descendants of *Sī’nLaē*, are found among the *Goasi’la*, *Nā’q’oaqtôq*, *Guē’tEla*, *Lau’itsîs*, and Nimkish. The *Yaai’x·aqEmaē*, the descendants of *Yix·ā’qEmaē*, are found among the *Q’ō’moyuē* and *T’Ena’xtax*. I believe that in all these cases part of the original clan has drifted away from its original home, keeping its old name. This view is sustained by the tradition that the clans were divided at the time of the great flood, one part drifting here, another there.

Still another case that gives evidence of the gradual development of the present system of clans and tribes is furnished by the *Mā’malēleqala* and *Wi’wēqaē*. Both these names are the collective forms of the names of the ancestors. Nevertheless the *Mā’malēleqam* and *Wi’wēaqam*, the *Mā’lēleqala* group, and the *We’qaē* group appear as subdivisions of these tribes. It seems to me that this proves that these subdivisions must have formed the original stock, which the other clans joined in course of time.

All this evidence proves that the present system of tribes and clans is of recent growth and has undergone considerable changes.

The traditions of the clans show clearly what we must consider the original unit of society among the Kwakiutl. Each clan derives its origin from a mythical ancestor, who built his house at a certain place and whose descendants lived at that place. In a great many cases these places prove to be old village sites. In some, large accumulations of shells are found, which show that they have been inhabited through

long periods. We conclude, therefore, that the clan was originally a village community, which, because of changes in population or for purposes of defense, left its old home and joined another community, while retaining its independence to a certain degree. This corresponds exactly to the social organization of the Salishan tribes of southern Vancouver Island and of all the coastal tribes of Washington and Oregon. The simple division into village communities, which seems to have been the prevalent type of society along a significant portion of the Pacific Coast, has undergone such changes among the Kwakiutl that a number of tribes divided into clans have emerged.

While it would be natural in the former stage for the child to be considered a member of the village community to which his father or mother belonged, we can expect disruptions in the organization that developed among the Kwakiutl. Among the village communities of Oregon, Washington, and southern Vancouver Island, the child belongs to the father's village, where the married couple generally live, and it seems that among many of these tribes, the villages are exogamic. Among the Kwakiutl, the clans are also exogamic, and certain privileges are inherited through the paternal line, while a much larger number are obtained through marriage. The existence of the former category suggests that the organization must have been purely paternal at one time. Three causes seem to have disrupted the original organization: the development of the more complex organization mentioned above, the influence of the northern tribes which have a purely maternal organization, and the development of legends regarding the origin of the clans that are analogous to similar traditions of the northern groups of tribes. Taking up the last point first, we find that each clan claims a certain rank and certain privileges based on the descent and adventures of its ancestor. These privileges, if they originally belonged to a tribe that was once in a paternal stage, would likely not deviate from the laws governing that stage. However, if they originated under the influence of a people in a maternal stage, an unusual development seems likely. In the north, a woman's rank and privileges always descend to her children. Practically the same result has been achieved among the Kwakiutl, but in a manner suggesting that a people with paternal institutions adapted their social laws to these customs. Here, the woman brings her father's position and privileges as a dowry to her husband; however, he is not allowed to use them himself but acquires them for the use of his son. Since the woman's father, for his part, acquired his privileges in the same way through his mother, a purely female law of descent is secured, though only through the medium of the husband. It seems to me that this exceedingly intricate law, which will be described in detail in the course of this paper, cannot be explained in any other way than as an adaptation of

<summary>The author argues that Kwakiutl clans evolved from independent village communities and developed a unique inheritance system that blends paternal traditions with northern maternal influences. This system allows a woman's rank and privileges to pass to her son through her husband, effectively creating a matrilineal descent through a male intermediary.</summary>

maternal laws adopted by a tribe that was at a paternal stage. I cannot believe that this is a transition from a maternal society to a paternal society, because there are no traces of the previous stage beyond those found everywhere, which do not prove that the transition was recent at all. There is no trace left of an inheritance from the wife's brothers; the young couple does not live with the wife's parents. But the most important argument is that these customs could not have been prevalent in the village communities from which the present tribal system originated, because in these, the tribe is always identified as the direct descendants of the mythical ancestor. If the village communities had been in a maternal stage, the tribes would have been identified as the descendants of the ancestor's sisters, as is always the case in the legends of the northern tribes.

Names and all the privileges connected with them may also be obtained by killing the owner of the name, either in war or by murder. The slayer then has the right to place his own successor in the position of the enemy he killed. In this way, names and customs have often spread from tribe to tribe.

It remains to support what I have said by telling the legends of a few clans. I shall give a fuller account of these legends later on, while here I will merely refer to those passages that are important to our current consideration. The clan Ō'manits'ēnôx of the L'ā'sq'ēnôx derive their origin from Ts'ī'lqoalōLela, the husband of L'ē'sElaqa (Sun woman). The former descended from heaven while his wife stayed there because she had to attend to the moving sun. He was accompanied by his children Sē'paxaēs (Shining down), Yā'q'Ent'Emaē (First speaker), G·ē'xdEn, and Dā'doqanaqēsEla (Seeing from one corner to the other). From these the clan originated (Appendix p. 665).

The following genealogy of the clan Lā'la-uiLEla of the La'Lasiqoala is an even better example:

A great number of examples of this kind could be given. It is true that these traditions are probably not very old and have been modified along with the changing social life of the people; but from what we know of the development of myths, we should expect to find in them at least some traces of the old maternal institutions if they had ever existed. The fact that they are invariably and always explained by genealogies, such as the one above, seems to me conclusive proof that a paternal organization of the tribe preceded the present one.

I referred several times above to the fact that the clans have certain rights in which the others do not share. These are mainly the use of certain crests and semi-religious performances. All of these are acquired by marriage, as described above. In the village communities of the southern tribes, we find no trace of a crest, while among the Kwakiutl, it is not strictly hereditary but descends through marriage in the female line, in a similar way as the crest of the northern tribes descends. The legends of the acquisition of the crest are also similar to the northern legends on the same subject; I conclude, therefore, that the present stage has developed through contact between these two cultural areas. I do not mean to say that the ideas have been bodily borrowed by the Kwakiutl, but that their manifestation in the social organization of the tribe is largely due to suggestions from the northern tribes. The American idea of the acquisition of the <term>manitou</term> <note>a personal guardian spirit or tutelary genius</note> was evidently also fundamental among the Kwakiutl, as all their tales refer to it, and, as we shall see later on, the whole winter ceremonial is based on it. However, it has assumed a peculiar form in that the <term>manitou</term> was acquired by a mythical ancestor and is now handed down from generation to generation. The connection has in many cases become so slight that the tutelary genius of the clan has declined into a crest. This decline, together with the descent through marriage, I take to be due to the influence of northern totemism.

I give a few stories illustrating the acquisition of the crest through the ancestor, which will bring out the close analogy with the acquisition of the <term>manitou</term>, and also show the manner in which the crest is used for adorning persons and utensils.

The legend of the *Ō'manits'ēnôx*, which I quoted above (Appendix, p. 665), goes on to tell how *G·ē'xdEn* fell in with a number of killer whales, which had assumed the shape of men and were mending their canoes. Their chief gave him the quartz-pointed whaling harpoon, his names, and the right to use the painting of the killer whale on his house front.

Another good example is the following tradition of the clan *Lâ'xsē* of the *Q'ō'moyuē* or *Kuē'xa*. I give here a translation:

The first *Kuē'xa* lived at *Tsā'Xoyō*. Their chief, *Yē'iqoLalasamē*, went bear hunting up the river of *LîXsī'wē* until he came to *Sā'x·sox·*. After he had been away four days, he saw the *Hō'Xhôq* (a fabulous bird, supposed to be similar to the crane) and heard its cry. It was larger than a man. Then *Yē'iqoLalasamē* hid. The *Hō'Xhôq* tried to find him, and finally discovered the place where the chief was hiding at one side of a cedar tree. It tried to peck him with its beak, but missed him. *Yē'iqoLalasamē* merely jumped to the other side of the tree, and the *Hō'Xhôq* could not kill him. He came home at night. Then he carved the crane out of yellow cedar, and now it is the carving of his clan (Plate 3). He invited all the tribes and gave away cedar-bark blankets, all kinds of skins, canoes, and slaves. Then he placed the image of the *Hō'Xhôq* on top of a pole outside of his house.

Later on, a chief of the Qoē'xsot'ēnôx wanted to have the carved Hō'Xhōq. His name was LEk·amā'xōt. He tried to find out how to obtain it and learned that he had to marry the daughter of Yē'iqoLalasamē to acquire it. He then became engaged to marry Mā'xalayuqoa, that chief's daughter. Yē'iqoLalasamē agreed, and they were married. Still later, NEqā'p'Enk·Em, chief of the Ku'kwā'kum of the Guē'tEla, obtained the Hō'Xhōq from the Qoē'xsot'ēnôx through marriage.

The first part of this legend again shows the close analogy with the acquisition of the <term>manitou</term>; the end shows how the privilege of using the carving was acquired, first by one tribe and then by the other.

It is not necessary to provide more of these examples. There is, however, another category of traditions according to which the crests or emblems of the clan are not acquired in this manner but were brought down by the ancestor of the clan from heaven, from the underworld, or from the ocean—wherever he may have originated. This is the case with the Sī'sīnLaē, whose emblem is the sun (figure 1). To this category also belong the numerous tales of ancestors who came down from heaven, took off their masks, and became men; in all these cases, the mask has remained the crest of the clan. The traditions of the G·ī'g·ilqam of the Q'ō'moyuē, the Ts'E'nts'Enx·qaiō, and many others belong to this class.

There is yet another class of privileges connected with these traditions which I will only briefly mention here, as I will discuss them more fully later. I am referring to membership in secret societies. Many ancestors, when obtaining their <term>manitous</term>, were given the right to perform certain dances, or were given secret songs or the power to eat human flesh. These rights have also become hereditary, but they differ from the crest in that the character of the initiating spirit (the <term>manitou</term>) has been more clearly preserved. Every individual who is entitled to membership in one of the secret societies by descent or marriage must nevertheless be initiated by its presiding spirit before joining the society.

In all festivals, references to these traditions are very frequent, and it is quite necessary to be familiar with them to understand the proceedings and speeches, as will become clear in the later parts of this description.

Summing up the preceding points, we may say that in earlier times, the Kwakiutl consisted of a series of village communities in which descent was traced through the paternal line, and the members of each community were considered descendants of a single ancestor. These communities combined into groups, but the constituent elements of these groups maintained a certain degree of independence and continued to be regarded as relatives. Each clan—as we may call the constituent elements of the tribe—developed a clan tradition founded upon the acquisition of a <term>manitou</term> by the mythical ancestor, the <term>manitou</term>

So far we have considered the clan as a unit. However, the individuals composing the clan do not form a uniform group but differ in rank. All the tribes of the Pacific Coast are divided into a nobility, common people, and slaves. The last of these may be left out of consideration, as they do not form an integral part of the clan but are captives taken in war or purchases, and they may change ownership like any other piece of property. The clan of the Kwakiutl is organized so that a certain limited number of families are recognized. The ancestor of each of these families has a tradition of his own, apart from the general clan tradition; and, because he possesses this tradition—which almost always concerns the acquisition of a <term>manitou</term>—he has certain crests and privileges of his own. This tradition and the crests and privileges connected with it descended, along with the name of the ancestor, to his direct descendants in the male line or, as indicated above, through the marriage of his daughter to his son-in-law, and through him to his grandchildren. But there is only one man at a time who personifies the ancestor and who, consequently, holds his rank and privileges. The individuals personifying the ancestors form the nobility of

At all festivals, they sit in the order of their rank, which is called the "seat" of the person (Tā'qoē). Legend says that the order of seats was established by the deity at a festival of the tribes, during the time when animals were still able to speak. <header>THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.</header>

### III. THE POTLATCH.

Before proceeding any further, it will be necessary to describe the method of acquiring rank. This is done by means of the potlatch, or the distribution of property. This custom has been described often, but it has been thoroughly misunderstood by most observers. The underlying principle is that of the interest-bearing investment of property.

The child, when born, is given the name of the place where it is born. This name (g·i′nLAXLĒ) it keeps until it is about a year old. Then its father, mother, or some other relative gives a paddle or a mat to each member of the clan, and the child receives its second name (nā′map'axLēya). When the boy is about 10 or 12 years old, he obtains his third name (gōmiatsExLā′yē). In order to obtain it, he must distribute a number of small presents, such as shirts or single blankets, among his own clan or tribe. When the youth thus starts out in life, he is liberally assisted by his elders, particularly by the nobility of the tribe.

I must say here that the unit of value is the single blanket—nowadays a cheap white woolen blanket—which is valued at 50 cents. The double blanket is valued at three single blankets. These blankets form the Indians' means of exchange, and everything is paid for in blankets or in objects whose value is measured by blankets. When a native has to pay debts and does not have a sufficient number of blankets, he borrows them from his friends and must pay the following rates of interest:

For a period of a few months, for 5 borrowed blankets, 6 must be returned (Lē′k·ō); for a period of six months, for 5 borrowed blankets, 7 must be returned (mā′′Laxsa Lē′k·ōyō); for a period of twelve months or longer, for 5 borrowed blankets, 10 must be returned (dē′ida or g·ē′La).

When a person has poor credit, he may pawn his name for a year. The name must then not be used during that period, and for 30 blankets which he has borrowed, he must pay 100 in order to redeem his name. This is called q'ā′q'oaxō (selling a slave).

The rate of interest for the Lē′k·ō varies somewhat around 25 percent, according to the kindness of the lender and the credit of the borrower. For a very short time, blankets may be loaned without interest. This is designated by the same term.

When the boy is about to take his third name, he will borrow blankets from the other members of the tribe, who all assist him. He must repay them after a year, or later, with 100 percent interest. Thus he may have gathered 100 blankets. In June, the time set for this act, the boy will distribute these blankets among his own tribe, giving proportionately to every member of the tribe, but a few more to the chief. This is called Lā′X'uit. When any member of the tribe distributes blankets after this time, the boy receives treble the amount he has given. The people make it a point to repay him within a month.

It details the use of blankets as currency and the specific interest rates required for borrowing property or redeeming a pawned name.</summary>

Thus, he owns 300 blankets, of which, however, he must repay 200 after one year has passed. He loans the blankets out among his friends, and thus at the close of the year, he may possess about 400 blankets.

The next June, he pays his debts (qoana') during a festival at which all the clans from whom he borrowed blankets are present. The festival is generally held on the street or in an open area near the village. Up to this time, he is not allowed to take part in feasts. But now he

may distribute property in order to obtain a potlatch name (p'ā'tsaxLäyē). This is also called Lā'X'uit.

At this time, the father gives up his seat (Lā'Noē) in favor of his son. After the boy has paid his debts, the chief calls all the older members of the tribe to a council, in which it is resolved that the boy is to receive his father's seat. The chief sends his speaker to call the boy, and his clan goes out in company with the speaker. The young man—for from this time forward he will be counted among the men—dresses with a black headband and paints long vertical stripes, one on each side of his face, running down from the outer corners of the eyes. These stripes represent tears. He gives a number of blankets to his friends, who carry them into the house where the council is being held. The speaker enters first and announces his arrival. The young man follows, and after him enter his friends, carrying blankets. He remains standing in front of the fire, and the chief announces to him that he is to take his father's seat. Then the boy distributes his blankets among the other clans and sells some for food, with which a feast is prepared. His father gives up his seat and takes his place among the old men (Nō'matsēil). The blankets given away at this feast are repaid with 100 percent interest. In this manner, the young man continues to loan and distribute blankets and is thus able, with due caution and foresight, to amass a fortune. Sometimes it happens that the successor to a man's name (Lawu'lqame) already has a name of his own. In all such cases (as well as when the name is acquired by inheritance), the successor gives up his name and his property to his own successor.

Possession of wealth is considered honorable, and it is the goal of every Indian to acquire a fortune. But it is not so much the posses-

<meta>This page continues the explanation of Kwakiutl social advancement, specifically how the possession and distribution of wealth through festivals allows a man to increase his prestige and influence within the tribe.</meta>

possession of wealth as the ability to give great festivals that makes wealth a desirable object to the Indian. As the boy acquires his second name and man’s estate by means of a distribution of property—which in the course of time will return to him with interest—the man’s name acquires greater weight in the tribal councils and greater renown among all the people, as he is able to distribute more and more property at each subsequent festival. Therefore, boys and men vie with each other in organizing great distributions of property. Elders pit boys of different clans against each other, and each is encouraged to do his utmost to outdo his rival.

And as the boys strive against each other, so do the chiefs and the entire clans; the single objective of the Indian is to outdo his rival. Formerly, feats of bravery counted as much as distributions of property, but nowadays, as the Indians say, "rivals fight with property only." The clans are thus perpetually pitted against each other according to their rank. The Kwakiutl tribes are considered the highest in the order given in the list above. In intertribal rivalry, they do not strive against each other, but rather:

Gue'tEla against the Ma'malēleqala.
Q'o'moyuē against the Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx.
Q'ō'mk·ūtis against the NE'mqic or Laō'koatx.
Wā'las Kwakiutl against the Lau'itsīs or Ts'ā'mas.

I have referred several times to the distribution of blankets. The recipient of such a distribution is not at liberty to refuse the gift, although, according to what I have said, it is nothing but an interest-bearing loan that must be repaid at some future time with 100 percent interest. This festival is called *p'a'sa*, literally, "flattening something" (for instance, a basket). This means that the rival's name is flattened by the amount of property given.

<column-break/>

There is still another method of rising in the social scale: namely, by showing oneself superior to a rival. This can be done by inviting the rival and his clan or tribe to a festival and giving him a significant number of blankets. He is compelled to accept these, but is not allowed to do so until after he has placed an equal number of blankets on top of the pile offered to him. This is called *dāPentg·ala*, and the blankets placed on top of the first pile are called *dā'pEnō*. Then he receives the entire pile and becomes a debtor for that amount; that is, he must repay the gift with 100 percent interest.

# REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

A similar process occurs when a canoe is given to a rival. When the gift is offered to him, the recipient must place blankets totaling half the value of the canoe upon it. This is called *dā'g·ōt*, or "taking hold of the bow of the canoe." These blankets are kept by the original owner of the canoe. Later on, the recipient of the canoe must return another canoe, along with a sufficient number of blankets to serve as an "anchor line" for the canoe. This act of giving a canoe is called *sā'k·a*.

The purchase or gift—whichever one chooses to call it—of a "copper" is even more complicated. All along the North Pacific Coast, from Yakutat to Comox, curiously shaped copper plates are used. In ancient times, these were made of native copper found in Alaska and likely also on the Nass River, but today they are crafted from imported copper. The typical shape of these copper plates can be seen in figures 2 and 3 and Plate 4. The T-shaped part (*qa'lā's*), which forms two ridges, is hammered. The top is called "the face" (*ō'nuxLEMē*), and the lower part is the "hind end" (*ō'nutsexstē*). The front of the copper is covered with black lead, into which a face representing the owner's crest animal is engraved. These coppers serve the same function that high-denomination banknotes do for us. Although the actual value of the piece of copper is small, it is made to represent a large number of blankets and can always be sold for blankets. The value is not set arbitrarily but depends on the amount of property given away at the festival where the copper is sold. Generally, the more often a copper is sold, the higher its value becomes, as each new buyer attempts to invest more blankets in it. Therefore, the purchase of a copper also brings distinction, because it proves that the buyer is able to gather a vast amount of property.

Each copper has its own name, and from the following list of coppers that were in Fort Rupert in 1893, the values attached to some of them can be seen:

*Mā'xts'ōlEM* (meaning "all other coppers are ashamed to look at it"), 7,500 blankets. <note>This copper has two crosspieces.</note>
*L'ā'xolamas* (meaning "steelhead salmon," i.e., it glides out of one's hands like a salmon), 6,000 blankets.
*Lō'pēLila* (meaning "making the house empty of blankets"), 5,000 blankets.
*DE'nt'alayō* (meaning "about whose possession everyone is quarreling").
*Mau'ak''a* (meaning "sea lion").
*Qau'lō'ma* (meaning "beaver face").
*Lē'ita* (meaning "looking below," namely, in order to find blankets with which to buy it).
*Nū'sē* (meaning "moon"; its engraving represents the half-moon, in which a man is sitting).
*G·ā'waqa* (meaning "a spirit." This is the Heiltsuk dialect name, corresponding to the Kwakiutl *Ts'ō'nōqoa*. See page 372).
*NE'lqEmāla* (meaning "day face").
*NE'nqEmāla* (meaning "bear face").
*K·'ā'na* (meaning "crow"; Heiltsuk dialect).
*Qoayī'm* (meaning "whale").
*Mā'x'ēnôx* (meaning "killer whale").
*Qoayī'mk·in* (meaning "too great a whale").
*Wi'na* (meaning "war," directed against the blankets of the purchaser).

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of Kwakiutl customs, specifically detailing the ceremonial purchase of a "copper" and how the blanket posts shown on the previous page (Plate 5) are used during this process.</meta>

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

The purchase of a high-priced copper is an elaborate ceremony, which must be described in detail. The trade is discussed and arranged long beforehand. When the buyer is ready, he gives the owner of the copper blankets worth about one-sixth of the copper's total value. This is called "making a pillow" for the copper (<term>qē'nulīLa</term>); "making a feather bed" (<term>ta'lqoa</term>); or "the harpoon line from which game hangs" (<term>dō'xsEmt</term>), meaning that the copper is attached to the long line of blankets in the same manner. It is also called "taken in the hand in order to lift the copper" (<term>dā'g·ilēlem</term>). The owner of the copper loans these blankets out, and when he has collected them again, he repays the total amount received, plus 100 percent interest, to the purchaser. On the following day, the tribes assemble for the sale of the copper. The prescribed procedure is as follows: The buyer first offers the lowest price at which the copper was previously sold. The owner declares that he is satisfied, but his friends demand gradually higher and higher prices, based on all the previous sales of that copper. This is called <term>g·i'na</term>. Finally, the amount offered is deemed satisfactory. Then the owner asks for boxes to carry away the blankets. These are counted at five pairs per box and are also paid for in blankets or other objects. After these have been paid, the owner of the copper calls his friends—members of his own tribe—to rise, and he asks for a belt, which he values at several hundred blankets. While these are being brought, he and his tribe generally return to their house, where they paint their faces and dress in new blankets. When they have finished, drums are beaten in the house; they all shout "hī!" and go out again, with the seller's speaker leading the way. As soon as the speaker has left the house, he turns and calls for his chief to come down, who returns to where the sale is taking place, followed by his tribe. They all stand in a row and the buyer puts down the blankets which were demanded as a belt, "to adorn the owner of the copper." This entire purchase is called "putting the copper under the name of the buyer" (<term>Lā'sa</term>).

In this procedure, the blankets are placed in piles of moderate height, one pile close to another, so that they occupy a considerable amount of space. In Fort Rupert, there are two high posts on the beach bearing carved figures on top, between which the blankets are piled in this way (Plate 5). They stand about 40 steps apart.

On the following day, the owner must distribute all the blankets that have been paid for the copper among his own tribe, paying his old debts first and, if the amount is sufficient, giving new presents. This is called "doing a great thing" (<term>wā'lasila</term>).

Coppers are always sold to rivals, and often a man will offer his copper for sale to a rival tribe. If the offer is not accepted, it is an acknowledgment that nobody in the tribe has enough wealth to buy it, and the reputation of the tribe or clan would consequently lose status. Therefore, if a man is willing to accept the offer, all the members of the tribe must assist him in this undertaking with loans of blankets.

<summary>This page describes the complex ritual and economic protocol for purchasing a ceremonial copper, including the use of "pillows" of blankets, the role of interest, and the communal effort required to maintain a tribe's prestige.</summary>
<keywords>copper sale, ceremonial exchange, blankets, debt and interest, Fort Rupert, tribal prestige, Kwakiutl rituals</keywords>

### REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

Debts which are repaid in the <term>wā'lasila</term> were mostly contracted in this manner.

In order to better illustrate this unusual proceeding, I will describe the sale of a copper which took place in the winter of 1894–95.

First, a feast was held, in which the Mā'malēleqala offered the copper Mā'xts'ōlEm for sale to the Kwakiutl. Mā'Xua, chief of the Maa'mtag-ila clan, invited all the tribes to his house. Then he spoke:

"Come, tribes, to my house. This is the house of the first Mā'Xua at G·agaxsdals.

"This is the feast house of Mā'Xua here.

"This is the house to which Mā'Xua invited guests at Ēg·isbalīs.

"This is the house to which Mā'Xua invited guests at Qalō'gwīs.

"This is the feast house of Mā'Xua at G·ā'qīs.

"This is the house to which my father invited guests at Tsā'xīs.

"I take the place of my father now.

"I invited you, tribes, so that you should come and see my house here.

"I am proud to speak of my ancestor, the chief who at the beginning of the world had the name Mā'Xua."

Then Mā'Xua turned to his own tribe and said: "Yes, K·'ēsōyag·ilîs. Yes, Mā'Xuag·ila. Let me speak of my ways. Wa, wa! Thus I speak, my tribe." Then he turned again to the other tribes and told them to sing, saying, "Go on, tell the whole world, tribes! Go on and sing; this was given to our ancestors in the beginning of the world by Kuēkuaxā'oē.¹"

Now Mā'Xua stopped speaking, and Qoayō'Llas, chief of the Wā'las clan of the Mā'malēleqala, spoke: "Yes, Chief! It is true what you said. I thank you for your words, Chief! Our ways are not new ways. They were created by our chief (the deity) and marked out for us when he made our ancestors men. We try to imitate what the creator told our ancestors to do. Keep to your old ways, Kwakiutl; keep to the ways of your grandfathers, who established the customs for you." Then he turned to his own tribe and said: "That is what I say, Wā'k·as. That is what I say, NEg·ē'. The word of the chief shall not harm me." Now he took the copper (Plate 6) and said: "Now sing my song!" His tribe sang, and after they had finished, Qoayō'Llas spoke again: "Yes, my tribe! I cannot help how I feel; I have nothing against the way you treat me and my tribe, Kwakiutl. Now I will promise blankets to you, Kwakiutl; blankets to you, Guē'tEla; blankets to you, Q'ō'mōyuē; blankets to you, Q'ō'mk·ūtîs; blankets to you, Wā'las Kwakiutl; this copper belongs to Ts'ā'xts'agits'Emqa, the son of Wā'las NEmō'gwīs. Now take care, great tribe! This great copper has a high price; its name is Mā'xts'ōlEm (the one of whom all are ashamed). Now I am going to lay it down before you, Kwakiutl. Do not let me carry it myself, Lā'bid! Take it to the chiefs."

### REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

Debts which are repaid in the <term>wā'lasila</term> were mostly contracted in this way.

To better illustrate this unusual proceeding, I will describe the sale of a copper that took place in the winter of 1894–95.

First, a feast was held, in which the Mā'malēleqala offered the copper Mā'xts'ōlEm for sale to the Kwakiutl. Mā'Xua, chief of the Maa'mtag-ila clan, invited all the tribes to his house. Then he spoke:

"Come, tribes, to my house. This is the house of the first Mā'Xua at G·agaxsdals.

"This is the feast house of Mā'Xua here.

"This is the house to which Mā'Xua invited guests at Ēg·isbalīs.

"This is the house to which Mā'Xua invited guests at Qalō'gwīs.

"This is the feast house of Mā'Xua at G·ā'qīs.

"This is the house to which my father invited guests at Tsā'xīs.

"I take the place of my father now.

"I invited you, tribes, so that you should come and see my house here.

"I am proud to speak of my ancestor, the chief who at the beginning of the world had the name Mā'Xua."

Then Mā'Xua turned to his own tribe and said: "Yes, K·'ēsōyag·ilîs. Yes, Mā'Xuag·ila. Let me speak of my ways. Wa, wa! This is how I speak, my tribe." Then he turned again to the other tribes and told them to sing, saying, "Go on, tell the whole world, tribes! Go on and sing; this was given to our ancestors at the beginning of the world by Kuēkuaxā'oē.¹"

Now Mā'Xua stopped speaking, and Qoayō'Llas, chief of the Wā'las clan of the Mā'malēleqala, spoke: "Yes, Chief! It is true what you said. I thank you for your words, Chief! Our ways are not new ways. They were created by our chief <note>the deity</note> and marked out for us when he made our ancestors men. We try to imitate what the creator told our ancestors to do. Keep to your old ...

Then Lā'bid stood up and spoke: “Say this again, my chief! Now pay attention, chiefs of the Kwakiutl; this is Sē'xitg·ila Mā'xts'ōlEm.¹ I will bring this to you.”

Then he stepped toward the Kwakiutl and placed the copper on the floor where they were sitting. Then Owaxā'lag·ilīs stood up, took the copper, and spoke: “Thank you, Wālas NEmō'gwīs. Come now, salmon, for which our ancestors have been waiting. This is Mā'xts'ōlEm. I will buy this Mā'xts'ōlEm. Now, Kwakiutl, pay me what I loaned to you, so that I may buy it quickly and keep our name as high as it is now. Do not let us be afraid of the price of Mā'xts'ōlEm, my tribe, wa, wa! Owaxā'lag·ilīs sat down, the young man distributed the dishes, and all the tribes ate. Then Mā'Xua stepped forward again and spoke kindly to the people who were eating. “Go on,” he said, “eat, Wālas NEmō'gwīs; eat, Hē'Lamas; eat, NEg·ē'; eat, you Ma'malēleqala; eat, Lā'qōLas; eat, G·'ōtē, you NE'mqic; eat, Sē'wit'ē; eat, E'wanuX; eat, you Lau'itsīs; eat, Wā'k·as; eat, Pō'tLidē, you Mā't'ilpē; eat, Wāts'ē; eat, Hē'was, you T'Ena'xtax. Eat, all you tribes. Now it is finished. I have already told you about my grandfather. This food here represents the goodwill of our ancestor. It is all given away. Now, pay attention, Kwakiutl! Our chief here is going to buy this copper; let us help him, wa, wa!” Then Hâ'mEsk·inîs spoke and said: “Your words are true, Chief! How true your words are. I know how to buy coppers; I always pay high prices for coppers. Now take care, Kwakiutl, my tribe, or else you will be laughed at. This is what I say, Ō'ts'ēstalīs; this is what I say, Wa'nuk"; this is what I say, young chiefs of the Kwakiutl; this is what I say, Tsō'palīs; this is what I say, Ō'gwîla; this is what I say, Ō'mx'it, young chiefs of the Q'ō'moyuē; this is what I say, Qoē'mālasts'ē; this is what I say, Yēqawit, chiefs of the Q'ō'mk·ūtīs; this is what I say, Quayō'Llas; this is what I say, Wā'kidīs, young chiefs of the Wālas Kwakiutl. This is my speech for our children, Mā'Xuag·ila, so that they may take care, wa, wa!” Then Quayō'Llas stood up again and said: “Thank you; did you hear, Lā'bid? Now, Q'ō'mōyuē, see the dance of ĀomōLa, the daughter of Wālas NEmō'gwīs. Now, Q'ō'mk·ūtīs, see the dance of Mā'mx·oyūkoa, the daughter of Wālas NEmō'gwīs. Now, Wālas Kwā'kiutl, see the dance of Mā'Xualag·ilīs, the son of Wālas NEmō'gwīs. These are my words, wa, wa!”

morning on the beach. Then all the tribes assembled. Ōwaxā’lag·ilîs stood on the beach and spoke. He said:

“Now, come, chiefs of all the tribes. Yes, come, because we want to perform a great work. Now, I am going to buy the copper Mā’xts’ōlEm from Wālas NEmō’gwîs. Only do not ask too high a price for it. And you, young chiefs of the Kwakiutl, take care and help me. Go now and bring the blankets from my house.”

Then the young men went and piled up the blankets on the beach. Mā’Xua and O’ts’ēstalis counted them. One man of the Ma’malēleqala, one of the Nimkish, and one of the Lau’itsis kept the tally.¹

Mā’Xua spoke: “It is my duty to take care of the property of our chief. It was the duty of my ancestors. Now I will begin.” Then he counted one pair, two pairs, three pairs, four pairs, five pairs, six pairs, seven pairs, eight pairs, nine pairs, ten pairs. As soon as ten pairs were counted, he said aloud, “ten pairs,” and the counters repeated, “twenty blankets,” and put two stones aside. When Mā’Xua had counted another ten pairs, the counters said, “forty blankets,” and put two more stones aside. They continued to put aside two stones for each ten pairs of blankets (Plates 7 and 8). Two men kept on piling up the blankets, and when they had piled up 1,000 blankets, Mā’Xua said aloud, “One thousand blankets.” The blankets were piled up alongside of a carved beam standing on the beach (Plate 5). When the pile was high enough, a new one was begun right next to the first pile.

Then Ōwaxā’lag·ilîs arose and spoke: “Tribes, I buy the copper Mā’xts’ōlEm with these 1,000 blankets. I shall not give any more unless the chiefs of all the tribes should ask for more, wa! That is my speech, chiefs of the Kwakiutl.” Now he sat down and Wālas NEmō’gwîs arose. He said: “Ya, Ōwaxā’lag·ilîs! Are your words true? Did you say it was enough?” Then he turned to his tribe and said, “Ya, Ōlsī’wit! Now rise, chief, and speak for me. That is what I say, Lā’bidē.”

Then Ōlsī’wit arose (see Plates 9 and 10) and said: “Are those your words, Kwakiutl? Did you say this was all that you were going to give for the copper? Are there 1,000 blankets?” The counters replied, “Yes, there are 1,000 blankets.” Ōlsī’wit continued: “Thank you, Chief Ōwaxā’lag·ilîs. Do you think you have finished? Now take care, Kwakiutl! You, Chief, give twenty more sets of ten pairs, so that there will be 200 more.” Then he turned to his tribe and said, “Chiefs of the Ma’malēleqala! Now, I have said my words, Chief Wālas NEmō’gwîs.”

Then Ōwaxā’lag·ilîs arose and said: “Your speech, Ōlsī’wit, is good. It pleases my heart.” And he said to the young men: “Go and bring 200 blankets from my house.” They went at once and brought those blankets.

Then Yā'qaLEnlîs arose and uttered the cry of Ts'ō'nōqoa: "hō, hō, hō, hō!" and he acted as though he was lifting the heavy weight of the copper from the ground. "You all know, Kwakiutl, who I am. The Hō'Xhoq <note>A mythical crane-like bird.</note> came down to Xō'xop'a, took off his bird mask, and became a man. Then he took the name Yā'qaLEnlîs. That was my ancestor, the first of the Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx. He married Lā'qoag·ilayūqoa, the daughter of Wālas NEmō'gwîs, the first chief of the great clan WēwamasqEm of the Ma'malēleqala. That is the reason why I speak. I know how to buy great coppers. I bought this copper Mā'xts'ōlEm for 4,000 blankets. What is it, Chief? What is it, Ōwaxā'lag·ilîs? Come! Did you not give any thought to my copper here? You always say that you are rich, Chief. Now give more, so that the price may be as great as I am. Give only ten times 100 blankets more, Chief Ōwaxā'lag·ilîs. It will not be much; give 1,000 more for my sake, wa, wa. This is what I say, Hā'wasalaL; that is what I say, Hē'Xuayus; that is what I say, Wawilapalasō; that is what I say for all of you, chiefs of the Ma'malēleqala, Wā, wā!"

Then Ōwaxā'lag·ilîs arose and spoke: "Yes, yes, you are feared by all, Great Chief! Do not show mercy in your speech. Now I am going to ask all of you, chiefs of the Ma'malēleqala: will you stop talking if I give you these 1,000 blankets in addition to the 1,600 blankets on this pile? If you say it is not enough after I have added the 1,000 blankets, then I will not force the purchase of the copper.

"Now answer me, Wālas NEmō'gwîs. I have seen no one giving 1,000 blankets more. I would be lying if I said I had ever seen it done as you demand, wa! That is what I say, chiefs of all the Kwakiutl."

Now Wālas NEmō'gwîs arose and spoke: "Chiefs, it is not my desire; it is the desire of all those chiefs who asked for more; I am satisfied."

It was described above how a boy is introduced into the distributions of property occurring among the tribe. It remains to state how he acquires his first copper. When the young man has acquired a certain number of blankets, one of his older friends invites him to take a share in the purchase of one of the cheaper coppers, which may have a value of, say, 500 blankets. The boy contributes 200 blankets as his share and the other man purchases it, announcing the young man as his partner in the transaction. The copper is delivered to the young man, who becomes a debtor to his partner for the amount of blankets contributed by the latter. He announces at once that he will sell the copper the following year, but that he is willing to deliver the copper on the spot. With these words he lays it down before the tribe. One of the chiefs of a rival tribe takes the copper and pays 100 blankets as a first installment. Then the boy promises a distribution of blankets (tsō’Xua) for the following year and loans out the 100 blankets which he has received. The next year he calls in his outstanding debts and invites all the neighboring tribes to a feast, to which his own tribe contributes food and fuel. In the course of the festival he pays the chief who took his copper 200 blankets, being the value of the 100 blankets received the previous year, together with 100 percent interest (see p. 341). Then the purchaser pays the sum of 750 blankets for the copper, including boxes and belt, as described above. Of this amount 700 are distributed on the following day in the prescribed fashion among the neighboring tribes. Now the young man proceeds to loan out his blankets until within a few years he is able to repay the share of his partner who first helped him to buy the copper. When the time has come for this transaction, his partner pays him double the amount of what he (the partner) has contributed, and the young man returns to him double of this amount.

The rivalry between chiefs and clans finds its strongest expression in the destruction of property. A chief will burn blankets, a canoe, or
