<meta>This page continues the discussion of the social and economic significance of coppers among the Kwakiutl, specifically focusing on the ritual destruction of property as a means of establishing superiority and prestige over rivals.</meta>

break a copper, thus showing his disregard for the amount of property destroyed and proving that his mind is stronger and his power greater than that of his rival. If the latter cannot destroy an equal amount of property without much delay, his name is "broken." He is defeated by his rival and loses his influence within his tribe, while the other chief’s name gains a corresponding amount of renown.

Feasts may also be counted as the destruction of property because the food provided cannot be returned except by hosting another feast. The most expensive kind of feast is the one where enormous quantities of fish oil (made from oulachon) are consumed and burned, the so-called "grease feast." Therefore, it also enhances the reputation of the person who can afford to give it, and neglecting to return it quickly results in a severe loss of prestige. Even more feared is the breaking of a valuable copper. A chief may break his copper and give the broken parts to his rival. If the rival wants to maintain his prestige, he must break a copper of equal or higher value and then return both his own broken copper and the fragments he received to the chief. The chief may then pay for the copper he has thus received. However, the chief who is given the fragments of the first copper may also break his own copper and throw both into the sea. The Indians consider that by this act, the challenged rival has shown himself superior to his aggressor, because the aggressor may have expected to receive his rival’s broken copper in return, which would have prevented an actual loss.

<note>* The order in which the sections are broken off and thrown away is indicated by the letters (*a*—*d*).</note>

In the vast majority of cases where coppers are broken, the copper is preserved. The owner breaks or cuts off one part after another until finally only the T-shaped ridge remains. This is valued at two-thirds of the copper’s total value and is the last part to be given away. The order in which the parts of the copper are usually broken off is shown in the accompanying illustration (fig. 4). The rival who receives the broken piece breaks off a similar piece and returns both to the owner. In this way, a copper may be broken up during contests with different rivals. Eventually, someone succeeds in buying up all the broken fragments, which are then riveted together, and the copper attains an increased value. Since a broken copper indicates that the owner has destroyed property, the Indians take pride in possessing them (see Plates 11 and 12).

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Kwakiutl social rituals and the prestige associated with "coppers," providing the textual context for the ceremonial destruction of property illustrated on the previous page.</meta>

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

The rivalry between chiefs, when carried so far that coppers are destroyed and grease feasts are given in order to destroy the prestige of a rival, often develops into open enmity. When a person gives a grease feast, a great fire is lit in the center of the house. The flames leap up to the roof and the guests are almost scorched by the heat. Still, etiquette demands that they do not move, otherwise the host's fire has conquered them. Even when the roof begins to burn and the fire attacks the rafters, they must appear unconcerned. The host alone has the right to send a man up to the roof to put out the fire. While the feast is in progress, the host sings a scathing song ridiculing his rival and praising his own clan, the feats of his forefathers, and his own. Then the grease is poured into large spoons and passed to the rival chief first. If a person thinks he has given a greater grease feast than the one offered by the host, he refuses the spoon. Then he runs out of the house (<term>g·ē'qEmx'it</term>=chief rises against his face) to fetch his copper "to squelch the fire with it." The host proceeds at once to tie a copper to each of his house posts. If he should not do so, the person who refused the spoon would, upon returning, strike the posts with the copper, which is considered equal to striking the chief's face (<term>k·î'lxa</term>). Then the man who went to fetch his copper breaks it and gives it to the host. This is called "squelching the host's fire." The host retaliates as described above.

The following songs show the manner in which rivals mock each other.

First, <term>NEqā'pEnk·Em</term> (=ten fathom face) let his clan sing the following song at a feast which he gave: <note>See Appendix, page 667.</note>

1. Our great, famous chief is known even outside of our world, oh! He is the highest chief of all. [Then he sang:] The chiefs of all the tribes are my servants; the chiefs of all the tribes are my speakers. They are pieces of copper which I have broken.

[The people:] Do not let our chief rise too high. Do not let him destroy too much property, otherwise we shall be made like broken pieces of copper by the great breaker of coppers, the great splitter of coppers, the great chief who throws coppers into the water, the great one who cannot be surpassed by anyone, the one surmounting all the chiefs. Long ago you went and burned all the tribes to ashes. You went and defeated the chief of all the tribes; you made his people run away and look for their relatives whom you had killed. You went and the fame of your power was heard among the northern tribes. You went and gave blankets to everyone, chief of all tribes.

2. Do not let us stand in front of him, of whom we are always hearing, even at the outermost limits of this world. Do not let us steal from our chief, tribes! Otherwise he will become enraged and will tie our hands. He, the chief of the tribes, will hang us.

[<term>Neqā'pEnk·Em</term> sings:] Do not mind my greatness. My tribe alone is as great as four tribes. I am standing on our fortress; I am standing on top of the chiefs of the tribes. I am Copper Face, Great Mountain, Supporter, Obstacle; my tribes are my servants.

At another feast he let his people sing: <note>See Appendix, page 668.</note>

1. Do not look around, tribes! Do not look around, otherwise we might see something that will hurt us in the great house of this really great chief.

> 2. "Do not look around, tribes! Do not look around, otherwise we might see something formidable in the great house of this truly great chief. His house has the Ts'ō'noqoa.<sup>1</sup> Therefore, we are paralyzed and cannot move. The house of our double chief,<sup>2</sup> the truly great chief, is taking our lives and our breath."

> 3. "Do not make any noise, tribes! Do not make any noise, otherwise we shall cause a landslide of wealth from our chief, the overhanging mountain."

> 4. [Neqā'penk'em sings:] "I am the one from whom the red cedar bark<sup>3</sup> comes down and is untied for the chiefs of the tribes. Do not grumble, tribes! Do not grumble in the house of the great double chief, who makes everyone afraid to die at his hands, and over whose body is sprinkled the blood of all those who tried to eat in the house of the double chief,<sup>4</sup> the truly great chief. Only one thing enrages me: when people eat slowly and take only a little of the food given by the great double chief."

While these songs merely praise the deeds of the singer, the following reply by Hē'nak'alasō, the rival of Neqā'penk'em, is extremely bitter. In it, the singer ridicules him for not yet having returned a <term>grease feast</term>.<sup>5</sup>

> 1. I thought someone else was causing the smoky weather? I am the only one on earth—the only one in the world—who makes thick smoke rise from the beginning of the year to the end for the invited tribes.<sup>6</sup>

> 2. What will my rival say now—that 'spider woman'? What will he pretend to do next? The words of that 'spider woman' do not take a straight path. Will he not brag that he is going to give away canoes, that he is going to break <term>coppers</term>, and that he is going to give a <term>grease feast</term>? Such will be the words of the 'spider woman,' and therefore your face is dry and moldy—you who are standing in front of the stomachs of the chiefs.

> 3. Nothing will satisfy you; but sometimes I treated you so roughly that you begged for mercy. Do you know what you will be like? You will be like an old dog, and you will spread your legs before me when I get excited. You did so when I broke the great <term>coppers</term> 'Cloud' and 'Making Ashamed'—my great property—and the great <term>coppers</term> 'Chief' and 'Killer Whale,' and the one named 'Point of Island,' 'The Feared One,' and 'Beaver.' I throw this in your face—you, whom I always tried to defeat, whom I have mistreated, and who does not dare to stand upright when I am eating; the chief whom even every weak man tries to defeat.

> 4. Now, my feast! Go to him, the poor one who wants to be fed by the son of the chief whose own name is 'Full of Smoke' and 'Greatest Smoke.' Never mind; give him plenty to eat, and make him drink until he is nauseated and vomits. My feast steps over the fire right up to the chief.<sup>7</sup>

To make the effect of the song even stronger, an effigy of the rival chief is sometimes placed near the fire. He is lean and is represented in a pose as if begging for the fire not to be made any hotter, as it is already scorching him (Plate 13).

...prestige over a rival, but also for the sole purpose of gaining distinction. This is done mainly when houses are built, when totem poles are erected, or when a son has been initiated by the spirit presiding over the secret society of his clan, a ceremony which has been mentioned previously. It seems that in ancient times slaves were sometimes killed and buried under the house posts or under totem poles. Later, instead of being killed, they were given away as presents. Whenever this was done, the inverted figure of a man, or an inverted head, was placed on the pole. In other cases, coppers <note>Ceremonial copper shields used as a high-value currency and status symbol</note> were buried under the posts or given away. This custom still continues, and in all such cases, coppers are shown on the post, often in such a way that they are being held or bitten by the totem animals (Plate 14). At the time of a clan member's initiation, slaves were also killed or coppers were destroyed, as will be described in greater detail later. The property destroyed in this way is called the <term>ō'mayū</term>, the price paid for the house, the post, or the initiation.

->Fig. 5.<-
->POTLATCH MASK OF THE K<sup>u</sup>KWĀ'KUM.<-

Double mask capable of being opened and closed by means of strings. (*a*) Outer view, representing the ancestor in an angry state of mind, defeating his rivals. (*b*) The mask opened, representing the ancestor in a pleasant state of mind, distributing property.

<note>IV A, No. 1243, Royal Ethnographical Museum Berlin. Collected by A. Jacobsen.</note>

The distribution or destruction of property is not always done solely to gain prestige for oneself; it is just as often done for the benefit of the successor to the name. In all such cases, the successor stands next to the host during the festival—or, as the Indian terms it, "in front of" him—and the chief states that the property is distributed or destroyed for the one "standing in front of him" (<term>Lawu'lqamē</term>). This is therefore the term used for the chief's eldest son, or, in a more general sense, for the heir presumptive.

At all these festivals, masks are occasionally worn that represent the ancestor of the clan and refer to its legend. I will give one example: In the potlatch of the Kᵘkwā'kum clan of the Q'ō'moyuē, a mask appears that represents one of the forefathers of the present clan (not their first ancestor), whose name was Nō'lis or Wa'tsē. It is a double mask topped by a bear (fig. 5). The bear broke the dam that prevented Nō'lis’s property from going up the river. The outer mask shows Nō'lis in a state of rage, defeating his rivals; the inner side shows him kindly disposed, distributing property in a friendly way. His song is as follows: <note>¹ See Appendix, page 670.</note>

1. A bear is standing at the river of the Wanderer who traveled all over the world.
2. The bear is wild at the river of the Wanderer who traveled all over the world.
3. A dangerous fish is going up the river. It will put a limit on the lives of the people.
4. Ya! The *sī'siuL* <note>² See page 371.</note> is going up the river. It will put a limit on the lives of the people.
5. Great things are going up the river. The copper of the eldest brother of our tribes is going up the river.

Another song used in these festivals is as follows: <note>³ See Appendix, page 671.</note>

1. The heat of the chief of the tribes will not have mercy on the people.
2. The great fire of our chief, in which stones <note>⁴ Stones heated in the fire to boil the food for the feast.</note> are glowing, will not have mercy on the people.
3. You, my rival, will eat what is left over when I dance at my grease feast—when I, the chief of the tribes, perform the fire dance.
4. What you are doing is too great, our chief. Who equals our chief! He is giving feasts to the whole world.
5. Certainly the chief of the tribes has inherited from his father the fact that he never gives a small feast to the lower chiefs.

The Haā'naLino clan has the tradition that their ancestor used the fabulous double-headed snake for his belt and bow. In their potlatches, the chief of the <term>gens</term> <note>The author uses the term 'gens' to refer to a clan or social group.</note> therefore appears dancing with a belt of this description and with a bow carved in the shape of the double-headed snake. The bow is simply a long, carved, and painted stick. A string runs through a number of rings and connects to the horns and tongues of the snake. When the string is pulled, the horns are raised and the tongues are pulled out. When the string is slackened, the horns drop down and the tongues slide back again (Plate 15).

### IV. MARRIAGE.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Kwakiutl social structure, moving from the symbolism of potlatch masks to the specific laws governing marriage and the inheritance of clan privileges.</meta>

<page-num>359</page-num>
<header>THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.</header>

As mentioned previously, many privileges of the clan descend only through marriage to the son-in-law of the possessor. The son-in-law, however, does not use them himself; rather, he acquires them for the use of his successor. These privileges are, of course, not given as a gift to the son-in-law; instead, he becomes entitled to them by paying a certain amount of property for his wife. The wife is given to him as the first installment of the return payment. The <term>crest</term> of the clan, its privileges, and a considerable amount of other property are given later, once the couple has children. The rate of interest is higher the more children they have. For one child, 200 percent interest is paid; for two or more children, 300 percent. After this payment, the marriage is dissolved because the wife's father has redeemed his daughter. If she continues to stay with her husband, she does so of her own free will (*<term>wulē'L</term>*, meaning "staying in the house for nothing"). To avoid this situation, the husband often makes a new payment to his father-in-law to maintain a formal claim to his wife.

The law of descent through marriage is so rigid that methods have been developed to prevent the extinction of a name when its bearer has no daughter. In such a case, a man who desires to acquire the use of the <term>crest</term> and the other privileges connected with the name performs a symbolic marriage with the son of the bearer of the name (*<term>Xuē'sa</term>*; in the Newettee dialect: *<term>dā'xsitsEnt</term>*, meaning "taking hold of the foot"). The ceremony is performed in the same manner as a real marriage. In the event that the bearer of the name has no children at all, a symbolic marriage is performed with a part of his body—such as his right or left side, a leg, or an arm—and the privileges are conveyed in the same way as in a real marriage.

It is not necessary for the <term>crest</term> and privileges to be acquired specifically for the son of the person who married the girl; they may be transferred to his successor, whoever that may happen to be.

Because the acquisition of the <term>crest</term> and its associated privileges plays such an important role in the arrangement of marriages, references to clan traditions and dramatic performances of portions of their myths occur frequently, as can be seen from the following descriptions:

First, I will describe the marriage of a <term>Ma'malēleqala</term> Chief.

<term>NEmō'kulag·ilîsts'ē</term> called all the young men of all the tribes to come to his house. After a second summons, all the young men arrived. Then he stood up and spoke: "Thank you, my brothers, for coming to my house. You know what is on my mind—that I want to marry today. You know that I wanted you to come so that I might ask my brothers to invite all the people. Now, dress yourselves; here is the paint and the eagle down."

The <term>Lā'g·us</term> stood up and spoke: "Yes, <term>NEmō'kulag·ilîsts'ē</term>, these are your words. My friends and I will go now to make war upon the daughters of all the chiefs throughout the world. Now, take care, my friends!"

He said: "These are blankets for you, <term>Guē'tEla</term>; blankets for you, <term>Q'ō'mōyuē</term>; blankets for you, <term>Wālas Kwakiutl</term>; blankets for you, <term>Q'ō'mk'ūtîs</term>. They belong to <term>Tā'qoaqa</term>, the daughter of <term>NEmō'kulag-ilists'ē</term>," and he said, "Now go to fetch my wife and the blankets."

Then the men went to the house of <term>Lā'lawig-ila</term>, and after a short time they came back. <term>Ts'ā'ts'alkoalis</term>, his daughter, was among them. Then all the men went home. He did not give away the blankets immediately. She went to live with her husband.

Here is the description of another marriage: The successor of <term>Mā'Xua</term>, chief of the <term>Gua'ts'ēnôx</term>, was engaged to marry <term>Hē'nEdemîs</term>, daughter of <term>Ya'qaLasaMē</term>, chief of the <term>Qō'sqēmuX</term>. Then <term>Mā'Xua</term> sent four men—<term>Kasā'lis</term>, <term>Ā'witē</term>, <term>NEmē'mâlas</term>, and <term>Yā'ƶidē</term>—to ask if <term>Ya'qaLasaMē</term> agreed to the marriage. As soon as the four men entered his house, <term>Kasā'lis</term> spoke: "I come, Chief! sent to you by the son of <term>Mā'Xua</term>. He has 400 blankets ready to be given to you to marry your daughter, and also to take your daughter home, <term>Ya'qaLasaMē</term>. We beg of you, O Chief! to open your heart to our wishes, for you have nothing to complain of. We are all of the same descent. We are sent by your uncle, Chief, and by your great-grandson, the successor to <term>Mā'Xua</term>. This I say, <term>NEmē'mâlas</term>. Now we have finished our speech, <term>Ā'witē</term>, <term>Yā'ƶidē</term>. Now, <term>Ā'witē</term>, you speak to our uncle here."

Then <term>Ā'witē</term> spoke: "Let me speak next, <term>Kasā'lis</term>. I came, sent as a messenger by your uncle. Let us try to obtain our relative. Now, <term>Yā'ƶidē</term>, you speak next." He said: "I am the double-headed snake.<note>See page 371.</note> There is nothing in the world that I am unable to obtain. Now speak, and give us an answer."

Then <term>Ya'qaLasaMē</term> spoke: "You have finished the speeches that you were to deliver to me, chiefs of the <term>Gua'ts'ēnôx</term>. Only let your tribe take care, <term>Ā'witē</term>. Then she came and went into the Gua'ts'ēnôx's canoe. They all boarded the canoe and returned home.

I will give yet another example, namely the marriage ceremony of the L'ā'sq'ēnôx, which is based on the following tradition: A chief of the L'ā'sq'ēnôx speared a sea otter which pulled his canoe out to sea. He tried to cut the line, but it was stuck to the canoe. Eventually, the mountains of his country disappeared from sight. After a long time, he saw a black beach, and when he drew near, he saw it was the place where all the charcoal from fires goes when it drifts down the sea's northward current. He passed this place and came to the place where all the dry sand drifts back and forth. The sea otter continued to pull him along, and he arrived at the place where bird down is drifting on the water. He passed those and came to the place where the toilet sticks<gloss>1</gloss> go. Finally, he discovered a village on a beach. The sea otter jumped ashore and was transformed into a man, who entered the chief's

The bridegroom's tribe go in canoes to the girl's house. When they arrive in front of her house, four old men wearing the masks that represent the four men previously mentioned step ashore. They walk four steps and then perform a dance. They look at the girl's tribe and point toward the house as though directing their friends. Then they go back into the canoe and take their masks off. Figure 6 represents the mask of <term>Xa'yā'la</term>. I have not seen the three other masks belonging to the ceremony. The broad band on top of the mask represents the head ornament of cedar bark which <term>Xa'yā'la</term> is said to have worn. The four men each receive one blanket from the bridegroom as payment for their dance.

At this point, I can describe only a portion of the ceremony prescribed for the return of the purchase money and the delivery of the crest to the son-in-law, as in most cases it is performed as a part of the winter ceremonial and must be treated in connection with that later subject. (See p. 421.) The return of the purchase money is called <term>qautē'x·a</term>, and the particular manner of return which will be described here is <term>LENE'mXs'a</term>.

The people are all invited to assemble in the house of the wife's father.

<meta>This page continues the description of Kwakiutl marriage customs, specifically detailing the ceremonial transfer of property and status from the father-in-law to the son-in-law, and introduces the importance of clan legends to these rituals.</meta>

<page-num>366</page-num>
<header>REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.</header>

When all the guests have gathered, the young man’s father-in-law enters, accompanied by his clan. Four of them carry the mast of a canoe; one holds it at the top, another at the base, and two at points in between. They walk to the right and stand on the right side of the door at the front of the house, facing the center. <note>Refers to footnote 1</note> Then the wife’s father calls his son-in-law, who steps forward and stands in the right-hand rear corner of the house. The other speaker tells him that the mast represents box lids (<term>g'i'SExstâla</term>, see p. 421) tied together (<term>LEnkᵘ</term>), and that they contain everything he owes his son-in-law. The son-in-law replies, asking if the coppers, the house, its posts, and his father-in-law’s names are also included. Even if the old man did not intend to give all of this, he must comply with the demand and promise to give it all to his son-in-law. Next, the young man’s wife is sent by her father to fetch the copper. She returns, carrying it on her back, and the young men of her clan bring in blankets. All of this is given to the young man, who immediately proceeds to sell the copper on the spot. This is called “holding the copper at its forehead” (<term>dā'g·iuē</term>). In such a case, less than half of the actual price is paid for the copper. If it is worth 6,000 blankets, it will bring only 2,500 blankets. The buyer must pay the price immediately, and the blankets the young man receives in this manner are distributed by him right away. By this distribution, he obtains the right to live in the house that his father-in-law has given to him.

Although in most marriages the house and name of the bride’s father are promised to be transferred to the young man, this is not necessarily the case. The dowry agreed upon may consist only of coppers, canoes, blankets, and the like.

I learned about a curious instance of how a man punished his father-in-law, who had long delayed the return of the purchase-money and was evidently evading the duty of giving up his name and home to his son-in-law. The son-in-law carved an image representing his wife and invited all the people to a feast. Then he put a stone around the neck of the image and threw it into the sea. In this way, he destroyed the high rank of his wife and, indirectly, that of his father-in-law.

### V. THE CLAN LEGENDS.

It appears from what has been said before that, in order to fully understand the various ceremonies, it is necessary to be familiar with the clan legends. In the following chapter, I will provide a selection of legends that will clarify their connection with the carvings used by each clan and the ceremonies performed on various occasions.

It seems desirable to introduce at this point a fuller description of

Sometimes these beams are supported by additional uprights (U'), which stand near the center of the house. The rafters (R) are laid over these heavy timbers and the beams that form the tops of the sides. They are about 8 inches in diameter. Light poles about 3 inches thick are laid across the rafters. They rest against the vertical poles (C) in the front and rear of the house. After the heavy framework which supports the central part of the roof is erected, a bank about 3 feet high is raised all around the perimeter of the house, its outer side aligning with the lines where the walls are to be built. Long, heavy boards 4 or 5 inches thick are set lengthwise along the front of the house, with their upper edges standing 2 1/2 or 3 feet above the ground. Then the earth forming the bank is packed against them, and thus a

<meta>This page continues the technical description of Kwakiutl house construction, specifically detailing the completion of the walls, the unique roofing system, the interior layout for multiple families, and the design of personal living spaces.</meta>

<page-num>369</page-num>
<header>THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.</header>

A platform is built running along the front of the house. Later, this is continued all around the house. The framework of the front is the next part to be erected. The poles (C) stand in the earth that forms the platform. The upper edges of the front boards, which were set into the ground, are grooved, and the boards forming the front wall stand in this groove. They are tied or nailed to the crossbar (E) and to the foremost rafter, which is connected to the framework of the front. The next step is to construct the rear wall and the sides. The rear wall corresponds exactly to the front, except that it lacks a door. The boards forming the side walls are set vertically into the ground, with their upper ends tied to the beam that forms the top of the framework. The platform running along the inner sides of the walls is finished by tamping the earth against the side walls. The roof consists of a unique type of boards which run from the gable to the sides of the house. They overlap at their edges like Chinese tiles. This arrangement ensures that the rain runs off the roof without leaking into the house. The house front is generally finished by cutting the boards to follow the roofline and finishing them with a molding. A few logs are placed in front of the door to form steps (T) that lead to the platform. Steps of the same kind lead from the platform to the floor of the house. The board forming the inner side of the platform slopes slightly inward. The house has no smoke vent, but several of the boards forming the roof can be pushed aside. During the night these openings are closed, but in the morning, one board over every fireplace is pushed aside using a long pole. As it is necessary to inspect the roof from time to time, a fixed ladder is leaned against the side of the house. It consists of half of a tree trunk or a heavy board into the upper side of which steps have been cut.

The house is inhabited by several families, each of whom has their own fireplace. The corners belonging to each family are separated from the main room by a rough framework of poles, the top of which is used for drying fish or other types of food. On each side of the fire stands an immense <term>settee</term> (fig. 11), which is large enough for the whole family. It has no feet, is about 7 feet long and 4 feet deep, and its sides slope slightly backward to provide a comfortable backrest. Boards are laid along the base of the rear and front platforms and on the side of the fire opposite the <term>settee</term>. The arrangement is sometimes slightly different; for instance, the <term>settee</term> might be missing, or in some cases, it may be placed at the rear. Often, long boards are placed edgewise near the fire to serve as a backrest. They are supported by stakes driven into the floor and lean slightly backward, thus forming a convenient support for the back. The bedrooms are shaped like small houses and are built on the platform that runs around the interior of the house. Most of these bedrooms have gable roofs, and their fronts are finished with moldings. The cross-section $c-d$ (fig. 8) explains the

I now proceed to a discussion of the clan legends. First of all, it is necessary to describe and list a number of supernatural beings who may become the supernatural helpers of humans, as they appear repeatedly in the clan legends. Besides a number of animals, such as wolves, bears, sea lions, and killer whales—which, however, do not play a very important part as protectors of humans—we primarily find a number of fabulous monsters whose help was obtained by the ancestors and who have therefore become the crest of the clan.

<image-desc>Fig. 12. THE SI'SIUL. A stylized drawing of a Sisiutl serpent. It has a central human-like face looking forward and two profile monster heads at either end with large eyes, curved snouts, and sharp teeth. The body between the heads is decorated with scales and fin-like appendages.</image-desc>

->Fig. 12.<-
->THE <term>SI'SIUL</term>.<-
->From a painting by a Kwakiutl Indian.<-

Perhaps the most important among these is the <term>sī'siuL</term>, the fabulous double-headed snake, which has a head at each end, a human head in the middle, one horn on each terminal head, and two on the central human head. (Fig. 10.) It has the power to take the shape of a fish. To eat it, or even to touch or see it, results in certain death, as all the joints of the unfortunate person become dislocated and the head is turned backward. I present here a few forms in which the <term>si'siuL</term> is represented (figs. 11, 12. See also, figs. 166-169, pp. 514, 515, Plate 15). In fig. 12 only one-half of the <term>si'siuL</term> is shown. The terminal head, with its horn laid backward, is plainly seen. Another being who figures prominently in the clan legends of the Kwakiutl is the <term>Ts'ō'noqoa</term>, a wild woman who resides in the woods. She is represented as having enormous breasts and as carrying a basket into which she puts children whom she steals in order to eat them. Her eyes are hollow and shine with a wild luster. She is asleep most of the time. Her mouth is pushed forward because, when awake, she is constantly uttering her cry, "ū, hū, ū, ū." This figure belongs to a great many clan legends and is often represented on house posts or on masks (figs. 13, 14).

She carried them far into the forest. Then she put gum on their eyes and carried them to her house. She was a cannibal. Among the children were two sons of the chief of the Wī'sents'a. Lō'pek'axsteLîL<note>This is not entirely clear. The name means "Rooted to the floor" and appears later as the name of a woman living in the Ts'ō'noqoa’s house.</note> was the name of the chief. His wife was LE'wag·ilayuqoa. She wept, and at times she would blow her nose and throw the mucus on the ground. Suddenly, she discovered a little boy lying on his back on the floor. He had been created from the mucus of her nose. She picked the boy up and carried him into the house. He grew very quickly; after four days, he was quite strong. Then he asked for a bow and two arrows. Now he was called LE'ndeqoayats'Ewal. When he had received his bow and arrows, LE'wag·ilayuqoa asked him not to cross the river, but he did so against her wishes. He followed the trail he found on the other side. He came to a house and entered. There he saw children sitting on the floor and a woman named Lō'pek'axsteLîL, who was rooted to the floor. She spoke: "Don't stay long, Chief! She has gone for water; if she comes back, she will kill you." Then he went out and followed the trail. Suddenly, he saw the Ts'ō'noqoa coming. She carried a bucket in each hand. The little boy climbed a tree to hide in its branches. The Ts'ō'noqoa saw his reflection in the water and made love to him. She looked up and discovered him. Then she called for him to come down. He came down to her, and the woman asked him: "How is it that you look so handsome?" The boy said: "I put my head between two stones." She replied: "Then I will use two stones as well." He sent her to fetch two stones, and soon she returned carrying them. She put them down. The boy said: "Now lie down on your back." Then the boy placed one stone under her head and told her to close her eyes. Then he took the other stone and dropped it as hard as he could on her head. Her head was smashed and her brains were scattered. She was dead. The boy broke her bones with the stones and threw them into the water. Then he went into her house. As soon as he entered, the woman who was rooted to the floor said: "Now, do not stay long. I know that you have tried to kill the Ts'ō'noqoa. This is the fourth time that someone has tried to kill her. She never dies; she has nearly come back to life. Her life is there in that covered hemlock branch <gloss>(knothole?)</gloss>. Go there, and as soon as you see her enter, shoot her life. Then she will be dead." She had hardly finished speaking when the Ts'ō'noqoa came in, singing as she walked:

> I have the magical treasure,
> I have the supernatural power,
> I can return to life.

That was her song. Then the boy shot at her life. She fell dead to the floor. Then the boy took her and threw her into the hole in which she

The spirit of the sea, Q'ō'mōqoa, the protector of the seals who kills hunters, appears less frequently. There are a number of tales relating how he took the ancestor of a tribe to the bottom of the sea and gave him his crest. I will give a legend here of the G·ēxsEm clan of the La'Lasiqoala, which shows how they came into possession of the Q'ō'mōqoa carving: Õ'meāl, the Raven, the ancestor of the G·ēxsEm clan, had a daughter named Hā'taqa. One day the crow, who was Õ'meāl's sister, and Hā'taqa went down to the beach to gather sea urchins. They soon filled their baskets. The crow carried them into the woods, broke the shells, and prepared them. Then she offered some to Hā'taqa, who refused them for fear of her father. The crow, however, promised that she would not tell on her and prompted Hā'taqa to eat the sea urchins. She had hardly begun to eat when the crow jumped upon a log of driftwood, shouting, "Qāx, qāx, qāx, qāx! Hā'taqa is stealing sea urchins." Hā'taqa asked her, "Please stop, and I will give you my blanket." The crow, however, did not stop shouting, even though Hā'taqa offered her her bracelets of abalone shells. But Õ'meāl had already heard what the crow said. He was enraged and ordered his tribe to load their canoes and extinguish the fires. Then he and his whole tribe left Hā'taqa all alone in the deserted village. Hā'taqa's grandmother, however, had pity on the girl, and before she left, she hid some fire in a shell. A dog and a bitch were the only living beings left in the village besides Hā'taqa. As soon as the canoes were out of sight, the dog attracted her attention to the shell by scratching and howling. She found the glowing embers and started a fire. She built a hut of cedar twigs where she lived with her dogs. The following morning she sent them into the woods and ordered them to fetch withes. They obeyed, and Hā'taqa made four fish baskets. At low tide, she placed them on the beach, and at the next tide, she found them full of fish. But on looking more closely, she discovered a man in one of them: Aik·a'a'yōlisāna, the son of Q'ō'mōqoa. He came out of the basket, carrying a small box. He said to her, "Carry this small box to your house. I have come to marry you." Although the box was small, Hā'taqa was unable to lift it, and he had to carry it himself. When he arrived in front of the house, he opened it, and, behold! A whale was inside. Aik·a'a'yōlisāna built a large house and married Hā'taqa. Then he invited all the tribes and distributed the whale meat. His descendants use his mask (fig. 15), and when it is shown, they sing as follows:

> It is a tale which has come down to us from the beginning of the world.
> You came up, bringing the house of Q'ō'mōqoa, you "Growing rich,"
> "Wealth coming ashore," "Covered with wealth," "Mountain of property."
> "Really great Mountain." It is a tale which has come down to us from the beginning of the world.¹

Figure 21 represents a totem pole which stood until a few years ago in front of a house in Xumta'spē (Newettee). The crest belongs to the subdivision G·'ēk·'ō'tē of the G·ī'g·îlqam clan. According to the legend, these people are the descendants of G·'ōtē, the son of K·ēpusalaōqoa, who was the youngest daughter of Kuē'xag·ila, the son of Hātaqa, the daughter of Ō''meaL (See p. 374). They have the Ts'ō'noqoa, a man split in two, another man, a wolf, a beaver, and the sea monster ts'ē'qic as designs for dishes. A man named NE'mqEmalis married a daughter of the G·'ēg·'ō'tē chief, and he had all these dishes made. Later on, a man named Qoayō'LElas married NE'mqEmalis's cousin. He was then told to unite the designs of the dishes and to carve a totem pole. He did so. The second figure from the bottom is placed upside down because the dish was on the man's back, while all the others were in the bellies of the carvings. This history may also explain why all the figures are separated on this column, whereas on most other totem poles they overlap, with one holding another or one standing upon another.

A very characteristic tradition is that of the clan NūnEmasEqâlis of the Lau'itsîs:

In the beginning, NōmasE'nxēlis lived at Â'g·iwa'laa, in front of Tsā'xis. He had a house there. His son was L'ā'qoag·ilaqEmaē. NōmasE'nxēlis came up with his copper. It is said that in the beginning he lay on it with his knees drawn up, and therefore his child was called L'ā'qoag·ilaqEmaē. Then Yix·ā'qEmaē, NōmasE'nxēlis's uncle, asked him to get a wife for him. Yix·ā'qEmaē lived at LîXsī'waē. He induced NōmasE'nxēlis to come there and live with him. His son was to marry the daughter of Sâ'g·iyē. Yix·ā'qEmaē desired to have Sâ'g·iyē's house and carvings; therefore, he wanted to marry Sâ'g·iyē's daughter.

There is one legend that is important in this connection because the rank of the various names and the laws governing the <term>potlatch</term> and feasts are derived from it. I give a version of the story here, which, however, is not quite complete and requires some additional remarks. It is the legend of Ō'maxt'ā'laLē, the clan legend of the G·ī'g·ilqam of the Q'ō'moyuē:

A bird was sitting on the beach at TE'ng·is. He took off his mask, and then his name was NEmō'gwîs. He became a man. Then he moved to K·ā'qa. He had a son whom he named Ō'maxt'ā'laLē. The child grew up quickly; he became a real man. He was very strong. He walked with his uncle Lō'La'watsa on the beach at Tsā'xis and clubbed seals. They were walking back and forth, clubbing seals. Then NEmō'gwîs spoke to his younger brother Lō'La'watsa: "Friend, let us not continue in this way. Let us try to arrange for our son to go out to sea." He desired to have more game than the sea otters and seals they were able to club on the beach at Tsā'xis. Therefore, they wanted to go to the islands. Then NEmō'gwîs and his younger brother burned out the inside of a cedar and burned its ends, thus making a canoe. They finished it. Then they launched the canoe they had made for the child. They tested the canoe the child was to use when going to Deer Island. Ō'maxt'ā'laLē was annoyed, and when he came back, his canoe was full of sea otters and seals. He kept going out every day and caught many sea otters and seals. Then he said: "Let us try to discover how many tribes there are. Let someone go and call them." Then NEmō'gwîs's younger brother, Lō'La'watsa, paddled. He went to La'lā'tē to call Hai'alîk·awaē. Then he arrived at Qag·'axstE'ls and called Mā'tag·i'la. He arrived at G·'ōtaqa'la and called

L'ā'xLaqoaXLa of the Lau'itsis, who, it is said, was a man, arrived at Sē'lats'ē and called for Mā'leleqala. He moved on and came to Lā'L'aq'uxla. There he called for Ts'E'nXq'aiō. He arrived at Tā'yaxqōL and called for Lā'laxsent'aiō. Then he went to the town at Q'ō'quē'taxsta'yō and called for Wā'xap'alasō. Then he went up the bay to Â'g·iwa'laa and called for Nū'mas. Then he went up the Sound to LîXsī'waē and called for Sâ'g·iyē. He came to XutsEtsâ'lis and called for YīXā'qEmaē. Then he went to the right side of the river of LîXsī'waē and called for SE'nLaē. Then he paddled to Ō's'eq and called for Hē'ilik·inakula; then to Nā'laxLala near the mouth of Ts'ā'watē and called for Yā'xLEN.

Meanwhile, the child of Nemō'gwîs was clubbing and harpooning seals for his father's feast. His house was already full of sea otter furs, which were used for blankets by the people of old. They were sewn together. Now the tribes gathered. He met his guests and distributed seals among them. He gave them their seats and gave his gifts to the chiefs. Nemō'gwîs kept the belly parts for them. He gave the hind legs to the chiefs of another tribe. He gave the flippers to the second-class chiefs, and the bodies to the common people. He assigned each clan its place. He gave the bellies to the highest chief. It is said he bit off these parts and had messengers pass them on to his guests; he bit off whatever he gave to his guests. Then he was called Wālas Nemō'gwîs, and he named his successor Ō'maxt'ā'laLē. Then he gave out the blankets to all the clans, establishing the law for later generations. Some of the guests stayed with him and became his tribe.

Now Ō'maxt'ā'laLē said to his father: "I shall go a little farther this time. Do not expect me; but first I will go bathing." Then Ō'maxt'ā'laLē went out in the morning. After he had bathed, he heard the sound of adzes. He made up his mind to see where the sound came from, because the sound was near when he first heard it. But it moved away as he followed it, and Ō'maxt'ā'laLē came to a pond. He bathed again and the sound came even nearer. He followed the sound, which moved ahead of him. He came to another pond and bathed again. Then the sound of adzes came still nearer. He followed it as it went before him. Now he found yet another pond. He bathed, and the sound came still nearer. He went toward it and now he saw a canoe. A man was sitting in the canoe, working on it with his adze. In the bow of the canoe lay a harpoon shaft and two paddles. Ō'maxt'ā'laLē stood behind the man. The man was the grouse. Then Ō'maxt'ā'laLē spoke: "Thank you, for I have found what you are working on." The grouse looked at him and disappeared. Thus Ō'maxt'ā'laLē found the canoe, the harpoon shaft, and the paddles.

Then he put his nettle line into his canoe. He and his uncle L'ō'L'awatsa went out. He went across the Sound, trying to reach Noomas Island. Then he saw a canoe coming from YaaiXugiwanō. They met at Noomas Island and held onto the sides of each other's canoes.

<summary>The narrative details the travels of L'ā'xLaqoaXLa, the establishment of potlatch laws through a seal feast held by Nemō'gwîs, and Ō'maxt'ā'laLē's spiritual quest to find a supernatural canoe.</summary>

“Good day, brother,” said <term>O'maxt'ā́laLē</term> to <term>Qā'watiliqala</term>, “I do not come without a purpose. My father sent me because you are the only person whose daughter I wish to marry.” <term>Qā'watiliqala</term> replied: “Paddle behind me and follow me to my house.” <term>Ō'maxt'ā́laLē</term> said: “I will give you my harpoon line, friend, my nettle line, my harpoon shaft, and my mat.” <term>Qā'watiliqala</term> then gave his leather line to his brother, and they exchanged their canoes and all the equipment they were using within them. Then <term>Ō'maxt'ā́laLē</term> said: “Let us go back. That smoke belongs to our house.” “No,” replied <term>Qā'watiliqala</term>, “Let us go on to my house. You said you wanted to be engaged to my daughter.” Then the two paddled side by side. They reached the lower part of the river at <term>Gua'ē</term>. “Be careful, brother, when we enter my house. When we enter, follow closely behind me,” said <term>Qā'watiliqala</term>. He warned his brother that the door of his house was dangerous. They walked up to the door together. The door was shaped like a raven. It opened, they jumped in, and the raven snapped at him. All the carvings in <term>Qā'watiliqala’s</term> house were alive—the posts were alive, as were the <term>sī'siuL</term> beams. Then <term>Ō'maxt'ā́laLē</term> married <term>Wilx·stasīlayuqoa</term>, the daughter of <term>Qā'watiliqala</term>. The house, the carvings, and all kinds of food were given to him as part of the marriage, as well as blankets made of lynx, marmot, wolverine, mink, and tanned elk skins. Then his father-in-law and his tribe brought him home. They brought everything, including the house itself. He built a house at <term>K·ā'qa</term>. That is why the place is named <term>K·ā'qa</term>: because logs were placed all around for the foundation of the house he had received through his marriage. Then <term>Omaxt'ā́laLē</term> invited all the tribes to a feast using the wealth he had obtained through his wife. (See Appendix, p. 675.)

In the feast mentioned in the previous legend, <term>NEmō'gwīs</term> is said to have assigned each of his guests a seat, which their descendants have kept to this day. He also established how the parts of the seal used to feed his guests were to be distributed. The chest was given to the head chief, the next in rank received the hind flippers, and the young noblemen received the fore flippers. At the feast, he also established the laws governing how blankets are given away and later returned.

This legend is so significant that I will provide another version which I obtained at <term>Fort Rupert</term>:

<term>NEmō'gwīs</term> lived in a village at <term>Wēkawāyaas</term>. He was the ancestor of the <term>G·i'g·îlqam</term> of the <term>Q'ō'mōyuē</term>. He wore a sun mask upon his face. He had a slave named <term>T'ō'tatsa</term> and a son. This son grew up quickly and became a man. One day, <term>NEmō'gwīs</term> went for a walk and saw a village at <term>Tā'yaguL</term>. There he saw a man wearing a bird mask sitting on the ground. The mask featured a small, hooked nose. Then <term>NEmō'gwīs</term> spoke to him: “O brother! Thank you for meeting me here. Who are you?” The other replied, “I am <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term>, brother.” Then <term>NEmō'gwīs</term> asked <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term>: “Who lives in the house beyond?” <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term> replied: “I do not know him.” <term>NEmō'gwīs</term> walked on to the east end of <term>Tā'yaguL</term>, where the other house was located.

When he arrived there, he told his younger brother and his son what he had seen.

He spoke to his son: “Oh, child, see the sea otters, the seals, and the sea lions on <term>Shell Island</term>.” Then his son wanted to go there. <term>Bō'nakwala</term> and <term>TO'Tatsa</term> rolled a drift log into the water. The son of <term>NEmō'gwîs</term> was to use it in place of a canoe. They brought it to the beach in front of <term>NEmō'gwîs</term>'s house and showed it to the young man. He sat on top of it and went to the island in order to club sea otters and seals. When he arrived at the island he began clubbing the sea otters and seals. He finished, and put them on his drift log. Then he went home. <term>Bō'nakwala</term> and <term>TO'Tatsa</term> met him on the beach and they unloaded the log. <term>NEmō'gwîs</term> spoke: “Oh, child, now your name is <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> because of your game.” He invited <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term> and <term>Lā'laXSEnt'aiō</term> and <term>Kuax·ilanō'kumē</term> and <term>Mā'tag·ila</term>. The four men came to the house and sat down. Then <term>Bō'nakwala</term> put stones into the fire and singed the seal. When he had done so, he cut it up. He filled the kettle with water and then threw the red-hot stones into the water until it began to boil. Then he put the pieces of seal meat into the boiling water and added more red-hot stones. After a short while the seal was done. <term>Bō'nakwala</term> took the meat out of the water, and <term>NEmō'gwîs</term> took the breast piece first. He bit it and gave it to <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term>, saying: “You shall always be the first one to receive his share, and you shall always have the breast piece.” Next he took the hind leg and gave it to <term>Kuax·ilanō'kumē</term>, saying: “You shall always have this piece, and it shall be given to you next to <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term>.” Then he took up the foreleg of the seal, bit it, and gave it to <term>Mā'tag·ila</term>, saying: “You shall always have this piece.” Then he gave a whole seal to <term>Ts'E'nXqaiō</term>, <term>Kuax·ilanō'kumē</term>, and <term>Mā'tag·ila</term>, and told them the name of his son. He said: “I invited you to show you my son. This is <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term>.” <term>Bō'nakwala</term> now addressed the guests. Because of this, people nowadays make speeches at their feasts, because <term>NEmō'gwîs</term> began the tradition of making speeches and distributing blankets and canoes among all the tribes.

<summary>NEmō'gwîs encounters various tribal leaders and establishes his son's name, Ō'maxt'ā'laLē, after a successful hunt. The story explains the origin of potlatch traditions, including ceremonial meat distribution and the making of speeches during feasts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of <term>NEmō'gwîs</term> and <term>Bō'nakwala</term>, detailing the construction and acquisition of canoes for <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> to hunt sea otters.</meta>

<page-num>386</page-num>
<header>REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.</header>

After the feast, they all left the house. <term>Bō'nakwala</term> looked for a good log of cedar wood. He found one and brought it to the beach in front of <term>NEmō'gwîs</term>'s house. When the tide had fallen, he burnt its ends and the middle, thus hollowing it out. It was to be the canoe of <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term>. As soon as it was completed, he gave it to <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term>. The latter went at once to <term>Shell Island</term> and clubbed sea otters. He did not club any hair seals. When he came home, <term>Bō'nakwala</term> and <term>7o'7atsa</term> skinned the sea otters. Then <term>Bō'nakwala</term> spoke: "O child! <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term>! I will go now. Do not feel uneasy if I should stay away for a long time." <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> replied: "Go on, but take good care of yourself." His uncle <term>Bō'nakwala</term> left and came to <term>Gā'yux</term>. At night, he bathed in water and rubbed his body with hemlock branches. On the following morning, he went on and heard the sound of an adze close to where he was. He went toward the sound. Then it stopped and reappeared a long way off. Then <term>Bō'nakwala</term> went again, bathed in the water, and rubbed his body with hemlock branches. He went on and again he heard the sound of an adze nearby. He went to see what it was, and again the sound stopped and reappeared a long way off. He went at once to the water and bathed again and rubbed his body with hemlock branches. He went on and heard again the sound of an adze nearby. When he went toward the sound, it stopped and reappeared a long way off. Again he bathed and rubbed his body with hemlock branches. When he had finished, he went on and suddenly he saw a beautiful hunting canoe lying on the ground. He went up to it and pushed it into the water, into the river of <term>Gā'yux</term>. He went in it down the river. In the canoe were two paddles and a harpoon. He rested at the mouth of the river and then paddled home to <term>Wēkawāyaas</term>.

When he arrived at the beach of <term>NEmō'gwîs</term>'s house, <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> came down to meet him. Then <term>Bō'nakwala</term> spoke: "O child, I have obtained a canoe for you." <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> made ready at once to go to <term>Shell Island</term> and asked the slave <term>7o'7atsa</term> to steer the canoe. They started, and when they arrived at <term>Shell Island</term>, <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> clubbed the sea otters. Then he loaded his canoe, which was full of sea otters. When they were going home, the slave said: "O master, let me see how you spear a sea otter with your harpoon." Then <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> said: "Steer toward that sea otter and I will spear it." The slave turned the bow of the canoe toward the sea otter and <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> threw and hit it.

Then they returned home. When they arrived at the beach, <term>Bō'nakwala</term> came to meet them. They unloaded the canoe, and <term>Bō'nakwala</term> and <term>7o'7atsa</term> skinned the sea otters and stretched the skins. After that, they ate. Then <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> spoke: "O father! I will go and see who lives east of us." <term>NEmō'gwîs</term> replied: "Child, beware of storms when you cross the sea. Go, and take <term>7o'7atsa</term> along." Early the next day, <term>Ō'maxt'ā'laLē</term> and <term>7o'7atsa</term> started. They spread the sea-otter skins over the bottom of their canoe and paddled straight across to the north end of the island at the mouth of <term>Knight Inlet</term>.

<summary>Bō'nakwala uses ritual purification to locate a superior hunting canoe for Ō'maxt'ā'laLē, who proves his skill by hunting sea otters and spearing them with a harpoon. Following this success, Ō'maxt'ā'laLē sets out with the slave 7o'7atsa to explore the regions to the east toward Knight Inlet.</summary>

When he approached YaaiXugiwanō, he saw a canoe with two men coming up. Ō'maxt'ā/laLē paddled toward this canoe. When the canoes were side by side, the men took hold of each other’s gunwale and Ō'maxt'ā/laLē said: “Where are you going, brother?” The one in the bow of the other canoe replied: “Brother, I am hunting among these islands here. I thank you for meeting me here. I am Qā'watiliqala. Who are you, brother?” Ō'maxt'ā/laLē replied: “Thank you, brother, for meeting me here. I am Ō'maxt'ā/laLē. Let us go to my house, the smoke of which we see there on the other side. It is not far. Come, take my canoe; it is yours now.” Then Qā'watiliqala spoke: “Brother, now this canoe of mine is yours and everything that is in it.” He meant the mountain goat skins with which it was covered and his harpoon. But Ō'maxt'ā/laLē's canoe was all covered with sea-otter skins. His blanket was made of sea otter and his harpoon line was made of the guts of the sea lion, while Qā'watiliqala’s line was of cedar bark and his blanket was made of mountain goat skin. Ō'maxt'ā/laLē spoke: “Thank you, brother. Now come across to your canoe and let me go into the canoe you gave me.” Qā'watiliqala arose and went into Ō'maxt'ā/laLē's canoe, and Ō'maxt'ā/laLē arose and went into Qā'watiliqala's canoe. This was as though they had exchanged their hearts so that they had only one heart now.

Then Qā'watiliqala spoke: “That is done. Now, brother, come to my house. It is beyond this point.” They paddled on, and when they had nearly reached Qā'watiliqala's house, he said: “Brother, take care. When I jump into my house, you and your slave must jump in at the same time.” Now they arrived at the beach in front of the house of Qā'watiliqala. They went ashore and walked up to the house. When they arrived in front of the house, the mouth of the door of Qā'watiliqala's house opened. They jumped in all at the same time, and it bit only a corner of Lo'Latsa's blanket. Then the posts at the sides of the door spoke, and the one on the right-hand side said: “You made them come to your house, Qā'watiliqala;” and the post on the left-hand side said: “Now spread a mat and give your guests food to eat, Chief.” It is said that the cross-beams over the rear posts were double-headed snakes (<term>si'siuL</term>), which were constantly playing with their tongues. The posts in the rear of the house were wolves, and a grizzly bear was under each of the wolves. Carved images were all around the house. Ō'maxt'ā/laL and Lo'Latsa were sitting in the house and were given mountain goat meat to eat. When they had finished eating, the speaker of the house said: “What do you want here?” Now Ō'maxt'ā/laLē saw the daughter of Qā'watiliqala, who was sitting in the rear of the house. He thought: “I will say that I came to marry her.” Then the thought-hearer of the house spoke: “Chief Ō'maxt'ā/laLē came to marry Qā'watiliqala’s princess.” Qā'watiliqala said at once: “O, brother! thank you that you want to marry my daughter. It has been my desire that you should marry her, brother Ō'maxt'ā/laLē. Now you marry my princess and you shall have this house for your house as a gift from your

<summary>Ō'maxt'ā/laLē meets Qā'watiliqala at sea and the two exchange canoes and belongings as a sign of brotherhood. They travel to Qā'watiliqala's supernatural house, where Ō'maxt'ā/laLē is welcomed and offered the Chief's daughter in marriage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Ō'maxt'ā'laLē's encounter with Qā'watiliqala, describing the transfer of names and the initiation of the wolf dance ceremonial.</meta>

wife and the great wolf dance *Walas'axa'*.¹ Its names are *G·alg·ayalis* and *G·alqEmalis* and *QEmō'ta'yalis* and *QEmōtilelag·ilîs*, and your summer names will be *NEg·e'* and *NEg·e'ts'ē* and *Quaxō'L* and *G·īg'esLEn*. The great dance *Walas'axa'* has forty songs. You will use this house for the celebration of the winter ceremonial, my son-in-law. That is all." Thus spoke Qā'watiliqala to O'maxt'ā'laLē. The latter replied: "Thank you, Chief Qā'watiliqala. I am glad on account of your speech, father-in-law. Now teach me the songs of the dance *Walas'axa'*, for I will at once invite all the tribes when I reach home." Thus spoke O'maxt'ā'laLē.

The speaker of the house said: "O, Chief Qā'watiliqala! Let us have the winter ceremonial tonight, so that our son-in-law may see our ways." Qā'watiliqala answered: "My speaker, your advice is good," and, turning to the wolf posts of the house, he continued: "Now take care, friends, you, *QEmō'ta'yalis*, and you, *QEmōtilelag·ilîs*. Howl, so that our friends *G·alalaLila* and his children may come." When he had finished, Ō'maxt'ā'laLē said: "O, father-in-law! I now invite you and your tribe to bring my house, myself, and my wife to my place. I cannot withstand your words, father-in-law! I say, thank you! Now let me watch your supernatural dances tonight, otherwise I shall not know what you are doing in this great dance."

At night the speaker of the house said: "Now, magicians, howl! so that *G·alalaLila* and his children may come." Then *QEmō'ta'yalis* and *QEmōtilelag·ilîs*, the posts of the house, howled four times each. At once a howl like theirs was heard behind the house. Then Qā'watiliqala called his tribe, the ancestors of the *Ts'ā'watEēnôx*. They entered their chief's house, and as soon as they had assembled, the wolves came in. All the men cried: "Yīhū, hū, hū, hū, hū, hū!" Four times they did so, and then they sang:

->I.<-

1. He was made to sit between the wolves, *hāi*.
2. He was taken around the world by *Lālistālaqa*, the wolf, *hāi*.

->II.<-

->For four years I was coming home. Then Mā't'Em took me away.<-

->III.<-

1. My poor younger brother, *TāTukuēdanuLas*, who lives on the other side, lies *ihī a*, for you said long ago that he was the first to show the wolf dance; my younger brother, *TāTukuēdanuLas*, who lives on the other side, *i hayo ihī, iyihō ō, ihī, iyihō, ō iyi, hayō, ō, ihī, iyihō, ō, iyī, ihī, iyihō, ō*.
2. My poor younger brother *ŋamtalaL* the *T'Ena'xtax*, lies, *ihī a*, for you said that long ago he was the first to show the wolf dance; my younger brother, *ŋamtalaL* the *T'Ena'xtax*, *i hayō ihī, iyihō ō, ihī, iyihō, ō iyī, hayō, ō, ihī, iyihō, ō, iyī, iyihō, ō*.

->IV.<-

1. Come, come, come, come and make love to the son of the wolf! Come! *yihī, yihī, ī ī, wō ō ō ō ō ō*.
2. *LēLatalaēnôx*, the wolf, has been all around the right-hand side of the world.

These are all the songs I know. If you go to the Ts’ā’watEēnôx, you can learn all forty songs of the Wālas’axa’.

When the wolf dance ended, Qā’watiliqala said: “O, friends, I invited you, my tribe, so that you may know that I am giving my daughter in marriage to Ō’maxt’ā’lalē, chief of the G·i’g·îlqam on the other side. Now let us go and take our son-in-law, his wife, and his house home. And he shall take this great dance. Let us go tomorrow!” Then the people left the house, and the next day they prepared to start. They crossed over, taking the house and Qā’watiliqala’s daughter. They stopped at Gā’yuX. They built a foundation of drift logs. In four days they finished the house.

Then Ō’maxt’ā’lalē went to tell his father, NEmō’gwîs. He entered the house and said: “Come, father! Let us go to my house at Gā’yuX. I have married the daughter of Qā’watiliqala. I brought my father-in-law and his tribe, and also the house and the great dance Wālas’axa’, as well as a great box and three baskets. I do not know what is in them.” NEmō’gwîs replied: “Let us invite Ts’E’nXqaio, Lā’laxSEnt’aiō, and Kuax·ilanō’kumaē so that they may see your house.” And he sent Bō’nakwala to invite the tribes. Then Ō’maxt’ā’lalē and his father went, and Ō’maxt’ā’lalē said: “Take care, father! As soon as I jump through the door of my house, you jump with me.” When they arrived at the house, the mouth of the door opened and the father and son jumped in. Then the posts said: “Go on! Greet those who come into your house, Chief!” NEmō’gwîs spoke: “Welcome, Brother Qā’watiliqala. I have heard about you. I thank you for having given your daughter and your house to my son.” Qā’watiliqala replied: “O, brother, I am glad that I have seen you. From now on your name will be Great NEmō’gwîs (Wā’las NEmō’gwîs). This box filled with curried skin blankets is for you, along with the basket filled with marten skins, the one filled with mink skins, and this one filled with lynx blankets.” Then Ō’maxt’ā’lalē left his house because he heard men speaking outside. He saw his uncle Bō’nakwala and the guests whom he had invited. Then Ō’maxt’ā’lalē said: “Now let us all jump into my house at the same time.” When they were all ready, the door opened and they all jumped in. Then the posts said: “Go on! Greet those who come into your house, Chief!” The guests sat down and were given food. When they had finished, they performed the winter ceremonial. Ō’maxt’ā’lalē showed the Wālas’axa’. Afterward, he gave sea otters to Qā’watiliqala’s tribe, and he gave blankets made of curried leather, marten blankets, mink blankets, and lynx blankets to Ts’E’nXqaio, Lā’laxSEnt’aiō, and Kuax·ilanō’kumaē. His winter dance lasted four days. He was the first who gave away blankets to all the tribes and who gave a seal feast. That is the end.

Before leaving this subject, I must mention that all the clans authenticate their claim to rank and the greatness of their ancestor by telling of a meeting between him and one of the two deities who prevail in the mythology of these tribes: Q’ā’nig·ilakᵘ in the Newettee

I do not need to go into these legends any further, because they are all of the same character and are simply intended to show that the ancestors of these clans were present at the time of the transformation of men into animals, and that they were as strong as the deity himself. For the details of the Q'ā'nig·ilakᵘ legend, I refer the reader to my book. <note>"Indian Legends of the North Pacific Coast," Berlin, 1895, p. 194.</note>

With this, I will leave the clan legends and their connection with the crest and the potlatch. I will mention here in passing that figures commemorating the distribution of property, the breaking of coppers, and grease feasts are often placed on top of houses or on poles. To this class belongs the statue of the speaker under the sun mask (fig. 1, p. 338), and the speaker on top of a house in Alert Bay (fig. 25). Other statues of the same class are shown in Plate 18, representing a chief who gives away coppers at a feast, and Plate 19, representing a chief breaking a copper. This last figure is placed on top of the house at the time when the father-in-law refunds the purchase price paid for his daughter.

To provide a better idea of the arrangement of the whole village, I include here a sketch of the village of Newettee as it appeared in 1886, based on a sketch I took at that time (fig. 26). The names printed in Roman letters indicate the names of the houses, those in italics are the names of mountains on Galiano Island, and the one in italic capitals is the name of the bay. The house Wā'tsuxūioa will be recognized as fig. 17 (p. 377). The post in front of it is shown in fig. 21 (p. 380).

It seems to me that the strong impulse the art of these people received from the development of totemic ideas must have resulted in the general application of animal designs for decorative purposes. That this is the case can be seen particularly in the case of dishes. The favorite designs for dishes throughout the cultural area to which the Kwakiutl belong are the seal and the canoe. The seal is not a totem animal, but merely the symbol of plenty, as no animal of its size provides a larger amount of meat and fat. Therefore, the seal feast is also reserved for the highest tribes of the Kwakiutl. The seal design is used by every tribe and by every clan. The same is often the case with the sea-lion design. I have selected a number of the most characteristic seal dishes (figs. 28, 29, 30), and also a sea-lion dish (fig. 31). The dish represented in fig. 30 shows the characteristic change of style that takes place in the extreme north, beginning at Yakutat. The deep, round forms become flatter and wider, and the carving is less elaborate.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between Northwest Coast art and totemism, transitioning from the decorative use of animal motifs to the spiritual legends of the Kwakiutl and neighboring tribes.</meta>

A process of euhemerism contributed to the prolific growth of the totem. We have seen that the tendency to decorate objects with animal designs was encouraged by an art style that was applied almost exclusively to representations of the totem. Thus, the animal became the dominating decorative element. The force of analogy must then have led the people to interpret certain animal figures—which were originally only decorative—according to the principles of totemism.

<image-desc>A line drawing of a carved wooden dish in the shape of a seal (Fig. 30). The dish is hollowed out in the center of the seal's body. Text below the drawing reads: "Fig. 30. SEAL DISH. Alaska. U. S. National Museum."</image-desc>

Other objects, such as drums (fig. 35, p. 395), boxes, house posts, etc., seem to be exclusively decorated with designs representing the totem.

## VI. THE SPIRITS PRESIDING OVER THE RELIGIOUS CEREMONIAL AND THEIR GIFTS.

It is a common feature of all the legends referred to so far that the supernatural powers obtained by the ancestors became the crest of a clan, and there is no mention of a direct relationship between the descendants of the ancestor and his crest. We are dealing only with legends commemorating the early history of the clan. They do not indicate that the being who helped the ancestor continues to protect his descendants.

<image-desc>A line drawing showing a detailed carving from a sea-lion dish (Fig. 31), depicting a stylized face or head profile with an eye and large mouth. Text below reads: "Fig. 31. DETAIL OF SEA-LION DISH. U. S. National Museum."</image-desc>

We must now deal with another class of legends that relate entirely to spirits who are still in constant contact with the Indians, whom they endow with supernatural powers. In order to gain their help, a youth must prepare himself by fasting and washing, because only the pure find favor with them, while they kill the impure. Every young man strives to find a protector of this kind. It is clear that this idea corresponds exactly to the *manitou* of the Algonquin Indians, and that we are dealing here with the elementary idea of acquiring a guardian spirit, which has reached its strongest development in America. Its specific character on the North Pacific Coast lies in the fact that the guardian spirit has become hereditary. This is the case among the northern tribes of British Columbia. It is also the case among the Kwakiutl and among the Chinook. When a youth prepares to meet a guardian spirit, he does not expect to find any except those belonging to his clan. This is probably the reason for the relatively small number

of such spirits—since among the Plains Indians, where each man has his own individual spirit, their number is unlimited—and this has also provided the opportunity for the development of a more elaborate mythology relating to these spirits.

<image-desc>Line drawing of a carved wooden canoe dish from Alaska, labeled Fig. 32. The dish has a curved, bowl-like shape typical of Northwest Coast indigenous art. Below it: "Fig. 32. CANOE DISH. Alaska. Cat. No. 9250, U. S. N. M. Collected by A. H. Hoff, U. S. A."</image-desc>

I will provide a list and brief descriptions of these spirits and the gifts they bestow.

I. *Wīnā'lag·ilīs* (=making war all over the earth). The descriptions of this being are very vague. He is a warrior and lives in the far north. He travels about constantly and never leaves his canoe. As far as I am aware, he is never represented in masks or other carvings. By obtaining his protection, a youth may acquire one of the following powers. He may become a—

(1) *Tō'X'uīt*, who is invulnerable and has power over the *sī'siuL*, which assists him and his friends on war expeditions.

(2) *Mā'maq'a*. The *mā'maq'a* has the power to catch the invisible disease spirit, which is constantly flying through the air in the shape of a worm. He is able to throw it into his enemies, who die from its effects immediately.

<image-desc>Line drawing of a carved canoe dish featuring a sea-lion design, labeled Fig. 33. The carving shows a human figure at one end and a sea-lion-like head at the other. Below it: "Fig. 33. CANOE DISH WITH SEA-LION DESIGN. U. S. National Museum."</image-desc>

(3) *Hawī'nalaL* (=war dancer), who, with the help of *Wīnā'lag·ilīs*, is immune to the pain of wounds and cannot be killed, regardless of how severely he is injured.

II. *BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē* (the first one to eat man at the mouth of the river; that is, in the north, because the ocean is considered a stream flowing northward). He is a cannibal living in the mountains who is always hunting humans.

<image-desc>Line drawing of a carved canoe dish with intricate animal designs on its exterior, labeled Fig. 34. This piece is also from Alaska. Below it: "Fig. 34. CANOE DISH WITH ANIMAL DESIGN. Alaska. Cat. No. 9244, U. S. N. M. Collected by A. H. Hoff, U. S. A."</image-desc>

Red smoke rises from his house. His servant (or wife) is *Q'ō'minōqas* (=the rich woman), who provides food for him. He has a female slave, *K·ī'nqalaLala*, who also provides food for him by catching men and gathering corpses. Near the door in his house sits his slave *Qoā'xqoaXualanuXsi'waē*, the raven, who eats the eyes of the people whom his master has devoured. In his house also live the *hō'Xhōk<sup>u</sup>*, a mythical bird with an immensely long beak that lives on the brains of men, whose skulls he fractures with his beak, and the

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of spirits, specifically focusing on the supernatural gifts they bestow upon their initiates and the ritualistic dances that dramatize these spiritual encounters.</meta>

REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

...describe what the gift of the spirit consists of. This difficulty appears even in the preceding list of the most important spirits.

Because these spirits are hereditary, their gifts are always contained in the legend detailing their acquisition by a clan's ancestor. The principal gifts in these tales are the magic harpoon, which ensures success in sea-otter hunting; the death-bringer which, when pointed against enemies, kills them; the water of life which revives the dead; the burning fire which, when pointed against an object, burns it; and a dance, a song, and cries which are peculiar to the spirit. The gift of this dance means that the protégé of the spirit is to perform the same dances that have been shown to him. In these dances, he portrays the spirit. He wears his mask and his ornaments. Thus, the dance must be considered a dramatic performance of the myth relating to the acquisition of the spirit, and it shows the people that the performer, through his visit to the spirit, has obtained his powers and desires. When a spirit appears to a young Indian today, he gives him the same dance, and the youth also returns from the initiation filled with the powers and desires of the spirit. He confirms his initiation by his dance in the same way as his mythical ancestor did.

The process of obtaining magical gifts from these spirits is called <term>Lō'koala</term>, while the person who has obtained them becomes <term>nau'alak"</term>, or supernatural, which is also the quality of the spirit himself.

The ornaments of all these spirits are described as being made of cedar bark, which is dyed red with the juice of alder bark. They appear to their devotees only in winter; therefore, the dances are also performed only in winter. For this reason, they may conveniently be called the winter ceremonial. I shall return to this subject more fully later on.

The following legend regarding the origin of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> (told by the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term>) will clarify what I have said:

The first of the <term>Awī'k·'ēnôx</term> lived at <term>Wā'waLala</term>. Their chief was <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term>. He had four sons who were mountain-goat hunters. At one time, the members of his tribe were disappearing one after another, and he did not know what became of them. <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term> wanted to eat mountain-goat meat. His sons offered to go out hunting. These are the names of the sons of <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term>: <term>Ta'wix·amayē</term>, <term>Qoā'qoasililag·ilis</term>, <term>Yā'qois</term>, and the name of the youngest was <term>Nū'Lilokuē</term>. The young men made themselves ready, and then <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term> advised them. He said, "Do not enter the house where the smoke looks like blood; otherwise, you will never return home. It is the house of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. The smoke of the house of the goat is white; go there when you see it. Do not go to the house where the smoke is grey on one side; it is the house of the grizzly bear. Otherwise, harm will befall you. Now go, my sons, and remember what I told you." <term>Ta'wix·amayē</term> replied, "We will try to avoid misfortune." The young men left early in the morning. About noon, they discovered the grey smoke of which their father had spoken. <term>Ta'wix·amayē</term> said, "Now let us see if our father's advice is good."
