"Just take care, dear brothers, so that no harm comes to us." They went on and soon they met the grizzly bear. They fought with him and he almost killed them, but finally they overcame the bear and killed him. The brothers continued on. At night they slept. In the morning Yā'qois woke up his brothers. They traveled for a long time; then Ta'wix·amayē said: "My dear brothers, do you see that smoke over there? That is what our father meant when he spoke of the bloody smoke of the house of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. Let us go there!" They walked on and came to the door of the house. It was open and the brothers entered. As soon as they came in, a woman called to them. Ta'wix·amayē stepped up to her and the woman said: "I am rooted to the floor. I will help you. This house you have entered belongs to <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. Now do as I tell you and pay attention to what you see. Dig a deep hole in that corner of this house. Then put stones into the fire, and when they are red-hot, put them into the hole." When the brothers had done so, she continued: "Now cover the hole with boards. As soon as <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> comes home he will dance, wearing his mask on his forehead." As soon as the brothers had finished their work, a whistling sound was heard. Then the woman said: "Now sit down. I will say that I found food, so that he does not see what we have planned." <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> entered crying "hāp." Then the <term>hō'Xhoku</term> and <term>QoāxqoaxuālanuXsi'waē</term> began to shout. <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> lay on his back. His body was covered all over with mouths. Then he arose. He became excited and went four times around the house crying "hāp." Then he went into his bedroom (*mā'wiL*). As soon as <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> had gone in there, the raven with feathers on his head that reached down to his waist came out and danced, going around the fire. The raven went back into the bedroom. Then <term>QoāxqoaxuālanuXsi'waē</term> came out crying "hāp, hāp, gō'u, gō'u!" and danced around the fire. Then he went back into the bedroom and out came <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> crying, "hāp." He danced around the fire and went back into his bedroom. Then came the <term>hō'Xhoku</term> crying "Hāp, hāp, hō, hō." He danced around the fire and went back into his bedroom. Now <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> and his four <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term>, and the four <term>q'ō'minōqa</term> came out. "Hāp, hāp," said <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. The <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> sang and said "hōîp," and sometimes the <term>q'ō'minōqa</term> sang "hai, hai, hai, hai." <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> danced. As soon as he came to the hole that the men had dug, Ta'wix·amayē pulled away the boards with which it was covered. <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> was looking upward while he was dancing. Then he fell into the hole upon the red-hot stones. Then they covered the hole up. Now he was dead. As soon as he died all the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> and <term>q'ō'minōqa</term> died also. The singers also fainted. While they were unable to see, Ta'wix·amayē took off all their ornaments of red cedar bark. He took the masks, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> pole, and the whistles. The old woman told him what to do. She taught him the song of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>.

<summary>Ta'wix·amayē and his brothers defeat a grizzly bear before trapping and killing the cannibal spirit BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē and his attendants with the help of a woman rooted in the spirit's house. Following the spirit's death, Ta'wix·amayē claims the ceremonial masks, whistles, and songs, establishing the origin of these ritual items.</summary>

When <term>Ta'wix·amayē</term> came home, he told his father <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term> what had happened. <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term> went at once to see <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term>'s house. He followed his sons. When they arrived at the house, the woman who was rooted to the floor gave them food and spoke: "My dear <term>Nā'nwaqawē</term>, you will dance and keep the <term>hā'mats'a</term> mask, the raven mask, the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term> mask, and the <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term> mask, and all the different kinds of red cedar bark. The <term>q'ō'minōqa</term> will have mixed red and white cedar bark, and the "Bear inside the door of this house" will have whistles. Then the boy nudged his mother and said: “Mother, I want to lick the blood,” but his mother restrained him. The boy began to scratch his head and finally started licking the blood, despite his mother's order. Then the eldest of the brothers nudged the youngest one and said: “Oh, why did we not follow father's advice?” The boy continued to lick the blood. Then the eldest brother took his bow and shot an arrow out of the house through the door. He asked his youngest brother to go and bring it back. As soon as he had left the house, he ran homeward as fast as he could. Soon the eldest brother took another arrow and shot it through the door. He asked his next youngest brother to fetch it, and he also took the opportunity to escape. Finally, he shot a third arrow, and the next brother went to fetch it. He also ran homeward as fast as he could. Then the boy began to cry. The woman asked the only remaining visitor: “Are your brothers not coming back?” and he replied: “They only went to fetch my arrows.” Then he shot a fourth arrow and went to fetch it himself. As soon as he had left the house, he ran homeward. When, after some time, the brothers did not return, the woman knew that they had escaped. She stepped out of the house and called her husband: “<term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>, I have allowed our good dinner to escape.” <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> heard her, although he was far away. He pursued the boys, crying “ham, ham, ham” (eating, eating, eating). The four brothers heard him crying and ran as fast as they could. Then <term>Nō'aqaua</term> and <term>Tsō'ēna</term> pulled back their seat and they fell into the ditch. They threw the red-hot stones on top of them. After some time they pulled out the bodies. <term>Nō'aqaua</term> cut them to pieces and scattered them in all directions, singing: “<term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>, you shall pursue mankind.” They were transformed into mosquitoes.

Here is another legend explaining the initiation of the <term>Oē'alîtx</term>, a subdivision of the <term>Hē'iltsuq</term>.

A woman named <term>Ts'u'mkwalaqas</term> came to the Stikine River. There she gave birth to a boy who was at once transformed into stone. It is now a large mountain at the Stikine. It has a name, but I do not know it. She had two brothers named <term>Wā'k·as</term> and <term>Dō'kwa-lēsala</term>, who lived in a village on Goose Island. She wanted to go to see her brothers. She went on in her canoe and came to the Skeena River. There she gave birth to a boy. He was also transformed into stone. It is now a large mountain at the Skeena River named <term>Kuga</term>. Again she was pregnant. She came to <term>Xā'exaēs</term>. There she gave birth to a boy, who was also transformed into stone. It is now a large mountain at <term>Xā'exaēs</term> named <term>Gugasp'its'awē</term>. Again she was pregnant. She started in her canoe and came to <term>Dā'yasiowē</term>. There she built a house of cedar bark. After four days she gave birth to dogs.

At night, the woodcarver took the houses and placed them on the ground on each side of his mother's house. The large house was in the middle of that village. Then the canoe builder placed his toy canoes in front of the houses. In the morning, <term>Ts'u'mkwalaqas</term> went out. What she saw were many people and large canoes. Now she was rich. The woodcarver went to the small river nearby and made a salmon trap. He carved salmon out of alder wood. This is why the flesh of the salmon is red. On the following day, he went to check his salmon trap. He found one fish in it and gave it to his mother, who cut it open and dried it. On the following day, he went again to check his salmon trap. He found eight salmon. He went home, carrying them on his finger, and gave them to his mother. Then he told his mother to look after the trap from time to time. By this time, the killer of monsters had killed all the monsters living in the sea near the coast.

Lā'wag·is. He was in love with a girl. Once upon a time, she went up the river to pick berries, and Lā'wag·is followed her. He walked along the bank of the river while she traveled up in her canoe. When it grew dark, he heard cries in the woods. Then he jumped into a pond and rubbed his body with hemlock branches. He continued on. He heard the cries the entire time and bathed in another pond. He walked on. Now the cries were close to him. He bathed again. Now the cries came quite close to him. He bathed for the fourth time. As soon as he had finished, he saw a woman with a large head, matted hair, and a face that was full of scratches. Lā'wag·is went up to her and put his arm around her waist. As soon as he had done so, they both fainted.

He recovered first, but he only held his arms around her waist tighter. Then the woman with the great head recovered and spoke: "I am the crier of the woods. Now let me go, and I will help you to obtain everything with ease. I will be your magical helper. You shall easily obtain all kinds of property." Lā'wag·is only held her more tightly. Then she spoke again: "I will provide wealth for you." But he held her even tighter. Then she spoke again: "I will give you the water of life. Let me go." But he held her tighter still. She spoke again: "Let me go. Take my name; it shall be yours. You will be <term>Qoā'dasgamāls</term>. I will give you the apron that burns everything." Then he let her go. She disappeared at once. She only left the four gifts, which she had given him, on the ground. Then Lā'wag·is took his magical treasures. He went on and tested his apron against the trees of a mountain. Immediately they were burned, and you can see even now that the mountains of <term>Ts'a'watē</term> are scorched. 

Now he was glad. He hid his magical treasures under a cedar tree and went on. He arrived at the village where his sweetheart was living. She asked him: "Why did you not come sooner?" He replied: "I lost my way." That night they went to bed and played together. After a short time, he was poked in the side through a hole in the boards of the house. He got up and went to look. As soon as he went out, his face was covered and he was led away by a man. He did not dare to speak or ask questions, but he knew that he was led three times up a mountain and three times down. During all this time, his face was not uncovered. Then he knew they were going up a mountain again, and he heard a cry, "hāp, hāp, hāp; haō, haō; gaō, gaō" (the cries of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, the <term>hō'Xhoku</term>, and of the raven). 

Then the man spoke: "My dear, do not be afraid. I want to give you magical power. This is my house. I am <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term>. You shall see everything in my house." They entered, and he uncovered the face of Lā'wag·is. "Now look, friend!" said <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term>. "You shall have my name, <term>Wilgasā'lag·ilīs</term>, and your name shall be <term>Hā'mats'a</term>. Now watch the dance of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>." Then he heard the cries, "hāp, hāp, hāp; haō, haō; gaō, gaō." Then the raven that was painted on the front of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>'s secret room opened its mouth and the <term>hā'mats'a</term> came out, vomited by the raven. Then he danced. ...see the singers. After the first song, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> went back and the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term> came out and danced. After one dance, he went back and the raven came out and danced. With the next song, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> came out carrying a corpse in his arms, which he ate. When he had eaten it, he danced again and went back. He had four songs. <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term> spoke: “This will be your <term>hā'mats'a</term>; your names will be <term>Wilgasā'lag·ilîs</term>, <term>Hamigā'lagalits'akᵘ</term>, and <term>Naxnawisā'lag·ilîs</term>. Now that he had learned the first song, <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term> taught him the second song:

1. You are looking for food, you great magician, mahamai, hama, hamamai; yi hama ma mai hama.
2. You are looking for men whom you want to eat, great magician; mahamai, hama, hamamai; yi hama ma mai hama.
3. You tear men’s skins, great magician, mahamai. You try to eat many men, great magician, mahamai, hama, hamamai; yi hama ma mai hama.
4. Everyone trembles before you, you great magician. You who have been to the end of the world, mahamai, hama hama mai; yi hama ma mai hama.

After the song, <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term> called <term>Lā'wag·is</term> and asked him: “Do you not want this harpoon shaft? It kills everything. Now it is yours, and also this red cedar bark and the fire with which you may burn everything, the water of life, and the quartz for killing your enemies.” Then <term>Lā'wag·is</term> went home. That is the end.

The following legend belongs to the <term>Nimkish</term>:

There were two friends. One of them had gone into the woods to be initiated by the spirits of his clan, while the other was not yet prepared to meet these spirits. Nevertheless, he went to search for his friend, and after four days, he found him. When he returned, his father asked him where he had been, and he told him that he had found his friend, who was being instructed by the spirits. Then his father struck him, saying: “Do you not know that it is forbidden? I will be killed because of you.” Then the youth became sad. At night, he put on his ornaments, which were made of abalone shells, and went into the woods. He went up the river and washed with hemlock branches. The following morning he went on, and the next day he washed again. Then he heard the voice of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term>. At the end of the

On the fourth day, he came to a precipice and lay down at its base to rest. Early in the morning, he saw the rock open and out came <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term>. He hid, and the spirit flew away over his head. His body was entirely covered with red cedar bark. The boy stayed there for four days. On the fifth morning, when <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term> came out again, he followed him and saw how he took off his cedar bark ornaments on the bank of a pond and went to swim in it. When he dived, the youth jumped forward and put on the cedar bark ornaments. Now the spirit emerged. When he saw the boy decorated with his cedar bark ornaments, he said: “You have done well to take my ornaments. Now I can do you no harm.” He took him along to his home inside the rock. There he asked him: “What do you want to have? Do you want this harpoon? Do you want the water of life? Do you want the death-bringer? Do you want my <term>hā'matsa</term>?” He gave him all of these. The youth stayed with him for four days. Then he was able to fly. Then <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term> instructed him to fly to a place where his father was accustomed to fetching water for cooking. Soon his younger brother came, and when he saw him, he discovered that he had been away a long time. What had seemed like four days to him were actually four years. He asked the young boy: “How is father? I am your elder brother. Go and ask father to clean his house.” The boy went back and told his father, who beat him for speaking of his dead son. Then the boy ran back and complained to his brother that his father had beaten him for carrying the message. The elder brother sent him back to the house, asking him to repeat his request. The boy obeyed, and when his father had heard the message again, he went out to see for himself. As soon as his eldest son saw him, he grew excited. He flew across the river to the graveyard, tore corpses out of their coffins, and devoured them. Then he flew into his father’s house and bit everyone whom he saw.

There are a number of tales referring to the acquisition of the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term>. The <term>Naqô'mg·ilisala</term> have the following legend on this subject: <note>Appendix page 680.</note>

A number of women went to the island <term>Yū'Lē</term> to dig fern roots. They put some dried whale meat over the fire, and a red-breasted owl came and picked up some of it. It is said that there are many red-breasted owls there. Then all of a sudden, the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term> came and landed on top of a tree. He came downward, pecking the tree. He came down to the bottom of the tree, but it was hard on his beak. Now he walked up to the women. He covered his nose and was transformed into a man. He reached a woman who put some dry whale on the fire. She laid a mat before him and put the whale meat on it. The <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term> said: “I do not eat whale meat; I eat only human brains.” So saying, he pecked the woman’s head, broke her skull, and ate the brain. One of the women had hidden when he came down. She went home and told the story. Then the <term>Naqô'mg·ilisala</term> resolved to make war upon the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term>. <term>Qō'mg·ustals</term> and <term>Waxalalaa</term> took the blood of a woman

The following tradition of the <term>Awī'k'ēnôx</term> referring to the <term>*hō'Xhokᵘ*</term> is of interest because it describes the ceremony or dance performed by every novice initiated by this being:

A young man named <term>Q'ō'mkilig·a</term> went into the woods to collect cedar bark. There the <term>*hō'Xhokᵘ*</term> caught his scent. He found that the youth was clean, and therefore rushed down upon him to kidnap him. When <term>Q'ō'mkilig·a</term> heard the spirit coming, he trembled with fear. He hoped to control his fears by smoking, but he failed. He fainted and lay there as if dead. The <term>*hō'Xhokᵘ*</term> came down to him and filled him with his powers.

When the youth did not return, his friends went into the woods to search for him. They found him lying in a deep faint. They sprinkled him with cold water, but he did not wake up. They carried him back to the village. When his father saw him, his heart was sad. However, he soon noticed that the boy was still alive. He called a <term>shaman</term> and asked him to heal his son. The <term>shaman</term> ordered the house to be swept and the floor to be covered with sand. He took the youth into the woods and stayed there for four days. Then he returned. After four more days, <term>Q'ō'mkilig·a</term> also returned. He had been given the name <term>QoaLqoā'oē</term>.

He sang of the <term>*hō'Xhokᵘ*</term>, and suddenly he jumped up to devour his father, who was sitting on the opposite side of the fire. He wore the cedar-bark ornaments of the <term>*hā'mats'a*</term> around his neck and head. His head ring slipped down and fell right over his mouth, so that instead of biting his father, he bit a piece out of his own ring. His grandfather took a large black blanket and wrapped it around the youth's head. He tore it with his teeth. Then the people tied a rope over his mouth, but he tore that as well. Nobody was able to restrain him. All the people fled out the door in fear. They heard him singing in the house and looked through the cracks and knot-holes to see what he was doing. They saw him climbing the house posts and pushing the roof boards aside. He wanted to chase the people. Then they stationed two men at the doors, while others held the roof down so that he could not escape. Others entered and threw a bearskin over him. But he crawled about the house, and his skin was so slippery that nobody could hold him. In the evening he quieted down and lay so still that the people thought he might be asleep. They made a jacket of cedar bark in which they tried to catch him. But as soon as they approached, he jumped up and ran out of the house. On the island of <term>Nalkuitxôi'as</term>, there were a number of women busy splitting salmon. He scented them and jumped into the water to devour them. They escaped in their canoe when they saw him coming.

At last <term>Qoalqoā'oē</term> regained his senses. He spoke to his father: "When I grow excited again, do not try to defend yourself; I will do you no harm." After a short time, he fell again into a state of ecstasy. He lay flat on the floor, face down. The people threw a net made of cedar bark over him in order to catch him. Sometimes they succeeded in placing a foot on his neck, but they were unable to hold him, even by winding his long hair around their hands. He escaped, and nobody knew what had become of him. He ran about in the woods, and when he came back to the village, he bit whoever he met. When he regained his senses, he asked his father to boil oulachon oil and to give it to him as soon as he fell into a renewed ecstasy, as this would restore his senses. One time when he was excited, he smelled the mussels in a canoe which was approaching the village, but which was still far away. He ran down to the beach, and as soon as the canoe landed, he ate all the mussels that were in it. Then he became quiet.

Another group of initiating spirits are the ghosts; their protégés are the ghost dancers. The following is a legend of the <term>L'ā'sq'ēnōx</term> regarding the origin of the ghost dance:¹

<term>Goā'xLa</term> and his children lived in a village in heaven. His sons were <term>Qō'masdôx</term>, the eldest; <term>Hai'aqoālal</term>, the next; <term>Nō'lak·as</term>, the following; and <term>A'nqolak·as</term>. His rival was <term>TsîlqoalōLela</term>. He had three sons: <term>Sepā'xis</term>, <term>YaqanLamayē</term>, and <term>G·ē'xden</term>. Then <term>TsîlqoalōLela</term> wanted to come down to our world. He made a copper ladder on which he was going to climb down with his children. His rival wanted him to pay for it(?). Now <term>Goā'xLa</term> heard what <term>TsîlqoalōLela</term> had said. Then he walked and walked for four days. All of a sudden, he saw a mountain growing up from this world of ours, reaching up to the sky. Then he went home and told his sons. They got ready and came to the place where he had been before. After a little while, they saw the mountain rising up again. As soon as it reached heaven, <term>Goā'xLa</term> said to his sons: "I shall not follow you. Go now and call your tribe the <term>Pē'pawilēnôx</term>. You shall take my dancing implements." Thus he spoke to his sons. Then <term>Qō'masdôx</term>, <term>Hai'aqoālal</term>, <term>Nō'lak·as</term>, and also <term>A'nqolak·as</term> came down to Raspberry Beach. Then they went on looking for a river. They were walking in the woods and came to Cape Cook. There they found a pole at the point of Cape Cook. Then <term>Qō'masdôx</term> and <term>Hai'aqoālal</term> went back, keeping close to the beach. They came to <term>Ots'ō'lis</term> and went to the head of the bay. There they saw smoke. They came up to it and saw a house, which they entered. There were two women who were roasting clams. Then <term>Qō'masdôx</term> and <term>Hai'aqoālal</term> asked the women: "Where do you come from?" The women replied: "We came from the upper world and we have no husbands." Then <term>Qō'masdôx</term> said, "We have no wives. How did you come down?" Then <term>Wī'yolēneqa</term>, one of the women, spoke: "These geese brought us down here, and we came to be your wives." The brothers were glad to hear this, and they went home with their

wives, Wī'yolēneqa and WīyoLasoguilakᵘ. When they came to Raspberry Beach, the women were pregnant. They gave birth to boys, and Qō'māsdôx gave his son the name Lā'qoasqEm. The boys grew up quickly. One day the children were playing at the river at one end of Raspberry Beach. Then Lā'qoasqEm fainted on that side of the river. The other boy went back to tell Qō'māsdôx. He came at once to look after his son, and indeed, he was dead. He buried him immediately. In the evening the boy returned to life, but what could he do? He was inside the coffin box. At night he heard people talking to each other. Then he was able to open the lid of the box. Right away he was called, and they went to a house in which the beating of boards was heard. Three ghosts were asked to take care of the boy. Then they led him into the dancing house, but they did not go to the rear of the house. They sat in the middle of the right-hand side. Now they spoke to Lā'qoasqEm: "Now be careful; remember what you see and the songs which you will hear. Do not eat any of the food they offer you." There was a chief standing in the house holding a rattle. His name was Hā'mamaxayals. He was chief of all the ghosts. He said, "Come, let my boy go to the rear of the house." But the three ghosts replied, "He is alive." They finished their dance. The boy felt uneasy. Then Hā'mamaxayals said: "Be careful, my tribe. We will take that little boy to his house." Then all the ghosts took some moss and put it on their heads. Then the little boy also put some moss on his head. At once, he sat on the ground of our own world. A shaman named Hē'lilalag·ilīs was told to take some urine to wash the people. Then all the ghosts cried "hamamā'" where he was sitting. Qō'masdôx and his wife were eating when they heard the sound, "hamamā', hamamā'." He ran out of his house to look, and there he saw his son sitting on the ground. He called his wife, "Come." His wife came to see and recognized her own son. Then Lā'qoasqEm called his father, "Go and take some urine to sprinkle your people with." Qō'masdôx brought his chamber pot. Then the whole tribe came. But the ghosts opened their mouths. As soon as a person passed their mouths while they were saying "hamamā'," he died. Then Lā'qoasqEm shouted, "Sprinkle some urine on the people." As soon as it was done, all those who had been dead were resurrected. Then he entered his father's house, and the noise of the ghosts came with him. The boy was singing their song and the tribe learned it from him. Thus they learned the song of the ghosts. Now listen to the song of the boy! His name was NēnLaxstals, now that he was a ghost dancer. No other kind of dance and carving came to him. This is his song:

> 1. Ya xamamē, ya xamamē, ya xamamē ya.
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now ghosts, go all to that upper world!
> 2. Ya xamamē, ya xamamē, ya xamamē ya.
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For your wealth in the ground is great, ghosts!
> 3. Ya xamamē, ya xamamē, ya xamamē ya.
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For your fire is great and many are your hot stones, ghosts!

<summary>This page recounts the legend of Lā'qoasqEm, a boy who dies and is taken to the house of ghosts, where he learns their rituals and songs. Upon his return to the living world, he uses a ritual involving urine to resurrect those killed by the ghosts' cries, establishing the tradition of the ghost dancer.</summary>

The origin of the sunrise dance is given as follows:

Kuēxala'lag·ilîs and his tribe, the first of the G·ō'p'ēnôx, were living at G·ē'damîs. At that time it was always dark and daylight never came. The first G·ō'p'ēnôx were sad. Then Nag·ēisilakua invited his tribe to meet. As soon as they had all assembled in the chief's house, he spoke: "G·ō'p'ēnôx! I did not invite you to eat. I will talk about our world. It is not good that it never becomes daylight. Now, councilors of the G·ō'p'ēnôx, deliberate on how we can obtain daylight for our world. That is what I wanted to say." He stopped speaking, and an old man named Yaqantayig·ilakᵘ, the father of Kuēxala'lag·ilîs, said: "Yes, G·ō'p'ēnôx, let us try to find where Nēnalaats'ēqa is living and let us go to her." Then another old man said: "My tribe, she is living at Xuā'tîs; and it is said that she keeps the sun in her box. Let us go and make war upon the Koskimo, for Nēnalaats'ēqa is of their tribe. Let us take away the daylight that she keeps in her box." With this, the old man finished speaking.

Then Kuēxala'lag·ilîs, who had magical powers, said: "My tribe, you all know I am Kuēxala'lag·ilîs; I have magical powers. Do not make war upon the Koskimo, for I will go to Nēnalaats'ēqa with my friend Ts'ēqaxsdō'kuilakᵘ. Now, get yourself ready, my friend! Let us go to Xuā'tîs. But you, my tribe, take care in case misfortune should happen to me." Then all the people said: "We are happy after being discouraged, because you have magical powers and therefore you always succeed in your undertakings."

Now Kuēxala'lag·ilîs and Ts'ēqaxsdō'kuilakᵘ started their journey. The former said to his friend: "We will not go directly to Xuā'tîs. I will go to the woods and try to find a truly supernatural power. Do not lose patience if you have to wait for me for a long time; otherwise, we shall not defeat Nēnalaats'ēqa. Hide here and do not let anyone see you." Then he left the canoe and went into the woods at night.

After a short time, he discovered a squirrel. Kuēxala'lag·ilîs spoke to him and asked: "What are you doing here, friend?" The squirrel replied: "I am picking crab apples." He asked in turn: "What are you doing here?" Kuēxala'lag·ilîs replied: "I am trying to bathe in that lake, so that I may obtain possession of the box in which our sun is kept, and which Nēnalaats'ēqa is guarding." The squirrel said: "Do you not know how to transform yourself into a baby and enter Nēnalaats'ēqa's womb? Then, when you are born, you must cry for the box." 

Then Kuēxala'lag·ilîs was glad to have the advice of his friend the squirrel. He went to his canoe and told his friend: "You may go home. I am not going with you, and do not worry if I stay away long." He pushed the canoe into the water, and Ts'ēqaxsdō'kuilakᵘ paddled home to G·ē'damîs. He told the G·ō'p'ēnôx what had happened.

Then Kuēxala'lag·ilîs walked until he saw the village at Xuā'tîs. There he saw Nēnalaats'ēqa sitting in her house, eating salmon. Then he transformed himself into a baby and entered her womb. She vomited at once. Her belly swelled rapidly, and after four days she

Then he went to the upper world.

In this manner, the G·ō'p'ēnôx obtained the sunrise mask (<term>na'xnak·aqEML</term>) and its red cedar bark. It was inside the box. That is the end. (See figures 129–133, page 484.)

The Mā'tEm ceremonial originates from the following legends of the Nimkish:

At Pāpēk·īn, above Nimkish Lake, lived a young man named Ō'mEaLEMāē. He was always playing with other children. One night he was very hungry. He took salmon roe out of a box and roasted it. When the roe burst, some of it jumped against the neck of the boy's father, who was sitting near the fire warming his back. He grew angry and struck Mā'tEm with a stick. The boy became sad and went into the woods. After walking a long time, he came to a place where there was a logjam of driftwood in the river. He wanted to die and jumped into the water above the logjam, but he came up again below it, none the worse for his long dive. He came to a second logjam and jumped into the river above it, but he came up below it, healthy and well. Then he arrived at a steep cliff. He climbed up and flung himself down the precipice, but he did not hurt himself. He went on and soon he arrived at a mountain which was resplendent with light. It was the cliff Nā'oalakoa. There it was raining quartz crystals all the time. He took up four crystals and placed them in a row on the midline of his head. He climbed the moun-

Then the people knew that he had returned and that he had obtained magical power from Mā'tEm. They bathed and went down to the shore, each carrying a staff with a crystal fastened to it. The youth, who was then given the name Mā'taanoē, followed him. He asked the people to sweep the house and to place a plank on the roof. When they had done so, Mā'tEm landed on the plank. Three times he flew up again, but the fourth time he came down into the house, accompanied by Mā'taanoē.

Later on, Mā'tEm went out with his slaves to cut wood. His canoe capsized and he descended to Bē'benaqaua. There he saw many dances and he received the <term>lōlō'LalaL</term>, the <gloss>ghost dance</gloss>, and the name Lō'LEmaē.

I obtained another version of this tale from a Kwakiutl, although the tale also belongs to the Nimkish:

A youth used to spend his time with his sweetheart, and despite the urgent pleas of his mother, he refused to marry. Late one night he came home and asked his mother to prepare food for him. She was angry and said: "Go back to the place where you came from and get your food there. I will not give you anything." The youth was saddened. He lay down and stayed in bed for four days without eating any food. His mother began to worry and asked him to get up, but he did not listen. Then she called the youth's sweetheart to call him, but he did not listen to her either. At last, after four days, he arose and went into the woods without knowing where he was going. He had lost his senses. He came to a lake. There he stripped off his clothes and swam and dived in the lake. He remained under water for a long time. When he surfaced, a totem pole rose with him. He came to a third and to a fourth pond, and after having bathed, he knew that he would find the bird. He put on his blanket and went on. Soon he saw the bird flying ahead of him. He threw off his blanket in order to be able to follow him more rapidly. Suddenly the bird turned and called, "What do you want from me?" The youth replied, "My mother mistreated me. Now I have come to find a magical treasure." The bird retorted: "Do you see that mountain? That is my home. Let us climb it!" He flew ahead and the youth followed him. When they had arrived at Mā'tem's house, the bird gave him quartz and other things: the water of life, the fire of death, and the seal harpoon. He put the quartz crystals into the youth's joints, and thus he obtained the power of flight. He sent him to the mountain Ts'ī'lk·împaē (feathers on top) in the far north, in order to get eagle down for his dances. The youth started on his journey. When he approached the mountain, it was snowing, hailing, and raining. The people who lived near the mountain kept great fires burning in order to see and catch anyone who came to the mountain seeking eagle down. But with the help of the quartz, the youth passed them without being seen. He gathered the eagle down and thus obtained the power to take the shape of a bird. Then he returned to his own village in the form of a bird. When his younger brother saw the bird approaching, he laid a snare to catch it. The bird put the snare over its own neck and resumed his human shape. He sent word to his father, asking him to clean his house. When this was done, he came home in the evening and danced as Mā'tem. On the following morning, the bird Mā'tem brought a totem pole and threw it down in front of the youth's house.

The Mē'iLa is a legend which belonged originally to the Hē'iltsuq and Awī'k'ēnôx. I obtained the following tale from the Awī'k'ēnôx regarding its origin:

A young man named Mē'iLa went up to the sky ten times within a single year. On his first visit, he found a gull, which he brought down. On his second visit, he found a puffin (?); on his third visit, the salmonberries, then a diver (a bird), and the bird xē'xēxē. After his sixth visit, he brought the bird atE'mkuli. But when he had gone up the tenth time, he did not return again. His mother, Lēelaiaqs, and his father, Q'ōmxto-îs, mourned for him. Finally, they fell asleep. His mother thought she saw a beautiful house in her dream, but upon waking, she realized that what she believed to have been a dream was real. The house was nearby, and her son Mē'iLa was sitting in front of it. She woke her husband so that he might see him. They jumped up and ran toward the house. But it retreated from them, and finally they saw that it was actually up in heaven. Then they sat down and cried, singing, "Our son is in heaven playing with Nūsnū'sELîs (the moon)."

In several cases, the dance or the powers obtained by an ancestor are also represented on totem carvings. I will give a few examples of this kind:

There were the first of the Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx at Hē'qams. Lā'liliLax became their chief. One day, he said he wanted to go to the river of Gā'yux to see if the sockeye salmon were traveling up the river. He went far upstream but did not find a single salmon. Then he forgot why he had gone up the river. He felt dizzy. Suddenly, he saw a handsome man sitting on a stone. His face was like that of a bird. The man did not see Lā'liliLax. The chief went up to him and stood behind him while the other man’s head was turned away. He said, "Friend, what are you doing here?" Now the man turned his head and spoke: "Thank you, friend, for coming so that I could see you. I am the one who thunders from one end of the world to the other." Lā'liliLax replied: "O, master, I came here for your sake. Now give me a magical treasure." Then the man spoke: "Build a house and invite all the tribes." He showed him the carving of the thunderbird with its legs spread wide. They say it was as long as a forefinger. The man spoke: "Its legs are the door of the house. The following legend belongs to the subdivision Mē'Emaqâaē of the Naqô'mg·ilisala and explains the post shown in fig. 36 (see also pp. 332 and 376):

A man lived in a house at G·igē'LEM. He tried to find the <term>sī'siuL</term> for his magical treasure, but he was unsuccessful. He simply died. Then his tribe put up a false grave for him. But he had actually found a magical treasure and went up to heaven. Blood was put on his false grave, and a sun was painted on it.

After four days, it began to thunder. Lē'laxa thundered. He came down to the beach early in the morning in the shape of the thunderbird. He took off his mask, and they recognized Lē'laxa. Then he showed his magical treasures: the thunderbird mask, the two-face mask, and the morning mask. He was a <term>mā'maqa</term>. He threw the worm against his enemies (see p. 485). The clan Đ'a'm'amtElaL of the Ts'a'watEēnôx has a number of carvings and ornaments, the use of which is authorized by the following tradition, which tells of the meeting of the clan's ancestor with the deity:

Đ'a'mtalaL was the name of the chief who lived on one side of the river Ts'a'watē. X·i'nt'alaqa was the name of his wife. B'a'Lalag·ilak<sup>u</sup> was his son. Nau'alagumqa and Ts'e'stalis were his daughters.

Đ'a'mtalaL was making a salmon trap. A man came and looked at him, and his hammer fell into the water. But Đ'a'mtalaL just said "hoî'p," and the hammer floated. It was Qā'niqilak<sup>u</sup> who was watching him.

Now they went down the inlet and came to Dōx'ualits'ēnaē. Then B'ā'Łalag·ilakᵘ moved in the canoe and flew away. In vain they tried to catch him with their paddles. He flew home. Wē'qaē traveled on and came to Qā'qētEn. There he saw the <term>thunderbird</term> sitting on a rock. He went down and heard Wē'qaē saying: “I thought he always made it hail.” Then the wind maker went back to tell the <term>thunderbird</term> what he had heard. Now the <term>thunderbird</term> arose and went into his house. He put on his <term>eagle dress</term> and came out again.

->VII. THE ORGANIZATION OF THE TRIBE DURING THE SEASON OF THE WINTER CEREMONIAL.<-

In the previous chapter, I described a number of spirits that appear to the Indians and are believed to bestow supernatural powers upon them. From the legends I have told, it appears that these spirits first appeared to the ancestors of the clan, and I have stated that these same spirits continue to appear to the descendants of those mythical ancestors. The number of spirits is limited, and the same spirit appeared to the ancestors of various clans across different tribes. However, in these cases, the spirit gave each of his protégés his powers in a slightly different form. In fact, each noble name (as described on page 338) has its own tradition regarding the acquisition of supernatural powers, which have been passed down to those who hold the name. As indicated in some of the traditions, the spirits give new names to the men to whom they appear, but these names are only used during the time when the spirits live among the Indians—that is, in winter. Therefore, from the moment the spirits are believed to be present, all summer names are dropped, and the members of the nobility take their winter names.

It is clear that when the names change, the entire social structure based on those names must break down. Instead of being grouped into clans, the Indians are now grouped according to the spirits who have initiated them. All those protected by BaxbakūālanuXsi'waē form one group; those who stand under Winā'lag·ilīs form another group, and so on. Within these groups, divisions are made according to the ceremonies or dances bestowed upon the individual.

Thus, at the start of the winter ceremonial, the social system is completely changed. The period when the clan system is active is called *bā'xus*, a term that also designates those who have not been initiated by any spirit and might be translated as "profane." The period of the winter ceremonial is called *ts'ē'ts'aēqa*, or "the secrets," a term that also refers to the ceremonial itself. It is also called *ts'ē'qa* (the singular of *ts'ē'ts'aēqa*); *aik·'ē'gala* (making the heart good); and *g·ā'xaxaakᵘ* (brought down from above). The Indians express this alternating of seasons by saying that in summer the *bā'xus* is on top and the *ts'ē'ts'aēqa* is below, and in winter it is the other way around.

During this period, societies take the place of clans. These societies consist of groups of all those individuals who have received the same, or nearly the same, power or secret from one of the spirits. Thus, the *hā'mats'a*, *nū'LmaL*, bear dancers, and others each form a society, which consists of a limited number of names, because the

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

Each member of the society derives their membership from the initiation of one of the ancestors of the nobility. These ancestors each have only one representative at a time. However, many of them are grouped together, as will be described shortly.

Because of these facts, a new member can be admitted to a society only when another member is dropped, whose place the new member then takes. This custom is similar to the transfer of a position in the nobility to a youth; the old member transfers his rights to a young man and leaves the ranks of the society.

The dancers (or societies) are organized into two main groups, which the Kwakiutl proper call the seals (*mē'êmqoat*) and the *quē'qutsa*. The former includes several dancers and societies of dancers—the *hā'matsa*, *ha'mshamtsEs*, *k·înqalalaLa*, *nō'ntsîstalaL*, *qoē'qoasElaL*, *q'ō'minōqa*, *nā'nē*, and *nū'LmaL*. These hold the highest rank. All others are *quē'qutsa*. These are subdivided into smaller groups based on age and sex, as follows:

| 3. *D'ō'd'ōpa* (rock cods), young men, about twenty-five years old. | 10. *Mō'smōs* (cows), old women. |
| 4. *L'ē'L'ēXEn* (sea lions), older men. | |

The number of these societies has changed frequently, but the *Maa'mx'ēnôx*, *D'ō'd'ōpa*, *L'ē'L'ēXEn*, and *Qoē'qoîm* have always remained. The current societies for women are quite new, as shown by their names—hens and cows. Until about twenty years ago, the former were called *wa'xwaxoli*.

The *La'Lasiqoala* are divided in the following way: The group corresponding to the seal group is called *q'ā'q'anas* (a small black shellfish). They include the *hā'mats'a*, *mā'maq'a*, *t'ō'x'uît* (*ō'lala*), *hai'alik·ilaL*, *ts'ē'koîse*, *sē'lics*, *ts'ē'koa'tâ'*, and *yiyā'LalaL*.

The Nā'q'oaqtôq are divided as follows: The group corresponding to the seals is called the *wu'n'awunx-îs*, or the "troublesome ones." They include the *hā'mats'a*, the bear, and the *mā'maq'a*. I do not have a complete list of the subdivisions for the *quē'qutsa*.

The *L'ō'L'Epana* (cormorants) are the chiefs; the *ēSElālîLtsawē qoayî'm* (the whales for whom one waits) are the young men; and the *ts'ē'ts'eg·inaqa* (gulls) are the older boys.

Among the Koskimo, the group corresponding to the seal group is called the *ts'ē'qolag·ilîs*, and it includes the wolves and the *hā'mats'a*. The chiefs of this tribe are called *t'ō't'opa* (rock-cods), and the higher chiefs are called *nā'nē* (bears). The middle-aged men are called *guē'gusō* (pigs).

The *quē'qutsa* groups of all these tribes consist of individuals who, for the time being, are not possessed by the spirits. A member of the *quē'qutsa* may be initiated by a new spirit at any time, at which point he or she leaves their ranks. Alternatively, a person may become possessed by their spirit and perform their dance or ceremony. In that case, they are temporarily not considered a member of the *quē'qutsa*, but simply one of the dancers. Therefore, the *quē'qutsa* correspond very closely to the group of people who have resigned their positions in favor of younger ones, as these individuals may also re-enter the ranks of the nobility by marrying and thus obtaining a new name.

The seal society is subdivided into two groups: the *la'xsâ* (those who have "gone into the house"), who have gone through the house of BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē and learned all his secrets; and the *wī'xsâ* (those who have "not gone into the house"), who have only "leaned against its walls." All the dancers who are instructed by BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē—the *hā'mats'a*, *ha'mshamt sES*, BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē's grizzly bear, *k·î'nqalaLala*, and *q'ō'minōqa*—belong to the *la'xsâ*; the others are *wī'xsâ*.

Each dance (*lē'da*) has two names associated with it: the dance name (*lē'laēnēXLä'ya*) and the *quē'qutsa* name (*quē'tseXLä'ya*). An individual assumes the latter name when giving up their dance in favor of a younger man, or uses it when they are not performing their dance or ceremony.

The two groups—the seals and the *quē'qutsa*, and the corresponding groups among the other tribes—are hostile toward one another. When the seals are excited, they attack and torment the *quē'qutsa*; the *quē'qutsa*, on the other hand, tease and torment the members of the seal society. While most dancers join the *quē'qutsa* for the greater part of the *ts'ē'ts'aēqa* season and perform their dances only on certain occasions, the members of the seal society—particularly those of the highest rank, the *hā'mats'a*—must stay with their society. Even when they intend to give up their dance, the *quē'qutsa* try to prevent them by all possible means.

It will be noticed that most of the subdivisions of the *quē'qutsa* have animal names. The Indians explain that the ceremonial was established at the time when men still had the form of animals, before the Transformer had put everything into its present shape. The present ceremonial is a repetition of the ceremonial

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

These ceremonies are performed by the man-animals (*nu'xnēmîs*) or, as we might say, are a dramatization of the myth. Therefore, the people who do not represent spirits instead represent these animals.

As might be expected from the laws governing the clan system, the "dance" is primarily acquired through marriage. Along with the house, the carvings, and the names of the father-in-law, the young man receives his dance name and *que'qutsa* name, though not for his own use. These are given to his successor (*Lawu'lqamē*), who is initiated in the prescribed way and then performs the ceremony. However, the son-in-law of the previous owner controls the dance. It can be performed only with his consent, and when another man marries his daughter, he may take it away from his current successor and give it to this new person, who then owns and controls it.

Through marriages with the Awi'k'ēnôx and Hē'iltsuq, the number of Kwakiutl dances has significantly increased.

I can now describe how these privileges, which are obtained through marriage, are transferred from a man to his son-in-law. I stated previously (p. 359) that, depending on the number of children the couple has, the purchase money given by the young man to his father-in-law at the time of marriage is returned with 100 to 300 percent interest.

As the time approaches when this money must be returned, the father-in-law calls in all his outstanding debts and gathers all his property until he has a large stock of food, blankets, boxes, dishes, spoons, kettles, bracelets, coppers, and ceremonial box lids (*g·i'sexstâla* or *koqētayâ'nō*). These are old lids for boxes, some clearly of a very great age. Their shape is the same as the lids still in use, but the front section is much higher, painted with designs representing faces, and inlaid with sea-otter teeth (fig. 41). The bracelets are tied to sticks, ten to each stick; in addition to the large coppers, small ones about an inch or two in length are used. Four of these are tied together and fastened to the end of a stick. Once the father-in-law has collected the necessary amount of property, he is ready for the ceremony of returning the purchase money (*qautē'x·a*). This may be done either in the *bā'xus* season or during the *ts'ē'ts'āēqa*. The ceremonies in both seasons are very similar. I will describe the former here, as the latter forms part of the winter ceremonial. The father-in-law calls his clan together.¹ They all arrive, and

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of the transfer of social privileges and property through marriage among the Kwakiutl. At this meeting, he informs the people what amount of property he is going to give to his son-in-law, and what names the latter is to receive from him; he also states if the son-in-law is to receive his house, his carvings, and his dance. The clan offers the father-in-law their help if he should not have enough property. The following morning, the father-in-law and the son-in-law each call their respective clans. The young man assembles his people in his house and tells them what he expects his father-in-law to give him, and he requests the people to dress as nicely as they can.¹ They put on their button blankets and bird's down and paint their faces. They remain in front of their house while the father-in-law's people take the ceremonial box lids and place them on the beach in the form of a square, the sides of which are about 100 feet long. This is called the canoe (*mā'wa*), and all the property that is to be given to the son-in-law is placed in this enclosure. From one or two corners of this "canoe," cedar bark ropes are stretched to the front corners of the young man's house. All the spoons and dishes which the father-in-law is going to give away are tied to them. They are called the anchor line of the canoe. The father-in-law calls his clan inside the square.² They all carry staffs. One of them sings out "hū, hū, hū!" and all respond, "wū!" This is repeated four times. The clan of the son-in-law, who are on the summer seat in front of the house, repeat the cries. After this, each party sings ten songs in turn. Then the wife of the son-in-law steps out of the canoe dressed in her best. She wears a blanket decorated with abalone shells. A large abalone shell is fastened to her nose by strings which pass over her ears, as the shell is too heavy to be worn suspended from the septum. For the same reason, her earrings are worn suspended from her hair. She performs a dance, after which her ornaments are given to her husband.

The mother-in-law is also in the "canoe." It is customary that during the time preceding this festival, people of her own and other tribes send her small presents of food or help her carry water. In return, she gives bracelets from the "canoe" to those who have been kind to her.

Now the speaker of the father-in-law calls the son-in-law, saying: "Come, take care of yourself, otherwise you will have bad luck."³ He calls four men of his own clan and says to them: "Come! Take hold of our property that we have in our canoe."⁴ Then turning again to the son-in-law, he continues: "I made an anchor line of spoons.⁵ I pay you—"

After all the presents have been given, the son-in-law and a few of his friends go to his house. The rest of his friends go behind the houses and walk secretly to the end of the village. > I will go and tear to pieces Mount Stevens, I will use it for stones for my fire,

The breaking of the canoe indicates that all the property given to the young man will be distributed among the tribe immediately. This is done on the following day.

There is still another way by which a dance may be obtained—the same as the crest and *bā'xus* (clan) names—namely, by killing its owner. It is said that many dances were introduced among the Kwakiutl and related tribes in this manner. I will give a few examples of this custom, which I briefly mentioned earlier, but which I could not discuss fully there because the custom is so closely connected with the winter ceremonials. The first instance I learned about is the following:

Formerly the *Mā'tilpē* had no *hā'mats'a*, but only *ha'mshamtsEs*, and the other tribes would not allow them to obtain one through marriage. At one time, a canoe of northern tribes passed near the village of the *Mā'tilpē*. Two young men observed it and saw that there were four men and two women in the canoe, one of whom wore the badges of the *hā'mats'a*. Then the two *Mā'tilpē* youths determined to kill the *hā'mats'a* in order to obtain his dance. They paddled up to the strangers, who asked the two young men to direct them to a camping place. They did so. Then they hid their guns in the bushes nearby and told the strangers that they were on their way to look after their traps. They asked to borrow the strangers' guns. When they had received them, they went to the place where they had hidden their own weapons, loaded them, and shot the four men and the two women. One of the youths took the cedar bark ornaments of the *hā'mats'a*. He found his whistles in a bag. At once he began to utter the *hā'mats'a*'s cry "hāp, hāp," for now he had the right to use the dance owned by the man whom he had killed. He also took two coppers which he found in the canoe. This method of obtaining a dance and other objects is called *kuē'xanEm*, meaning "obtained by killing."

It is the same when a novice who is being initiated is found in the woods—the person who finds him may kill him. The murderer then obtains his dance, and the relatives of the novice are not allowed to take revenge.

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

The following very characteristic descriptions were given to Mr. George Hunt in the summer of 1895. He recounts them as follows:

I was walking on the street of the Nimkish village when I saw Hē'x·hak·En, who was sitting on his summer seat. He called to me and said: “O, my dear friend! Your days, young men, are good. But our past ways were evil when we were all at war with each other. I mean that you face no such troubles nowadays. I was pursued three times by northern Indians during the time when we still went naked.” Then I asked Hē'x·hak·En, “Where did this happen?” And he said, “At Gā'widē. We were out in two canoes harpooning porpoises. I was in one, and my friend, NemōXtsaXqô'lag·ilis, was in the other. I had killed two porpoises. When day broke, I saw four canoes, and I told my friend. He said to me: ‘I will go to the island of Gā'widē’; and I said, ‘I will go to Ō'gwamalis. Take good care of yourself. Goodbye.’ Then I paddled away. My canoe was flying like a bird. Two of the canoes pursued me, but they could not overtake me. Then I looked back and saw that they could not catch up with my friend, who had nearly arrived at Gā'widē. Then I watched them and saw how the warriors were searching for my friend. Night fell and I felt distressed, for I saw that the warriors had a fire on the beach. I asked my steersman: ‘What do you think? Shall we look for my friend and see if they have enslaved him?’ He agreed, and we paddled to the island. When we arrived there, I took my gun and went ashore. I went to where the fire was burning on the beach and saw that the warriors had unloaded their canoes. I said to my companion: ‘Take care, my friend, I am going to shoot them.’ We hauled up our canoe and hid. As soon as we reached there, we sat down close to them. They were eating. There were five men in a line from where I sat, and my friend said that there were three in a line from where he sat. We each put thirty balls of buckshot in our guns and fired both at the same time. I had killed three and wounded the two others. My friend had killed two and wounded the third man. And I saw two more men running away. Then we ran to the wounded ones and killed them. We took one man and four women alive and made them our slaves. We took the property of the northern people. I looked into a large box, and when I opened it, I saw a lot of red cedar bark and abalone shells which were attached to it, as well as the whistles of a <term>hā'mats'a</term>. I asked one of the women: ‘What is that in this box?’ She only replied: ‘Hōm, hōm, hōm, hōm, hōm, hām, hām, hām, hū, hū,’ and she bit her own arm. Then I knew that one of these men whom we shot had been a <term>hā'mats'a</term>. I immediately cried <gloss>hāp</gloss> <note>The ritual cry associated with the hā'mats'a cannibal dance</note>. There were also two coppers in the bottom of that box. Then we came here to Alert Bay in the canoe of the dead men. Here we were met by our tribe, the Nimkish. We were invited at once by Chief Koax·ila-nō'kumē, along with our slaves. He gave us dried halibut to eat. As soon as we had eaten, the chief spoke and said: ‘My friend, tell us, where did you get these women?’ Then I spoke to him and told what

I put the ring of red cedar bark around my neck and I put the head-ring on my head. I obtained this cedar bark ornament by killing its owner. Therefore you must not say anything against me. Examine it closely, otherwise you will say later on when I give my winter dance that I invented it." Then L'ā'qōLas said: "Chief, what can we say against you since you killed these men? You have obtained this ornament from the man whom you have killed; therefore it is called 'obtained by killing.' It is the same as though you had obtained your *<term>hā'mats'a</term>* through marriage. Now go on and give a winter dance. Why should we not do it in the right way?" Then my brother’s son disappeared right away, and when he came back in winter he was my *<term>hā'mats'a</term>*. That is what I did in the past. Now you know it."

The hā'mats'a ceremonial was obtained in this way by killing a great number of Hē'iltsuq. The war in which this happened is one of the most famous in the history of these tribes. I provide here a version obtained by Mr. Hunt.

The Bî'lxula made war upon the Qoē'xsot'ēnôx. It was autumn. They landed above the village of Qoā'yastEm and hauled their canoes ashore. Late in the evening, they sent out spies to examine the village. About midnight, when all the Qoē'xsot'ēnôx were asleep, the Bî'lxula launched their canoes and divided. One half went to the east end of the village, and the other half to the west end. They stayed in their canoes not far from the beach until it was almost daylight. It was foggy. As soon as it became daylight, they landed and many men went to the rear of the houses. As soon as they were ready, the most courageous warriors broke through the doors of the houses and speared men, women, and children. Whoever tried to escape through the rear door was speared by the men stationed there. Others of the Bî'lxula looked after the valuable property and put it into their canoes. Now the Qoē'xsot'ēnôx were all killed; only seven men and five women were left. Then the Bî'lxula set fire to the houses. Their canoes were heavily loaded with men's heads. They went home. At that time, people of different tribes were staying at Qoā'yastEm: the Ma'malēleqala, Lau'itsîs, Nimkish, and Nā'qoaqtôq, all guests of the Qoē'xsot'ēnôx. They were all slain by the Bî'lxula, as were some who belonged to the Kwakiutl. Then four men came and told what had happened to NEqā'p'Enk·Em, chief of the Kwakiutl, who was Qoē'xsot'ēnôx on his father's side. Then he called the Kwakiutl and asked them to go to war against the Bî'lxula. Then four men were sent to ask the Ma'malēleqala, Nimkish, and Lau'itsîs to go to war as well. They also asked the La'Lasiqoala and the Nā'qoaqtôq. Four very strong men were selected, and after six days they returned. When they came back to Tsāxîs, NEqā'p'Enk·Em invited them, and when they were seated in his house, he called all the Kwakiutl to hear the reports of the messengers. When the people had arrived, he asked them to be silent and to listen to the words of the messengers. One of them said: "In four days they will all be ready to come, both men and women. All have decided to go to war against the Bî'lxula." Then Yā'xLEN said: "Now go, Kwakiutl! Prepare to go, so that we do not stay another night when they arrive. And let our wives wash for four days so that we may have good luck." After they had eaten, the men who were going to war took seaweed and blew into it until it nearly burst. Then they made neck rings out of it. When they had done so, NEqā'p'Enk·Em invited all the men and women to his house. He told them what to do, for he knew all the customs of ancient times. He spoke: "Thank you, Kwakiutl—thank you and your beloved wives. Now, Kwakiutl, we will soar up and catch the Bî'lxula in our talons. We will be the great thunderbird. We will avenge our fathers, our mothers, our uncles, our aunts, our sisters, and our younger brothers,"

On the next morning the great warrior YēqaLalasamē himself awakened them before the crows were moving. Then all the men and women rose. Only those who were menstruating were not allowed to go. First the men went to get hemlock branches, then the women did the same. Then they all went into the sea and sat down crying, "hū, hū, hū." They rubbed their bodies with hemlock branches. The women did the same, and then men and women pretended to fight. The women threw the kelp rings at their husbands, who tried to catch them. When a man missed his kelp ring or when it burst, he was not allowed to go on the war expedition. For four days the men and women continued to do this. When they had finished, they prepared their weapons. After five days the Ma'malēleqala arrived in four canoes, the Nimkish in six canoes, the Lau'itsis in two canoes, and the Ts'ā'watEēnōx in eight canoes. Then Neqā'p'Enk'Em invited all the tribes. When they were in his house, he gave them dried salmon and afterwards clover root. Before they finished this course Neqā'p'Enk'Em stood up and said: "Fathers, uncles, brothers, children, thank you for coming. Early the following morning they started. When all the tribes had come to the island opposite Gua'ts'ē, NEqā'p'Enk·Em and Yē'qaLalasamē arose and the former spoke: "Friends, now our season will change from *bā'xus* to *ts'ē'ts'aēqa* as soon as we cut off the head of a man. Then our *hā'mats'a*, bears, and *nūLmaL*, the *hawī'nalaL*, and all the other winter dancers, will become excited. Now let spies go ahead in four canoes. Now we are no longer men; we are killer whales. When you see a canoe, fire a gun so that we may know it. Then take hold of the canoe, but do not hurt them until we come." NEqā'p'Enk·Em finished speaking and sat down. Then one canoe of the Kwakiutl, one of the Ma'malēleqala, one of the Nimkish, and one of the Lau'itsîs went ahead. They steered to G·î'lsg·iltEm. When they had passed the island, the other war canoes followed. At night they stopped at Nux·saqōīL. Early the next morning Yē'qaLalasamē sneezed. Then he awakened all the men and said, "Slaves! I sneezed with my right nostril. Today we shall stain our hands in blood." Then the four spies started again. They did not see a canoe or smoke, and all the warriors grew discouraged. Now they arrived at the mouth of Rivers Inlet. Then Mā'Xua, chief of the Ma'malēleqala, spoke: "Listen to me, friends. My heart feels badly because we have not yet seen anyone whom we might slay. Let us play with the Awī'k·'ēnôx, the tribe of this place, to gladden my heart." The warriors did not want to do it, and while they were still talking, the report of two guns was heard. "Now, slaves, paddle! Those were our spies." Then all the men paddled on. The Kwakiutl came to a place where six canoes of Hē'iltsuq were lying along with the four canoes of their spies. The Nimkish were the next to arrive. Then came the Lau'itsîs, and far behind the others the Ma'malēleqala. Let us meet them with our *ts'ē'tsaēqa* during the dancing season. We will compete with the dances of our brothers O'ts'ē'stalîs, Ō'mx·'it, Wā'k·as, and Quina. We cannot kill the He'iltsuq. Let us go to war against the Bî'lxula.” He was speaking in this way just as the Ma'malēleqala came into sight around the point of the bay. They saw the canoes drifting, and MāXua arose at once and said: “Why do you let your canoes drift about?” And Ya'yaqadalal took up his lance and killed the steersman of one of the He'iltsuq canoes. As soon as he had done so, he cried, “*hūp, hūp, hūp*.” Then all the tribes attacked the He'iltsuq. Only Ō'mx·'it was not killed. As soon as the *hā'mats'a* killed a man he cried, “*hāp, hāp, hāp*,” the bear growled, and every dancer became excited as soon as he killed a man. When all the He'iltsuq were dead, they took their cargo and divided it. But the red cedar bark and the whistles of the *hā'mats'a* and the *Laō'laxa* were given to the war chiefs. All the chiefs of the He'iltsuq were *hā'mats'a*. Now, Ō'mx·'it became a slave of Mā'Xua, the chief of the Ma'malēleqala. Then NEqā'p'Enk·Em said: “Friends, what do you think? Shall we go on to the Bî'lxula? Think of it, friends! We have done a great thing. The chiefs O'ts'ē'stalîs, Bā'salaL, Wixwaqoqamaya, and Wā'yats'uLa have not come here. They are close relatives of those whom we killed. Are you not afraid of them? Then there are all the sons of O'ts'ē'stalîs. I think we ought to go home.” Then they all returned. They had obtained all the names and all the dances of the dead chiefs of the He'iltsuq. Since that time, the tribes have possessed the cedar bark ornaments of the He'iltsuq and their names. They obtained them by spilling the blood of these men in war.<sup>2</sup>

I have given these reports in some detail, as aside from the light they throw upon the acquisition of names and dances by war, they show

It is also noted that these societies are recognized during war expeditions. I will return to this subject later.

Despite the fact that every dance must be obtained through marriage or by killing its owner, there are several offices connected with the ceremonies of the societies that are strictly hereditary through the male line and therefore always remain within the same clan. To this class belongs the office of the master of ceremonies—the officer in charge of the drum, the batons, the eagle down, and others that will be detailed in the description of the ceremonial (Chapter IX). This provides further evidence for the theory mentioned earlier: that Kwakiutl institutions were once patrilineal but were later modified by the influence of northern tribes, who follow a matrilineal system.

### VIII. THE DANCES AND SONGS OF THE WINTER CEREMONIAL.

The purpose of the entire winter ceremonial is, first, to bring back the youth who is believed to be staying with the supernatural being who protects his society. Then, once he has returned in a state

<image-desc>Line drawings of two carved wooden batons. The top baton (Fig. 42) is shown horizontally, featuring several carved bands or rings along its length. of ecstasy, the goal is to exorcise the spirit possessing him and to restore him from his sacred madness.

These goals are achieved through songs and dances. To bring the youth back, members of all the secret societies perform their dances. It is believed that these will attract the attention of the absent novice, until finally one of the dances may excite him so much that he will approach, flying through the air. As soon as he appears, his friends try to capture him. Then the second part of the ceremony begins: the exorcising of the spirit, or, as the Kwakiutl call it, the taming of the novice. This is achieved through songs sung in his honor, dances performed by women in his honor, and the efforts of the shaman. After the novice has been restored to his senses in this way, he must undergo a ceremonial purification before he is allowed to take part in the ordinary activities of life. The strictness and severity of this purification depend on the character of the dance. Novices must drink water through the wing bone of an eagle, as their mouths must not touch the brim of the cup; they must suck

Errors in rhythm, turning the wrong way during a dance, smiling, and chewing gum are all counted as mistakes. The error must be atoned for by an initiation of the person who made the mistake. When the members of the seal society notice a mistake, they jump from their seats and bite and scratch the person who made the error. He drops down immediately

When a <term>hā'mats'a</term> falls during his dance, he must lie down as if he were dead. Then the master of ceremonies calls a man named <term>Ē'k·istōlis</term> (meaning "sand in eyes," referring to a drowned person), whose office is hereditary. He is a <term>quē'qutsa</term>, and in his official capacity, he is called <term>ts'ā'ts'exsilaēnôx</term> (one who acts secretly). He carries a large staff (<term>k·'ē'lag·aiū</term>) which is split like a pair of tongs and has blood hidden inside it. With this staff, he takes hold of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>'s neck, and blood is apparently seen flowing from it. Then all the <term>hē'lig·a</term> (see p. 438) lift the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, place him on their mat, and carry him four times around the fire. After they have circled the fire four times, his whistle is heard in the woods. When the mat is set down, it is discovered that he has disappeared and only his blankets and ornaments are left behind.

<image-desc>Line drawing of a carved wooden baton (Fig. 50). This baton is shorter and thicker than Fig. 49, featuring multiple stacked figures. He stays away for four days, and his father must organize a new festival for him. When the <term>hā'mats'a</term> falls, everyone places their hands over their eyes and drops their heads, crying *hā*.<note>With a falling tone.</note> As the expense of such a festival is very great—the amount being equal to the return of a marriage dowry—few people can afford a second initiation. While every effort is made today to enable the <term>hā'mats'a</term>'s father to provide the new festival, it is said that in former times the unfortunate dancer was killed by the other <term>hā'mats'a</term>, the bear dancers, and the <term>nū'LmaL</term>, often at the urging of his own father.

When a <term>hā'mats'a</term> falls during his dance, it is considered an evil omen, indicating that he will die at an early age.

The perspective held by the Kwakiutl is clearly that the falling of a <term>hā'mats'a</term> or of another dancer indicates either ill will from the spirit or a defeat of their spirit by that of another tribe. For instance, I was told that at one time the Kwakiutl had invited the <term>Ma'malēleqala</term> for a winter ceremonial. When one of their dancers fell, their own <term>nū'LmaL</term> tried to kill him, and he was rescued with difficulty by the <term>quē'qutsa</term>. The song that was used during his dance was never used again. They believed the event was proof that the spirit presiding over the winter ceremonial of the <term>Ma'malēleqala</term> was stronger than their own.

<image-desc>Fig. 51: Two line drawings of wooden ceremonial rattles representing human heads. The rattle on the right (captioned "Breadth, 8 inches") is wider and flatter with prominent ears and closed lips.</image-desc>

->Fig. 51.<-

When one of the dancers of an inferior society falls, he also disappears to be initiated, but his father does not need to go to the expense of a complete festival, as these initiations are much less expensive.

The ritual gear of the dances consists largely of ornaments made of cedar bark, which is dyed in the juice of alder bark; of masks, whistles, and carvings of various kinds. All of these must not be seen by the uninitiated. If any of the uninitiated happened to see them, they were killed without mercy. As an example of this, I was told the following incident:

<image-desc>Fig. 52: Line drawing of a wooden rattle in the shape of a human head. A snake or larva-like creature is shown crawling out of the mouth and extending up the side of the face towards the ear.</image-desc>

->Fig. 52.<-
->RATTLE OF <term>HĒ'LIG·A</term>.<-
->Representation of the head of a dead person, out of whose mouth a snake is crawling. Height, 8 1/2 inches.<-

One of the <term>quē'qutsa</term> was preparing a carving to represent the <term>sī'siuL</term>. His daughter happened to see him at work. He then called her into his room and dug a hole directly under the fireplace. He asked her to put her head into his lap, pretending that he wanted to clean the lice from her hair. Then he killed her with a hammer. He put her body into the hole, covered it, and replaced the ashes. His wife looked for the girl, but he did not tell her what he had done until the following summer, when he became ill. Then he asked his wife to bury the remains of their daughter. As a survival of this custom, a saying remains which is used by the initiated to warn away the uninitiated: "Go away, else we shall bury you."<note>Hā'g·a qoē'tax ā'Lanô'x tsamē'sōL.</note>

...a house set apart for this purpose. It is called <term>lō'pEkᵘ</term> (emptied) because it is emptied of everything that is profane. Only when dances are performed are the uninitiated or the profane allowed to enter the house. They must stay on the left-hand side of the entrance.

Most of the dances are performed in connection with feasts. Others are shown in connection with distributions of property. As the clans are suspended during the ceremonial, the seating order that prevails in summer is also suspended, and a new arrangement takes place. The seal society has the seats of honor in the rear of the house, and among them, the highest <term>hā'mats'a</term> has the first seat, in the middle of the rear of the house. On both sides of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> society sit the bear dancers and other members of the seal society. At the extreme ends of this society sit the <term>nū'LmaL</term>, the messengers of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The killer whale and rock cod societies sit in front of the seal society. They are the singers.

This order prevails in summer and is also suspended, and a new arrangement takes place. The seal society has the seats of honor in the rear of the house, and among them the highest <term>hā'mats'a</term> has the first seat, in the middle of the rear of the house. At both sides of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> society sit the bear dancers and other members of the seal society. At the extreme ends of this society sit the <term>nū'LmaL</term>, the messengers of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The killer whale and rock cod societies sit in front of the seal society. They are the singers.

The <term>hē'mElk</term> and the whale society sit next to the <term>nū'LmaL</term>—the former to the left of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, the others to his right. The Koskimo sit next to them near the front corners of the house. The women sit all along the sides of the house in the rear row, the chicken society farthest in the rear, the dam society and the <term>Kē'ki'xalakᵘ</term> in front. The person who gives the feast and all his relatives are in the "kettle corner," the right-hand front corner of the house. The profane sit on the left-hand side of the door. When one tribe has invited another, all the members of the invited tribe sit in the front part of the sides of the house. The seal society of the hosts sits in the rear, and their singers are positioned as described previously. The rest of the inviting tribe is in the kettle corner.

Sometimes on such occasions, all the members of the seal society and of the corresponding societies of the other tribes sit in the rear of the house. Then the <term>hā'mats'a</term> of all the tribes sit in the middle—first those of the Kwakiutl, and at each side those of the Ma'malēleqala, and at their sides those of the Nimkish and Lau'itsîs. The other groups arrange themselves in the same manner, the Kwakiutl members sitting in the rear row nearest the rear of the house; then toward the door follow the Ma'malēleqala, continuing in the next row nearer the fire. Then follow the Nimkish and Lau'itsîs.

The singers are arranged so that the rear rows face the fire while the front rows face toward the back of the house. In their midst sits the song leader (nâ'qatē) and his two assistants (guā'nuLEmē, meaning "sitting at his sides"). It is the duty of the song leader to compose new songs, to create new words for old tunes, to quickly learn the songs of a returning novice, and to teach them to the singers. He also gives signals for changes in rhythm and starts the tunes. His position is hereditary through the male line. His assistants call out the words for each verse. The singers are seated so that they can spread their mats in front of the board that serves as their back support; while kneeling on these mats, they have long planks within easy reach on which they beat the rhythm with batons. These batons are generally made of split pine wood and are created at the time of opening

It is a very beautiful sight to see the many guests going home, each carrying a torch and lighting up the logs and canoes on the beach on one side and the dark row of houses on the other.

I will now proceed to describe the ceremonials of various societies.

BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē, as stated above, initiates several dancers, the most important of whom is the hā'mats'a, or the cannibal. He is possessed by a violent desire to eat men. The novice is taken away by this spirit and is supposed to stay at his house for a long time. The period of his absence extends over three or four months, during which time he actually stays in the woods. In the middle of this time

I received another report regarding the killing of a slave. A female slave was asked to dance for the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. Before she began dancing, she said: "Do not get hungry; do not eat me."¹ She had barely finished saying this when her master, who was standing behind her, split her skull with an ax. She was then eaten by the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. This occurred in <term>Newettee</term>, and <term>Q'ōmEna'kula</term>, who participated in the performance, was living until a few years ago. He told me that it is exceedingly difficult to eat fresh human flesh—much more so than eating dried corpses.
