The bones of the killed slaves were kept on the north side of the house, where the sun does not shine upon them. During the fourth night, they were taken out of the house, tied up, weighted with a stone, and thrown into deep water. This was done because it is believed that if they were buried, they would return and take their master's soul.

When the <term>hā'mats'a</term> had bitten a piece out of the arm of one of his enemies, he drank hot water after swallowing the flesh. It was believed that this would cause the wound to become inflamed. Nowadays, as the ceremonies have lost much of their former cruelty, they do not actually bite a piece of flesh out of the arm. Instead, they merely pull the skin up with their teeth and suck hard to remove as much blood as possible, and then secretly cut off a small piece of skin with a sharp knife. the ear until after the dance, when it is returned to the owner to assure him that it will not be used against him for purposes of witchcraft.

Besides devouring slaves, the hā'mats'as also devour corpses. When a new hā'mats'a returns from the woods after being initiated, he will sometimes carry a corpse, which is eaten after his dance. The bodies are prepared for this ceremony. The skin is cut around the wrists and ankles, as they must not eat the hands and feet. It is believed that otherwise they would die immediately. The hā'mats'a must use the corpse of one of his deceased relatives for this ceremony, which the hē'lig·a must prepare. The Kwakiutl used to bury their dead in trees. The body was placed in a box, and these boxes were placed on branches a considerable distance up a tree. There, the boxes were piled one on top of the other (Plate 27). When the bodies are exposed to the action of the freely circulating air in this way, they mostly mummify. A corpse is taken down from the tree and soaked in salt water. The hē'lig·a takes hemlock twigs from which the leaves have been removed and pushes them under the skin, gradually removing all the decayed flesh until nothing but the skin remains. After this is done, the body is placed on top of the small hut in which the novice (*g·ī'yakila*) lives while staying in the woods. The corpse's hands hang down. Its belly is cut open and spread with sticks. The hā'mats'a keeps a fire under it and smokes it.

<image-desc>Line drawing of a rock carving at Fort Rupert. It depicts a stylized human-like face with large, circular eyes, a broad nose with flared nostrils, and a wide mouth, all incised into the rough surface of a rock.</image-desc>

Four days before he returns to the village, he sends for all the old hā'mats'as. When they arrive, he tells them: "These are my traveling provisions, which I received from BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē."¹ He asks them to point out which portions they desire to have when he returns. They take the body down and place it on a clean mat. Each points out what he desires to have. His return will be described later (p. 527). His *k·î'nqalaLala* returns with him. She carries the corpse that has been prepared. She walks backward, facing the hā'mats'a. When she reaches the right side of the fire, the hā'mats'a enters the house. He stoops so that his face is close to the ground. Upon entering, he turns four times, descends to the middle of the house, and when he is four steps away from the door, he turns again four times. When the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> reaches the rear of the house, she turns again. A drum is placed bottom-up in the middle of the rear of the house. The <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> pretends to put the corpse on the drum but walks past it, with the <term>hā'mats'a</term> following her. At the door she turns again and proceeds around the fire; when she reaches the drum a second time, she turns again and pretends to put the body down. At this time, all the veteran <term>hā'mats'as</term>, who have been outside the house, jump down from the roof and rush in through the doors. They are all naked and follow the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> in a state of high excitement. When they have run around the fire four times, the body is placed on the drum.

The master of ceremonies (see page 501) begins to cut the body and distributes the flesh among the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. But first, the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> takes four bites. The people count how many bites each of them swallows. They are not allowed to chew the flesh; instead, they swallow it whole. The <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> brings them water to drink in between.

After this part of the ceremony is finished, the <term>hē'lig·a</term> rise; each takes one <term>hā'mats'a</term> by the head, and they drag them to the salt water. They go into the water until it reaches their waists, and, facing the rising sun, they dip the <term>hā'mats'a</term> four times under the water. Every time he rises again, he cries "<term>hāp</term>." Then they return to the house. Their excitement has subsided. They dance during the following nights. They look downcast and do not utter their distinctive cries, "<term>hāp, hāp</term>." They do not dance in a squatting position, but in an erect

After the ceremony is over, the hā'mats'a compensates those he has bitten, as well as the owners of slaves he has killed, by paying them with blankets.

The ceremony of the hā'mats'a's return will be described later, when a full account of the entire winter ceremony is provided. My goal here is to describe the style of dancing so that I do not need to return to the subject again later.

The hā'mats'a has two ways of dancing—one representing him in a state of extreme excitement, and the other when he is becoming calm.

<image-desc>Fig. 65. Head ring of hā'mats'a. A ring of dark, twisted cedar bark with a large, loose bundle of shredded bark tied on one side. IV A, No. 578, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by A. Jacobsen.</image-desc>

first dance represents him searching for human flesh to eat. He dances in a squatting position, with his arms extended sideways and trembling violently (fig. 62). He first extends them to the right, then to the left, shifting his feet at the same time so that when extending his arms to the left, he rests on his left foot while the right foot is stretched backward; when extending his arms to the right, he rests on his right foot while the left foot is stretched backward. In this way, he moves forward slowly with long steps. His head is tilted upward, as if he were looking for a body being held high in front of him. His eyes are wide open, his lips are pushed forward, and from time to time he lets out his terrifying cry, *hāp*. His attendants surround him, and two of them hold him by his neck ring so that he does not attack the people. When he is at the back of the

upward. In his second dance, the *hā'mats'a* dances standing erect. While in his first dance he is naked, he is now clothed in a blanket. Now he holds his forearms upward, with his elbows near his sides, his palms forward, and his fingers lightly bent. His hands are still trembling violently. His dance consists of rhythmic steps matching the beats of the batons. He takes very high steps, so that his knees almost touch his chest. When raising one foot, he simultaneously bends the knee of the other leg, and thus drops his torso considerably without changing his position (Plate 28). He always puts down the entire sole of his foot.

When he first returns from his initiation, he wears a head ring, neck ring, waist ring, bracelet, and anklets made of hemlock branches. The form of these rings varies according to the legend from which the *hā'mats'a* derives his origin. While most of them have plain hemlock rings, one *hā'mats'a* of the *Koskimo* has his decorated with small rings of white peeled twigs, which contrast clearly against the dark green ring of balsam pine (see p. 595).

The painting of the *hā'mats'a's* face also depends upon the legend from which he derives his origin. Most of them have their faces painted black all over, while others have two curved red lines on each cheek running from the corner of the mouth to the ear in a wide curve

If the dancer is not a novice, he performs the first dance with his cedar bark ornaments, which the new <term>hā'mats'a</term> does not wear until his fourth dance. These consist of a heavy crown of plaited cedar bark and a corresponding neck ring, anklets, and bracelets (figs. 63–68).

The head ring in figure 63 is set with four crosspieces. These crosspieces signify the gifts of the spirits who have initiated the cannibal dancer. The front piece represents the Milky Way, the cannibal pole of <term>Baxbakuālanuxsī'waē</term>; the two side pieces represent the <term>hō'Xhok<sup>u</sup></term>. The rear crosspiece is said to be merely an ornament. Some <term>hā'mats'as</term> wear a bear skin decorated with the scalps of the slaves they have eaten or of the enemies they have killed.

<image-desc>A line drawing of a ceremonial mask or painting of a face. The face features two large, almond-shaped eyes with thick, dark brows and heavy pupils. Below the eyes is a wide, grinning mouth that spans the lower half of the face, filled with numerous sharp, triangular teeth.</image-desc>

->Fig. 75.<-
->**PAINTING ON THE FRONT OF A MĀ'WIL, REPRESENTING THE FACE OF BAXBAKUĀLANUXSĪ'WAĒ.**<-
->From a sketch.<-

The symbolic meaning of several crosspieces will be described in detail further on (p. 449).

During the dances of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, whistles are heard (figs. 69–74) which represent the voices of the spirits. Most of these whistles are small. They are made of red cedar. A few are made of bone.

After his first dance, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> disappears into a room set apart for this purpose at the rear of the house. It is called the <term>mā'wiL</term> and is supposed to be the house of <term>Baxbakuālanuxsī'waē</term>. Its front is painted with designs representing either the face of <term>Baxbakuālanuxsī'waē</term> himself or that of his servant, the raven. The top of the front is decorated with fringes of red cedar bark (fig. 75). The room is always arranged so that when the <term>hā'mats'a</term> reappears, he comes out through the mouth of the painting on its front. Plate 29 shows the <term>hā'mats'a</term> emerging from the secret room, which is painted with the raven design. As soon as he appears, his attendants run up to the secret room and hold the <term>hā'mats'a</term> by his neck ring. Then he comes forward and performs his dance.

This room is used only by the novice. For him, a high pole is also erected in the middle of the rear of the house. It is called the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term>, the cannibal pole. It is a mast thirty to forty feet high, wound with red cedar bark. At the top is a short crosspiece about four feet long. The cedar bark extends up to it so that it forms a triangle at the top of the pole. Sometimes a triangle painted with the face of <term>Baxbakuālanuxsī'waē</term> is attached to it instead.

As mentioned before, the novice disappears into his secret room after his first dance. Soon his cries are heard again, and he is seen coming out backward from the side of the <term>mā'wiL</term>. He wears the mask of the raven, <term>Qoā'qoaXualanuXsī'waē</term> (fig. 76), which is supposedly growing

After the dancer has moved around the fire four times, he disappears behind the <term>mā'wiL</term>. Then the <term>hā'mats'a</term> comes forward again out of the <term>mā'wiL</term> and dances in a squatting position as before, but perfectly naked. He disappears, and next a dancer—the same one who wore the first mask—appears, coming out backward from the side of the <term>mā'wiL</term>. He wears the mask of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> himself, and dances and moves in the same position as the <term>Qoā'qoaXualanuXsi'waē</term>. (Fig. 77 and Plate 30.)

It will be noticed that some of these masks are decorated with skulls carved from wood. These have various meanings. They may indicate that the mask was obtained in war, or that as many slaves were killed for the novice as there are skulls attached to the mask, or finally they may belong traditionally to the particular <term>hā'mats'a</term>. Each has a separate tradition, and therefore, their masks and ornaments differ. While the dancer who wears the mask of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> is dancing, the singers sing the following song:

> He carries the <term>hā'mats'a</term> head mask, which he obtained from <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>, all around our world.<note>See Appendix, page 687.</note>

After he has danced around the fire four times, he disappears. Then the <term>hā'mats'a</term> comes out from the <term>mā'wiL</term> again, dressed in his red cedar bark ornaments, and dances in an upright position.

When an experienced <term>hā'mats'a</term> performs these dances, the masks are not used. Instead, he dances four times in a row: first in a squatting position, then upright during the latter part of the second dance and for the entire third and fourth dances.

a mouse coming out of a hole and calling him. He threw off his blanket and spoke to the mouse, who invited him to enter. She warned him, however, to be careful of the door. The chief followed her. The chief jumped through the door when it opened. Q'ō'moqoaē gave him the hā'mats'a dance and the raven mask.

Following is the legend of the origin of the G·agg·aēnôx:

The first of the A'wa-iLala lived at Ts'ā'watē. Their chief was Gu'mg·ila. His sons were Qoā'wiLpē and Xa'niats'amg·ilak<sup>u</sup>. They were always very happy because their tribe was numerous. One night they were attacked, and only Gu'mg·ila and his two sons were saved. When morning came, Xa'niats'amg·ilak<sup>u</sup> felt very uneasy and told his father: "I will go into the woods. Do not try to find me, my dear father!" His father replied: "Just be careful, my son, lest something happen to you. Do nothing wrong, because you intend to go and obtain a magic treasure. Rub your body for four days with hemlock branches, otherwise you will smell like a human." Then they separated. The young man

<meta>This page continues the description of ceremonial cedar bark ornaments. While the previous page focused on the legend of Xa’niats’amg·ilakᵘ and his first few rings, this page details the specific symbolic components of the head and neck rings—such as "death-bringers" and "fire-bringers"—and describes the ritual progression of the hā'mats'a dancer among the La'Lasiqoala.</meta>

According to tradition, NōmasE'nxelîs, an ancestor of the Naqô'mg·ilisala, had a son named LExx·ā'lix·ilagū (p. 335), who obtained his dances from the sī'siuL and from the wolves. His first head ring (fig. 92) shows six crosspieces in front. These are the death-bringers, and the upright piece on top is the fire-bringer, while the square behind represents the bucket containing the water of life.

<image-desc>Line drawing (Fig. 89) of a ceremonial neck ring. It is composed of a thick, braided circular band with a horizontal bar across the top. Long, braided fiber pendants hang from the sides and center.</image-desc>
->Fig. 89.<-
->NECK RING WORN BY XA'NIATS'AMG·ILAḲU<-
->IN FEASTS.<-
->Cat. No. 175508, U. S. N. M. Collected by F. Boas.<-

In his second head ring (fig. 93), only four death-bringers are shown. This ring is worn in his second dance. As will be described below, the Naqô'mg·ilisala and La'Lasiqoala remove some of the symbols that designate the supernatural powers of the dancer after each dance. The ring shown in fig. 94 is stripped of all these crosspieces and is worn by the dancer during feasts. The dancing neck ring (fig. 95) has two crosspieces on the sides. These symbolize the gifts of the sī'siuL, while the gifts of the wolves are symbolized by the attachments in the front and back.

Another hā'mats'a of the La'Lasiqoala, upon returning from the woods, dances for four nights with wreaths of hemlock branches; the following four nights (the fifth to the eighth) without any ornaments; then four nights (the ninth to the twelfth) with ornaments of red cedar bark. He wears eight bundles over his forehead, which are called k·'ā'siwē, and four on each side. The next night, after he has finished dancing, one of the k·'ā'siwē is removed, which is publicly announced the following morning. On the fourteenth night, two more of these bundles are taken away; the next night, two more; and finally, on the sixteenth night, one more is removed, which is also publicly announced each morning.

<image-desc>Line drawing (Fig. 90) of a head ring. It is a thick, braided circular band with several small, rounded bundles (k·'ā'siwē) attached to its exterior. A small measurement scale is positioned below the drawing.</image-desc>

On the seventeenth night, a black line is drawn across his face from the left side of his forehead to the right side of his chin, and then he rises to bite people. <meta>This page continues the description of the ceremonial regalia and ritual progression of the hā'mats'a among the Kwakiutl people, specifically detailing the symbolic markings of the initiate and the transition between different societal ranks.</meta>

The size of the ring is said to signify the waning moon. When the hā'mats'a returns, a bloody line is drawn across his face, beginning on the cheeks and curving up toward the nose, crossing its upper portion. This is said to represent the moon. The line is made by rubbing the face with dogfish skin. It is said that this line indicates the effect of Wina'lag·ilis's canoe, which rubbed against the face of the novice.

Each hā'mats'a has eight of his own songs, which are composed for him by the nâ'qatē at the time of his return from the woods, and these are sung whenever he dances.

A young man who first becomes a member of a secret society cannot join the hā'mats'a until after a number of years. For seven years, he must have been a member of societies of lower rank. Then, in the eighth year, he may become a hā'mats'a.

<image-desc>A drawing of a ceremonial neck ring (Fig. 91) made of thick, braided or twisted cedar bark. It features several stiff, branch-like protrusions radiating outwards, also wrapped in bark. The ring is worn around the neck as part of ceremonial regalia.</image-desc>

->Fig. 91.<-
->NECK RING OF XA'NIATS'AMG'ILAKU.<-
->Cat. No. 175493, U. S. N. M. Collected by F. Boas.<-

The hā'mats'a's first initiation is called g·ī'yak·ila. After four seasons, he may be given another hā'mats'a initiation by his father. This is called tâ. After he has been initiated four times (yuduXp'Ena tâ = having gone into it three times), he may leave the ranks of the hā'mats'a and become a quē'quatsa. This is called "locking the whistles into the box." This is accomplished in the following way: When the master of ceremonies assembles all the people (qap'ē'ku, see p. 502), all the hā'mats'as stand up; then the one who desires to join the quē'quatsa says:¹ "I will not stand up before you. I want to be a quē'quatsa." He is asked why he desires to do so, but only replies:² "I have finished being a hā'mats'a." Then the people reply:³ "Let your whistles be quiet," and he says:⁴ "I will keep my whistles quiet." The same statements must be made by other members of the seal society who desire to become quē'quatsa.

On the following day, the master of ceremonies sends his messengers to invite the people to the qap'ē'ku. The man who desires to become a quē'quatsa

<meta>This page continues the description of the hā'mats'a initiation rituals, specifically detailing the symbolic body painting and the initiate's interaction with messengers and the Seal Society.</meta>

must join them. He is painted with the particular design that used to excite him—a head, maggots, the raven, the x·ā'wayū, or the corpse. When painting them, the people hold them tight and torment them. The skull is painted in black on the hā'mats'a's face; the maggots are represented by numerous little dots, and the x·ā'wayū is indicated by a rope. The painting representing the corpse shows feet, because when the hā'mats'a enters the house carrying a corpse, its feet are always visible under the blanket.

Painted in this manner, he accompanies the messengers, who carry long staffs (quē'sp'ēq). The hā'mats'a pretends that he cannot properly do the work assigned to the messengers. When they call a name, they always strike the threshold with their staffs. The hā'mats'a stands in their midst, and they strike his feet with their staffs when calling a name. In short, he is mistreated in every conceivable way, particularly by his rival. If he can no longer endure the torments, he will rush to the seat of the Seal Society. The people pull him back, push him, and tear his clothes. Then he becomes excited and bites the people.

Following are a number of songs of the hā'mats'a:

### HĀ'MATS'A SONG COMPOSED RECENTLY BY QOAYŌ'STĒTSAS.<note>1 Appendix, page 688.</note>

1. I am going all around the world eating everywhere with BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē.

Moving forward and backward indicates that the dancer is referring to himself. For the phrase “eating everywhere,” the right hand stretches far out, as if taking food, and is then brought to the mouth, while the left hand describes a wide circle to indicate "everywhere." For “BaxbakualanuXsi’waē,” both hands are bent inward and the fingertips are moved toward the mouth, signifying “the eater.”

I did not see the dance for the second line. In order to explain the gestures of the third line, I must provide a literal translation:

“I went, you cried ‘hāp’ for me, BaxbakualanuXsi’waē, at the center of the world.” For “I went,” the gesture is the same as described above. For “you cried ‘hāp’ for me, BaxbakualanuXsi’waē,” both hands are bent inward and move toward the mouth, as before, designating the cannibal spirit. Then the arms are stretched far backward, the palms are turned downward, and the head is lowered; this is the cannibal spirit’s posture when crying “hāp.” The same posture is taken by the dancer wearing the mask (fig. 77) when he clatters its movable jaw while crying “hāp.” For the phrase “At the center of the world,” when these words are sung, the dancer stands in front of the fire and looks up toward the rear of the house in BaxbakualanuXsi’waē’s posture, as before, because he is then looking at the center of the world. The last line is the same as the third.

The mention of the north refers to the fact that the composer is a descendant of the <term>Tongass</term> on his mother's side. He claims to have obtained his <term>hā'mats'a</term> from her tribe.

### <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> SONG COMPOSED ABOUT FIFTY YEARS AGO. <note>See Appendix, page 690.</note>

1. Food will be given to me, food will be given to me, because I obtained this magic treasure.
2. I am swallowing food alive; I eat living men.
3. I swallow wealth; I swallow the wealth that my father is giving away.

The presents given away at the time of the initiation of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and at his later dances are said to be swallowed by him. The song means, therefore, that through his ecstasy, his father was compelled to give away much wealth.

### <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> SONG OF THE <term>LAU'ITSÎS</term>. <note>See Appendix, page 690.</note>

1. I went all around the world to find food.
2. I went all around the world to find human flesh.
3. I went all around the world to find human heads.
4. I went all around the world to find corpses.

### <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> SONG OF THE <term>KOSKIMO</term>. <note>See Appendix, page 690.</note>

1. You will be known all over the world; you will be known all over the world, as far as the edge of the world, you great one who safely returned from the spirits.
2. You will be known all over the world; you will be known all over the world, as far as the edge of the world. You went to <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>, and there you first ate dried human flesh.
3. You were led to his cannibal pole in the place of honor in his house, and his house is our world.
4. You were led to his cannibal pole, which is the <term>Milky Way</term> of our world.
5. You were led to his cannibal pole at the right-hand side of our world.

This song was sung for a youth who had taken the place of another who had died. Therefore, the song says that he safely returned from the spirits. The text says: “You returned from <term>Ia'lag·ilîs</term>,” which is another name for the spirit of the winter dance. The <term>Milky Way</term> is the cannibal pole of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>; in other cases (see p. 405) it is the rainbow.

### SECRET SONG OF THE <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> WHO CARRIES A CORPSE.—<term>AWI'K'ENÔX</term>. <note>See Appendix, page 691.</note>

### <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> SONG OF <term>WA'NUK</term> COMPOSED ABOUT EIGHTY YEARS AGO. <note>See Appendix, page 692.</note>

> That is the way of the real <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>.
> Are you the real <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>?

This refers to <term>Wa'nuk</term>'s war expedition. He had cut off the head of his enemy, and, holding it with his teeth, he said: “That is the way...”

### <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> SONG, <term>LA'LASIQOALA</term>.^1

1. The <term>hō'Xhok<sup>u</sup></term>'s voice is heard all over the world. Assemble at your places, dancers, at the edge of the world!
2. The raven's voice is heard all over the world. Assemble at your places, men, at the edge of the world!

### <term>HĀ'MATS'A</term> SONG, <term>LA'LASIQOALA</term>.^2

1. Truly! He travels around the whole world, the great <term>hā'mats'a</term>, looking for food everywhere—the great <term>hā'mats'a</term> on both sides of the world.
2. Truly! He wants to eat plenty, the great <term>hā'mats'a</term>. He is trying to eat everything himself, the great <term>hā'mats'a</term>, but he did not reach the food that he was going to obtain at the edge of the world.
3. He wants to eat with both hands, the great <term>hā'mats'a</term>, at the house of the one who is trying to eat everything himself all over the world; but he did not reach the <term>coppers</term> that he was going to obtain at the edge of the world.

This translation is not entirely certain. The song refers to the <term>Goasi'la</term>, who in ancient times had many dances and did not want to give them to the other <term>Kwakiutl</term> tribes who desired to acquire them through marriage. The <term>La'Lasiqoala</term> heard that the <term>Goasi'la</term> intended to invite them to their winter dance. They were invited and set out, but it seems their chief was afraid and returned without attending the feast.

### <term>K·Î'NQALALALA</term> SONG.¹

1. Begin! You whose eagle down, which is strewn all over her body, fills the house; you who bring all the people together from all over the world.
2. Begin! You who make the people weak, tempting those who have eaten too much with food; your body makes the people of the whole world over-saturated.
3. Begin! You who pile the red-hot stones up to the roof of the house all over the world.

The girl who danced this <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> was a prostitute in her tribe. She is shamed in this song. By the eagle down and the piles of red stones, the composer meant the young men who came in crowds to her house. The meaning of the second verse also becomes clear from this perspective.

### <term>K·Î'NQALALALA</term> SONG.²

1. <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> cries 'hāp' for me; he utters the <term>hā'mats'a</term> cry for me. I possess great supernatural power.
2. <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> and his companion have thrown the sound of whistles and the sound of magic power into me. I possess great supernatural power.
3. I reached the place where the exciting cry of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> and his companion is heard. I possess great magical power.

### <term>K·Î'NQALALALA</term> SONG.³

1. The sounds of the winter dance are heard wherever you are, great one.
2. <term>Hā'mats'a</term> cries are heard wherever you are, great one.
3. You went right up to the raven, and the sound of fighting ravens is heard wherever you are.
4. You went right up to the shutting mouth, and the sound of the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term> is heard wherever you are.
5. You went right up to him who carries one corpse on each arm for you.

The <term>hā'mats'a</term> cry “hāp” was obtained by the <term>Kwakiutl</term> through intermarriage with the <term>Awī'k·'ēnôx</term>. The dancer was partly of <term>Awī'k·'ēnôx</term> descent. Therefore, the song says that he carried the <term>hā'mats'a</term> cry through the world. (Line 4, "shutting mouth" refers to the <term>hō'Xhokᵘ</term>.)

### <term>K·Î'NQALALALA</term> SONG.⁴

1. I have the winter dance song; I have magic powers.
2. I have the <term>hā'mats'a</term> song; I have magic powers.
3. I have <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>'s song; I have magic powers.
4. Your magic power killed the people, and therefore they all hide from you, fearing your great power.

This song belonged to a man who had killed a chief of the <term>Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx</term>, and the song refers to this event. Later, he was killed by a <term>Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx</term>, who now owns the song.

### <term>K·Î'NQALALALA</term> SONG OF THE <term>NIMKISH</term>.⁴

1. I tame the wildness of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> when I see it.
2. I cut the veins of the wild monster in the north when I see it.

The skull indicates that the <term>hā'mats'a</term> is filled with the desire to eat skulls. The form of the rattle is evidently suggested by the beautiful northern raven rattles. (See pp. 623, 629.)

This song was also composed for a girl of bad reputation who had spread syphilis among her tribe. The remark "I cut the veins of the wild monster" refers to this. The singers mean that she is infecting everyone, even the wild monster.

->Q'Ō'MINŌQA.<-

The <term>q'ō'minōqa</term> dance was recently acquired from the <term>La'Lasiqoala</term> through intermarriage. The novice also disappears into the woods to be initiated by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. 

When she is brought back by the tribe, her hair is falling out and her head is covered with blood because it has been torn by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. She carries a skull in each hand. As soon as she is seen, the <term>hā'mats'as</term> begin to cry "hāp" and dance toward her in a squatting position with trembling hands, eager to devour the heads she is carrying. The other <term>q'ō'minōqas</term> and those who have previously been <term>q'ō'minōqa</term> join her dance and move as if they are carrying heads. In this way, she dances into the house, always surrounded by the <term>hā'mats'as</term>, who finally take the skulls out of her hands, lick them, and eat the maggots and the dry skin still attached to them.

## THE <term>HA'MSHAMTSES</term>.

The Kwakiutl state that before obtaining the <term>hā'mats'a</term> from the <term>Hē'iltsuq</term>, they had only the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term>, who is also initiated by <term>BaxbakuālanuX sī'waē</term>. Nowadays he is considered inferior to the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, and the dance belongs almost exclusively to women. The ceremony following the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term>'s return from his or her initiation is the same as the return of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The ornaments are also of the same description, except that his cedar bark is not twisted and plaited, but simply wound around his head, neck, wrists, and ankles. He does not use a <term>mā'wiL</term>. His cry is not <term>hāp</term>, but <term>wîp</term>. He does not dance in a squatting position, but always standing, with his forearms stretched forward and his elbows close to his sides. His hands tremble. After his first dance, which, like all others, consists of four rounds, he reappears wearing a mask. This is either a head mask, similar to the <term>QoāqoaXualanuX-sī'waē</term> mask described on page 447, or it is a full-face mask. Almost all of these represent animals, which are the protectors of the dancer. It has not become clear to me why so many different animals may become the protectors of the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term>.

<image-desc>Fig. 98. A technical sketch of a ceremonial head ring. It is composed of thick, fibrous bundles of cedar bark, wrapped or tied together to form a circlet with a protruding knot or bundle at the top. Below the image is the text: "Fig. 98. HEAD RING OF Q'Ō'MINŌQA. La'Lasiqoala. IV A, No. 6869, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by F. Boas."</image-desc>

I will describe a few of these masks and give the songs that belong to them. Figure 99 is a <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term> mask, the outer figure of which represents the grizzly bear. The inner face represents <term>BaxbakuālanuX sī'waē</term>. The red rim around the mask represents blood, which is shown because the bear is cut open in order to make the inner face visible.

<summary>This page details the ritual songs and cedar bark ornaments of the Q'ō'minōqa and introduces the ha'mshamtsEs dance, describing its historical precedence over the hā'mats'a and its specific ceremonial characteristics.</summary>
<keywords>Q'ō'minōqa, ha'mshamtsEs, BaxbakuālanuX sī'waē, La'Lasiqoala, cedar bark, ceremonial masks, grizzly bear mask, Kwakiutl ritual songs</keywords>

--- Page 230 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term> masks, specifically focusing on the symbolic meaning of the face painting and the ceremonial names and songs associated with the performers.</meta>

The painting on the face represents parts of his body. The chin tuft also represents the uvula. The <term>Kwakiutl</term> believe that the uvula is the cause of hunger, and that <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> has a very large uvula, which causes his insatiable hunger. The mustache represents his legs, and the green spots on the cheeks represent his body. The ears are painted over the eyes and have the shape of a raven's ears. The blue ornament on the forehead is merely a painting, intended to fill a space that did not satisfy the artist. The distinct shape of the nose is called the "voracious nose," and it is meant to indicate that he can smell a person from a long distance away. The name of the owner of this mask, while a member of the "<term>seal society</term>," is always <term>Nā'wîs</term>. After he joins the

Image (b) shows the mask opened, revealing an interior human-like face representing BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē. The interior face is white with a red border and mustache, blue around the eyes and eyebrows, and green spots on the cheeks.</image-desc>

### NŌ'NTSISTĀLAL.

This dance is also said to have been obtained comparatively recently by marriage from the <term>Awī'k·'enôx</term>. The novice is also initiated by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> and has the power to handle fire with impunity. In his ecstasy, he takes up glowing coals, puts them into his mouth, and throws them upon the people. At the end of the dancing season, he must pay for all the damage done in this manner. His ornaments are made of red and white cedar bark. Following is a song of the <term>Nō'ntshistālal</term>:¹

1. The gift of the spirit that destroys man's reason—O real supernatural friend!—makes the people afraid.
2. The gift of the spirit that destroys man's reason—O real supernatural friend!—scatters the people who are in the house.

<columns>1</columns>

### NĀ'NĒ, THE GRIZZLY BEAR.

There are two degrees of this society: <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>'s grizzly bear and the ordinary grizzly bear. The former is the higher in rank. Both are among the most important members of the seal society. While all the preceding ones belong to the <term>laxsâ</term>, these are <term>wī'xsâ</term>.² Therefore, at the time of initiation, they are not taken away by the spirit but are only hidden in a corner of the house, from where they come

...they come forward when they are ready to show that they have been initiated. They are perhaps the most dreaded helpers of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, as it is their duty, along with the <term>nū'LmaL</term>, to punish all violations of laws regarding the privileges of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> or the winter ceremonial in general. I stated before that the penalty for some mistakes was death. The unfortunate individuals were killed by the grizzly bear dancers and the <term>nū'LmaL</term>. They also guard the dancing house and often assemble on the roof with the other members of the seal society, where they frighten everyone away with their wild cries and threatening attitudes. They always wear bear claws on their hands and sometimes appear dressed in bearskins. Their faces are painted to look like the enormous mouth of a bear. Their head rings and neck rings are made of red and white cedar bark. Each of these is twisted into a tight rope; then they are twisted around each other and tied at the ends.

## THE <term>NŪ'LMAL</term>.

The <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> (plural of <term>nū'LmaL</term>) or "fool dancers" are also messengers and helpers of the <term>hā'mat'sa</term>, who help to enforce the laws referring to the ceremonial. Their method of attack is by throwing stones at people, hitting them with sticks, or in serious cases stabbing and killing them with lances and war axes.

<image-desc>Line drawing (Fig. 103) of a "MASK OF HA'MSHAMTSES." The mask is highly stylized with prominent, rounded features, including large eyes, a broad nose, and an open mouth. Fibrous material, possibly hair or shredded bark, sprouts from the top and bottom of the mask. Text below the image: "Height, 17 3/4 inches; white, red, black. IV A, No. 917, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by A. Jacobsen."</image-desc>

The <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> are initiated by a legendary people, the <term>Ā'Lasimk·</term>, who are believed to live near a lake inland from <term>LīXsi'waē</term>. Their village is believed to be on an island floating on the lake. They have enormous noses and their bodies are covered with mucus. In olden times a man went beaver hunting and encountered these people. He came back exhausted and "crazy." His nose was running all the time; he ate the mucus and smeared it all over his body. He urinated and defecated in the house, and only after a long time did the people succeed in restoring him to his senses.

From him the <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> are said to derive their origin. They are supposed to be out of their senses and to have long noses. They are as filthy as the first <term>nū'LmaL</term> is said to have been. Some of them when initiated are taken away by the <term>Ā'Lasimk·</term>, while others are initiated in the house. The <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> are <term>wī'xsâ</term>. Those who are to be initiated in the house will all of a sudden begin to scratch their heads and bodies. They scratch more and more violently. This indicates that they are

possessed by the winter dance spirit. After four days, they are confined in the corner of the house and appear as <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> at the time of the next dance. When a young man is to be initiated into this order, the old <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> will throw mucus from their noses onto him and thus "throw the spirit of the winter ceremonial into him."

The <term>nū'LmaL</term>, according to what was stated above, is filthy and acts as though he is out of his senses. His cry is *wē, wē, wē*. Paintings of fool dancers are shown on Plate 33. They do not dance, but, when excited, run about like madmen, throwing stones, knocking people down, and crying. They turn to the right instead of to the left, and make the circuit of the fire by turning to the left. Then the <term>quē'qutsa</term> try to correct them, but they only grow more excited. They dislike seeing clean and beautiful clothing. They tear and soil it. They break canoes, houses, kettles, and boxes; in short, they act like madmen in every conceivable way. At the end of the dancing season, they must compensate the owners for all the property they destroyed.

<image-desc>A detailed line drawing of an indigenous mask, identified as Fig. 104. The mask features a face with wide, circular eyes and a large, bulbous nose. Technical details below indicate it is the mask of Ha'mshamtses, measuring 13¾ inches in length, and is part of the collection at the Royal Ethnographical Museum in Berlin.</image-desc>

The <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> carry lances and war clubs during the ceremonials, which they use to kill those who offend the <term>hā'mats'a</term> (figs. 113–116, pp. 475, 476). Many of these lances are carved and painted with the design of the raven. The <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> wear rings of red cedar bark, which are simply tied around their heads and hung around their necks. The bark is not plaited.

When they first appear after their initiation, and also when performing their ceremonial dance, they use masks. All these masks are characterized by long noses of a curiously round shape. The face is surrounded by a red ring which represents red cedar bark. The style of these masks has not changed during the last century. There is one in the U.S. National Museum that was collected by the Wilkes Expedition (fig. 117, p. 477). Another old specimen is in the British Museum (Plate 34). The similarity between this style of mask and the newer ones collected in recent years will be noticed (figs. 118–122, pp. 477–479). Any mention of a long nose excites the <term>nū'LmaL</term>. He does not allow his nose to be touched.

### SONG OF <term>NŪ'LMAL</term>, <term>LA'LASIQOALA</term>.<note>Appendix, page 707.</note>

1. Oh wonder! He is causing a turmoil on the earth.
2. Oh wonder! He makes the noise of falling objects on the earth.
3. Oh wonder! He makes the noise of breaking objects on the earth.

There is a chief <term>nū'LmaL</term> who is called <term>G·ē'qamēq'ōLEla</term> or <term>Ō'maq'ō'LEla</term>. It is stated that nine generations ago, <term>TsEx'uē'tē</term>, chief of the <term>Sī'sīnLaē</term>, had a son who was a <term>nū'LmaL</term>. He gave a feast and said that he wanted to make his son chief of all the <term>nōō'nLEmaLa</term> and call him <term>G·ē'qamēq'ōLEla</term>. He sent him to be initiated as a <term>nū'LmaL</term> once more, and when he returned, he distributed an immense amount of property: sea-otter skin blankets, canoes, slaves, coppers, etc. As he was unable to bring all this property into the house, he scattered eagle down, which symbolized the property, all over his guests. Since that time, “property is the lance of the <term>G·ē'qamēq'ōLEla</term>,” and the father of a new <term>G·ē'qamēq'ōLEla</term> must distribute all his property at the time of the novice's initiation.

<image-desc>A line drawing of a Kwakiutl bear mask (Fig. 106). The mask features a long, protruding tongue or snout, stylized carvings including a large eye with concentric circles, and a thick ruff of shredded cedar bark or fur at the back. Text associated with the image reads: "Fig. 106. MASK OF <term>HA'MSHAMTSES</term>, REPRESENTING THE BEAR. Length, 15 inches; white, red, black. IV A, No. 1255, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by A. Jacobsen."</image-desc>

The <term>Hā'wayadaLaL</term> is one of the highest fool dancers. He carries a knife in his right hand and moves it along his neck as though he were cutting it. Then he changes the knife to his left hand and repeats the same motion. In doing so, he stabs himself—or pretends to do so—actually stabbing his neck ring, which is filled with a bladder containing blood.

### <term>NĀ'NAQUAUALIL</term>.

The dance of the <term>Nā'naquaualiL</term> consists of very rapid motions of the body from right to left, according to the rhythms of the song. The trunk is slightly inclined forward, the hands are open and held upward,

<summary>This page describes the ritual return and song of the hā'maa dancer, who mimics a voracious spirit by biting people, and introduces the Salmon dance of the La'Lasiqoala tribe. people hide all the eagle down, the symbol of wealth, but put it on when he enters, indicating that the salmon brings prosperity. He is greeted with the cry “haiohō'.” The amount of property distributed by the dancer’s father is as large as that needed for initiating a <term>hā'mats'a</term>. His dance is intended to imitate the motions of a jumping salmon. He holds his head sideways and dances with stiff legs, keeping his feet in the same spot while turning his body first to the right and then to the left. His forearms are bent upward, with his open palms stretched forward. His song is as follows:

1. Many salmon are coming ashore with me.
2. They are coming ashore to you, the pillar of our heaven.
3. They are dancing from the salmon’s country to the shore.
4. I come to dance before you at the right-hand side of the world, surpassing, outshining, and exceeding everyone; I, the salmon.

### SONG OF A SALMON DANCER.¹

1. The salmon came to search for a dancer.
2. He came and put his supernatural power into him.
3. You have supernatural power. Therefore the chief of the salmon came from beyond the ocean. The people praise you, for they cannot carry the weight of your wealth.

### THE SALMON WEIR DANCE.²

In the legends of the Kwakiutl, the weir is a toy of the salmon. The salmon weir dancer is initiated by the salmon. At present, the dance belongs to the <term>Maa'm-tag·ila</term>, who acquired it through marriage from the <term>Awī'k·'ēnôx</term>. The novice remains in the woods for about one month. When he returns, he is naked. His body is smeared with the juice of a plant that makes it very slippery. His cedar bark ornaments are similar to those of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, but much smaller. The dancer first balances on one leg, with his body bent almost horizontally to one side and his other leg extended to the opposite side. Then he switches to the other leg, bending his body to the other side and extending his opposite leg. Here is his song:

1. I went to work at my salmon weir. When I took out the salmon, the crows had picked out their eyes.
2. (Speaking to the chief of the tide:) Stand still, chief! You who make the tide rise, who cause whirlpools where the tides meet, whose seaweed skirt makes the tide rise.
3. (Chief of the tide says:) Cry <term>hāp</term>! supernatural one! Cry <term>hāp</term>!

### WASP DANCE—HA'MASELAL.¹

According to the legend, this dance belongs originally to the Ts'E'nts'Enx'qaiō, to one of whose ancestors the female chief of the Wasps appeared. Only one person at a time owns this dance. I obtained only one line of the song:

1. Do not let us go near the house of the wasp.² There is great danger.

### KU'NXULAL, THUNDER BIRD DANCE.³

1. You are swooping down from heaven, pouncing upon a whole tribe.
2. You are swooping down from heaven, burning villages, killing everything before you, and the remains of the tribes are like the leftovers of your food, great thunder bird; great thunderer of our world.
3. You are swooping down from heaven, going from one tribe to the other. You seize with your talons the chiefs of the tribes.

### KU'NXULAL, LA'LASIQOALA SONG.³

This will be the dance of the thunder bird. Wonderful will be the dance of the thunder bird.

## THE WOLF.<note>Appendix, page 711.</note>

> 1. I go to the seat of the chief of the wolves. Yihihi ahahi.
> 2. I am taken to the middle of the back of the house of the wolves. Yihihi ahahi.
> 3. Thus I obtained all the supernatural powers of the wolves. Yihihi ahahi.

### WOLF SONG, LA'LASIQOALA.<note>Appendix, page 711.</note>

> 1. I come barking on the beach. I make the noise of distributing blankets, for you will be as great as your ancestor, the first of all the chiefs.
> 2. Wonderful are the words of our chief, the wolf. It is said: We shall assemble with our children, asking him to give blankets—to give blankets to each tribe, even to all the tribes of the world. Yihēi.
> 3. Let us try to pacify our chief, otherwise he will swing his bringer of death and cut short our lives, and we shall fall before the chief of the wolves. Yihēi.

### WĀLAS'AXA'.<note>The great one from above.</note>

<image-desc>Fig. 117. MASK OF NŪ'LMAL. A wood-carved mask shown in a three-quarter profile, featuring a prominent brow, large circular eyes, and a carved hand motif placed over the mouth area.</image-desc>

->Fig. 117.<-
->MASK OF NŪ'LMAL.<-
->Cat. No. 2659, U. S. N. M.<-
->Wilkes Expedition.<-

The Wālas'axa' is a unique wolf dance. It belongs to the legend of O'maxt'ā'laLē (see p. 382), who obtained it by marrying the daughter of Qāwatiliqala. The Wālas'axa' is danced in the following way: All the men of the tribe dress in blankets and headdresses representing the wolf. They hide behind a curtain which stretches across the back of the house, and when the singers begin their song, they come out from the right-hand entrance of the curtain. Two criers are stationed there, who hold staffs and announce their arrival. As soon as a dancer appears, he turns and proceeds on a march around the fire. The fists are held forward with the thumbs held up (Plate 36). When the dancers arrive in front of the door, they turn once and then proceed around the fire, disappearing again behind the curtain at the left-hand side. When all have disappeared, two more circuits are made in the same manner. In the fourth circuit they stop when everyone has come out. They squat down on their hands and feet, imitating the motions of wolves. They rest on their toes and knuckles and turn their heads to the right and to the left.

->THE LŌ'KOALA.<-

There is still another wolf dance, which is derived from traditions regarding the initiation of men by the wolves. The tradition underlying this dance is that of Mink and the wolves. The sons of the chief of the wolves were preparing to be initiated. Mink found and killed them, and thus obtained their names and positions. He returned wearing the wolf's scalp as a head mask. Three times he danced around the fire, covering his face and head with his blanket. Then, the fourth time, he uncovered it and showed that he had killed the wolves. All the animals tried to kill him, but were unable to do so. I shall provide the full legend later on. Mink, whose quē'qutsa name is K·ēx·, thus obtained the wolf's name, Nūn, as a member of the seal society, and also the wolf's Lō'koala, or supernatural power. This tradition belongs to the clan

Before singing, the dancer goes three times around the fire, covering his head with his blanket. Then he unfolds it. He wears the headdress. Each of his cheeks is painted with a black circle, the inside of which is red. He puts his hands flat to his nose (both in the center line, one close to the other), dances, and sings the previous song. Then the <term>nōō'nLEMaLa</term> all try to attack him while the <term>quē'qutsa</term> protect him.

### <term>TS'Ō'NOQOA</term>.

Although the <term>Ts'ō'noqoa</term> is not an animal, but a fabulous being, as described before, this seems the most appropriate place to mention her dance and songs. She is a member of the <term>seal society</term>. She is represented as always being asleep. When the dancer enters the house, a rope is stretched from the door to her seat, along which she feels her way.

### SONG OF THE IA'K'ÎM.

1. The great <term>Ia'k'îm</term> will rise from below.
2. He makes the sea boil, the great <term>Ia'k'îm</term>. We are afraid.
3. He will raise up the seas, the great <term>Ia'k'îm</term>. We shall be afraid.
4. He will throw blankets out of the sea, the great <term>Ia'k'îm</term>.
5. He will distribute blankets among all tribes, the great <term>Ia'k'îm</term>.
6. We fear him, the great <term>Ia'k'îm</term>.

### SONG OF THE SĪ'SIUL DANCE, LA'LASIQOALA.<note>Appendix, page 713.</note>

1. Great is the <term>sī'siul</term> dance of our chief.
2. They say by his dance he will cut a whole tribe in two.<note>He will destroy them.</note>

### AŌ'MALAL, OR CHIEFTAINESS DANCE.

I did not see the dance and do not know any details regarding initiation, etc. I received the following description: The <term>Aō'malal</term> is said to sit on a stage in front of the <term>mā'wiL</term>. She wears the chieftainess's ornaments of abalone shells in her ears and attached to her nose. She does not move, but is merely shown behind the curtain while the people sing her song.<note>Appendix, page 713.</note> It is probable that this dance is a recent introduction from the north. In the winter ceremonial of the <term>Tsimshian</term>, the dancer appears in the manner described here on a stage, and after the song, the stage is hidden again behind a curtain.

### SONG OF AŌ'MALAL.

1. We are told that our great chief lets his daughter dance as chieftainess.
2. Great is the song of the chieftainess; great is the <term>hā'mats'a</term> song of the supernatural chieftainess.
3. At the place of the great supernatural chieftainess, the sound of copper is heard, the ringing of copper.

### GHOST DANCE.

I stated in Chapter VI<note>Page 408.</note> how the ghost dance of the <term>L'ā'sq'ēnôx</term> originated. There are a number of traditions of similar character explaining the origin of the ceremony among various tribes. All these traditions contain descriptions of a visit to the world of the ghosts, which is believed to be located beneath our world. Then the visitor was given the secrets of the ghost dance and other magical gifts. This dance is a mimic representation of a visit to the lower world. The dancer wears the head ring and neck ring (figs. 146, 147)<note>Page 497.</note>, which are set with skulls, indicating that the ghosts have initiated him. Elaborate preparations are made for this dance. During the days preceding it, the members of the <term>seal society</term> keep a close watch so that nobody enters the dancing house in which they remain assembled. Then a ditch is dug behind the fire, and speaking tubes made of kelp are laid under the floor of the house so as to end in the fire. The ghost dancer appears, led by a rope by one attendant. He goes around the fire four times, summoning the ghosts. After he has made the fourth

As he completes a circuit, he slowly disappears into the ditch near the fire. The people try to hold him by the rope, but he apparently sinks out of reach. Then many voices are heard coming from the fire—actually the voices of people hidden in the bedrooms who speak through kelp tubes. It is announced that the ghosts have taken the dancer away and that he will return after a certain number of days. When the time of his return is near, another dance is held. A carving representing a ghost is seen to rise out of the ground carrying the dancer.

> 2. The chief of the ghosts made me dance. Therefore, I have supernatural power.
> 3. He put a beautiful ornament on my forehead. Therefore, I have supernatural power.

## <term>MĀ'TEM</term>.

I have told the legend of the <term>Mā'tem</term> in the previous chapter.<note>Page 411.</note> The dancer, when his song is sung, appears first on the roof of the house, perfectly naked. Five pieces of wood, which are covered with mica and cut in the form of hexagonal prisms in the shape of quartz crystals, are fastened along the midline of his head. They are attached to a thin wooden frame, which is shaped according to the curvature of the head and hidden in the hair. The frame consists of a middle piece which is attached to a ring and held by two crosspieces. All of these

## NA'XNAK·AQEML AND ME'ILA.

Two dances derive their origin from the heavens—the <term>Na'xnak·aqemL</term> and <term>Mē'ila</term>. I have already told the legend of both (p. 413). The <term>Mē'ila</term> dance and the ornaments of the dancer are shown in Plate 38 and fig. 149 (p. 501). His club (<term>kuē'xayu</term>), the gift which he received in heaven, represents the <term>sī'siuL</term>. His cedar bark ornament is made of red and white cedar bark. The large flat attachments in front represent the Pleiades. He carries a small clapper (fig. 150, p. 502) in place of a rattle.

The <term>Na'xnak·aqemL</term> wears an immense mask, the mouth of which is made so that it can open wide. Therefore it is also called <term>hā'x·ilaqam</term> (the yawning face). The opening mouth means that the day is yawning when the dawn appears. A mask of this kind was among the collections at the World's Columbian Exposition and has been transferred to the Field Columbian Museum. The song belonging to this mask is as follows:<note>Appendix, page 714.</note>

1. You will arise, you who are known throughout the world.
2. You will arise, you who are famous throughout the world.
3. You will arise; before you sinks down your rival.
4. It is said that I buy food for my feast even from my rival.

Finally, I will describe the dances established by <term>Wīnā'lag·ilīs</term>, namely the <term>mā'maq'a</term>, <term>t'ō'X'uît</term>, <term>hawi'nalaL</term>, and <term>ā'mlala</term>. All of these dancers wear ornaments made of hemlock, not red cedar bark. They are all considered war dances.

### <term>MĀ'MAQ'A</term>.

The <term>mā'maq'a</term>, or "thrower," performs a dance in which he is supposed to throw disease into the people. He enters the house naked except for a head ring, neck ring, waistband, bracelets, and anklets made of hemlock. His hands are held flat against his thighs. In this position, he runs around the fire with short, quick steps, looking upward with sudden movements of his head—first to the right, then to the left. As he does this, he is looking for his supernatural power to come to him. Suddenly, he claps his hands together and holds his palms flat against each other. He then moves his hands somewhat like a swimmer: upward, then in a long circle forward and downward, and finally drawing them close to his body and upward again. Now he is holding his supernatural power, "the worm of the <term>mā'maq'a</term>," between his palms. During all of this, he continues his path in short, quick steps, but he no longer looks upward. Gradually, he moves his palms apart,

<image-desc>A line drawing of a ceremonial mask featuring a prominent, curved bird-like beak, stylized eyes, and painted or carved geometric designs on the face. The mask appears to be made of wood and is labeled as Fig. 131.</image-desc>

->MASK OF <term>NĒNALAATS'ĒQA</term>.<-

The stick consists of several tubes that fit into each other so that the dancer can lengthen and shorten it. While the worm is seen to increase and decrease in size, the <term>mā'maq'a</term> resumes his throwing motions, moving his closed palms in circles as described above. Suddenly, he seems to throw the object he is holding. At once, all the people stoop and hide under their blankets. The object has disappeared. He repeats the performance. The second time he throws the worm, it is

The worm flies into some of the people, who immediately jump up and rush toward the fire, where they fall down lifeless. Blood streams out of their mouths. The mā'maq'a continues to dance around them and blows upon them until finally they are carried away as if dead. The mā'maq'a follows them, and either he or the shaman restores them to life. During this entire ceremony, the singers beat the boards rapidly and silently, only stopping when the mā'maq'a is not dancing. His song is sung after he has finished his dance. ### MĀ'MAQ'A SONG.<note>Appendix, page 715.</note>

> 1. Go and look everywhere for his supernatural power, for his supernatural power.

Among the <term>La'Lasiqoala</term>, the <term>mā'maq'a</term> wears cedar bark ornaments as shown in figures 151 and 152 on pages 502 and 503. > 4. Truly the supernatural power cuts short their lives.

## T'Ō'X'UÎT.

The <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> is almost always danced by women. The dancer is decorated in the same way as the <term>mā'maq'a</term>. She enters singing the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> cry:

<image-desc>Musical notation for the t'ō'X'uît cry, featuring three short melodic phrases on a treble clef staff.</image-desc>

->Yā yā yē    yā yā yē<-

She holds her elbows close to her sides, her forearms forward, and her palms upward. She walks around the fire limping, raising both hands slightly with every second step, as though she were trying to conjure something up from underground. She is followed by four attendants. Her spirit is in most cases the <term>si'siuL</term>, and she is conjuring him. She moves around the fire four times, and then the ground opens in the rear of the house and a huge <term>si'siuL</term> comes out. Its horns move and its tongues flicker. This carving is raised either by strings that pass over the beams of the house or by men who lift it from underneath. A carving of this sort was exhibited at the World's Columbian Exposition and has been transferred to the Field Columbian Museum. As soon as it appears, there is a great commotion in the rear of the house so that it cannot be seen very distinctly. After it has disappeared again, the singers begin its song, which is as follows:<note>Appendix, page 715.</note>

> 1. Let us show what we gained by war!
> 2. (<term>Winā'lag'ilis</term> says:) I did not turn my face backward to look at those who were bothering me when I went to make war on you, friend.

> 3. Throw your power that is killing everyone, throw your fire of death, throw what makes them turn their faces downward, throw it against those who went to make war upon you.
> 4. I surpass them; they are the lowest in the whole world.
> 5. I pulled them into my canoe to be my slaves, so that they may bail out the war canoe.<note>This song is a modified version of an older song belonging to the Sī'sinLaē of the Kwakiutl. It was adapted when the Nimkish invited the Kwakiutl to a feast and is directed against them. In this context, references to war refer only to the rivalry in the distribution of property (potlatches), and the song suggests that the Kwakiutl are superior to the Nimkish. The dancer is called "friend" because he had not yet received his new name when the song was first performed. In line 3, "makes them turn their faces downward" means the Nimkish are lying flat on the ground while the Kwakiutl step over their backs. Line 4, "the lowest of the whole world," again refers to the Nimkish, exaggerating their inferiority.</note>

Another <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> will take a stick, a lance, or a paddle and, after conjuring up the <term>sī'siuL</term>, split it in two. This is done with a smaller carving consisting of two parts that can be separated and joined again by using strings. A <term>sī'siuL</term> of this kind was collected by Mr. Hunt for the Anthropological Department of the World's Columbian Exposition and is now in the Field Columbian Museum. Its song, which is four generations old, is as follows:<note>Appendix, page 716.</note>

> 1. I have been on the other side of the world, I, the great supernatural being.
> 2. There I obtained all the supernatural power.
> 3. I bring with me all the supernatural power.

Still other <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> will conjure up a small <term>sī'siuL</term>, which flies through the air like that of the <term>mā'maq'a</term>. At other times, the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> will succeed in bringing the <term>sī'siuL</term> up just far enough for its horns to show. She tries to grasp it and it takes her down to the underworld. Then her friends try to hold her, but she disappears. Her attendant, who holds on to her, sinks into the ground with his forearms and seems to

Still other <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> invite the people to kill them. The dancer says "hup, hup," moving the edge of her palm along her throat, meaning, "Cut my neck!" or she moves the tips of the fingers of both hands down her stomach, meaning "Open my belly!" or she moves them along her head, shoulders, or other parts of her body. Finally, she is placed on a seat behind the fire, and one of her attendants complies with her request. He appears to drive a wedge through her head from one temple to the other. The wedge is first shown to the people and then secretly exchanged for another one, which consists of two parts attached to a wooden band that is slipped over her head and covered with hair. A pair of seal's eyes are hidden in her hair and lowered over her own eyes when the wedge is driven in, so that it looks as though her eyes were coming out of their sockets. Then she rises and walks around the fire to show the wedge sticking in her head. After one circuit, she is seated again, the wedge is removed, and she is healthy and sound. On other occasions, the head or shoulder is struck with a paddle which seems to split it; when withdrawn, it leaves a bloody line that looks like a wound. In this case, the paddle is secretly exchanged for another one which is notched so as to fit her head or shoulder. She walks around the fire showing it, and then it is removed.

Other <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> request their attendants to kill them with a spear.

In some dances, the dancer’s head is cut off, and the person who performs the decapitation displays a carved human head with a deathly expression, which he holds by its hair. These heads are portraits of the dancer, as accurate as the carver's skill allows (figs. 153, 154, pp. 503, 504).

<image-desc>Fig. 137. Two side-profile drawings of wooden masks representing a wasp dancer. The masks have stylized eyes and pointed, beak-like snouts.</image-desc>
->Fig. 137.<-
->MASKS OF WASP DANCER.<-
->Height, 6 1/4 inches; blue, black, red.<-
->IV A, Nos. 422 and 423, Royal Ethnographical Museum,<-
->Berlin. Collected by A. Jacobsen.<-

Sometimes the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> is burned. A box with a double bottom is prepared for this performance. The dancer lies flat at the back of the house, and the box is placed on its side so that she may be pushed into it from behind. A pit is dug at the spot where she lies; she hides in it while being concealed from the audience’s view by the box standing in front of her. After the pit has been covered again, the box is lifted, closed, and thrown into the fire. Before the box is brought in, a skeleton is placed between its two bottoms. While the box burns, the dancer’s song is heard coming from the fire. A speaking tube made of kelp runs under the floor from the pit where she hides to the fireplace, and she sings through it. When the fire has died out, charred bones are found in the ashes. They are collected and laid on a new mat, and for four days the people sing over them. The mat is positioned so that it lies over the opening of another speaking tube. The <term>shaman</term> attempts to resuscitate her, and after four days, a voice is heard coming from the bones. Then they are covered with a mat. The woman crawls up from a ditch, where the bones are thrown while she takes their place. She begins to move, and when the mat is removed, she is seen to have returned to life. In many of these dances, after the performer has been "killed," the <term>d'E'ntsiq</term> (Plate 39 and fig. 155)<note>Page 506.</note> emerges from underground. It consists of a series of flat, carved boards joined on their narrow sides by plugs that pass through spruce root rings or through tubes carved from cedar. The joints are somewhat loose, so that the entire structure can be given an undulating motion forward and backward. It has two

Other <term>t'ō'X'uît</term>, instead of conjuring the <term>sī'siuL</term>, bring up the <term>nō'nLEmg·ila</term> (making foolish) (figs. 156–158),<note>Pages 501–509.</note> a small human figure with a movable head and arms. It dances about, and then one or two birds are seen to fly down from the roof and alight on its head. In fig. 158, the bird is seen sitting on the figure's head. Fig. 159 represents a bird which is let down by means of strings, at the same time flapping its leather wings. Often the bird takes hold of the figure's head and carries it away, only to return it after a while. The face of the <term>nō'nLEmg·ila</term> is always painted in the same manner. It is white, and two black lines, onto which mica is glued, run downward from the eyes. The head is decorated with tufts of human hair. The figure is also operated from underground. In some dances, only the head of the <term>nō'nLEmg·ila</term> is used (fig. 160, p. 510). It is worn by a dancer who wraps a blanket over his head and carries the head in front of his stomach.

The <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> is supposed to be able to make every object he touches rattle. A stone, a staff, a pipe, etc., is handed to him by any member of the audience, and, when he shakes it, it rattles. He wears a small rattle concealed under his hemlock bracelet, which produces this sound.

The <term>La'Lasiqoala</term> call the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> <term>ō'lala</term>, and have special names for the various performances. They use ornaments of red cedar bark. The ring of the <term>ō'lala</term> is shown in fig. 161 (p. 510). The <term>ō'lala</term>, when returning from the woods, has many bloody lines on his cheek, "the rubbing of <term>Wīnā'lag·ilîs</term>’s canoe." Four horizontal lines run over each cheek, nearly reaching the nose. Above them is one line just under the eyes crossing the bridge of the nose, and two short vertical lines run down the temples outside the eyes. Another painting of the <term>ō'lala</term> consists of one pair of parallel black lines running from one cheek over the upper part of the bridge of the nose to the other cheek, and of a pair running horizontally across the middle of the forehead. Following is one of the <term>ō'lala</term>'s songs:<note>Appendix, page 716.</note>

> 1. (<term>Ō'lala</term> sings:) The world knows that I have reached the dancing pole of our world.
> 2. (The people sing:) Hold upright the great post in the middle of the world.
> 3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You who hold up the world.
> 4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You keep the sky from falling down like a foundation built of interlocking logs.

The last of the dances, the origin of which is attributed to <term>Wīnā'lag·ilis</term>, is the <term>hawī'nalaL</term>, the war dance. The legend of this dance belongs to the clan <term>Maam'tag·ila</term>. In the beginning of the world, there was a man named <term>Wi'naXwīnag·im</term>, who was a great warrior. He wanted to go on war expeditions all the time. The people who desired peace tied him with strong ropes. He, however, broke them without difficulty. He held a knife in his hands, the handle of which represented the <term>sī'siuL</term>, and ran out of the house and killed everyone who set foot in the street. The blood ran in streams down to the water. The people finally took hold of him again, cut holes through his thighs and through his back, and pulled ropes through them. Thus they hung him from the beam of the house and began to sing songs which they hoped would appease him. While he was swinging from the beam, he still held his knife; and as he could not cut anyone else, he cut his own head. His wounds did not hurt him; on the

The performance of the <term>hawī'nalaL</term> is a repetition of the deeds of this man. When he is being initiated, he fasts in the woods until he grows very thin. When he returns, he wears ornaments of hemlock branches. Small, thin slabs of wood carved in the shape of paddles (fig. 165, p. 513) are sewn along his arms and legs, across his chest, and down his sides. Then, a rope of red cedar bark is stretched from the roof of the dancing house to the beach. No one is allowed to go under it, and no canoe may pass in front of it. If a canoe should violate this law, it is seized, carried into the house, and hung from the beams, where it remains for four days. When

Two horizontal rectangular illustrations stacked vertically, depicting traditional Northwest Coast Indigenous artwork (specifically Kwakwaka'wakw style). Both panels are set against a background of vertical lines representing wooden planks.

The top panel features two primary figures. On the left is a stylized humanoid figure in a splayed, front-facing position, showing anatomical details such as ribs and joints. Here is a song of the <term>hawī'nalaL</term>:

1. They tried to hang me and to kill me in war.
2. But the water where they tried to kill me only turned into curdled blood.

I also give (figs. 170, 171, p. 516) the mask of the earthquake dancer (<term>Xoā'ēxoē</term>). He wears a rattle consisting of a ring on which perforated shells are strung (fig. 172, p. 516). His dance is believed to shake the ground and to be a certain means of bringing back the <term>hā'mats'a</term> who is being initiated.

I will add here a song of a mask in regard to which I have not been able to obtain any definite information. It is called <term>Hai'alik'îmL</term> and belonged originally to the <term>G·ē'xsEm</term> of the <term>Naqô'mg·ilisala</term>, whose ancestor, <term>Hē'lig·ilig·ala</term>, it is said to represent. The dancer is initiated in the house. In his first and third dances he wears ornaments of red cedar bark which have a horn on each side, one behind, and a flat crosspiece in front. In his second and fourth dances he wears a curious mask.

After the mask has disappeared, the people sing:<note>See Appendix, page 717.</note>

1. Everybody goes to him to obtain dances.
2. In the beginning the never-stopping one spread his wings over your head.<note>The "never-stopping one" refers to <term>Winā'lag·ilis</term>.</note>

<meta>This page continues the list of ceremonial dances and societies, detailing the specific hierarchy and organizational structure of the winter ceremonial (ts'ē'ts'aēqa) among various Kwakiutl-speaking tribes.</meta>

The <term>Ts'ā'watEēnôx</term>, <term>Guau'aēnôx</term>, <term>Haxuā'mîs</term>, <term>T'Ena'xtax</term>, and <term>A'waiLEla</term> follow this order, as far as I have been able to learn:

1. <term>Mā'maq'a</term>.
2. <term>Hā'mats'a</term>.
3. <term>Hai'aq'antELaL</term> (<gloss>speaker dance</gloss>).
4. <term>Hawē'xaqulaL</term>, who persuades chiefs to destroy property, coppers, and other valuables.
5. <term>Walas'axā'aL</term>.
6. <term>Hauā'iadalaL</term> (a <gloss>fool dance</gloss>).

Among the <term>Koskimo</term>, <term>G·ō'p'ēnôx</term>, <term>L'ā'sq'ēnôx</term>, and <term>Gua'ts'ēnôx</term>, the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> is first in rank. Next is the <term>mā'maq'a</term>, followed by the <term>hā'mats'a</term>.

The <term>La'Lasiqoala</term>, <term>Naqô'mg·ilisala</term>, <term>Nā'qoaqtôq</term>, and <term>Goasi'la</term> do not include all the dances listed above in the winter ceremonial (<term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term>). A large number, particularly the fool dancers, the <term>hawī'nalaL</term>, and all the animals, are included in a ceremonial called <term>nō'nLEM</term>, which is neither <term>bā'xus</term> (<gloss>secular or non-sacred</gloss>) nor sacred. Songs belonging to both seasons are used in this ceremonial. I will discuss this ceremonial more fully later on (Chapter XII, page 621). Consequently, the number of members of the <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term> is small. They are arranged in the following order, beginning with the highest:

1. <term>Mā'maq'a</term>.
2. <term>Hā'mats'a</term>.
3. <term>Ha'mtsetsōē</term>. This is a <term>hā'mats'a</term> who is not taken away by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē</term>, but only dreams of him. Consequently, his initiation is performed in the house. He has neither the <term>hā'mats'a</term> cry (*hāp*) nor the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term> cry (*hwîp*). His song has words only. His badges are like those of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>.
4. <term>Ts'ē'kois</term>.
5. <term>Ts'ē'koa'tâ</term>.
6. <term>H·ai'alik'auaē</term>.
7. <term>Ō'lala</term> (corresponding to the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term>).
8. <term>Lolō'LalaL</term>.
9. <term>YiaiatalaL</term>, or <term>Q'ō'minōqisaL</term>.
10. <term>Pa'xalalaL</term>, <gloss>shaman dance</gloss>.
11. <term>Wā'tanEm</term>. These are the novices who have just entered the <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term>. After the <term>hā'mats'a</term> has been initiated four times, he is <term>wā'tanEm</term>—meaning he is "pulled out" of the dancing house. He becomes a <term>quē'qutsa</term>. During this transitional period, he is <term>wālawē</term>, that is, <term>wā'tanEm</term> in a transitional stage. When a <term>bā'xus</term> offends the <term>q'ā'q'anas</term> (which include the above dancers), he is made <term>wā'tanEm</term>. He dances in four houses and becomes a novice. The following year, he will be initiated into one of the higher societies.

## IX. THE WINTER CEREMONIAL OF THE KWAKIUTL.

I can now describe the ceremonial at which all these dancers perform their ceremonies. Generally, it is connected with the refund of the purchase money for a wife, the <term>qautē'x·a</term>, as described on page 421.

I will first describe the great ceremonial, which is the same for all the <term>laxsâ</term>, but most elaborate for the initiation of a <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The whole

The ceremonial is in the charge of a master of ceremonies, whose ceremonial names are <term>Nū'xnēmîs</term> and <term>LE'mwala</term>, while his secular name is <term>Ō'mx·'it</term>; the winter name of his speaker is <term>Hō'LElitē</term>. A number of other officers will be described throughout this chapter. All these officers and their titles originate from a myth telling how the animals held their first winter ceremonial. I shall relate that myth later on (page 538). Plate 42 represents the current master of ceremonies and his speaker.

<image-desc>Fig. 148. A woven head ring for a Ghost Dancer. It features three tall, feather-like cedar bark plumes standing upright from a thick woven ring, with shredded cedar bark fringe hanging down.</image-desc>
->Fig. 148.<-
->HEAD RING OF GHOST DANCER.<-
->La'Lasiqoala.<-
->IV A, No. 6874, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by F. Boas.<-

At the time of marriage, the bride's father promises to transfer his membership in one of the secret societies to one of his son-in-law's children. When a son of the latter has reached the age of 10 or 12 years, or even earlier, he is initiated into one of the lower secret societies, through which he must pass before he can become a member of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> society. 

<image-desc>Fig. 149. Two ceremonial items: a carved wooden club with a face and bark attachments, and a thick woven neck ring with a large decorative bundle and hanging shredded bark fringe.</image-desc>
->Fig. 149.<-
->CLUB AND NECK RING OF ME'ILA.<-
->From a sketch made at the World's Columbian Exposition.<-

As soon as he is entitled to become a member of this society, his father invites the three principal chiefs of the tribe to his house and informs them that he wants his father-in-law to make his son a member of the secret society. The celebration of this event is exceedingly expensive, and for this reason, the three chiefs investigate the debts and the property of the man and of his father-in-law, in order to make sure that they can meet the expenses associated with the ceremonies. If they find the amount of property is sufficient, they give permission for the celebration of the festival. In this case, they order the father to invite all the chiefs of the tribe to meet on the fourth day. When they assemble, the three head chiefs inform the young chiefs of the plan, and the latter give their consent.

At this meeting, the man who hosts the dance notifies his father-in-law that he wants the blankets which he paid for his wife returned, and that he wants to receive the box containing his father-in-law's dance.
