<keywords>Nū'xnēmîs, LE'mwala, Ō'mx·'it, Hō'LElitē, hā'mats'a, winter ceremonial, secret societies, initiation, tribal chiefs, marriage debt</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the description of the preparations for the Kwakiutl winter ceremonial, specifically detailing the formal invitation of the tribe and the symbolic transfer of wealth from a father-in-law to his son-in-law's child through a ceremonial pole.</meta>

# 502 REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

Then the chiefs order the man to invite the whole tribe to a meeting which is to be held four days later. The three head chiefs inform the tribe, in a speech made in a low voice, of their intention to hold a winter dance, and the young chiefs request everyone to prepare themselves for this festival. In particular, they are asked to clean themselves and to refrain from sexual relations with women, as the spirit <term>Wīnā'lag·ilis</term>, who has his home in the north but dwells among the Indians during the dancing season, dislikes people who are unclean or those who have had sexual relations. The young man who is going to host the winter ceremonial is called the <term>yē'-wix·ila</term>.

<columns>2</columns>
<image-desc>Two carved wooden clappers shown from the side. Each has a paddle-shaped striking end decorated with Northwest Coast style ovoid and U-form carvings, narrowing to a textured handle.
->Fig. 150.<-
->CLAPPER OF MĒ'ILA.<-
->Length, 9 1/8 inches.<-
->IV A, No. 1005, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by A. Jacobsen.<-</image-desc>
<column-break/>
At this meeting, the father-in-law calls one of his speakers, who must step into the middle of the house, holding a pole that is from 6 to 8 feet long. It is called the <term>winter-dance pole</term>.
<column-break/>

The speaker delivers a speech in which he outlines the amount of property represented by the pole and announces the father-in-law's intention to give it to the young man. He asks the latter to step up to the pole and touch it as a sign of acceptance. The whole assembly joins in this demand, and the young man, accompanied by a chief—who is paid for this service later on—steps up to the pole. The chief who speaks for the young man asks the father-in-law what the pole represents, and the latter's speaker explains once more the amount of property, such as blankets, copper bracelets, food, and grease, which is to be used in the dance.

<image-desc>Two ceremonial head rings made of woven or braided cedar bark fiber. They are circular and bulky with multiple fibrous tassels or ends protruding from the top.
->Fig. 151.<-
->HEAD RINGS OF MĀ'MAQ'A OF THE LA'LASIQOALA.<-
->IV A, No. 6864, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by F. Boas.<-</image-desc>

Then the chief representing the young man takes the pole, places it over his shoulder, and runs around the fire, stooping and shouting, "Whoo! whoo! whoo!" The meaning of this action is that the weight of the property represented by the pole is too heavy for him to carry. Then he sings the following song: <note>Appendix, page 718.</note>

> The Spirit of the Winter Dance came down,
> The Spirit of the Winter Dance came down and stays here with me.

Then the master of the ceremonies rises and orders everyone to bathe early in the morning for four days before the crows begin to cry.

and thus to prepare to meet Wīnā'lag·ilīs.

At this time the winter-dance whistles are heard for the first time. These whistles represent the voices of the spirits of the winter dance. When first heard, they appear to be far away from the house in a northerly direction. The

->Fig. 152.<-
->NECK RING OF MĀ'MAQ'A.<-
->Lā'Lasiqoala.<-
->IV A, No. 6865, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin. Collected by F. Boas.<-

second time they come nearer the house, and thus they are heard four times, getting closer and closer. This indicates that the spirit is approaching the village from the north. Finally, the whistles of the spirit of the cannibal society are heard near the house. Then the sound is heard on the roof and moves around it four times. At this time the son of the man who hosts the festival suddenly disappears (<term>x·is'ē't</term>), and a few minutes later he is heard to cry in the woods "hāp, hāp, hāp," the sound which is attributed to the cannibal spirit <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. The master of ceremonies asks the people if they know the meaning of all this, and another chief replies that <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> has taken the young man to his house to initiate him into the cannibal ceremonies.

To this the master of ceremonies replies that in four days the people are to assemble again to receive the ornaments of cedar bark. He asks them to sing their summer songs during this time, to use their summer names, and to make merry, because as soon as the four days are over, they will be forbidden to use their summer names or to sing their summer songs. following morning when the crows begin to cry, everyone, young and old, takes a bath in the sea. They rub their bodies with hemlock branches in order to clean themselves in preparation for the arrival of the spirit <term>Wīnā'lag·ilīs</term>. On the evening of the third day, the master of ceremonies distributes plain head ornaments and neck rings of cedar bark among twelve messengers, who must blacken their faces and go to the houses of the people to invite them to the meeting to be held the following day. They receive in payment a button blanket from the master of ceremonies, which is not returned. Their positions are not hereditary. People who have good voices are selected to act as messengers. They carry staffs in their hands about 8 feet long.

<meta>This page continues the description of the preparations for the Kwakiutl winter ceremonial, following the invitation for the people to assemble and the transition from summer names to winter names.</meta>

<page-num>504</page-num>
<header>REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1893.</header>

When they come to a house, they open the door and invite the people, the women first, with one of the residents of the house prompting the speaker. When they call the names, they stand in the doorway and strike the threshold with their staffs.¹ After the women, the hā'mats'a is called, followed by the other men, and the que'quts'a last. Then the speaker for these twelve men says,² "Is that all?" The people reply,³ "That is all." Then they call a specific relative of the master of ceremonies named Ts'īx·ā'xtōlsE'lās.⁴ All the property distributed by the master of ceremonies is given in honor of this relative, who consequently is of high rank. He or she receives this name anew every year. After the messengers have called the people by their winter names, they are not allowed to use their summer names again until the ceremonies are ended.

<image-desc>Figure 154: A line drawing of a carved wooden head with long, wavy hair and closed eyes, depicting a serene or sleeping face. The carving is used in the T'ō'xuīt dance.</image-desc>

->Fig. 154.<-
->CARVED HEAD USED IN THE T'Ō'XUĪT DANCE.<-
->Height, 11 inches.<-
->IV A, No. 1249, Royal Ethnographical Museum, Berlin.<-
->Collected by A. Jacobsen.<-

By this time, the people begin to arrange themselves into groups, which are divided according to sex and age. These groups take the place of the clans, as previously described.

On the following morning before daylight, the same twelve men visit every house and call out to everyone: "Do not sleep! Go and bathe in the sea. We are walking around again to call you."⁵ The people rise and immediately plunge into the sea to cleanse themselves for the qap'ēk', or assembly, which is the formal beginning of the winter ceremonial.

Then they go to the house of the master of ceremonies, which is called the assembly house.⁶ The house has been prepared for this purpose. A heavy cedar plank has been laid along the rear wall of the house, and another one along each side. These are used for beating time. The doorway is surrounded by a ring of hemlock branches covered with eagle down, so that everyone who enters the house must pass through it. When passing through it, the people turn to the left, step through it with the right foot first, and then turn again.

The members of the seal society⁷ do not enter the house, but instead assemble in another building. During this day, the people sing and celebrate until after dark. Then the master of ceremonies rises and calls four officers to go and invite the seal society. These offices are hereditary, and the men who perform the ceremonies hold specific names which

belong to the offices: X·i'x·iqala, of the Gue'tela tribe; Q'ē'q'aqaualas, of the Walas Kwakiutl tribe; Lôxsâ', of the Hā'ialik·auaē clan; and Ā'Lō'lSela, of the Q'ō'moyuē tribe. The last is their leader. They are called pä'paxamē (head paxalas). One of these men must be a <term>paxala</term> (shaman). When starting, each takes a round rattle. They blacken their faces, put on their head rings and neck rings of red cedar bark, and cover their heads with eagle down. Then their speaker, Ā'Lō'lSela, says, "We are going to fetch our friends."¹ Then they go around the fire four times, singing as follows:²

> O friend, O friend, O supernatural friend (meaning Winā'lag·ilīs).

Then they go to the house in which the seal society is waiting for them. Meanwhile, the master of ceremonies calls up four other officers to invite the highest members of the seal society, the hā'mats'as. These offices are also hereditary. The names of the officers are: K·ā'qauLēE, of the Kue'xa tribe; Mē'goatExstāla, of the same tribe; K·ēx·, of the Maa'mtag·ila clan; and Nā'wulqalag·ilīs, of the Kue'xa tribe. The first three names are quē'qutsa names, and the last is a ha'mshamts'ES name. He is the leader of these four messengers. They are also called pä'paxamē (head paxala), and there must be one <term>paxala</term> (shaman) among them.

The master of ceremonies gives them tallow. The ha'mshamts'ES puts some of it into his mouth, chews it, and then rubs it all over his face, while the others simply rub it on their faces without chewing. Each is also given a cedar bark ring, charcoal, feathers, and a round rattle. They all wear quē'qutsa rings. After they have received the ornaments, they say, "We will go and fetch our great friends."³ They walk four times around the fire, singing:⁴

> You said, Winā'lag·ilīs, that I should capsize in rough weather. Your friend stayed here long in my canoe near the beach. You said that I should capsize in rough weather, but your friend capsized while sleeping during the rough weather.⁵

Then they walk around the fire and go on their errand. After about fifteen minutes, the eight men who were sent to fetch the seal society and the hā'mats'as return, and Ā'Lō'lSela sings:⁶

> BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē told me about the great supernatural means of killing people with my teeth.

<meta>This page continues the description of the messengers who summon the seal society and the hā'mats'as, following the ritual procedures for their entrance into the ceremonial house.</meta>

The four men who went to fetch the seal society enter first. Those who went to fetch the hā'mats'as follow them. Before they enter, the people who are assembled in the house clear their throats, as they are not allowed to cough or laugh after the seal society has entered. When the messengers enter, Ā'Lo'lsela says, “Our friends are coming.”¹

<image-desc>A detailed vertical illustration of a ceremonial carved board or totem pole (identified as Fig. 155, a D'entsiq). It features a stack of traditional Northwest Coast indigenous motifs. Now Nāwulqa'lag·ilis says, “Take care, our great friends are coming.”²

Then the four men who called the seals sit down in the front left-hand corner of the house, and the others in the front right-hand corner. Now everyone looks at the door where the fool dancers (nōō'nLEMALA) enter first. They strike the door with their swords or lances, open it, and stand in the doorway. Their faces are blackened, and they wear torn and soiled clothing. Their heads are strewn with eagle down. If anyone laughs or coughs, the fool dancer steps up to them and threatens them with his sword or lance. Then the fool dancers turn one by one, go to the right around the fire, and sit down in their seats. Their places are at both ends of the seal society’s seats, as they are the guards of the society. Then all the other members of the society enter, each group by themselves, and each dressed in their proper ornaments of red cedar bark. They stand in the doorway for a short time and then go to their places, turning to the right and moving around the fire. The hā'mats'as are the last to enter. They are preceded by the grizzly bear dancers, whose faces are blackened. They wear blankets and bear claws on their hands. If there happens to be an odd number of these, one of their number goes to the rear of the house. The others remain at the door and look around at the assembly. Then they divide into two parts, forming two rows, one on each side of the door. Now the hā'mats'as enter and pass between the two rows of bear dancers, which close behind them. The hā'mats'as step up to the fire and, standing side by side, face the rear of the house. They stand there for about ten minutes, during which time no one is allowed to move. Then the master of ceremonies rises and makes a speech in a very low voice, in which he warns the people to be careful and not to offend the hā'mats'as. The latter turn to the right and walk slowly to the rear

of the house, holding their blankets in a fold over their arms, which are held at some distance from their chest. If anyone coughs after the hā'mats'as have entered, the bear steps up to him and threatens him. The offender must give a feast to the seal society; sometimes also to the quē'qutsa. The hā'mats'as sit down in the middle of the rear of the house. Next to them on both sides sit the bear dancers; next to these the other groups of the seal society. Then the master of ceremonies asks the four messengers who went to invite the members of the lower grades of the seal society to fetch tallow and white cedar bark. The four men rise together and Ā'Lō'lsEla says: "We go to lift our grandfather from the floor."¹

All the ceremonial objects which are acquired by inheritance are called "grandfather." They are kept in four boxes in the right-hand front corner of the house. When the men lift them, the ts'ā'eqa spirits enter them, making them hungry. This is expressed in their song, which they sing while walking around the fire and carrying the boxes containing the tallow and cedar bark:²

->This is what makes us confused.<-

They carry these boxes four times around the fire and then stop in front of the hā'mats'as, to whom they give some tallow and cedar bark. They continue to distribute it, two men going to the right and two going to the left until they meet at the door.

Then the master of ceremonies calls the same messenger who went to fetch the hā'mats'as: "Come, friends, and lift from the floor your grandfather."³

They rise, walk around the fire four times, and, standing close to the door, the speaker says, "We are going, friends, to lift our grandfather,"⁴ which means in this case the drum. Then they turn to the right and walk out of the house. After about ten minutes, they are heard to return singing, and enter holding each one corner of the drum. They sing:⁵

> BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē said he would make me go through his own house.

They remain standing near the doorway, then turn to the right and go four times around the fire, and put down the drum. As soon as they do so, the small (<term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term>) winter dance whistles are heard blowing. The men say, "That is a good sign for us, friends."<sup>1</sup>

The master of ceremonies next calls the four men who summoned the seal society, saying, "Come, friends, go and fetch our batons."<sup>2</sup> They do not reply, but begin to sing their secret song, circling the fire four times and swinging their rattles:<sup>3</sup>

->I am the only one who owns the winter dance.<-

They walk out of the house and continue to sing until they come back, carrying the batons on their left arms. They go around the fire and lay the batons down in front of the people, beginning with the <term>hā'-mats'as</term>, and continuing on both sides until they reach those who sit nearest the door.

Then the master of ceremonies calls upon the four men who fetched the <term>hā'-mats'as</term>, saying, "Come, friends, take up our red cedar bark here."<sup>4</sup> They rise, and their speaker replies in a low voice, "Now I am going to take up this red cedar bark, your great real friend."<sup>5</sup> They all sing together:<sup>6</sup>

> BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē made me a winter dancer.
> BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē made me pure.
> I do not destroy life, I am the life maker.<sup>7</sup>

Then they walk out singing, and come back singing the same song and carrying the red cedar bark under their left arms. They bring it in a long bundle, about 12 feet in length and more than a foot thick. One man carries it in front, two in the middle, and one at the end. They carry their rattles in their right hands. He gives slow downward jerks with his round rattle, saying "ōp" with each movement and stooping toward the floor. This is the song of Hai'alik·auaē, the first shaman. Thus, he goes around the fire once, and then he sings his secret song:<note>See Appendix, page 723.</note>

> 1. My mind is not strong enough (to lift it).
> 2. My mind is afraid of it.<note>This refers to the cedar bark ornaments, which hold the power of the winter ceremony.</note>
> 3. I have seen the winter ceremonial.

After he has finished his song, Nā'wulqalag·ilis reaches his hand backward, and someone places a knife into it without being noticed. He gives this to the master of ceremonies, who steps up to the four men holding the cedar bark. Three times he pretends to cut it, and after each feigned cut, he makes one turn to the left. The fourth time he actually cuts through it, and at the same time, the sound of whistles is heard coming from the cedar bark.

After it is cut, the master of ceremonies distributes it, giving the <term>hā'mats'as</term> their portion first, then to the other members of the seal society, and finally to the <term>quē'qutsa</term>.

He then calls to the men who brought the members of the seal society, "Bring us our down, friends."<note>G·ā'xlax·ins qa'mxualāēns nēnēmō'k^u.</note> They then bring the dishes, with each man carrying one dish. Then he sends them in the same way to bring the tallow. After he has received all the dishes, he calls up the four men again and sends them to all the people gathered in the house to ask if anyone wishes to join in the celebration of the winter dance—that is to say, if there is another man ready to act as <term>yē'wix·ila</term> during the same ceremony. He asks, "Who is the one to whom the seal society will go?"<note>A'nguēla ä'ita lawultsāneMla'sa lē laēnēnōk^u.</note>

To return to the <term>qap'ē'k<sup>u</sup></term>. The master of ceremonies takes one of the dishes with feathers and, singing his secret song—

> 1. My mind is not strong enough,
> 2. My mind is afraid of it,
> 3. I have seen the winter ceremonial,¹—

goes around the fire four times, followed by the four men who carry the dishes with down. At the back and the front of the fire, they all turn once. Then the master of ceremonies returns the dish to the four men and orders them to distribute the feathers: "Go and feather our great friends."²

The men begin again with the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and place feathers on the heads of the people, beginning in the middle and proceeding toward both ends. Then they distribute tallow and batons in the same way.

Now the master of ceremonies puts on his head ring, which consists of a flat strip of cedar bark to which a long trail of the same material is attached. Again, he sings his secret song and goes around the fire four times, swinging the rattle, which he holds at approximately the height of his head. During this song, the people bow their heads and move in their seats to find a comfortable position. They hold their batons ready for use. After the master of ceremonies has gone around the fire four times, he stops in front of the <term>hā'mats'as</term> and says "wai, wai," while thrusting his rattle forward. At this signal, the people look up and begin to beat the boards for about ten minutes, during which time the master of ceremonies shakes his rattle.

Then he swings the rattle in a wide circle, giving a signal for the people to stop. During the following minutes, not a sound is heard except from the <term>shamans</term>, who utter the sound "h, h" from deep in their throats from time to time. This means that they are watching to see if the people make a mistake or break any of the rules. After about ten minutes, the master of ceremonies gives a new signal for the people to beat the boards. After ten minutes more, they stop again. Then everyone

After this, the master of ceremonies gives another signal and all the men begin to beat the boards again as hard as possible, and at the same time, the <term>bear dancers</term> utter their cries. The <term>fool dancers</term> are heard to cry "wai! hai! hai!" while throwing stones and swinging their swords and lances. The master of ceremonies gives a new signal, and all the people stop beating the boards at once. Then the <term>bear dancers</term> and <term>fool dancers</term> look down, and all the <term>que'qutsa</term> sing their own secret songs again. When the master of ceremonies gives the fourth signal for beating the boards, the whistles of the <term>hā'mats'as</term> are heard in the house. Then

<image-desc>A vertical illustration of a ceremonial object, identified as Fig. 164. WEAPON OF Ā'MLALA. The object features a handle and a head composed of radiating, star-like points. Below the title, it says "From a sketch made at the World's Columbian Exposition."</image-desc>

The people reply, "Come, friend, no one is stronger in supernatural power than you are."² Then all the other men say one after the other, "Let us go on the floor and beat time."³ Then they all (men, women, and children) get ready to sing the old song which is supposed to drive the spirits away. They cry "ye heee hu hu hu ye heee!" This is the song of the wolf. After this song, the master of ceremonies says: "That is wrong."⁴ Now they utter the bear's cry: "Hamama ma ma, hamamai." Again he says, "That is wrong." The people next utter <term>Hai'alik·auaē's</term> sound, "wô ip kf wô-ip kf wô-ip" (kf blown upward). They continue this for about five minutes. The whistles continue blowing, and the master of ceremonies says again: "That is wrong! That is wrong! Let us sing another song." Now they sing "wōi, wōi, wōi," which is also <term>Hai'alik·auaē's</term> song. After this song, the whistles stop, and at the order of the master of ceremonies, they sing the first song of the winter dance:⁵

->Wō, wō, ai, a, ai, really tormenting, ai, ai really tormenting.<-

Just before the end, the master of ceremonies joins the chorus, crying "ō hu," and all the people shout "wā!" hitting the boards together, which is believed to be a means of driving away the spirits. This song is sung four times. Then the speaker of the second <term>yē'wix·ila</term> says: "Friends, be happy. I received the name ——— from the supernatural being."⁶

Then all the people reply: "You received your great name from the supernatural being."⁷ After this, the speaker continues, saying that the people should be glad to hear the old songs and to have seen the

<image-desc>Fig. 170. A black and white drawing of an ornate wooden mask (Mask of Noā'ēxoē). The mask features a primary face with a wide mouth and large eyes, with several smaller carved faces or humanoid figures integrated into the sides and top of the headpiece.</image-desc>

The bears wear head rings of red and white cedar bark. Their faces are painted black, showing an enormous mouth set with teeth that stretches from ear to ear. They have bear claws on their hands. The fool dancers have their faces blackened all over. They wear red cedar bark, and their clothing is ragged and torn.

Now the people say, "Let us drive them out!" <note>Wai'g'a x'ins k'ā'yuwulsōq. Let us drive them out.</note> As soon as they try to do so, the *hā'mats'as* jump down from the roof and drive the people before them. The bears and fool dancers get excited at the same time and finally drive the people out of the house and down to the beach. The *hā'mats'as*, bears, and fool dancers pursue them. At last, they drive them into the sea and keep them standing in the water until they promise them the best food they have in their houses. Then the seal society returns to the *lō'bEk* <note>G·īlq'asāmas laxa hā'mats'a.</note> or the house of the first *yē'wix·ila*, while the *quē'qutsa* enter the house of the second *yē'wix·ila*.

Here the men take their seats according to the societies to which they belong. When they are giving a feast here, they send four dishes of each course to the *hā'mats'a*. This is called "making the *hā'mats'a* eat first." <note>G·īlq'asāmas laxa hā'mats'a.</note> The food is carried to the *hā'mats'a* by four messengers known as *qoē'tsē'sta*; this means people who were seals and are trying to become *quē'qutsa*. They alone are allowed to enter the *lō'bEk*.

If in any of these speeches a man should use a <term>bā'xus</term> (profane) name of a person, all the people cry out at once, and he must sit down. He may even be punished by the fool dancers.

The promised feast is given in the evening. The host sends the <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term> to call the people to come to his house on the following morning. They rise early and go as a group from house to house calling everybody until all the people are assembled in the house of the second <term>yē'wix·ila</term>. The host sends the same four messengers with four dishes of each course to the seal society or <term>ts'ā'ts'aqamtsEn</term> (that is, the <term>ts'ē'ts'aeqa</term> people), and the people ask him to send them quickly so that everyone may get their food.² The host sends four of the Koskimo with the food.

meal until they have learned that the <term>hā'mats'as</term> have eaten. Throughout the entire dancing season, this rule must be followed.

During all this time, the father-in-law of the first <term>yē'wix·ila</term> has been gathering all his property—principally food, blankets, boxes, dishes, spoons, kettles, bracelets, coppers, and box lids—in order to refund (<term>qautē'x·a</term>) to his son-in-law the amount promised at the marriage of his daughter (see p. 421).

When he assembles his clan to announce his plans, the members of the seal society must not come. This is the only time when the clans are recognized during the winter season. He informs the people what amount of property he is going to give to his son-in-law, what names the son-in-law is going to have, and how many songs he has had composed for him.

<image-desc>A ceremonial neck ring (Fig. 175) made of thick, braided or twisted red cedar bark. The ring is circular with four distinct protrusions or "crosspieces" extending outwards. These crosspieces are also made of twisted cedar bark and end in frayed or tasseled tips. The caption identifies it as the first neck ring of Hai'alik'auaē and states that the four crosspieces represent the powers of the shaman.</image-desc>

The son-in-law assembles his clan in the dancing house (<term>lōbEk"</term>) and has them paint their faces with charcoal. Meanwhile, the canoe of <term>g·ī'sExstâla</term> is built, as described on page 422. All the speakers' staffs which are carried at the festival are decorated with red cedar bark. The dances that are performed all belong to the winter dance, though <term>hā'mats'a</term> songs are not used. When the daughter of the father-in-law dances, she is also dressed in red cedar bark ornaments. The description of the ceremony will be found at the place referred to above (p. 421).

After the full amount of property has been turned over to the son-in-law, the father-in-law calls the master of ceremonies and, pointing to the box containing the winter dance implements—masks, whistles, and ornaments of red cedar bark—he says, "Come, I am afraid of this box here; you are the only one who is not afraid of it, because you went through all the ceremonies of the winter dances."¹ To this the master of ceremonies, who carries a small cane, replies, "Let me go there. Yes, your word is good, friends."

"It is good that you say I am the highest among you."<sup>1</sup> With this, he lifts the box, hides it under his blanket, and begins to sing his secret song, as follows:<sup>2</sup>

->O friend, O friend, O supernatural friend.<-

Then he calls the son-in-law, saying, "Stand up; it may be that this box is intended for you."<sup>3</sup> The young man rises and replies, "Hold it for a while until I dress."<sup>4</sup> Then he goes to the house, and after a few minutes he returns without a blanket, his face blackened. He presents himself to the master of ceremonies: "Here I am, friend;"<sup>5</sup> who asks him once more to be ready: "Go on, get ready, son-in-law."<sup>6</sup> Then he gives him the winter names belonging to the contents of the boxes. He receives both the <term>mē'emqoat</term> name and also the <term>quē'qutsa</term> name. He asks him to step near.<sup>7</sup> The young man turns to the left and walks slowly down to the beach where the master of ceremonies is standing. The latter takes off his neck ring and, holding it, sings his secret song:

1. My mind is not strong enough (to lift it).
2. My mind is afraid of it.
3. I have seen the winter ceremonial.<sup>8</sup>

Then he turns around and gives the young man the neck ring to which the arm and leg rings are tied. He turns again and takes off his head ring. The young man's wife, who stands next to the master of ceremonies, gives her dancing apron to the latter, who turns once and puts it onto her husband. Last of all, he gives him the box. Then the master of ceremonies says "hōp ōp" four times. (This is the sound of <term>Hai'alik'auaē</term>). The master of ceremonies continues:<sup>9</sup>

"Wait a while, son-in-law, you have no name for your <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term>, but I have seen what carried away our son. Her name is ———." With this, he secretly puts a whistle into the hand of the son-in-law. The latter turns to the right and calls "h! h!" (deep from the throat).

He turns around to the left, stooping down, and walks in a zigzag way up to the house.

When he approaches the house, he cries "hāp! hāp!" and all the people of his clan gather the property which has been given to him and follow him. As soon as he cries "hāp hāp," his son (the <term>g·i'yakila</term>), who is in the woods, is heard to reply with the same sound. Now, four men of the <term>yē'wix·ila's</term> family go down to the square, carrying an axe, and split the box cover forming one corner of the square. This is called "**sinking the canoe**" (<term>tsō'kunsa</term>), and it means that the son-in-law must distribute among the tribe everything he has received from his father-in-law.

When the people reach the house, the son-in-law gives them some food and gives notice that in four days he intends to try to bring his son back from the woods.¹ The next three days are spent in feasting and dancing. In the evening of the third day, the young man calls all the people to go into the woods in order to make eight new songs for the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and two for the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term>, the servant of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The singing master and his assistants go into the woods early in the morning, while the <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term> go in the evening. The old chiefs go last and sit by themselves. They give orders to the <term>quē'qutsa</term>, telling them what they have to do during the festival when the <term>hā'mats'a</term> is expected to return.

While learning the songs, the people sit mixed together, not arranged according to the societies to which they belong. Those who have good voices sit near the singing master. They always select a certain clearing in the thicket for this purpose (Plate 43). No women are allowed there. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> and the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> who are in the woods listen

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

They listen unseen to the songs, as they must dance to them when they first appear in the house. The people sit arranged in a square. At some distance from each corner, a fool dancer is placed to watch so that no uninitiated person comes near. If, nevertheless, one of these people should see what is going on, he is captured by the fool dancer, taken into the square, and initiated.

After all have learned the new songs, they scatter and go home individually so as not to attract the attention of the other people. Each family eats supper alone, and then they prepare for the dance. When darkness falls, the $y\bar{e}^{\prime}wix\cdot ila$ sends four messengers to invite the people to the dance. He gives each of them a button blanket, a head ring, and a neck ring made of red cedar bark, along with eagle down to strew on their heads. They walk out of the house to one end of the village and enter the door of the last house to invite the people. Each of them has a set speech. The first says, "Let us try the shamans!" The second says, "We shall try in vain to bring back what makes us remember our friends!" The third says, "Bathe, $G\cdot\hat{e}pLalai!$ Bathe, $Yaqo\hat{\iota}sai!$" calling the names of the dancers. The fourth says, "Rise, friends!" also naming the dancers.<note>The first man says: La $m\text{ENS}$ <gloss>We will</gloss> $h\bar{e}inax'al\bar{e}Lai'$ <gloss>try</gloss> $p\bar{e}paxalai'$. <gloss>shamans.</gloss>
The second says: La $m\text{ENS}$ <gloss>We will</gloss> $wul'al\bar{e}Lai'$ <gloss>try in vain</gloss> $n\bar{e}nEm\bar{o}koai'$ <gloss>friends</gloss> $k\cdot ik\cdot \bar{\iota}'lnala$ <gloss>to bring back</gloss> $x\text{ENS}$ <gloss>our</gloss> $q'\bar{a}lal\text{E}Laai'$. <gloss>what makes us remember.</gloss>
The third says: La ams <gloss>Ready you</gloss> $x\bar{o}s\bar{e}t'\bar{e}Lai'$ <gloss>bathe</gloss> $Gy\cdot \hat{e}pLalai.$ <gloss>(woman's name).</gloss> Laams <gloss>Ready</gloss> $x\bar{o}s\bar{e}t'\bar{e}Lai'$ <gloss>bathe</gloss> $Yaqo\hat{\iota}sai'$. <gloss>(Hā'mats'a name).</gloss>

In inviting the people, they begin with the women and mention the name of everyone living in that particular house, continuing with the names of the $h\bar{a}^{\prime}mats'a$ and finally calling the names of the $qu\bar{e}^{\prime}qutsa$. After the messengers have gone through the whole village, they return to the house of the $y\bar{e}^{\prime}wix\cdot ila$, saying: "We have been outside to the end of the village."<note>$Lam\text{En}\bar{o}X$ $l\bar{a}'pelsa$.</note>

Then the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> asks four other people to act as his messengers. Again, he gives each of them a <term>button blanket</term>, a head ring and neck ring made of red <term>cedar bark</term>, and <term>eagle down</term> for their heads. They go to all the houses and invite the people to come at once. They go to each house and say, "Walk back." <note>Qātsēstai'.</note>

As soon as the people begin to enter the house, the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> beats time on a board in quick measures, concluding with a sharp rap and the call, "hai, hai."

<image-desc>A line drawing of a ceremonial head ring, labeled as Fig. 179. It is a circular band of woven material with four upright, twisted, branch-like projections rising vertically from the ring at regular intervals.</image-desc>

->Fig. 179.<-
->SECOND HEAD RING OF <term>HAI'ALIK'AUAĒ</term>.<-
-><term>Nimkish</term>.<-

The <term>Koskimo</term> are the first to enter. Each man carries as many <term>hemlock wreaths</term> as he has killed enemies during war expeditions. They also carry bows and arrows. Then they step up to the middle of the house and throw one wreath after the other into the fire, calling the name of the enemy whom it represents. As soon as a wreath is thrown into the fire, they call "yē," and everyone repeats this cry. At the same time, they shoot arrows into the fire. This ceremony is called <term>yî'lxoa</term>, which means placing the head of an enemy on a pole. The fire is called <term>XusE'la</term>, which means "fighting place." The whole ceremony is called <term>al'Xts'âlīL wā'lastEm</term> (carrying blood into the house and giving away much property) or <term>k·'ā'g·'ēuLaxstā'la</term> (the sharp edge of a knife). At present, the wreaths represent the number of <term>coppers</term> that a man has given away. They have taken the place of heads because, according to the customs of the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, a man who has given away a <term>copper</term> becomes a victor over his rival by doing so. They also throw paddles into the fire; the meaning of this is that they are sending a canoe to call their rivals to a festival in which they are going to show their greatness.

After the <term>Koskimo</term> have entered, the <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term> come in. Pieces of board representing dorsal fins are attached to their backs. They carry wreaths of hemlock branches in their hands. Their arms are stretched back and they make the motions of swimming, blowing from time to time like whales. They drop their wreaths in the rear of the house, go out again, take their fins off, and reenter. Then the people beat time, and the <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term>, holding their blankets stretched out backward, enter. They take up their wreaths and call the name of the <term>copper</term> or other property that they are going to give away. Then they

throw the wreaths into the fire. This means that they are going to rival the other tribes in the amount of property that they will give away.

The wives of the Koskimo, the <term>qau'qōtsaxsEm</term> (?), are the next to enter. Each of them carries a number of sticks, which represent the amount of property that they are going to give to their husbands. Each says what amount of property these sticks represent. They are followed by the <term>qā'qaō</term> and <term>k·ē'k·ēxalāqa</term>, the wives of the <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term>. They also carry sticks and state how much property they are going to give away.

Last of all the <term>mEsē'q</term>, or Sea-egg, enters. Sharp sticks about 3 feet long are fastened to his clothing. Two men accompany him. When he comes to the rear of the house, all the sticks are pulled out from his clothing, and at the same time the names of all the <term>coppers</term> which were given away during the past year are called. Everyone who has given away blankets has one stick contributed to the ornaments of this unique dancer. The sticks are then thrown into the fire, while all sing out, "yē!"

<image-desc>A black and white illustration of a ceremonial neck ring. It is composed of thick, fibrous coils with three distinct wooden crosspieces. Each crosspiece features a carved face or head. Strands of long hair or fiber hang down from the sides of the ring.</image-desc>

The <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term> and <term>d'ō'd'opa</term> then arrange themselves behind the fire, facing the rear of the house. The singing master stands behind them, facing the door and looking at the singers. The Koskimo and <term>hē'mêlk</term> sit on each side of the house, the women in the rear row. (See p. 436.)

Finally the <term>seal society</term> enters in the same manner as described above (p. 506).

While they are going to their seats the singers slip out one by one through the secret door. Then suddenly they all re-enter the house with great noise, and the people say: "The great <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term> have become excited."¹ They go around the fire slowly, holding their blankets spread out. Sometimes they are led by one of the <term>mē'êmqoat</term>. Then they pretend to pursue the latter.² If the member of the seal society should happen to be a fool dancer, they try to hit his nose, and as soon as they succeed in doing so he gets excited and stabs the people. During all this time the singing master remains in his place.

¹ <term>Kuē'qōL la g·a maa'mx'ēnuxts'ē'!</term>
These are wild, the great maa'mx'ēnox.

² They act according to their names. The <term>maa'mx'ēnôx</term> are killer whales, while the <term>mē'êmqoat</term> are seals, who are the prey of the former.

<summary>The ceremony continues with wives presenting symbolic property for their husbands, followed by a ritual featuring the Sea-egg dancer and a dramatic hunt where the killer whale society pursues the seal society.</summary>
<keywords>Koskimo, property distribution, coppers, Sea-egg dancer, maa'mx'ēnôx, seal society, fool dancer, winter ceremonial, Nimkish</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the description of the winter ceremonial, moving from the entrance of the wives and the Sea-egg dancer to the evening performances intended to summon the novice back from the woods.</meta>

After the singers have rearranged themselves behind the fire, two of them are sent to the door. Each has a rattle. They are the heralds who announce the dances that are to be performed that night in order to bring about the return of the novice. When the singers and the members of the seal society are in their places, the people slip out one by one and return to perform their dances. On this evening, they do not show the highest dances they possess, but those they owned when they were children. On the whole, the lower grades of dances come first and the higher ones later, but there is no strict order. As soon as one of them approaches the house, the heralds shake their rattles, and at this signal, the singers begin to beat the boards rapidly and continue to do so during the dance, at the end of which they sing one song for the dancer.

<image-desc>Fig. 181. A ritual head ring made of shredded and twisted cedar bark. The ring has several vertical bundles of the same material protruding upwards, resembling stylized branches or flames.</image-desc>
->Fig. 181.<-
->HEAD RING OF <term>HAI'ALIK'AUAĒ</term>.<-
-><term>L'ā'sq'ēnōx</term>.<-
->Cat. No. 175522, U. S. N. M. Collected by <term>F. Boas</term>.<-

The character of these dances was described in the preceding chapter.

When about half of all the dances have been shown, and particularly after a dance that has been well performed, two messengers (<term>hō'Laq'is</term>, listeners) are sent out by the speaker of the master of ceremonies to listen if any sign of the <term>hā'mats'a's</term> return can be heard. They go out, listen, and come back saying that they have not heard anything.

While the people are waiting for the dancers to come in, teasing and jokes occur. The speaker of the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> sends the heralds: "Go to our friend (the bear dancer) and see if he has not washed."¹ The herald goes out, after turning in the doorway. When he comes back, and if the next dancer is to be a woman, he may say: "She will not come; she is fighting with her husband;" or, "She will not come; she and her husband are kissing each other."

The dances continue until early in the morning, when the ghost dancer appears. As soon as the people sing his song, all the old <term>hā'mats'as</term>, who have not entered the house until then, get excited. Their whistles are blown by the <term>hē'lig·a</term>, and they enter the house from all sides—through the roof, through the front door, and through the secret doors in the rear of the house. They jump down to the floor, squat, and, looking up, cry "<term>hāp hāp!</term>" They jump around the fire four times, looking up and crying "<term>hāp!</term>" all the time. Their cries are supposed to be heard by the novice in the woods, who is suddenly heard on the roof of the house. He runs around four times. Three times he pushes the boards of the roof aside, and then he jumps down. The

¹ <term>Ha'g·a laxens nemō'kua (nā'nē). Ē'saē xō'sit.</term>
<gloss>Go to our friend (the bear). He has not washed.</gloss>

<summary>During the ritual evening, community members perform childhood dances to summon the novice back from the forest. The ceremony involves heralds, ritual teasing, and the dramatic return of the hāmats'as and the novice through the roof and secret doors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the winter ceremonial, moving from the earlier dances to the specific ritual attempts to summon and capture the <term>hā'mats'a</term> novice through the assistance of the <term>Lēlē'L'alēnôx</term> official.</meta>

People surround him and try to hold him. He runs around the fire four times, but all of a sudden he disappears again, having exited through the secret door in the back of the house. Only the hemlock branches he was decorated with remain in the house. As soon as the people see that he has disappeared, they say that someone has made a mistake which angered the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and caused him to leave the house again.

The <term>hā'mats'a</term> is not always persuaded to return in the manner described here. Sometimes the <term>xoā'ēxoē</term> dances, and the earthquake produced by the dance brings him back; or the dance of the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> may bring him back.

In some instances, a specific official, the <term>Lēlē'L'alēnôx</term>, must try to call the novice. He is considered the chief of all the <term>quē'qutsa</term>. He wears a rough head ring and neck ring made of red cedar bark that is twisted four times. His face is blackened. He enters carrying a baton and stops in front of the fire. If anyone laughs, he points at him, and the person singled out must look down. He goes around the fire singing his secret song, as follows:<note>Appendix, page 724.</note>

> Ah, ah, supernatural power! Ah, ah, ah, supernatural power!
> Hoo!

In the back of the house, he turns once, cries "hu!" and stoops down to listen. Then he continues his circuit and repeats this action in front of the house. While he is doing so, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> appears on the roof, at the back right-hand corner of the house, runs around the roof, and opens a hole at the front left-hand corner to look down into the house. From there, he rushes to the back left corner of the house. Then he runs to the back right corner and then to the front right corner, pushes the boards aside, and looks down into the house. Then the people take a number of blankets, spread them out tight, and hold them under the place where the <term>hā'mats'a</term> is looking down. Finally, he jumps down into the blankets in the front right corner of the house.

They try to hold him and slowly go around the fire, attempting to lay their hands on him, but he disappears again. Only his hemlock branches are left in the hands of the people.

Then the <term>Lēlē'L'alēnôx</term> says that the laughing of the person whom he pointed out in the beginning was the cause of the disappearance of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The laugher must call his daughter to dance, and he must take a staff (the feast pole <term>qā'sōp'ēq</term>) in his hands and promise to give a feast after her dance.

If any other mistake has been made, the <term>Lēlē'L'alēnôx</term> points it out in a similar way. When, for instance, a woman has brought her uninitiated children into the house, he will say on entering, “I smell someone who is profane;”¹ and the people will reply, “Important is your word.”² Then he asks for red cedar bark, which is given to him. He makes a neck ring and a head ring (figs. 186, 187, pp. 527, 528). He asks one man to beat time. Then he sings his secret song, and suddenly the voices of birds (whistles) are heard on top of the house. He holds the red cedar bark in front of his face, pushing it forward with every step and crying, “ō, ō, ôp, ôp.” Then he puts the cedar bark on the child’s head. The birds' voices suddenly disappear, and are heard on the roof of the house of the child’s father. Then that child must disappear, as it is supposed that he has been taken away by these spirits.

After the novice has disappeared again, the chief’s speaker asks all the people to make themselves ready to expect the novice on the following morning. All this time his whistles are heard in the woods. Then the people go to their houses and have a short rest, but after about an hour or two the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> calls them to his house and asks them to try to catch the new <term>hā'mats'a</term>. He says: “Take care! we want to save our great friend.”³ Then the master of ceremonies requests the seal society to assemble, and the <term>quē'qutsa</term> to follow them. He says, “Gather seals!”⁴

The <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> lead the way, each singing her secret song. All the people follow them toward the beach. The first <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> sings:<note>Appendix, page 724.</note>

They go westward, and as soon as they come to the place called <term>Nau'alak'uas</term> (place of supernatural power), about one-eighth of a mile west of the village, four sons or relatives of the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> are sent out to gather hemlock branches.

People catch him and lead him toward the house, singing the new songs. (Plate 44.) The <term>hē'lig·a</term> sing their secret songs, and the uninitiated cry “hoî'p.” By this means, they attempt to tame the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The people lead him to the house of the <term>yē'wix·ila</term>, who steps out of the house with his entire family as they approach, dressed in red cedar bark ornaments and button blankets. Their faces are marked with black spots, and their heads are covered with down. They dance in front of the house, accompanying the new songs. Some of the <term>yē'wix·ila</term>'s relatives go down to the people leading the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and hold boards in their hands for the people to beat time on. Then the latter begin to sing as follows: “Woe! You are making your parents poor, <term>naualak</term>!”<margin>1</margin> Then they walk into the house. After they have all entered, the new <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term>—who returned from the woods with the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and who is completely naked during the ceremony—begins to sing her new song. She enters the house walking backward, facing the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, whom she intends to lead into the house. The <term>hā'mats'a</term>, however, seems unwilling to enter and stays in the doorway for about half an hour, where he turns four times while the <term>hē'lig·a</term> surround him the entire time. During this time, the people raise the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> and the <term>mā'wiL</term>. As soon as it is completed, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> leaves the doorway, goes to the right until he reaches the rear of the house, and climbs the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term>. He climbs onto the roof of the house, runs around once, and returns by descending the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term>, or he jumps down from the door of the <term>mā'wiL</term>. As soon as he jumps down, he rushes toward a man and bites his arm. He goes around the fire once, holding him in this way. Then he climbs the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> again, runs around the roof, and after he comes down again, he bites another man. This is repeated four times. During this time, the people sing the new songs, and the <term>hā'mats'a</term> dances around the fire, though not properly, as he is supposed to still be out of his senses. After he has danced around the fire for the fourth time, he enters the <term>mā'wiL</term>. Then all the people take off the hemlock branches and throw them into the fire. This is called smoking the wildness of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> out of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. Then they arrange themselves according to the societies to which they belong. "I am (Hē'iltsaqolîs)! Come, friends, and give away the bracelets and coppers."¹ The name by which he calls himself here is the one which he assumes at this festival. Then the members of the society to which he belongs take the brass bracelets and the coppers out of the box and give them to him. He says: "I obtained this property from my father-in-law, and I am going to distribute it now according to the laws of the winter dance."²

The *yē'wix·ila* turns everything over to the master of ceremonies or to one of his own relatives, who in their turn distribute the property among the assembly, giving to the women first, then the "seals," and lastly the *quē'qutsa*, each person receiving one stick of bracelets and one stick of coppers. After the property has been distributed, the people go home and eat their breakfast in their own houses.

In the evening the *yē'wix·ila* again requests four messengers to invite the people. He tells them the names of the new *hā'mats'a* and *k·î'nqalaLala*, and tells them to call the people to come to his house, in order to tame the new *hā'mats'a* and *k·î'nqalaLala*. Each of these messengers receives one button blanket. They go to the various houses and say:³

> "Shamans! We will pacify this supernatural one. We will soften (Tse'mqok·aLa)⁴ by means of our songs. Friends! We will pacify this supernatural one. We will restore her to her senses (Hē'lig·îxstēg·ilisa).⁵ Let us go into the dancing house before dark!"

After they return to the dancing house, the *yē'wix·ila* calls four more messengers, who also receive a button blanket each in payment for their services. They must go to the end of the village, and beginning at the last house they must say: "We come back to call you. The fire is going out. We have no fuel. Come quickly, shamans!"⁶ The people follow them at once, and all enter the dancing house.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonial, detailing the ritual efforts to pacify the hā'mats'a through dancing, the use of eagle down, and the mediation of specialized dancers and singers.</meta>

During the whole day, the whistles of the hā'mats'a were heard in the house. Then the speaker of the yē'wix·ila says the following: "Friends, do as I desire! Try to pacify our friend! Let all the women dance!"¹ This is a request for the women to dance with the hā'mats'a in order to tame him. The master of ceremonies calls upon all the ha'mshamtsEs, the hai'alik·ilaL, the t'ō'X'uît, and the k·î'nqalaLala to dance with the hā'mats'a. They blacken their faces, put eagle down on their heads, and begin to dance. Then the hā'mats'a shakes the ha'msp'ēq and comes out of the mā'wiL. At once, the people begin to beat the boards, but they do not sing. The hā'mats'a goes around the fire once and disappears again into the mā'wiL. The master of ceremonies says, "Someone must have made a mistake," and calls for the paxa'lalaL—which means the shaman dancer. He steps forward, asks for a round rattle, and as soon as the master of ceremonies has given it to him, he begins to sing the song of the paxa'lalaL.² "You took me around the world, BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē." He goes around the fire and then enters the mā'wiL at the same place where the hā'mats'a entered. He stays there for about ten minutes and then reappears, saying that the people have made too much noise, that they did not have enough down on their heads, and that the hā'mats'a had disappeared again for these reasons. The master of ceremonies calls for four dishes of eagle down. Then four men come out of the right-hand front corner of the house carrying the dishes and saying that they were waiting for the orders of the master of ceremonies. He sends the four men to put feathers on the heads of the people, beginning with the hā'mats'a, continuing with the other "seals," and finishing with the quē'qutsa. Then the master of ceremonies says that the eagle down brought supernatural power into the house (which is not supposed to be present where there is no down).

Now the hā'mats'a is seen to leave the mā'wiL again. He jumps down, goes around the fire once, and disappears again. Again, the paxa'lalaL is sent to discover if a mistake has been made which caused the hā'mats'a to leave again. He sings the same song as before and enters the mā'wiL, where he stays for some time. He reappears and says that the hā'mats'a was displeased because the hē'lig·a did not sing their secret song. Then four hē'lig·a are sent into the mā'wiL. The yē'wix·ila gives four button blankets to the master of ceremonies and asks him to do with them as he pleases. The master of ceremonies gives them to the hē'lig·a, who then begin to sing: "Wa

Now they enter the *mā'wiL*, and after a short time, they bring out the *hā'mats'a*, who bites the arm of one of them. As soon as they approach the door of the house, the *hā'mats'a* lets go his hold, turns around, and bites a second person in the same way. They continue their way, and when they reach the *mā'wiL*, the *hā'mats'a* disappears once more. The *hē'lig·a* follow him, and soon he reappears, biting a third person. As soon as they come to the door, he lets go his hold and bites a fourth person. When they reach the rear of the house again, the *hē'lig·a* do not allow him to reenter the *mā'wiL*. The people beat time rapidly. During these ceremonies, the *hā'mats'a* is entirely naked, except for a wreath of hemlock branches which he wears around his neck, one around his head, one around his waist, and bracelets and anklets of the same material.

Now the people begin to sing the new songs that were made for the *hā'mats'a*. After the first song has been sung, he disappears into the *mā'wiL*, and immediately the mask of *QoāqoaXuālanuXsi'waē*, the raven, appears. After the mask has disappeared, the *hā'mats'a* appears again, entirely naked. When he has finished his dance, the mask of *BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē* comes out (see p. 446). The mask disappears into the *mā'wiL*, and the *hā'mats'a* comes out again dancing slowly. He wears a crown of red cedar bark on his head, a wide neck ring of the same material, anklets, bracelets, a dancing apron, and a bear skin. Then the people continue to sing the new songs that were made for him. The master of ceremonies spreads a new mat in the middle of the rear of the house, in front of the singers. After his dance, the *hā'mats'a* sits down on this mat, facing the rear of the house. Then the *k·î'nqalaLala* comes out of the *mā'wiL* singing her new secret song. After she has finished, the people sing the new songs that were made for her in the woods. She dances until the two songs are finished. Then the master of ceremonies calls up a man named *Ts'ē'qamē* (*quē'qutsa* name): “Come, friend, try if you can reach our friend.”¹ This is the request for him to tame the *hā'mats'a*. *Ts'ē'qamē* asks for four pieces of soft white cedar bark, which are given to him by the *yē'wix·ila*.² *Ts'ē'qamē* takes them, crying “hoîp, hoîp.” This means that he is putting the secret of the winter dance into the bark. He asks for a pole (about 6 feet long), which is given to him by the *yē'wix·ila*, or by the latter's brother, who is looking after the fire. *Ts'ē'qamē* ties the four pieces of cedar bark to the end of the pole. Each piece is about 8 feet long. He tells the people to be ready to beat time when the signal is given. He asks one of the *k·î'nqalaLala* to take off the clothing of the *hā'mats'a*.

The k·î'nqalaLala goes around the fire saying "hoîp, hoîp, hoîp, hoîp," and then takes off the hā'mats'a's clothing and cedar bark ornaments. Then Ts'ē'qamē gives the signal to the people to begin beating time, and as soon as they begin, he puts one end of the cedar bark into the fire. He runs around the fire until he comes to the place where the hā'mats'a is sitting. Here he swings the burning bark over the hā'mats'a's head, and at the same time, the hā'mats'a turns around while squatting and crying "hāp, hāp, hāp." Ts'ē'qamē goes around the fire once more, keeping his eye on the hā'mats'a until he reaches him the second time, when he swings the burning bark over his head again. This is done four times. This is called nawa'qamā. Then the hē'lig·a lift the hā'mats'a, carry him around the fire, and take him into the mā'wiL. The master of ceremonies now calls the yē'wix·ila and asks him to pay Ts'ē'qamē for his work. The yē'wix·ila goes into his bedroom and brings out a button blanket, which he gives to him. Then the yē'wix·ila asks the master of ceremonies or one of his relatives to distribute the rest of the brass bracelets, coppers, and button blankets among the people. Each person receives one stick of bracelets, one stick of coppers, and one button blanket.

Now all the uninitiated must leave the house. The door is closed and the purification of the hā'mats'a begins. Four men must take part in this ceremony: the kuē'ts'ēnôx or the washer, the qa'nēnôx or the rubber, the ts'ē'silaēnôx or the tongsmaker, and the t'a'mtsēnôx or the time beater. Whatever these men ask for during the ceremony must be given to them, and they keep it as their personal property. When everything is quiet, the ts'ē'silaēnôx asks for a piece of cedar board about 6 feet long, for a wedge, and for a stone hammer. After these are brought to him, the t'a'mtsēnôx sits down in his place ready to beat time. Then the ts'ē'silaēnôx asks for a belt. After he has received it, he puts it on and goes around the fire four times, carrying a rattle in his hand, while the t'a'mtsēnôx beats time. He does not sing, but says "hoîp, hoîp." After he has gone around the fire four times, he stops, puts his rattle down, and stoops three times, as though he were going to pick up the hammer and wedge, but he does not actually take them until he stoops for the fourth time. Every time he stoops, the t'a'mtsēnôx gives a short rap on the board. Then the ts'ē'silaēnôx goes around the fire until he comes to the place where the board is lying on the ground. He steps up to it, turns once to the left, puts his wedge against the board, and pretends to drive it in with his stone hammer, but he takes it off again, turns once more to the left, and places it a second and third time against the board. The fourth time he actually drives the wedge into the board with one hard blow and splits it. Then he asks the yē'wix·ila for a knife, and after it is given to him, he makes a pair of tongs out of the cedar board. Then he asks for a clean mat and for a piece of soft white cedar bark. He takes it up with his tongs, goes around the fire, and gives it to the

*qa'nēnôx*. Every time these men go around the fire, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* must beat the boards.

Then the *qa'nēnôx* takes the mat and spreads it on the floor at the left side of the door, and lays the cedar bark on it. He begins to rub the bark and to cut it. When cutting, he draws his knife three times, pretending to cut, and every time he does so, he turns to the left. The fourth time, he actually begins to cut the bark. One of the pieces he cuts is about 6 feet long, and two other pieces are each about 2 feet long. A knot is tied in the middle of the long piece, which is then tied into the shape of a ring, with the ends crossing each other and leaving about 1 foot free. The two shorter pieces are tied near the middle of the long piece, so that the whole forms a ring with two ends on one side and two ends near the middle. The ring represents the body, the knot represents the head, the upper ends represent the arms, and the lower ends represent the feet of a person.

Now he rises and gives a signal to the *t'a'mtsēnôx* to beat time. He goes around the fire once and stops near the tongs that the *ts'ē'silaēnôx* made. Then he puts the ring down. Now the *ts'ē'silaēnôx* rises. He spreads the tongs with a small stick. Three times he pretends to take them up, turning each time. The fourth time, he actually takes them and goes toward the ring of white cedar bark, the *qa'nā'yu*. At this time, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* begins to beat time again. The *ts'ē'silaēnôx* goes around the fire with the tongs in his hands and keeps his eye on the *qa'nā'yu* the entire time. When he comes to the mat on which it is lying, he pretends to take it up with the tongs, but he does not touch it. Then he turns around to the left and extends his arms toward the place of the rising sun. Every time he does so, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* gives a hard rap on the board, and the people cry "wa!" This is repeated three times; the fourth time, he takes the *qa'nā'yu* and goes around the fire four times until he arrives at the east side of the house.

Then he pushes up the tongs three times. The fourth time, he turns them around and places the handle under the roof on the east side of the house. He goes around the fire four times. Then he pretends to take up four stones with his tongs. He does not actually take them until the fourth time. During this time, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* beats time again. Then the *kuēts'ēnôx* asks for a new dish, which is placed on the floor. He asks for water, which is brought to him in a bucket. When he takes the bucket, he gives a signal to the *t'a'mtsēnôx* to beat time. He walks around the fire with the water while all the people say "wa wa wa." Every time he comes to the point where he started—either opposite the door or in the rear of the house—he turns and lifts his bucket toward the sun. Every time he does so, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* stops with a loud rap. After he has done this four times, he goes to the dish, which is standing on the left side of the door. Three times he pretends to pour out water, and the fourth time he empties it into the dish. After this has been done, the new *hā'mats'a* is called to come out from the *mā'wiL*. He and the *k·î'nqalaLala* come out entirely naked. A new mat is placed

Every time he turns, he says, "hoî'p." The fourth time, after laying down the mat, the *k·î'nqalaLala* sings the *hē'lig·a* song.<note>It is my power to pacify you (see page 527).</note> The *k·î'nqalaLala* walks four times around the fire while singing. The *hā'mats'a* must follow her, and every time the *k·î'nqalaLala* turns, he must turn as well. They turn whenever they reach the point opposite the door and at the back of the house. After they have made four circuits, they sit down, with the *hā'mats'a* appearing wild the whole time, as though he wanted to bite the people. The *qa'nēnôx* rises and walks around the fire after signaling the *t'a'mtsēnôx* to beat time. He takes a small stick and places it in the wall of the house a little below the tongs on which the *qa'nāyu* is hanging, but before actually placing it there, he mimics the motion three times, turning after each movement. Then he attempts to take the *qa'nāyu* from the tongs, but he does not actually take it down until after he has made the motion three times. As soon as he finally takes it, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* gives a loud rap and says "ya." Then the *qa'nēnôx* turns once and puts the *qa'nāyu* on the short stick. Again, he walks around the fire while the *t'a'mtsēnôx* is beating time. He goes to the tongs, turns around once, and takes them down.

He walks around the fire holding the tongs downward. During this time, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* beats time. The *qa'nēnôx* stops at the door and holds the tongs toward the door. Then the *kuē'ts'ēnôx* rises, and with an ordinary baton, he strikes the small stick which spreads the tongs, thereby throwing it out of the door. If the stick should happen to strike the walls of the house and not go through the door, it predicts a short life for the *hā'mats'a*. Then the *ts'ē'silaēnôx* turns and walks around the fire. Three times he pretends to take the stones out of the fire, extending the tongs toward the sun each time. The fourth time, he actually picks the stones up. Then the people cry "wa wa." He turns, walks around the fire four times, and stops near the dish containing the water. Three times he pretends to throw the stones into the water, and every time he does so, the *t'a'mtsēnôx* beats time. The fourth time, he throws them into the water.

This ceremony is performed with each stone individually. Then he walks around the fire again and puts the tongs back under the roof in the same place where they were before.

Now the *kuē'ts'ēnôx* rises. He walks around the fire, stretching his right hand backward and shaking it. This is the signal for the *t'a'mtsēnôx* to strike the board as hard as possible. Every time he reaches the east and the west sides of the fire, he turns around and the beater gives one short rap. Every time he comes to the turning point, he extends his hands toward the *qa'nā'yu* as though he were going to take it down. His hands are shaking the whole time, like those of Bax-

He holds his left hand stretched forward. He goes around the fire, and at the turning point, he extends the ring toward the sun. Every time he does so, the <term>t'a'mtsēnôx</term> gives a short beat.

He walks around the fire four times and finally stops near the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. Then the <term>qa'nēnôx</term> calls the <term>kuēts'ēnôx</term> to come to the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. He does not actually take any water until the fourth time. He holds the water in his two hands, goes around the fire, lifts it toward the sun, turns around, and puts it on the head of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, softly stroking him. The <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> sits next to the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> first extends his right arm, then his left arm, through the ring. When the ring comes down to his feet, he raises his right leg first, puts it down outside the ring, turns all the way around on his right foot, then takes up his left foot, and sits down on the mat, facing east. The <term>qa'nēnôx</term> takes the ring up, turns around, and alternately drops his left hand and raises his right hand.

Again, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> extends his right arm, and the <term>qa'nēnôx</term> rubs him in the same way as the first time. This is repeated four times. Then the <term>qa'nēnôx</term> goes around the fire and performs the same ceremony with the <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term>. Then the people sing:

> “In olden times you went all around the world with the supernatural being.”<note>See Appendix, page 724.</note>

The <term>qa'nēnôx</term> takes the tongs down from the roof and takes up the <term>qa'nā'yu</term>, while the <term>t'a'mtsēnôx</term> is beating time. He goes around the fire swinging the ring, and turns at the front and at the rear of the house, raising the ring toward the sun. After he has gone around the fire four times, he swings the ring over the fire until it ignites. Then all the people say, “wa wa.” He walks out of the house and burns the ring on the street. Then he burns the tongs in the house. After this, all the people are allowed to enter the house.

After the song has been sung, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> gets excited, leaves the house, and runs around the village.

The <term>yē'wix·ila</term> now brings all his dishes, kettles, spoons, and mats, and distributes them among the people of his tribe; the people go to the pile and each person takes one piece. This celebration lasts until it is nearly daylight.

<meta>This page continues the description of the purification and taming rituals for the hā'mats'a, following the handling of the ceremonial rings and the ritual washing ceremonies.</meta>

Around this time, the four officers—the <term>kuē'ts'ēnôx</term>, the <term>qa'nēnôx</term>, the <term>ts'ē'silaēnôx</term>, and the <term>t'a'mtsēnôx</term>—leave the house, with the last-named officer carrying the baton. Then they say: $^1$ “Here is food for you, <term>quē'qutsa</term>.”

This is the notice for the final great feast in the winter dance ceremonies. At this time, they count all the mistakes made by the <term>hā'mats'a</term>.$^2$

For four days after this, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> runs around biting people. On the fourth night, the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> calls his society together and tells them that the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> is going to be burned. A messenger belonging to his society is sent out to call all the people together. He is given a button blanket and a new head ring and neck ring. This messenger goes to every house and says:$^3$ “Friends, we will tame our great friend ———.”

Then the entire tribe—men, women, and children—assembles. They sing the <term>hā'mats'a's</term> songs, and during the following day, the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> pays them for their bites; the price is one canoe for each bite. The women who danced receive bracelets, and the men who sang receive button blankets. These presents must be returned with interest when the recipients give a festival in a future year.

All the <term>quē'qutsa</term> must now leave the building. The fool dancers and bears are also required to go out. Only the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term>, <term>nō'ntsistalaL</term>, <term>qoē'qoasElaL</term>, <term>nā'ne</term> of <term>BaxbakualanuXsi'waē</term>, <term>k·i'nqalaLala</term>, and the <term>lāxsâ</term> remain. They nail the door shut and seal all the cracks and holes in the walls. The <term>k·i'nqalaLala</term> take the batons; then all the <term>hā'mats'as</term> begin to cry “hāp, hāp.” The <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term> cry “wip, wip, wip,” and all the others utter their distinctive sounds. The <term>k·i'nqalaLala</term> beat time, and each sings his own song. During this time, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> becomes excited and circles the fire and the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> four times. Then they lift the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> and pull it down, laying it so that it slants downward from the roof. During this ceremony, all the <term>hā'mats'as</term> are naked. Four times they go up and down the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> while it is in this position, crying “hāp, hāp.” Then the <term>ha'msp'ēq</term> is taken down entirely. The <term>hā'mats'as</term> cut it into four pieces, while the <term>k·i'nqalalala</term> and the others who are present make as much noise as possible. Then four <term>hā'mats'as</term> carry each piece. They carry it around the fire, turning in the front and in the rear of the house, and crying “hāp” the entire time. Then they throw the pieces into the fire. Next, the <term>mā'wiL</term> is pulled down and burned with similar ceremonies. For four days, they remain in the house singing the new <term>hā'mats'a</term> songs. On the fourth day, they dress in red cedar bark, sprinkle feathers on their heads, and blacken their faces. Then the <term>wä'lēqa</term>—the first meal of the <term>hā'mats'a</term>

<summary>This page details the final stages of the winter dance, where the hā'mats'a's ritual mistakes are tallied and the community is compensated for his ritual biting. The ceremony concludes with the symbolic destruction and burning of the ha'msp'ēq pole and the mā'wiL screen, followed by four days of singing new songs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the final stages of the hā'mats'a's ritual return and the conclusion of the winter dance ceremonies.</meta>

<page-num>537</page-num>
<header>THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.</header>

...after his return from the wilderness—is celebrated. The <term>k·î'nqalaLala</term> leaves the house, followed by the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, each singing his own song. They visit four houses and are fed by the people. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> must eat all that is given to him. Then they walk into the next house, where they are fed again.

Now the whole tribe assembles again in the house of the <term>yē'wix·ila</term>. A canoe mast is erected in the middle of the house, and the master of ceremonies asks, “Who will take the red cedar bark off of the people and keep it until next winter?” Whoever intends to host a winter dance the following winter must step forward and take hold of the pole. Then all the people take off their rings and throw them into the fire. Only four are kept until the next year. The people tie handkerchiefs around their heads in place of the cedar bark.

Then “the sound of the batons is driven out of the house.” The people beat time four times and then throw all the sticks into the fire. This is the end of the winter dance.

After biting people, and particularly after eating slaves or bodies, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> must observe a great many rules. Immediately after they have eaten from a corpse, the <term>hē'lig·a</term> brings them salt water, which they drink in great quantities in order to induce vomiting. If they do not vomit as many pieces as they have swallowed, their excrement is examined in order to ensure that all the pieces of human flesh have passed through the body. The bones of the body that they have eaten are kept for four months. They are kept alternately for four days in their bedrooms on the north side of the house where the sun does not reach them, and four days under rocks in the sea. Finally, they are thrown into the sea.

The <term>hā'mats'as</term> are not allowed to go out through the house door, but must use only the secret door in the rear of the house. When one of them goes out to relieve himself, all the others must go with him, each carrying a small stick. They must all sit down together on a long log. They must rise again three times and do not sit down until the fourth time. Before sitting down, they must turn four times. Before they rise, they must turn four times. Then they go back to the house. Before entering, they must raise their feet four times. With the fourth step, they actually pass through the door. They enter right foot first. In the doorway, they turn four times and walk slowly into the house. They are not allowed to look back.

For four months after eating human flesh, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> uses his own spoon, dish, and kettle, which are thrown away after the prescribed time has passed.

He must wear soiled cedar bark. He must stay alone in his bedroom. A grizzly bear dancer is placed in the doorway to ensure that no one enters.

Before taking water out of a bucket or before dipping it out of a brook, he must dip his cup three times into the water. He must not take more than four mouthfuls at one time.
