He must carry an eagle's wing bone and drink through it, as his lips must not touch the rim of his cup. He also wears a copper nail to scratch his head with, as his fingernails must not touch his skin; otherwise, they would fall off. For sixteen days after he has eaten human flesh, he must not eat any warm food, and for four months he is not allowed to blow on hot food to cool it. For a whole year he must not touch his wife, nor is he allowed to gamble or to work. When the dancing season is over, he pretends to have forgotten the ordinary ways of human beings and has to learn everything anew. He acts as though he were very hungry all the time.

The whole ceremony of bringing back the novice is, according to the ideas of the Kwakiutl, a repetition of the same ceremony performed by the wolves who attempted to bring back their novices; and the following tradition, which, however, is not complete in all its details, explains its origin: <note>Appendix, page 725.</note>

Mink made a salmon trap behind Qā'logwīs, the village of the Kwakiutl. The different tribes held a winter ceremony, and the sons of the chief of the wolves had disappeared in the woods. While there, they spoiled Mink’s salmon trap. They did this for three days. Then Mink became angry. He made up his mind to watch who was tampering with his salmon trap. He went there in the evening and hid near his salmon weir. Then the four sons of the wolf, who had disappeared in the woods, arrived. They went right up to the salmon weir and took out the salmon that had entered it. Then Mink said to himself, “You are the ones who tampered with my weir.” They sat down and ate the salmon raw. Mink crawled up to them from behind and killed them with his club. He cut off their heads and went home carrying the four heads. Nobody knew that he had killed them; even his mother did not know it.

Now the wolves were going to bring back their novices after two days. When the time came for bringing the novices back, Kuē'kuaxāoe was the master of ceremonies. Mink closed all the holes and cracks of his own house and tied ropes of cedar around it to strengthen it.

Before daylight, Mink went in his canoe to Mē'mk·umlīs. He made a salmon weir of stones. Then he went and sat down on a rock. He looked at his weir. “What fish is in my trap?” he said. “A small bullhead,” replied the trap. Then he scratched his head. “Oh, that is pretty; I am working hard looking after my trap! Throw it into the water!” He asked again, “What fish is in my trap?” It replied, “A small flounder.” He threw it into the water, and then the trap caught first an eel, then a dogfish, a perch, a silver perch, a coho salmon, a dog salmon, a humpback salmon, a steelhead salmon, a spring salmon, and finally a *sī'siuL*. Then he said, “That is it; that is it!” and he was glad. He took the *sī'siuL* out of his trap and put it down on the rock. He broke off hemlock branches, laid them in his canoe, and put the fish on top of them. Then he went home to his house at

Qā/logwîs. He went ashore to his house. His mother was lying down. Then Mink spoke: “Don’t stay here, grandmother, but carry my fish into the house.” His mother went down to the beach. She went to the canoe and looked in vain for the fish. Her body became contorted and her head turned backward because she had seen the sī'siuL <note>A legendary double-headed serpent.</note>. Mink waited for his mother for a long time. Then he got up and went to look for her. He found her and saw that her whole body was contorted. “Is that the way, grandmother? Are you so happy?” He took her and straightened her body. He carried the sī'siuL himself from the beach to the house. He put it into a box. Evening came. The people intended to bring back the novices that night. They beat the boards in vain for the ones they expected. They had been killed by Mink.

The people were still singing in the house. One of the chiefs said, “Dancers, let us try to bring back our novices.” But when they did not come after numerous attempts, one of them spoke: “Dancers, we are not going to succeed in bringing back our novices.” One of them replied, “Wash yourselves, friends.” Then the last one spoke: “You who are not initiated, turn your faces toward the back of the house. We will go in before dark.” Then the people thought they would have to give up trying to bring back their novices. They listened, but they did not hear the arrival of the supernatural power.

Up to this time, Mink had not made his appearance. Then the people said, “What is the matter with our chief K·ēx· (Mink)?” They went to fetch him. Now Mink and his cousins—the raccoon, the killer whale, and the squirrel—did what they had planned. His sister Ts'E'stayūkoa and the raccoon went and pulled out a board in the back corner of the dancing house. The raccoon sat down in that corner. Now K·ēx· came in. He danced for a little while and went out again. Then he came in and danced again with his sister. He sang:

->Spread your legs, Ts'E'stayūkoa,<-
->Spread your legs, Ts'E'stayūkoa,—<-

and he jumped through his sister's spread legs.

Then he came in again. He used the heads of the wolves as his mask, but he was hiding them behind his blanket. He sang:

->Mink is wearing the middle of the faces of the wolf chief's sons.<-

He went out again; and when he came back in, the heads of the wolves were attached to his blanket. Now the people tried to kill him because they saw that he had killed their chief's sons. Then he went out through the doorway in the rear while his friends, the squirrel and the raccoon, beat the drum. He came in again wearing the sī'siuL mask. As soon as he entered the door, he uncovered the mask, and everyone who saw it died in convulsions. Then K·ēx· selected all his relatives and the people he liked and brought them back to life. That is the end.

The initiation of members of the lower grades of the ts'ē'tsāēqa is not performed with ceremonies as elaborate as those of the la'xsâ.

Their initiation is called kue'xalakᵘ. Those who are initiated through the kue'xalakᵘ ceremonies are called g·ixsēg·i, which means "leaning against the wall of the mā'wıL." In most cases, they return from their initiations during the festivals held to bring back a novice of the la'xsâ. Sometimes, however, while the people are gathered at a feast, the wi'xsâ or kue'xalakᵘ novice is taken away by the spirits; then his father announces that he will be brought back in four days. He calls for the master of ceremonies of the kue'xalakᵘ, who wears a head ring decorated with five feathers—one in front, one on each side, and two in the back. His face is painted red. He enters and begins to circle the fire, swinging his baton from the elbow. When he reaches the back of the house, he turns around while swinging his stick and then strikes a board once, crying "ha'mamamama" very rapidly at the same time. As soon as he does this, all the people strike the boards. Meanwhile, the master of ceremonies turns around, strikes the board again, and cries "hamamai'." Again, all the people strike the boards together and cry "ha'mamamama." These cries represent the sounds made by the ghosts. The master of ceremonies continues his circuit, swinging his baton the entire time. When he reaches the door, he turns again and continues. When he reaches the back of the house for the second time, the same ceremony is repeated. He continues his circuit in the same way as before. When he reaches the back of the house for the third time, he turns and cries "yēhēē" and strikes the boards; then all the people cry "yēhēē'hōōōō." This represents the sound of the wolf. While the people are beating time, the master of ceremonies turns again and then strikes the boards, crying "yēhēē" and drawing out the last syllable as long as possible. Then the people strike the boards all at the same time and repeat his cry.

The master of ceremonies circles the fire for the fourth time, and when he reaches the back of the house, he turns and cries "wōwōwō" or "wōē'p." Then the people beat time and say "kf" (with the "f" drawn out very long). This is the sound of Hai'alik·ila. During this time, the whistles of the ghosts are heard continuously.

When the master of ceremonies turns for the last time, he smiles at the people, strikes the board, and cries "wō," to which all the people reply "hää." The ceremonies of this evening are called lōL.

Now the chief steps forward and says, "This is finished, friends; bring in your boxes." <note>Wā nēnemō'kᵘ, g·ā'xLax·is t'ā'miatse Laōs nēnemō'kᵘ.</note> While he remains standing, those who are willing to bring boxes leave the house and soon return, carrying them on their shoulders. The lids and ropes of the boxes are thrown into the fire. The boxes are placed in a row at the back of the house, with the openings facing backward. Then the yē'wix·ila asks one of his relatives or his daughter to dance. He holds a large staff in his hand, which is called a qā'sōp'ēq or "feast staff." He promises to celebrate the winter dance; and calling for his father-in-law, he says that he was compelled to

celebrate the winter dance without having had previous knowledge of what was coming, and requests his father-in-law to repay him for the property with which he was presented at the time of the marriage of his daughter. The father-in-law rises, asks the young man to give him the staff, which he grasps in the middle, holding it horizontally. Then he calls his friends to take hold of the staff with him. By doing so they pledge themselves to help the old man to repay his son-in-law. He says how much he is going to pay to his son-in-law and returns the staff to him. Then the latter takes it and carries it, pretending that it is exceedingly heavy, saying, “ō, ō, ō, ō!” It is supposed that the property is attached to the staff.

The father-in-law asks: “When will you want me to pay you all this property?” And the young man says that he wants it by the third day. The following days the people are invited to feast and to dance in the chief’s house. A sail is stretched across the rear of the house. The seal society have their seats close to this sail.

Now the master of ceremonies rises and calls one man (the <term>mā'MEnats'ēnôx</term>), whose office it is to look after the drum. This office is hereditary. The master of ceremonies says: “Go and bring your inheritance.” The man rises, steps up to the fire, goes around it, leaves the house, and soon returns carrying the drum on his shoulder. He stops in the doorway, turns around silently, and walks around the fire four times. He stops finally in the left-hand rear corner of the house, where he puts down the drum on its flat side. He carries a small whistle in his mouth and every time he pushes the drum he blows the whistle. It is of course supposed that this sound is produced by the drum. Then he says, “It is done; I have brought my inheritance.” The master of ceremonies asks, “Did you bring the baton with you?” To which the man replies, “My grandfather has been dead so long that I forgot this part of my inheritance.” He is sent to fetch it, and walks out of the house and returns in the same way as the first time. He deposits the batons in the middle of the rear of the house, and every time he moves them he blows another whistle.

Then the master of ceremonies calls another man, whose office it is to look after the eagle down. This office is also hereditary. He goes out in the same way as the other officer, and soon returns, carrying a painted bag filled with down. He says, “Here is the bag which my grandfather left for me to take care of.” He walks around the fire four times, turning in the front and in the rear, and finally deposits it in the right hand front corner of the house. Then four men take four dishes, each takes one handful of down out of the bag, and puts it into the dish. The down is pulled apart so that it fills the dishes entirely. The owner of the down shakes his bag, which then appears to be quite full again, and carries it back. It is supposed that the bag always remains full. Then the master of ceremonies takes up one of the dishes and asks his brother, who is chief of the <term>quē'qutsa</term>, to take

Another one. The name of this office is dā'sqamē xa kuē'xalak^u, holder of the kuē'xalak^u. The officer has the name Q'E'mtq'atas. <note>According to tradition, the first man of this name invited the people to a feast, but, instead of feeding them, only taught them four songs. The name means "eating songs."</note> Two other men take the other two dishes and they walk around the fire once. Then they begin to scatter the eagle down on the heads of the people. The master of ceremonies begins either with the ha'mshamtsEs or with the bear-fool dancers (nE'nq'olEla) (see p. 499 No. 16). Then he gives eagle down to the fool dancers and to all the other dancers.

Then the master of ceremonies goes around the fire again, swinging the baton. He stops in the rear of the house and strikes a box. All the people imitate him. Then a number of women, who are hired for the purpose, begin to dance. The people sing one song for each of the women. After this dance the chief of the quē'qutsa promises a feast for the next day, and the people go home.

The next morning a number of quē'qutsa go around from house to house to invite the people for the feast. The same women who danced the first night dance this evening. Again, a feast is announced for the following day. On this day, all the dancers who are allowed to wear masks enter first and arrange themselves behind the sail, wearing their masks. Then the people enter, and last of all the master of ceremonies, wearing his cedar bark ring, with his face painted red. Again he swings his stick from the elbow, turns in the house, says “wôi wôi,” and strikes the box. Then all the people beat the boxes for about ten minutes. Suddenly the master of ceremonies stretches out his arm and swings the baton slowly all around. The people stop beating time at once. He continues swinging his baton, and swings it faster and faster. Finally, he beats the box again, and again all the people begin to beat time. Now the dancers are heard behind the curtain, each with his distinctive sound. The curtain begins to shake and is lowered, revealing all the masks standing behind it. This is the end of the celebration of the third night. Again, a feast is promised for the next day. This evening the same ceremony is repeated, but after all the masks have appeared in the rear of the house, the young person who had disappeared at the beginning of the ceremonies comes out from the right-hand rear corner of the house. He sings his new song and dances. Then his father brings out all the property given to him by his father-in-law and distributes it among the people. Bracelets, <term>coppers</term>, and spoons are given to the women and children. Silver bracelets, kettles, and box covers are given to the men. Before the people go home, the chief promises another feast.

The following day the people assemble again, and a feast is celebrated in which everybody takes part. Before they begin to eat, the host brings all the button blankets which he has received from his father-in-law and distributes them. The women receive white blankets.

<meta>This page continues the description of Kwakiutl ceremonial procedures, moving from the conclusion of a feast and the naming of a novice to a specific ritual contest between the initiated dancers and the uninitiated "dogs."</meta>

This is called a present to wipe the mouth with (<term>dā'yaxstanō</term>). Each person receives one dish and spoons, which they take home after the *feast*. After this feast, the novice receives his name. Then the people leave the house. The purification of the novice is performed in the same way as described above (see p. 532).

Sometimes the <term>kuē'xalak<sup>u</sup></term> begins with a curious contest between the <term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term> and the profane. This ceremony is used by the Kwakiutl, Ma'malēleqala, Nimkish, Lau'itsīs, T'Ena'xtax, Ts'ā'watEēnôx, Axuā'mîs, and Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx. The tribes forming the Newettee and Koskimo groups use the ghost dance in its place. Mr. George Hunt told me the following instance of this ceremony's performance:

The Q'ō'mk'ūtīs, Walas Kwakiutl, and Kuē'xa had celebrated the <term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term> without inviting the Guē'tEla, the highest of the Kwakiutl tribes. Then the chief of the last-named tribe called all his people together in his house. He put up a long pole, the "winter dance pole," leaning it against the beam of his house, and asked his people, "Are you glad to hear the winter dance going on at the other end of our village while you are asleep in your houses? If you want to remain <term>bā'xus</term>, do so. If you want to join the winter dance, then one of you step up and touch this pole." As nobody stepped up to touch the pole, he put his hand on it himself and said: "I will be the <term>yē'wix·ila</term>; but first let us all turn ourselves into dogs" (<term>wā'tsē</term>; in the ordinary language, <term>waō'tsē</term>). Then all his people took off their clothing, even their earrings and anklets, with the women keeping only a small petticoat. They blackened their faces and hands and painted men's and dogs' faces all over their bodies. Then they cut the winter dance pole into pieces about a fathom in length each. The chief ordered them to cut a hole in the rear wall of the house. After this was done, they went out secretly and approached the house in which the other tribes were celebrating their winter dance from the rear. Then they barked like dogs, broke through the rear wall of the house, and drove out all the dancers, including even the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. They broke the canoes and all the belongings of the dancers. This was their revenge for not being invited to the festival. This ceremony is called <term>wā'ts'axt</term>, which means "dogs running from one house to the other."

Now the <term>ts'ēt'saēqa</term> assembled on one side of the street, while the "dogs" or the <term>bā'xus</term> assembled opposite them. The chief of the Guē'tEla, standing in front of his tribe, asked the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> of the other tribes, "Can you throw the supernatural power among us?" Then the <term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term> began to beat time, with the <term>que'qutsa</term> and <term>mē'emqoat</term> all standing together. Then the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> with the frog stepped out from among the <term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term> and danced like the <term>mā'maqa</term>, trying to catch her supernatural power. After some time, she apparently caught it in her hands and threw it against the "dogs." The first throwing is called the <term>laE'lk<sup>u</sup></term> (<term>dedā'LELAL</term> in the Newettee dialect), which means "laughing." The dogs laugh and bark all at the same time.

It also details the subsequent ritualized confrontation between the initiated dancers and these "dogs."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the ritualized contest between the ts'ē'tsaēqa (the initiated) and those acting as "dogs" (the profane or uninitiated) during the Kwakiutl winter ceremonial.</meta>

<page-num>544</page-num>
<header>REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.</header>

Then the <term>ts'ēt'tsaēqa</term> beat time again. Again the dancer caught her supernatural power, went forward and backward four times, turned around, and threw it against the dogs. Then they sat down, still laughing, and began to scratch their heads. Again they barked. The <term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term> beat time for a third time, and the dancer caught the supernatural power again. She went forward and backward with quick steps, turned around, and threw it again. Then the dogs rushed into the water, scratching and rubbing their bodies, which means that they are removing the <term>bā'xus</term> from their bodies. They barked and came out again.

Now the <term>quē'qutsa</term> of the other tribes assembled in a group by themselves and sent four men to the dogs, apparently to deliver some message, but actually in order to carry some red cedar bark to them. After they had returned, the dogs in their turn sent four of their number to fetch some more cedar bark. This is repeated four times, and is called <term>ts'ā'ts'ēxsila</term>—that is, pretending to carry messages.

Now the chief of the <term>quē'qutsa</term> spoke to his people: "Take care; do not give in, and remain what you are." All his people stood up. Then the <term>quē'qutsa</term> beat time again, and the dancer continued her dance. Suddenly she was seen to hold red cedar bark in her hands. Four times she went backward and forward holding the cedar bark and moving her hands up and down. She turned four times, and every time stretched her hands out as though she was going to throw the cedar bark against the "dogs." The fourth time she *really* threw it. Then all the people stooped, and when they stood up again they had cedar bark rings on their heads.

Then the <term>hāmats'a</term>, <term>nū'LmaL</term>, <term>nā'nē</term>, and the other <term>mē'emqoat</term> of the <term>Guē'tEla</term> began to get excited. The chief pushed his son toward them. They surrounded him and dragged him around until all of a sudden he disappeared. Then it was said that the supernatural power had taken him away from the <term>hā'mats'a</term>. This novice was now <term>kuē'xalak<sup>u</sup></term>. The chief next invited all the "dogs" and the <term>ts'ē'tsaēqa</term> into his house and announced that after four days he was going to try to bring the novice back. This is called <term>wā'sdana qap'ē'k<sup>u</sup></term>, or short assembly, and takes the place of the <term>qap'ē'k<sup>u</sup></term> ceremony described above. The <term>kuē'xalak<sup>u</sup></term> then continues as described before.

## X. THE WINTER CEREMONIAL AT FORT RUPERT, 1895-96.

In the preceding chapter I have given a general description of the ceremonial of the initiation of a single novice. When the ceremony is actually in progress, there are several novices to be initiated, feasts are being held, and numerous incidental ceremonies are performed which depend upon circumstances, such as atonement for mistakes, rivalry between chiefs, and so forth. In order to make clear the character of the ceremonial, I will describe in the present chapter the ceremonial as it actually took place and so far as I witnessed it in the winter of

1895-96. At that time three tribes had assembled at Fort Rupert (Tsā'xîs)—the Kwakiutl, the Koskimo, and Nā'q'oaqtôq. The Koskimo also included the G·ō'p'ēnôx, L'ā'sq'ēnôx, and Gua'ts'ēnôx. I reached Fort Rupert on November 15, 1895, and shall record here what I saw.

On the 16th of November, one of the Nā'q'oaqtôq gave a feast. The Kwakiutl had their seats in the rear of the house, the Koskimo on the right-hand side, and the Nā'q'oaqtôq on the left-hand side. When all had assembled, the chief speaker of the Nā'q'oaqtôq said: "Welcome, friends. Now that you have all come in, take the handles of your batons and sing."<note>1</note> Then the batons were distributed. Planks were laid for beating time. While the people were still coming in, one of the <term>quē'tsEm</term> (<term>quē'qutsa</term>) began to tease a fool dancer who intended to give up his dance and become a <term>quē'qutsa</term>. He pulled his nose, rubbed it with snow, and threw snowballs at it. As stated before, the fool dancer is supposed to have a long nose and to resent all allusions to the nose. He does not allow it to be touched. The <term>quē'qutsa</term> tried in this manner to excite him so as to prevent him from leaving the seal society and becoming a <term>quē'qutsa</term>. Finally, a number of <term>quē'qutsa</term> joined the first <term>quē'tsEm</term>. They pulled the nose of the fool dancer, spat on it, and smeared it with grease, despite his attempts to escape them. Finally, they tied him to one of the house posts and continued to maltreat his nose. Now the Kwakiutl sang two songs. They were followed by the Koskimo, who sang two songs in their turn. Meanwhile the meal, which consisted of soapberries, had been prepared, and the speaker held up a dish which was intended for the first <term>hā'mats'a</term>. He shouted: "This is the dish of Yaqoîs."<note>2</note> The dish was carried to him. The members of the seal society received their shares in order, then the women, and finally the <term>quē'qutsa</term>. Now the host turned to the fool dancer who was tied to the post and whom the people were teasing again. He said: "I will ask your friends to stay at their places for a little while because I am cooking for you and wish to feed you." Then several of the fool dancers came to his assistance. They licked the grease off his nose, untied him, and took him back to his seat. As soon as the dishes were distributed, the host's assistants began to prepare the second course, which consisted of rice. While the people were eating, the different societies uttered their cries:

> "The hens are pecking!"<note>3</note>
> "The great seals keep on chewing."<note>4</note>

When shouting these cries, the members of the societies lifted their spoons and seemed to enjoy the fun. Next, the Koskimo tribe lifted their spoons and all cried "yū." Then they ate as quickly as they could, and all the different <term>quē'qutsa</term> societies competed with each other, singing all at the same time.

Next, a man stood up who acted as if he were a Haida. He gave a speech during which he made violent gestures, imitating the sound of the Haida language. An interpreter who stood next to him translated the intended meaning of his speech, which was supposed to be a message of thanks to the host for the soapberries. This was because they were one of the main food articles of the Haida, and the speaker was pleased to eat the kind of food he was used to in his own country. He continued, saying that he carried a box filled with food which he was going to give to the person who could pronounce his name. Then the host's daughter was called upon and asked to say his name. He began, "Ga'tsō," which she repeated; "Sē'as," which she also repeated; then followed, spoken very rapidly, "Qoagā'ñ Gustatē'ñ Gusgitatē'ñ Gusoa't Qoag·ē'ns Qaqa'xsLā."<note>This joke has been known for about eight years and is often repeated.</note> Then she said, "I cannot say this; I must go to school in order to learn it." The Haida asked her to go to school with him for four nights; then she would know it. The girl's father interrupted them, saying that he wanted to wash his daughter before she went to school with him.

Now the Kwakiutl and the Koskimo sang two songs each before the rice was served. After the songs, the host's father-in-law, who had provided the rice for the feast, spoke as follows: "O friends! I have not finished providing food for the marriage of my daughter to my son-in-law"; and turning to his son-in-law, he continued: "Do not say that word. Do not refuse my kind offer, or else I shall be ashamed. I do not do the same as other people, who only pretend to give feasts, giving only to those who have to buy my property from me."<note>The son-in-law had hesitated to accept the rice for this feast, and the old man referred to this fact.</note>

*November 18.*—In the morning, the Kwakiutl assembled in their secret meeting place in the woods. A new bear dancer and fool dancer were to be initiated in the evening, and the plan for the festival was laid out. After their return, they were invited by one man of the tribe to a seal feast in which the Na'q'oaqtôq and Koskimo did not take part, because seal feasts are considered a privilege of the noblest tribe, namely, the Kwakiutl. The seal was singed and boiled. Then the skin, with the blubber still attached, was cut spirally all around the body and handed to the men who stood up all around the house. They received about a yard of blubber each. Then the host made a short speech; and after the four feast songs were sung, they all began to eat. After the blubber was finished, the meat was distributed in dishes and eaten.

In the evening, the father of the new bear dancer gave a feast. The Kwakiutl sat in the back of the house, the Koskimo on the left-hand side upon entering, and the Na'q'oaqtôq on the right-hand side. When everyone had entered, the members of the seal society came in—first the bears dressed in button blankets. They had bears' paws on their hands, worn like mittens. They remained standing in the doorway and looked around wildly. The next to enter was the Ts'ō'nōqoa, who, according to tradition, is sleeping all the time. She had her eyes closed and attempted to go to the back of the house, turning to the left, while the customary circuit is to the right. One of the messengers who was stationed at the door took her by the arm and led her to the right. A rope was stretched from the door to her place, along which she walked to her seat in the back of the house, feeling her way by means of the rope. The next to enter were the fool dancers. While they were going to the back of the house, a loud noise was heard outside. They pretended to be afraid, hid their faces among the people, and hurried to their seats in the back of the house. The noise came nearer, the door opened, and in came the killer whales—young men and boys dressed in blankets and having long carved fins attached to their backs. Some of these consisted of a sheath in which a carved board was placed so that it could be pulled out and dropped back by means of strings, thus giving the appearance of a fin which was alternately lengthening and shortening. The men came in stooping low, so that the fins stood upright. They blew like whales, turned in front of the fire, and slowly went to the back of the house, leaving the fire to their left, stopping and blowing on their way. After they had made one circuit, they disappeared again. Next, a number of people came in, spreading their blankets and imitating the motions and voices of ducks. They went to the back of the house. As soon as all had assembled, the people began to sing. Suddenly a man holding his young son in his arms rushed out of the right-hand back corner of the house, ran around the fire uttering the cries of the nū'L-

At the same time, he smeared his son's face with mucus from his nose, thus "imbuing him with the sacred madness of the *<term>nū'LmaL</term>*." The poor child was frightened and cried piteously during the ceremony. This was his initiation into the *<term>nū'LmaL</term>* society. It happened during an interval between the four songs that were sung before the meal.

After the people had eaten, the bear rushed out of the same corner from which the fool dancer had come. He was dressed in a bear skin and came out on all fours, pawing the ground, growling, and looking wildly at the spectators. The people began to sing the first of his new songs, and eighteen women danced to accompany the song in order to appease his holy wrath. The songs calmed him, and he disappeared again into the corner of the house from which he had come and where he was supposed to be initiated. After this, the second course was served, and then the people dispersed, each lighting his torch and making their way home along the dark street or down along the beach and up the narrow bridges that cross the stream leading from the beach to the street. Soon the flickering lights disappeared into the houses, where the fires were tended before everyone went to their bedrooms to rest.

On the 19th of November, the first *<term>hā'mats'a</term>* gave a feast of salmon and berries. Early in the morning, he himself, accompanied by the seal society, went from house to house with their faces blackened and dressed in their various ornaments—the fool dancers with their lances, the bears with their enormous paws. The fool dancers knocked at the doors with their lances. Then they entered and invited the people using the same words used on ordinary occasions. However, they did not raise their voices; they spoke the invitation in a low, growling tone. Whenever a person's name was mentioned whose meaning in some way offended the bears, they pushed the speaker—one of the fool dancers—so that he almost fell down. While the names were being called, the members of the seal society looked around angrily.

Generally, four calls are necessary to gather the people, but the seals do not allow them to linger. After they had called the first time, they went around appearing offended by the people's lateness. They carried a long rope, entered the houses, and the fool dancers pushed the people from their seats with their lances. The bear dancers scratched them and drove them toward the rope, which was stretched tight. Then the members of the society who held the rope pushed the people out of the house and onto the street. After arriving on the street, they drove them before the rope until they reached the dancing house. Thus, it did not take very long to bring the people together. About 3 o'clock in the afternoon, they began their second call, and by 4:30 p.m., all the people were assembled. By this time, the salmon was cooked; it was placed in long, flat dishes and fish oil was poured over it. The fool dancers and bear dancers distributed the dishes and the wooden spoons, with every three or four people receiving one dish. The Koskimo and Nā'q'oaqtôq were served first, and the Kwakiutl last. Etiquette requires that the guests eat as quickly as possible. Whenever the bear dancers and fool dancers saw someone eating slowly, they went up to him and pushed and scratched him. Throughout this time, a huge fire was maintained in the middle of the house, and grease was poured into it. The flames leaped up to the roof of the house, which occasionally caught fire, so that a man had to be sent up to put it out. It is considered improper for guests to pay attention to such fires, and they appear to take no notice of them until the host decides it is time to tend to the roof. He sometimes ignores the fire until it has grown to a considerable size.

When a number of fool dancers and bears began to eat despite his commands, some of the other members of the seal society took the food away and pulled them back. After all the guests had eaten, a large dish was placed on the plank that was laid in front of the door. When the people were teasing them, the friends of some of the members of the seal society stepped before them, spreading their blankets and thus hiding them from view, so that the people should not see them eating.

Now Hō'LElitē arose again and spoke: "This is the way of my chief. He gives a large feast on account of the nobility of my tribe." He asked the people to take the batons and to sing. The Nā'q'oaqtôq started and sang two songs. The Koskimo followed with four songs. In the fourth song, the word "raven" occurred. As soon as it was heard, one of the <term>hā'mats'as</term> of the Koskimo became excited. He jumped up, crying "hāp, hāp, hāp," trembling all over his body. His attendants rushed up to him, the people beat time violently, and the drummer beat the drum, while the <term>hā'mats'a</term> tried to rush up to the people and bite them. But he was held back by his six attendants. Slowly he moved to the rear of the house, where he went once to the left and once to the right, then continued his course around the fire. When he came to the door, he went out, followed by his attendants. Then the Koskimo called four times, "yū!"

While this was going on, NEg'e'ts'ē, the speaker of the Koskimo, arose, and as soon as quiet was restored, he spoke: "Take care, my tribe; the supernatural power has entered our <term>hā'mats'a</term> Nau'aqîs;" and turning to the Kwakiutl, he said: "Be ready, friends, you on both sides of the house; we will try to tame our <term>hā'mats'a</term>." This was said at the moment when the <term>hā'mats'a</term> ran out of the door. His attendants returned after an absence of about ten minutes.

November 20.—In the afternoon, the Koskimo sent their messengers to invite people to a feast. Around 6 p.m., the people had assembled in their dancing house. First, a Nā'q'oaqtôq distributed blankets among the people, and then one of their number stood up, holding a copper in his hands. He spoke about its value and said that he was going to buy it. Suddenly, whistles and noise were heard outside, and the Koskimo *hā'mats'a*, who had disappeared the previous night, entered, accompanied by his attendants. He danced around the fire once and disappeared again. Then the speaker of the Koskimo asked the Kwakiutl and the Nā'q'oaqtôq to sing. The Kwakiutl sang their two songs. The Nā'q'oaqtôq followed, but when they got out of time during their first song, Yā'qois—the principal *hā'mats'a* of the Kwakiutl—became excited. He jumped up, crying “*hāp, hāp, hāp*.” His nine attendants rushed to him, and while he was trembling violently, they moved once to the right and once to the left behind the fire, then around the fire; when they reached the door, they went out. During all this time, whistles were heard coming from the circle of attendants. While the Koskimo chief continued his speech, the whistles and the howling of the *hā'mats'a* were heard in the street. Soon he returned, dressed only in a dancing apron, two rings of cedar bark worn crosswise over his shoulders, and a heavy ring of red cedar bark worn on his head. For the first circuit, he danced in a squatting posture. When he was opposite the door, he was carried for a short time by his attendants. In the rear of the house, he turned once. The second circuit he danced standing, and the songs sung during this time were in a five-part measure. His feet were placed down with the beats of the batons. His knees were lifted high for each step, while his torso moved downward at the same time. After he had gone around the fire twice, his father dressed him in a fine *Chilcat* blanket and an apron and leggings of the same make, with which he made two more circuits around the fire. *November 21.*—Early in the morning, the old hā'mats'a of the Koskimo, with three attendants, was seen on the beach pursuing a number of women. It appears that they had taken some of the food that was intended for him, which had provoked his anger. He ran after them, trying to bite them, and they escaped into the water, which the hā'mats'a is supposed to fear. There he kept them for a long time; whenever they made an attempt to escape, he tried to bite them and drove them back.

"...you had a chief before this time, but now you have no chief." <note>This means that Nō'Lq'auLEla had become greater than all the other chiefs because of his numerous distributions of blankets.</note> Upon this, all the <term>Kwakiutl</term> said: "True, true; we cannot deny it." <note>K·'ēsnōX hē'Xoa.</note>

After these speeches were finished, food—which consisted of crab apples mixed with grease—was distributed among the guests. <note>The crab apples are picked while they are unripe, boiled, and kept in water.</note> When the people had almost finished eating, one of the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> gave a button blanket to his son-in-law as a promise of a great number of blankets which he was to give him at a later time. Then the recipient thanked his father-in-law. He took his staff, which he held horizontally on his shoulder, carrying it as though he were weighed down with the gifts from his father-in-law. Slowly he went around the fire singing his secret song—a <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> song, as he was a member of that society. He turned when he came to the front of the house and again when he reached the rear of the house. While he was still singing, all the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> singers assembled near the door. They held a plank to beat time on and began to sing. The man danced while they sang. After the second song, he put on the button blanket and danced, accompanied by the third song. During the fourth song, he took up some burning coals and laid them before one of the men. This was to indicate that he had power over the fire. Then he took another piece of burning coal between his hands and rubbed it; swinging his closed hands forward and backward, he suddenly threw them forward, and as they parted, the coals had disappeared. He had transformed the coal into a supernatural object which was to fly around the whole world to see if there was a chief greater than his father-in-law. He said it would return in four days to bring him an answer. Then he announced that he would keep the blanket which he had received and that he would not give it away, and the people replied: "Do as you say."

In the evening, the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> held their <term>kuē'xalakᵘ</term>. When all the people had assembled, the speaker thanked them for coming, and turning to his own tribe, he said: "Keep your batons in readiness!" As soon as he had said this, the door opened and two men came in wearing large blankets and imitating the motions of cormorants. They entered by twos and threes and gathered in the rear of the house, standing in a row. When all had come in, the speaker asked the first of the birds: "What is in your stomach?" He replied: "<term>Kwakiutl</term>." Then he asked the next one: "What is in your stomach?" He replied: "Four tribes," meaning the four tribes of the <term>Kwakiutl</term>. Turning to the third one, he asked: "What is in your stomach?" He replied: "The <term>Kwakiutl</term>, the <term>Koskimo</term>, and all other tribes." When he asked the next one, the man acted as though he were vomiting. This signifies that he was vomiting the property that was to be distributed at night. The fifth one said to the speaker that he had gone from tribe to tribe through

...the whole world swallowing the tribes.<sup>1</sup> After the speaker had questioned everyone in this manner, he thanked the cormorants for coming and said: "I am glad that you are not light cormorants, but that you are heavy with property."

Another signal was given to the singers to beat time, and the killer whales entered. They also came in by twos and threes. They had fins made of wood tied to their backs and entered blowing. They moved in a crouched position so that the fins stood upright. Blowing, they went around the fire, where they remained standing next to the cormorants. Now the speaker said: "Do you know why we open our ceremonial with the entrance of the cormorants and the killer whales? In ancient times, when <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term> traveled all over the world in his canoe <term>Dā'daLa</term>, he came to <term>Goā'LgoaL'ā'lalîs</term>, where the village of the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> stands. Both the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> and the killer whales were living there at that time. <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term> left them and went to <term>Ya'xoēstEm</term>. After he had left, difficulties arose between the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> and the killer whales. When <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term> heard of this, he transformed some of the whales into birds and others into sand. For this reason, the sand of the beach at <term>Goā'LgoaL'ā'lalîs</term> makes a sound when it is stepped upon."

After he had finished his speech, the women came in dressed as birds. They danced around the fire and stopped next to the cormorants and killer whales. Then the speaker continued: "Do you know what this means? The birds were living at <term>Ya'xoēstEm</term> when <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term> arrived there. They were living in a cave. <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term> painted them different colors. The crows and the cormorants wanted to be made more beautiful than all the others and waited until the very last; but then they found that <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term> had used all his paint and had only some charcoal left, which he used to paint them. Therefore, they are black. After the birds had been painted, they came dancing out of the cave. At that time, <term>Kuēkuaxā'oē</term>'s canoe was burned. If you do not believe what I have said, <term>Koskimo</term>, come and visit me and I will show you the place." After this speech, the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> distributed their blankets among the <term>Kwakiutl</term> and <term>Koskimo</term>.

After this was done, a messenger entered the house and said: "Some strangers are on the beach." The speaker of the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term> sent a man out, who took a torch and went down to the beach. Soon he returned and informed the speaker that some white men had landed and asked for permission to enter. The speaker sent for them, and the messengers came back leading a young Indian girl who was dressed in European costume, with a flashy hat, a velvet skirt, and a silk blouse. Then they asked <term>Nō'Lq'auLEla</term> what he thought of her—if he thought she was wealthy. They asked him to send her back if she appeared to be poor. He looked at her and said: "I can easily distinguish between the rich and the poor, and I see she is wealthy. Let her stay here." Then the speaker

...looked at her and said: “Oh, that is Mrs. <term>Nū'lē</term>.” They led her to the back of the house and asked her if she was carrying anything in her pocket. She produced a roll of silver quarters, which the speaker took and distributed among the people. By this time it was near midnight. Then the speaker said: “Let us take up the purpose of our gathering.” 

The festival was for the initiation of a new <term>q'ō'minâqa</term>. About two weeks before the festival, the host’s daughter, who was a <term>q'ō'minâqa</term>, had died, and he wanted his niece to take her place. The festival was to be her initiation. She had been hidden in a secret room at the back of the house, and when the singers began the songs of the deceased girl, she appeared wearing a blanket, a dancing apron, a round neck ring, and a high head ring that was covered all over with down. She danced very slowly around the fire, accompanied by two attendants. Her hands trembled. They were held horizontally forward and slightly bent, with her elbows resting at her sides. When she appeared, three women began to dance at the back of the house in order to calm her. After four circuits, she disappeared into her room, followed by her two attendants and the three dancers. 

When the second song began, she reappeared and danced in the same manner as before. At the end of the song, she went back to her room. During the third and fourth songs, she grew quiet and danced like the other women. When she appeared for the fourth time, she wore a huge, round head ring. She was accompanied by an old woman, the aunt of the deceased girl, who wore no ornaments and whose disheveled hair hung loosely over her face. This indicated that she was in deep mourning.

Soon after the ceremony ended, a man's song was heard in front of the house. He approached slowly. Then the door opened and a naked person appeared, wearing only an apron, a head ring of red cedar bark, and arm rings and anklets made of the same material. He stayed in the doorway for a long time, singing his secret song. Then he came forward, looking upward, with his hands laid flat against the back of his thighs. With short, quick steps, he ran around the fire. The audience became restless because they feared him—the <term>mā'maq'a</term>, the thrower of sickness. 

When he entered, all the <term>hā'mats'a</term> had to leave the house. As soon as he began his circuit, a man holding a rattle ran up to him and followed all his movements. As soon as the <term>mā'maq'a</term> reached the back of the house, he gave a high jump. The drummer beat the drum rapidly and, all of a sudden, the <term>mā'maq'a</term> had caught his magic stick, which he held between his palms, extending it and then shortening it again. Suddenly, he threw it into himself. The staff disappeared, and he fell backward in terrible contortions. Blood came pouring out of his mouth and chest. After some time, he pulled the stick out of his mouth, recovered, and continued his dance. He tried to catch the stick again, looking upward and holding his hands close to his thighs. As soon as he had caught it, all the people stood up, and when he threw it, they stooped down, hiding in their blankets and crying, “wā.” The first time he threw his stick, it did not

The man who had accompanied the mā'maq'a's dance with his rattle acted as though the stick had entered his throat and was suffocating him. As soon as the mā'maq'a had thrown a second time, he disappeared into the secret room at the rear of the house. Soon he reappeared, singing over the dead, who were carried into the secret room. Shamans were called, who sang over them and cried "hoîp," while the mā'maq'a danced a third and a fourth time, catching and throwing his stick, without, however, hitting anyone else. This was the end of the ceremony.

November 22.—In the morning, the Koskimo held a secret meeting, at which it was decided that Q'ē'q'anqoala was to perform the dance *Bā'baqoayūl* (soul catcher). In this dance, which is described on page 575, the dancer pretends to capture the soul of one of the audience members; however, a certain amount of property is used to symbolize the soul. Therefore, when a dancer catches a soul, it means that he takes a certain amount of property from the owner, which is then to be distributed among the guests. For this reason, the speaker asked at this meeting:

> "Q'ē'q'anqoala is going to perform his dance. I want to know if anyone wishes for him to capture their soul."

Whoever intended to distribute blankets offered his soul, saying:

> "Q'ē'q'anqoala, capture my soul, for I want to give away blankets to our rivals."

The speaker thanked them for their offer. The soul is represented in the dance by a small ball of eagle down attached to a string. As many balls are attached to the string at equal distances as there are men who offered their souls to be captured.

In the afternoon, the Kwakiutl held a meeting at the assembly place in the woods, where they laid out the plan for the *kuē'xalak<sup>u</sup>*, which was to take place that same evening. The Koskimo intended to have a festival on the same day but finally gave it up because of the one to be held by the Kwakiutl. The people assembled in the evening. The Kwakiutl sat in the rear of the house—the Koskimo on the right side upon entering, and the Nā'q'oaqtôq on the left side upon entering. The last to enter were the members of the seal society, who took their seats in the last row at the rear of the house. The singers sat in front of them, while the old chiefs occupied the front row. When all had assembled, the speaker of the Kwakiutl arose and said:

> "Welcome, friends, on both sides of the house. We are all here in our dancing house."

And turning to the members of the seal society:

> "Do not leave too soon, great friends."

Now turning to the Kwakiutl, he said:

> "Now be ready with your batons."¹

Everyone expected that the hā'mats'a would get excited and watched him anxiously, but everything stayed quiet. X·ī'x·ēqala continued: "This is the strength of my clan. No other Kwakiutl clan has ever broken as many expensive coppers as we have." With every copper that he named, he struck his staff down forcefully, bending his knees at the same time. Then he turned to the G·ē'xsem and said: "I thank you for the button blankets and for the 2,000 bracelets," and he immediately promised to distribute the blankets among the Nā'q'oaqtôq.

After he had spoken, Lē'Lēlaku asked his brother-in-law, "What happened to the 40 blankets which I gave you at the time of my marriage to your sister? If you do not want to pay them, say so; but if you do intend to pay them, let me know. Do as you please; I do not care." Then his brother-in-law replied that he was going to pay in due time. Lē'Lēlaku then promised to give the 40 blankets to the Koskimo.

Now Hō'Lelitē arose and said: "You have finished. Now let us take up the purpose of our gathering." The blankets were put aside. As was stated before, the festival was to be a kuē'xalak"—that means the initiation into one of the lower ranks of the secret societies. The person to be initiated was the son of Sē'g·ag'ila, who had arranged this feast. He gave his membership in the fool dancer society to his young son. The people began to sing a fool dancer's song. Then suddenly a fool dancer rushed out of the right-hand rear corner of the house, carrying his young son in his arms and crying, "wiē', wiē'." At the same time, he cleaned his nose and put the mucus on the boy's face. This is done because it is believed that the power of the fool dancer resides in the mucus. After he had run around the fire once, he disappeared again behind the curtain drawn at the back of the house. Hō'Lelitē arose again and said: "This is Nułt'aqā'lag·ilis," thus naming the place which the boy was to occupy. The people sang again, and a woman wearing the headdress of the Nā'naquauaLiL came out. Another woman danced backward in front of her. A man carrying a rattle accompanied her. This dance was not an initiation, but only a representation of the dance which X·ī'x·ēqala had obtained from his wife by marriage. After this dance was finished, a young boy was to perform another Nā'naquauaLiL dance. He came out and danced once around the fire, accompanied by one man carrying a rattle and three others who watched him. He wore a head ornament with four horns. After this dance, he disappeared behind the curtain, and when the second song commenced, a large mask representing the sunrise Na'xnaik·êmL appeared at the back of the house, coming from behind the curtain. It was a double mask, which in the course of the dance was to open. When the wearer of the mask opened it, one side of the cover broke. Although the attendants rushed up to the mask immediately, trying to cover it, the hā'mats'a had seen what had happened.

After a while, the Koskimo returned to the dancing house, with four men going first, each carrying a staff held horizontally, and each singing his own song.

They were *Wīnā'lag·ilîs*. They led a young girl who wore a head ring. She had just been initiated into a secret society.<gloss>2</gloss> Then two of the speakers spoke at the same time. "Koskimo, you have a hard task; you must kick against a high mountain. <note>This means that they had to strive against the Kwakiutl.</note> <term>Wīnā'lag·ilīs</term> or <term>Hai'alilaqas</term> has killed this boy, the son of <term>XExuā'NElq'ala</term>, the <term>pa'xala</term>. The supernatural power came and took him away. He is dead. We will try to resuscitate him."

As soon as he said so, the <term>mā'maq'a</term> tried to throw the body into the fire. <note>As this was entirely unplanned, the ceremony was not carried out as it is in other cases. If the performance had been planned beforehand, the <term>mā'maq'as</term> would have provided themselves with a skeleton, which they would have carried in their arms instead of the child. They would have thrown the bones into the fire, and after the charred remains had been seen by the people, they would have made them disappear in a ditch made for the occasion, and the boy would have risen at the place where the charred bones had been seen before.</note> <term>T'ē't'ēsumx·tsana</term> and <term>T'ō'pēwa</term> pushed them back and asked for assistance. Now they put the body down on top of a box and <term>T'ō'pēwa</term> asked the highest <term>pa'xala</term> of the tribe to try to resuscitate the boy. <term>Lō'Xoaxstaak<sup>u</sup></term> came and sang his secret song. Then he spoke to the Kwakiutl: "Friends, if you have a mask for the winter ceremonial which you want to show, do not let a stranger use it; teach your own people to show it, so that no mistake may occur. Only because a stranger showed your mask a mistake happened and brought about our great difficulty. I say so, <term>T'ō'pēwa</term>." <note>He spoke on behalf of the latter and therefore used his name.</note> Then he went around the fire singing. After he had made one circuit, the women joined his song and a deep-sounding whistle was heard, which represents the breath of the <term>pa'xala</term>. He sang four songs, and after every song the whistles were heard. Every time it sounded the Kwakiutl beat time and cried "hä, hä, hä, hä." Then the boy began to move again and pretended to come to life. This was the end of the festival.

When all was over, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> of the Koskimo appeared once more and ran around the fire, followed by his assistants. Then he disappeared again.

**November 23.**—Early in the morning the Koskimo dressed themselves to meet their novice. Two messengers went through the village and asked the people to clear the floors of the houses and to sweep them. They arranged themselves in two groups—first the <term>wī'xsâ</term>, then the <term>lā'xsâ</term>. One of the former carried a skin drum. The men walked first. They were followed by the women, among whom was the new <term>wā'tanEm</term>, who was initiated the previous night. The men were singing while the women were dancing. The <term>wā'tanEm</term> danced, raising her hands alternately, her elbows close to her sides, the palms of the hands upward. She had four feathers on her head ring. She did not dance with the first song, but joined the dance during the second, third, and fourth songs. The <term>lā'xsâ</term> followed the <term>wī'xsâ</term> at a short distance. The men were singing, a woman beat a skin drum, and others, among them another <term>wā'tanEm</term>, were dancing. Thus they walked from one house to the other. At times the <term>hā'mats'a</term>, accompanied by some of the <term>fool dancers</term> and <term>bears</term>, would leave the house and attack the people. In the afternoon, all the members of the <term>seal society</term> appeared on the roof of the house. Every society howled its unique cries, and the <term>fool dancers</term> threw stones at the people. During all this time, people were forbidden to pass in front of the house. Whenever anyone approached the house, the members of the <term>seal society</term> frightened them away. While they were on the roof of the house, all standing at the front edge of the roof, a man approached. Immediately, the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and <term>bears</term> jumped down and pursued him. The <term>fool dancers</term> climbed down the sides of the house, and they all went in hot pursuit until the man escaped into one of the neighboring houses. Whistles of the different societies were heard in the house all day long.

About 6:30 in the evening, <term>Lāgulā'g·alīL</term> and <term>Lō'Xuals</term> blackened their faces, put on blankets and belts, as well as head rings and neck rings of red cedar bark, and scattered eagle down on their heads. Then they left the <term>dancing house</term> and opened the door of the neighboring house. There they stood, and <term>Lāgulā'g·alīL</term> cried: “Now, <term>quē'qutsa</term> men and women, let us go into the house;” and <term>Lō'Xuals</term> added: “We will pacify our cannibal.” In this way, they went from house to house. When they had returned from their round, four young men went and called the people, saying: “Now we come to make you rise.” While they were still going around, some of the <term>Koskimo</term> gathered in the <term>dancing house</term>, beat the boards, and cried “<term>yū</term>” twice, giving a short final rap with each cry. As soon as the <term>Kwakiutl</term> heard the beating, they all went to the <term>dancing house</term>. There the beating and the cries were repeated twice.

About 8 p. m. all had assembled in the <term>dancing house</term>. The men of the <term>Koskimo</term> tribe were sitting in the rear portion of the house. Then <term>LoXuaxstaakᵘ</term>, a <term>Koskimo</term>, stood up and spoke: “Come, friends, so that you may see the way in which I perform the winter ceremonial. This was given to us by the creator of our ancestors. Your ways, <term>Kwakiutl</term>, differ greatly from ours. They were given to you in the beginning of the world. Take care and do not change your old customs, <term>Kwakiutl</term>!” Then he turned to his tribe and asked them to hold their batons in readiness. While he was speaking, he held his staff in a horizontal position. Then <term>Ho'Lelītē</term>, chief speaker of the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, replied: “Your speech is good, friend. It is true what you said. I am glad to see that you are adhering to the customs that were given to you;” and, turning to the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, he continued, “We must answer our friends.”

Now the rest of the <term>quē'qutsa</term> of the <term>Koskimo</term> entered—first <term>G·a'loīL</term>, the chief speaker of the dancers. He held a speaker's staff in his hands and carried a number of blankets over his shoulder. He was singing his secret song while the others were singing outside the house. He sang as follows:

1. I tried to tame them by the power of my magic, friends.
2. I blew water upon them to tame them, friends.

As soon as he entered, *Tō'qoamalīs* and *Lāgulag·ālīL*, the chiefs of the *Koskimo* who had been sitting at the back of the house, stood up, and with them their speaker, *Qoa/lx·ala*.

*NaqwaLayē*'s head ring belongs to the descendants of *Ya'xstaL* of the *Naqô'mg·i lisala*. According to tradition, the *Xōyā'lEs* <note>see also page 332</note> had killed all the *G·īg·ē'L'Em* except *Lēō'lExmut* and his three sons, the eldest of whom was *Ya'xstaL*. In order to make his sons strong, *Lēō'lExmut* dragged them over the beach around the island of *G·īg·ē'L'Em* so that the sharp shells cut their backs. Only *Ya'xstaL* survived this ordeal and gained supernatural strength. Then they went to wage war against the *Xōyā'lEs*. When they had reached *Ta'tsolīs*, a wolf came to their camp while they were asleep, threw *Ya'xstaL* on his back, and carried him away. From time to time, he put him down to see if he was still alive. When he felt his breath, he picked him up again and continued on his way. Finally, he reached the village of the wolves. He threw *Ya'xstaL* down in front of the chief's house and, having taken on human form, he whistled. Then many people came out of the houses to see who had arrived. They mistook *Ya'xstaL* for a sea otter, carried him into the house, threw him down, and began to butcher him. When they had cut open his chest and were about to open his belly, he jumped up and asked, "Will you help me take revenge on the *Xōyā'lEs*?" The wolves promised to help him and asked him, "What did you come here for? Do you want this wedge? It will help you build canoes so that you can reach your enemies." *Ya'xstaL* did not reply but only thought that he did not want the wedge. *WīLaqā'latit*, chief of the wolves, knew his thoughts at once. He asked, "Do you want the harpoon? It will enable you to kill enough seals at one time to fill your canoe." *Ya'xstaL* thought that he did not want the harpoon, and *WīLaqā'latit* knew what he was thinking. To this the speaker *Qoa'lx·ala* replied: “Your word is true, friend *G·ā'sa*. When I was young, I saw streams of blood shed in war. But since that time, the white man came and stopped up that stream of blood with wealth. Now we are fighting with our wealth. That is all.” Then he said, turning to his tribe, “Now, my singers, take your batons and be ready to sing.”

...to you, Kwakiutl. I promise to give its value to you, Guē'tEla, and to you, Q'ō'mōyuē, and to you, Walas Kwakiutl, and to you, Q'ō'mk·ūtīs. This is 'Killer Whale.' I want to sell it at once." Speaking thus, he gave it to Q'ēq'anqoala and said: "Go on! Place this copper before our friends." He did so. Then a Kwakiutl chief, Nō'Lq'auLEla, arose and spoke to Q'ēq'anqoala: "Bring the copper to me." He did so, and Nō'Lq'auLEla continued: "Oh, my tribe! My friends! Look at me. I, Nō'Lq'auLEla, took the copper for the sake of your name, Kwakiutl, because your name is above those of all other tribes and I do not want to see it mocked. Now, brother-in-law Nu'xnēmīs, look at me. I have nothing with which to pay for this copper, which I have taken a liking to. Therefore, I ask you and my wife, La'msitasō, to buy the copper for me. That is all, friends!"

To this speech, Mā'a, the Koskimo, replied: "There is no chief like you, Nō'Lq'auLEla. You are the first one to treat us well. You support your tribe with the strength of your wealth."

When he had finished, Tō'qoamalīs, chief of the Koskimo, took a pair of blankets and spoke: "Your word is true, Mā'a! Nō'Lq'auLEla is our chief, for he gave us more property than any other chief of the Kwakiutl. Go on, Nō'Lq'auLEla! Buy our copper," and, turning to his tribe, he concluded: "Thus I speak for our chief, Koskimo." Now he held up the pair of blankets and said: "Look at this, friend! This is our goodwill toward our friends on the other side" (meaning the Kwakiutl). "I want you to do as our friend G·ō'qoadē did, who brought the copper into our dancing house. Sell it for blankets and give them away! This pair of blankets served to keep our copper warm. I took it off in order to put it on some of our friends on the other side. This is for Yā'qoīs, Sē'īx, and Hō'LElitē. It is given by G·ō'qoadē, the daughter of Kō'kwīLala. That is all."

Then Mā'a and G·a'loīL went out, and immediately the <term>quē'qutsa</term> began to beat time and cried "yū!" all at the same time. When they had done so, the whistles of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> were heard on the roof of the house. Then Mā'a returned, carrying a staff to which an imitation of a scalp was attached. He was followed by G·a'loīL. Both remained standing at the door, one on each side, and Mā'a said: "Friends, did you hear that noise? If I am not mistaken, something dangerous is near us. Keep your batons ready."

While he was speaking, the door opened and the <term>hā'mats'a</term> Ya'xya-k·alag·īlīs appeared, crying "hāp, hāp, hāp." His face was blackened. He wore a head ring and a neck ring of red cedar bark. His neck ring was thin and set in two places with long fringes, indicating that this was the first initiation of the new <term>hā'mats'a</term>. He wore no blanket. He was accompanied by two attendants who carried rattles. One of them wore a large head ring of red and white cedar bark, the ring of the <term>mā'maq'a</term> of the <term>hēlig·iliqala</term> of the La'Lasiqoala tribe. <note>See "Indian Legends of the North Pacific Coast of America," Berlin, 1895, page 187.</note>

<summary>A Kwakiutl chief takes responsibility for purchasing a valuable copper to uphold his tribe's honor, followed by a ceremonial presentation of blankets and the dramatic appearance of a newly initiated hā'mats'a dancer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the Kwakiutl winter ceremonies, specifically detailing the ritual songs and dances used by the Koskimo to pacify the hā'mats'a initiate.</meta>

### THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

As soon as he entered, the Koskimo began to sing:

1. Your dance does not equal mine, for I am the giver of magic, hamē.
2. I have been in the secret room of BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē, the giver of magic, hamē.
3. BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē, the giver of magic, was in high ecstasy when I was near him and uttered his cannibal cry, BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē, the giver of magic, hamē.

The second song was as follows:

1. I am known here and all over the world, I the supernatural one.
2. I am renowned here and all over the world, I the supernatural one.
3. You are the great one who gives coppers, who gives property, the supernatural one.

While the people were singing, the hā'mats'a danced in the doorway in a squatting position, turned around, and danced toward the rear of the house. Two women danced for him, one to the right and one to the left of the door. When he had reached the left-hand rear corner of the house, Mā'a and G·ā'lōiL stepped forward and followed him, saying now and then: “Great is your magical power. Do not be too violent in your fury,” and the attendants cried “hōîp, hōîp.” Whenever the singers reached the end of a line, the hā'mats'a stopped dancing and cried “hāp.” The attendants gathered around him while the sound of whistles was heard.

After these two songs had been sung, Mā'a spoke: “Friends, we cannot pacify the great hā'mats'a with these two songs and by means of the dance of these two women. Now arise, women, and dance with him. If we do not succeed in pacifying him, we will always be troubled by him. We would not be able to eat in our houses because of him. Therefore, friends, sing again.” While he was speaking, the sound of the whistles continued. The hā'mats'a was crying “hāp.” Then Ā'Labala stepped up to him and dressed him in a black blanket and an apron and scattered eagle down on his hair.

Now the singers began the third song:

1. You are looking for food, great magician, you are looking for men, mā hā.
2. You are trying to eat as much as you desire, great magician, you tear off their skins, mā hā.
3. You go close to the secret room, great magician, you have been inside the secret room, mā hā.

During this song the hā'mats'a danced in a standing position. His movements were becoming less violent and the sounds of the whistles were becoming fainter. The cries of “hōîp” from his attendants, the singing of the men, and the dances of all the women were beginning to pacify him. At the end of the song the women took a rest. They had been dancing with their backs turned toward the fire, with the exception of two who were standing at the sides of the door and who stood facing the fire.

Now the speaker G·ā'sa joined Mā'a and G·ā'lōiL, who were standing near the door. Then the singers began the fourth song:

1. The chief cannibal of the whole world cried hāp; mē, hamā.
2. Now eat, chief cannibal of the whole world, mē hamā.
3. Do not try to hide from me, mē hamā.

The <term>hā'mats'a</term> was dancing even more quietly, first to the right and then to the left in the rear of the house, and then around the fire. In front of the fire, he squatted down, crying "hāp." His attendants gathered around him and shook their rattles, crying "hōîp." Then, at the beginning of the next line of the song, he continued his dance, and after four circuits, he disappeared behind the curtain which was stretched in the left-hand rear corner of the house.

Then Mā'a, who was still standing near the door with his two companions, spoke: "Friends on the other side of the house! Now our great friend is pacified." While he was speaking, Kō'kwiLala, the helper in the winter dance, swept the floor with hemlock twigs in order to prepare it for the following dances.

Then Ā'Labala, who was standing in the right-hand rear corner of the house, spoke: "Take care, friends on the other side of the house. Watch my customs, for they were given to my tribe—the Koskimo—and to the L'ā'sq'ēnôx and G·ō'p'ēnôx, and to you Gua'ts'ēnôx, by the Maker of the world. Your customs, friends on the other side of the house, differ from ours. They were given to you. I am glad to see that you, as well as we, are observing our old laws. Now Tabala, Ha'nk·ala, Tsā'xîs, and LōXuals, go and fetch our chief's blankets."

The four men left the house, and soon they returned carrying the blankets. G·ā'sa took one pair and said: "Hō'LElitē and Nu'xnēmîs, look at these blankets. That is the power of our winter dance. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> who just finished dancing is Ya'xyak·a'lag·ilîs, and these blankets will be given away in honor of his name and of his dance." Then he gave the first blanket to Yā'qoîs, the chief <term>hā'mats'a</term> of the Kwakiutl, and then to the other men in order. When all were distributed, Hō'LElitē spoke: "Friends, did you hear what G·ā'sa said? Everything he said is true, except for one remark in which he is mistaken. You said that your customs in regard to dances and festivals differ from ours; remember, we are all of the same name. That is all. Thank you for this red cedar bark that you gave us <note>meaning the blankets</note>. Now I have finished."

Then Qoā'qoaxst'ala walked around the fire, apparently without any purpose, but in fact as a signal for the dancers who were standing outside the house to enter. The door was flung open; Mā'a, G·ā'loīL, and G·ā'sa, who remained standing near the door, gave a signal to the singers, who began to beat time very rapidly. A song was heard outside the house, and now a dancer named K·uē'daqala entered with quick, short steps, his hands stretched backward under his blanket and his face blackened. He was both a <term>mā'maq'a</term> and a <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term>. As soon as he had come to the rear of the house, the singers ceased beating the boards. Mā'a said: "Thank you, friend, for coming to this dance."

Then G·ā'loīL gave another signal, and a female dancer named T'ē'La entered, her hands stretched forward. Again the singers stopped—

When he had finished, Lō'Xoaxstaakᵘ told the people to be careful, because he had heard the voice of Q'ē'q'anqoala, the <term>Bā'baqoayūL</term> (soul catcher).<note>This is a *t'ō'X'uît* dance of the G·ō'p'ēnôx. A string is fastened to his middle finger and a small ball of eagle down is fastened to the middle of the string. The details of this dance are described in the text. (See also p. 561.)</note>

As soon as he entered, all the dancers stooped down as though they were trying to hide, for fear that <term>Bā'baqoayūL</term> might take their souls. His aunt, Pō'sqaas, took a position to the left of the door, and while he was walking around the fire she danced the *ha'mshamtsEs* dance. When he came back to the place in front of the fire, all the people arose and he lifted his hands, the palms being held close together. This was repeated four times. When he stopped the fourth time in front of the fire, he opened his palms and the "soul" was seen between them. The speaker told the singers to stop beating the boards, and Mā'a went about among the people in order to find whose soul the dancer had caught. After a short while he turned to the people and said: "My friend Q'ē'q'anqoala has captured the soul of our chief Lā'qōlag·ilîs." Then the latter stepped forward and asked the singers to sing the song of Q'ē'q'anqoala and of his aunt Pō'sqaas.

1. I go to obtain your cedar bark ornaments, hā, your cedar bark ornaments, hamē me, hamē, hamē, hamē hē hamā hē hē hamā.
2. Now your dance will shine throughout the world wherever a winter dance is held; Giver of light, hamē mē, hamā.

During this song the <term>Bā'baqoayūL</term> was dancing on one spot in the rear of the fire in a bent position. Pō'sqaas was dancing the *ha'mshamtsEs* dance to the left of the door, and G·ā'sa and G·ā/loīL, the greatest *mā'maq'a* among the Koskimo, danced around the fire, their elbows held close to their sides, forearms held forward, hands closed, and thumbs stretched upward.

At the end of the dance Lā'qōlag·ilîs spoke to Q'ē'q'anqoala: "Come, my son! I thank you for bringing back my soul, for I am saved now." Then he called the two chief speakers, Ā'Labala and Lō'Xoaxstaakᵘ. They followed his summons, and he gave them a stick about 2 feet long. Lō'Xoaxstaakᵘ held it up and said, "Oh, friends on the other

This song and dance were given by the wolves to Ya'xstaL, and are used by his descendants to excite the <term>hā'mats'a</term> and warriors who go out to battle.

All the <term>Hahai'alik·awē</term> clans of all the tribes in the whole world have a right to a <term>hā'mats'a</term> with a raven whistle, for <term>Hai'alik·awē</term> had a <term>hā'mats'a</term> with a raven whistle at the place we name <term>Lala't'ē</term>, and his <term>hā'mats'a's</term> names were <term>Qā'yul</term> and <term>Qalamā'lag·ilîs</term>. We may use either of these names for our <term>hā'mats'a</term>. We will call him <term>Qā'yul</term> now, and if he should be taken away again by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>, we will call him <term>Qalamā'lag·ilîs</term>. You, <term>Kwakiutl</term>, always use hemlock branches for your <term>hā'mats'a</term>, for it was given to you in this manner by the <term>Maker of Man</term>. It was given to us to use balsam pine for our <term>hā'mats'a</term> and for all other dances. The white rings you saw on the head ornaments of our <term>hā'mats'a</term> are the same as those worn by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> when he was excited. The attendants passed ropes through these rings to tie him down, so that he might not leave his house and devour his people; and the trail of his ornament served for his attendant to hold him. You also saw the streaks of blood running from the corners of his mouth to the lobes of the ears. They indicate that <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> lives on nothing but blood. That is all."

He had hardly finished when <term>Lō'Xoals</term>, a <term>Koskimo</term>, came forward from the rear of the house holding a single blanket. He spoke: "Look at me. See this single blanket! I am tired of waiting so long at this place for one solitary, single blanket. Now I will show you that I do not care for a single blanket." He tore it, threw it into the fire, and continued: "Now, you who saw it in the fire, take good care to keep it warm. All single blankets will go there from now on. We are too great a tribe to receive only a single blanket each." Then <term>LamaLa</term> went up to him and stopped him. He held six <term>button blankets</term> and said:

"Friends on the other side! Each of us has something to say. <term>Lō'Xoals</term> has had his way by burning this blanket. <term>Kwakiutl</term>, he did not mean you. Do not feel offended by it. I have rivals in my own tribe and I must wake them up from their sleep, for they do not see that it is hard work for us to fight you with property. We are the <term>Koskimo</term>, who have never been vanquished by any tribe, neither in wars of blood nor in wars of property. Now I will ask you one thing: Treat me well. In olden times, the <term>Kwakiutl</term> mistreated my forefathers and fought them so that the blood ran over the ground.

About 7 p.m., November 23, <term>Hō'LElitē</term> sent two messengers, <term>NōLElag-ilīs</term> and <term>KuLE'm</term>, to call all the men of the <term>Kwakiutl</term> tribe to a secret meeting to be held in his house. > "Indeed, friends, you have fulfilled my wishes, for you all have come as soon as I sent for you.
