*November 24.*—Early in the morning, Hō'LElitē sent NŌLelag·ilîs and KuLE'm to call all the Kwakiutl. They went around and tapped at the outside walls of the bedrooms. The people rose at once and went out to the place where the <term>ĀmE'lk<sup>u</sup></term> is held. This place is about 150 yards from the east end of the village at the edge of the woods. The men went into the woods and cut off hemlock branches, from which they made head rings and neck rings; with these they adorned themselves, as well as the women. Then Nu'xnēmîs told the people to get ready for the first cry, and he himself sang out “hō” as loud as he could. Then all the people beat the boards, which were laid down at the place of meeting, and cried “hē.” Next, all the <term>ha'mshamtSēs</term> dancers—all of whom are women—were tied to a rope which was held by a man. The bear dancers were tied together in the same manner, and led by another man, one of the old bear dancers. Then the <term>ha'mshamtSēs</term> began to cry “wip wîp” and the bears began to growl. Now Nu'xnēmîs sang out again, “hō;” the people beat the boards and responded with the cry “hē.” The <term>ha'mshamtSēs</term> began to cry “wip,” the bears began to growl “wo hā,” and the fool dancers cried “wīhī'.” After a short interval, Nu'xnēmîs sang out “hō” for the third time, and the people and the dancers responded in the same manner. Then, while the men were still beating time and while the various cries were being uttered, Yā'qoîs, the chief <term>hā'mats'a</term>, rushed out of the woods, followed by his six attendants, and crying “hāp, hāp, hāp, hāp.” He ran about among the people in a state of great excitement.

When Nu'xnēmîs left the house, he cried again "hō," and all the people responded "hē," but the <term>hā'mats'a</term> cried "hāp, hāp, hāp, hāp," the bears cried "wo, hā," the fool dancers "wihī," and the <term>hā'mshamtsEs</term> "wîp, wîp." After they had visited four houses, Nu'xnēmîs led them back to the winter dancing house of Sē'g'ag·ila. They were marching in the same order as before. Just before they entered, HŌ'LElitē spoke: "Friends, I noticed one of our number is missing." The people asked who it was, and he replied: "It is the son of our friend Sē'g'ag·ila. The spirits have taken him away. Let us go into the house and see what we can do for our friend." Then the people entered. As soon as all were inside, the whistles were heard in the <term>hā'mats'a's</term> room. Then HŌ'LElitē spoke: "Enter this house of our ancestors and observe the rules that were laid down for the winter ceremonial. Now be happy. I thank you that you all have come to this morning's ceremonial, for I do not like to have the Koskimo or other strangers laugh at us. If any of you had gone home before we finished, they might have had cause for doing so. We have done well, and the spirit of the winter dance is pleased with our work; otherwise he would not have taken one of our number with him. Therefore I myself and my friend Nu'xnēmîs are pleased with you. We cannot do anything without you, for what is the power of a chief without the help of his tribe? You call me and Nu'xnēmîs chiefs of the winter ceremonial, but we have no power without you. Now I have finished." Then Nu'xnēmîs sang out once more "hō," the <term>t'ō'X'uît</term> repeated her secret song, and when she had finished HŌ'LElitē gave the signal for the people to beat the boards. She stretched her hands forward and caught the supernatural power in the same manner as described before, and threw it upon the people, who cried again. Three times she caught it and threw it upon the people. The fourth time after she had caught it she threw it up into the air. Then she sat down.

Now HŌ'LElitē arose and spoke: "O friends! Do you see how I look? I am almost ready to run away from this house of the supernatural power. I was standing near the post and next to me was standing K·ēx·'s son. As soon as our friend Wīlanqoā'lag·ilîs caught the supernatural power the fourth time and threw it upward, it came and took the son of our chief K·ēx· along. Friends, there was one taken away this morning,"

Then <term>Nu'xnēmis</term> called all the men together, struck the board once, and cried, “wō wō ai.” Then all the people struck the boards together and cried, “wō wō ai a ai a k·as ai,” beating time rapidly for a few minutes. Then <term>Nu'xnēmis</term> struck the board with one sharp stroke and cried, “wō.” Then all the people did the same, all striking the boards at the same time with one short, loud rap. Immediately following this rap, they beat the boards rapidly, crying “hē,” drawn out very long. Then they were quiet, but the whistles continued to be heard.

<term>G·a'lg·axōla</term> said: “You have failed to drive away the spirits with this song.” Then <term>Nu'xnēmis</term> gave another rap and cried, “hama ma ma.” Then all the people began to strike the boards rapidly and cried, “hama ma ma ma ma,” continuing to beat the boards for a few minutes. This cry is intended to drive away the grizzly bear. Then <term>Nu'xnēmis</term> gave a short rap, crying “hamam” at the same time, and all the people gave a short rap and cried, “hama ma ma,” and then stopped beating. The whistles were still heard.

Then <term>G·a'lg·axōla</term> said: “You have missed the spirit of the cedar bark again.” <term>Nu'xnēmis</term> struck the boards as before and cried, “yihi i i i.” Then the people took up the cry in the same manner as before, crying, “yo hi i i i hū ū ū ū,” and again <term>Nu'xnēmis</term> gave the signal to stop, as before, with the cry “yihi,” and the people finished by crying, “yihi i i i hū ū ū ū.” Still, the whistles continued to be heard.

Now the people ate, and when they had finished, most of them went home. The <term>hā'mats'a's</term> whistles were heard during this time in his room.

About 2 p.m. the people came to fetch blankets, which were to be given away in honor of <term>Ya'qoîs</term>, in payment of his last ecstasy <note>A state of ritual trance or religious fervor</note>. When the blankets were being brought into the house, the <term>tally keeper</term> of the <term>G·ō'p'ēnôx</term> came in to look after the proper distribution of the blankets. He gave the names of the clans and the number of blankets which were to be given to each name in each clan. The blankets were arranged in such a manner that those intended for each clan were laid in the same direction, while those of the next clan were placed crosswise on top of the preceding lot. Wherever a man was to receive blankets who still owed some to the giver, a number of sticks corresponding to the number of blankets due were placed in the pile; these were given to the debtor as a way of canceling the debt, according to the number of sticks. After the pile intended for the <term>G·ō'p'ēnôx</term> was arranged, the <term>tally keepers</term> of the other tribes came in and looked after the blankets which were to be given to them. In the evening a feast was given, the blankets were distributed, and shortly after the beginning of the feast the <term>hā'mats'a</term> <term>Ya'qoîs</term> came in and danced three times; the first and the second time in a squatting position with an ordinary blanket, but the third and fourth time in a standing position and wearing a <term>Chilcat blanket</term>. As everybody was tired on account of the long ceremonies of the preceding nights, the feast closed early.

November 25.—Early in the morning <term>T'ō'kuiL</term>, chief of the <term>Koskimo</term>, sent his two speakers, <term>Ā'Labala</term> and <term>WalkaLtsemt</term>, to the chiefs of the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, to inform them that on this day the <term>Koskimo</term> intended to perform their ceremonies, and requesting them to postpone their festivals to another day. They also asked them to keep the matter a secret from the young men. At the same time the speakers invited the <term>Koskimo</term> to come quietly to the house of their chief. other <term>hā'mats'a</term>, who is going to come back to us today. That is all. These are the rules of <term>G·ē'xdEn</term>, who came down from heaven. My grandfather was of the blood of <term>G·ē'xdEn</term>, according to the tradition. Be very careful, for the <term>Kwakiutl</term> tribes will watch us closely. They will try to find fault with our laws, for they have ways of their own which differ widely from ours. They have no winter ceremonial of their own, and they will try to learn from us. I am not ashamed to show our winter ceremonial, for it is derived from tradition. That is all."

With this he sat down and <term>Ā'Labala</term> arose. He said: "O <term>Koskimo</term>! You have heard the rules of our grandfathers. Try to remember them, and do not forget what our chief has said, for he might die and I might die as well, and then one of you must take my place. That is all, my grandchildren."

Next <term>Lā'gulag·ilis</term>, the chief of the painting, arose and said: "<term>Tō'qoa-malis</term>, it is true what you said. We have traditions which teach us our laws. We are not like our rivals, the <term>Kwakiutl</term>. I tried to discover the origin of the names which they use in the winter ceremonial, but no one could tell me, for they have no traditions. Therefore you, <term>Koskimo</term>, my tribe, may laugh at the little <term>Kwakiutl</term>; for each of our clans has a tradition, or even two, and we may justly be proud of it. Look at me and my name. According to the tradition that was told me by my grandfather, the first <term>Lā'gulag·ilis</term> was the chief of the paintings for the winter ceremonial. That is now my name. It belongs to the tradition of my clan, the <term>G·ē'xsEm</term>. And my name has existed from the beginning of the world. When the <term>Kwakiutl</term> desire to discover the true history of our ceremonials, tell them the tradition of <term>G·ē'xdEn</term>, for our chief, <term>Tō'kuil</term>, is giving his winter ceremonial. Now take care, my tribe. You are aware that I am the chief of the paintings and of the ornaments of the <term>quē'qutsa</term>. We are all prepared now, for we are painted with charcoal that we obtained from <term>Ya'xstaL</term>, according to the legend of the <term>Naqō'mg·ilisala</term>. You know how he obtained the fire of death from the wolves at <term>Ḹayail</term>. You also remember how he burned his enemies to ashes and transformed them into stone by means of his fire of death. Our paint is that of <term>Ya'xstaL</term>, therefore we use only black paint and no red paint. The other tribes use very little charcoal and much red paint, because they have no traditions to guide them. I do not allow any red paint to be used in the winter ceremonial, because our traditions do not say anything about the use of red paint. Only the <term>NaE'nsx·a</term> clan are allowed to use red paint, for their chief, <term>Nēna'laats'ēqa</term>, used red paint in the <term>nō'nLEm</term> dance, to indicate the blood of the tribes whom he had killed. Therefore they use no charcoal, but red paint only. They also use white paint in the <term>nō'nLEm</term> dance, because <term>Nēna'laats'ēqa</term> brought this ceremonial down from heaven, and the white paint symbolizes the white clouds. All our ceremonials are founded on traditions which our ancestors were careful to preserve. Now I have finished my speech." <note>See p. 410 and figs. 129–133, pp. 484–486.</note>

<summary>Leaders of the Koskimo tribe discuss the divine origins of their winter ceremonial and differentiate their strictly tradition-based customs from those of the Kwakiutl. The chief of paintings explains the symbolic use of charcoal, red paint, and white paint based on specific clan legends and ancestral spirits.</summary>

Then <term>G·ā'sa</term> arose and said: "Did you hear the speech of our old chief? It made me feel proud and happy, for I am a young man and did not know how we obtained our winter ceremonial. Let us remember the speeches and traditions of our ancestors. Take care, <term>mā'maq'as</term>, <term>hā'mats'as</term>, <term>maa'myaank^u</term>, and you, <term>quē'qutsa</term> of the <term>Koskimo</term>, <term>Gua'ts'ēnôx</term>, and <term>L'ā'sq'ēnôx</term>, for we are all one tribe now. Do not fall and do not laugh, so that the <term>Kwakiutl</term> may not sneer at us. I am going to watch you carefully, and if I see anyone breaking the laws of the winter ceremonial, he will be made a <term>wā'tanEm</term>. He will have to wear a long white feather and dance in all the houses of the <term>Kwakiutl</term>. After his dance, he will have to distribute at least one hundred blankets. This will be the punishment for any violation of the rules of our ancestors."

When he had finished, two men, <term>Nā'kualē</term> and <term>Walx·aLtsamt</term>, entered, and the latter spoke: "Be quiet, slaves of the red cedar bark! I have seen our two chiefs who were taken away by <term>G·ē'xdEn</term>'s <term>Baxbakuālan-uXsī'waē</term>. They look dreadful, dressed in ornaments of balsam pine. I narrowly escaped them." <term>G·ā'sa</term> asked, "Is that true?" When he said this, a man who was standing on the roof of the house secretly gave a signal to the two new <term>hā'mats'as</term>, who were waiting in the woods at the west end of the village. They rushed down to the beach, crying "hāp, hāp." When the people who were assembled in the house heard them, <term>Tō'qoamalīs</term> sent <term>G·ā'sa</term> to the roof of the house to look around. He came back and said: "Slaves of the red cedar bark, prepare to meet our two new <term>hā'mats'as</term>."

Then the people left the house, the four <term>mā'maq'as</term> first. They were followed by the six <term>hā'mats'as</term>, who wore ornaments of red cedar bark and eagle down on their heads. Cedar bark was wound in four turns around their arms and legs. Next followed the <term>maa'myaank^u</term>, the young women, who also wore rings of red cedar bark, but no arm rings or leg rings. They had a belt of cedar bark and wore button blankets. Their faces were painted black, with three horizontal lines (one over the eyebrows, one over the lower part of the nose, and one just under the mouth) and four vertical lines (one downward from the middle of each lower eyelid, and one from the middle of each temple). When these three groups had left the house, the remaining <term>quē'qutsa</term> shouted "yū" four times. Then they all rushed out of the house and followed, in a separate group, the three preceding groups. The <term>mā'maq'as</term> were singing. The <term>hā'mats'as</term> walked on silently. Their heads and arms were held downward. The <term>maa'myaank^u</term> were singing and dancing, and the <term>quē'qutsa</term> cried "yū" every few minutes.

When they had reached the new <term>hā'mats'as</term>, the four <term>mā'maq'as</term> surrounded them. The six old <term>hā'mats'as</term> formed a circle around the <term>mā'maq'as</term>. They in turn were surrounded by the <term>maa'myaank^u</term>, who held each other's hands. The <term>quē'qutsa</term> surrounded the last in a half circle, also holding each other's hands. Only the four speakers, <term>Mā'a</term>,

Then <term>Mā'a</term> spoke: "Friends, we have caught the grandson and the sister of our chief, who were taken away by <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. We thought they might be dead and that they might never return. What in the whole world can vanquish us? Even <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> is unable to overcome us. I thought the <term>Kwakiutl</term> might have killed these two young people, because they cannot overcome us in our war of property. I am glad that they were taken away by the spirit of the winter ceremonial. We are a long way from our village, and I believed that the spirit of the winter ceremonial had stayed behind, but he is following us wherever we go. Now let us return to the woods and learn the song of our novices. <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> gives four songs to all the novices who go to his house, and certainly he has given songs to these two."

The two novices now ran back to the woods, crying "hāp," and the people ran with them. There they sat down. <term>G·ā'loīL</term> and <term>Qoaqoax·st'ala</term> took their seats in the middle of the whole group. Then <term>Mā'a</term> said: "Now listen, <term>Koskimo</term>! I will ask our singing masters to sing four new songs for these <term>hā'mats'as</term>. Try to learn them as quickly as you can. Sing, singing masters! And <term>G·ā'loīL</term>, put some words against the <term>Kwakiutl</term> into your songs." The first singing master of the tribe commenced his song, and after he had sung one line, he began to beat time. The people joined him, and after he had sung through the whole song, they tried to sing it. Next <term>Qoaqoax·st'ala</term> sang his song in the same manner. Then <term>G·ā'loīL</term> sang the third song, and finally <term>Qoaqoax·st'ala</term> the last one. The two singing masters asked the people if they liked the songs, and <term>T'ō'kuiL</term> thanked them, saying that they were just what he had wished for. Then the people arose and started to return to the village in the order indicated in fig. 188.

Before starting, they all put on head rings and neck rings made of hemlock branches. As soon as they reached the village, <term>Lō'Xoaxstaak"</term> shouted "wē'i, wē'i," and all the <term>quē'qutsa</term> responded "yū." Then the <term>hā'mats'as</term> began to run about and to dance in the circle, and the people struck up the new songs, beating time on boards that were carried by some of the <term>quē'qutsa</term>. The <term>maa'myaank"</term> also began to dance, and thus they proceeded until they reached the dancing house (Plate 45). The novices were the last to enter the house. There they danced around the fire. The <term>maa'myaank"</term> danced in their honor, and the old <term>hā'mats'as</term> joined their dance. After the second dance, they were clothed by <term>Mā'a</term>, and then they began to dance more quietly. After the fourth dance, they disappeared into their secret room.

...was going to buy a copper. A number of speeches were made, and a woman danced for Wā'las, for whom the people sang a song of joy. During the feast that followed this purchase, the *hā'mats'as* of the Koskimo sat on a platform with blackened faces, behind the *quē'qutsa*. (Plate 46).

The members of the seal society of the Kwakiutl were still confined to the dancing house, but every now and then they rushed out of it and knocked people down. The *hā'mats'as* struck them, and they broke canoes, dishes, and other things.

In the evening, the Koskimo had their *t'E'msEla*. When the four messengers were sent out to invite the people, the host blew four times upon them, and their head rings were strewn with bird down. Now, people were heard singing outside, but before they entered, some blankets were distributed. Three or four speakers carrying lances stepped into the doorway. Then a dancer entered, singing; his entire face was blackened. The speaker covered the dancer's mouth with his hands, forcing him to stop singing, and spoke to him. The dancer replied, "Nothing is heard." The speaker then left him, and he continued his song. He danced forward and raised his hands alternately. No one beat time to accompany his song. His head ring had a horn in front. During this time, the speakers were talking. Finally, the dancer was led to the back of the fire by the speaker who held the lance. Now the singers began to sing again. *QE'ldētsEm* and another old man performed a dance, and blankets were given away. Some blankets were held around the fire while the distribution took place. During this time, the speaker who carried the lances went to the door, and four women exited.

Now the speaker ordered the people to sing, and a *hā'mats'a*, accompanied by one assistant, entered. The beating of time continued for a while before the singing began. When the *hā'mats'a* reached the back of the house, seven women entered dancing. One of them remained standing near the door, while the others danced around the fire. In the dances of the Koskimo, one woman—whose duty it is to sing all the secret songs—remains standing in the doorway throughout the entire ceremony. At the end of the *hā'mats'a*'s second dance, some of the women danced out of the house again. After his first circuit, the *hā'mats'a* danced once to the right and once to the left at the back of the house, and then disappeared behind the curtain.

Now blankets were again distributed in honor of the preceding dance. Again, the women were heard singing outside. They entered wearing blankets and imitating the motions of birds; in this way, they danced to the back of the house, where they remained standing. They were followed by the speaker carrying the lance. One of them sang while the others danced at the back of the house. Then blankets were distributed among the *Nā'q'oaqtôq*. Next, a speaker with a blackened face went out.

Then the *mā'maq'a* entered, wearing a blanket. Men and women were talking to him. He placed his hands on a baby sitting in its mother’s lap and blew on it. Then he spoke in front of the curtain, and the people replied, "*wō*." Next, *QE'ldētsEm* appeared from behind the curtain, dancing. He was followed by the speaker carrying a lance and a man carrying his child in his arms. The child wore a *hā'mats'a* head mask. After they had circled the fire once, the singers began their song and the women danced. Some speeches followed.

A new dancer was announced. The singers began to beat time, and a woman, a *t'ō'X'uît*, entered dancing, her palms stretched forward and upward. A second woman and two men who carried guns and blankets followed her. She was painted black in the following way: her right cheek was entirely black, while on the left cheek two vertical lines extended down her whole face near the nose. Two horizontal lines ran from her lips to her ear, one a little above and the other a little below the mouth. A long conversation developed between her and the speaker. The people beat time twice. They divided into two groups and discussed how they would test her. One group went to the door and brought back weapons, saying they would kill her to see if her guardian spirit would protect her. Others said they would much rather split her open. Then the mother-in-law of the *t'ō'X'uît* stepped between the two groups and asked them to kill her instead; but when she began to strip off her blanket and shirt, they ridiculed her, asking if she was not ashamed to strip in front of so many people, and led her away. The young woman spoke again. Then the men went out. The speakers who held their lances talked, and after a short time, the three men returned. Some men holding paddles and staffs were standing in the front row in the back of the house. Then a woman and a girl ran out of the door, and there was great excitement among the people in the back of the house. One man cried, "I am the *sī'siuL*." Now the *t'ō'X'uît* took off her blanket and shirt and sat down. Then they led a girl around the fire to the back of the house. The girl carried a knife. During this time, one of the *Koskimo* women was singing. Now the speaker, whose face was blackened, took a paddle out of the hands of one of the men. The woman sat down behind the fire, in front of the singers. He stepped up to her while the other woman was dancing, her hands raised and trembling. Four times the man went around the woman. Every time he stood behind her, he raised his paddle as though he were going to strike her. The fourth time, he actually struck her, and the paddle entered deeply into her shoulder, and blood was seen to flow down. QE'ldētsem also put his hands on her head, chest, and shoulders, crying “hōî, hōî, hōîfff.” While this was going on, some of the women arose from their places and danced. Then the two shamans who had been working over her raised her to her feet and led her around the fire. The blood had ceased to flow, but a deep cut, beginning at the right breast and going across her shoulder far down the back, was clearly visible. Then all the people cried “hū,” and she went out. Now a Nā'q'oaqtôq spoke, and blankets were distributed.

At 12:30, a new dance began. The girl who in the preceding dance had carried a knife came from behind the curtain and danced. A number of women danced in her honor, and the same old woman who had stayed in the doorway continued dancing there. One old woman was dancing while holding her pipe in her mouth. A song was sung, and then one of the Koskimo delivered another speech, holding a short staff in his hands. Whenever a name was called, he raised the staff high and held it so that the ends rested against his palms.

As the people became hungry by this time, a woman threw dried salmon among them—first to the members of the secret society of the Koskimo, and then to the others. While they were eating, the societies again uttered their calls.

Now a new dance was announced. A woman entered, wearing a flat ring, the front of which was set with feathers. She carried a bundle of red cedar bark in her hands. Her eyes and cheeks were painted black. When she shook the bundle of bark, it made a rattling noise. The people gave her a pipe, a stick, and other things, and whatever she carried made a rattling noise. The people took these items from her again but were unable to produce the same sound. Then they beat time again. She went once around the fire, looking upward and shaking her bundle of bark, holding it as though she were going to throw it. Then she stood in the rear of the fire and sang her song. She gave her cedar bark to one of the messengers and took a staff in its place, which she carried around the fire and made it rattle; another person tried it, but it did not make a sound. Next, she took a pipe from one of the Nā'q'oaqtôq and made it rattle in the same manner. Then she disappeared behind the curtain. <note>See page 492.</note> After some speeches, four young men went out, and several old people followed them, bringing food.

Then members of the Wā'tanEm danced. After their dance, more blankets were distributed. While the people were still eating, whistles imitating the raven's cry were heard outside. This was about 1:30 a.m. The speaker asked the people to beat time. Then the hā'mats'a entered.

In the middle of the back was a painting of a squatting man whose palms were represented by carved wooden skulls sewn onto the blanket. The knees and the head were represented in the same way. When they stopped in the rear of the house, both squatted down, and their attendants stood around them. After the fourth dance, they disappeared behind the curtain. Then more blankets were distributed.

At 3:15, women were heard singing outside. A man entered singing, followed by a woman. Two pairs of bloody lines were drawn on her cheeks, running downward in a wide circle from the mouth to the ear. She sang her secret song. She danced as a <term>t'ō'X'uît</term>, trying to catch her supernatural power. As soon as she moved her hands upward, trying to catch it, the women began to dance in her honor. Then she caught it between her hands and threw it forward. At once a flying <term>sī'siuL</term> was seen in the rear of the house, moving rapidly to the right and left and trembling constantly. As soon as the <term>sī'siuL</term> disappeared again, all the dancing women put their palms together as if they had caught the supernatural power. Then blankets were distributed.

Now a song was heard outside. The speaker asked the singers to beat time. A man entered singing. His body was bare, but he wore a dancing apron and had cedar bark rings around his arms and wrists. He was a <term>Bā'bakuaūLa</term>, a <term>t'ō'X'uît</term>. After some speeches, there was singing, and a woman and a man danced. They held their elbows close to their sides, stretched their hands forward with the palms upward, and moved their hands up and down in jerky motions. The <term>Bā'bakuaūLa</term> was then placed on a seat behind the fire in front of the singers, and the speaker was asked to pierce him with his lance. The singers beat time, and the speaker took up the lance and struck its point against the floor to show that the lance was solid, and displayed it to the people. Then he took up the lance and walked around the <term>Bā'bakuaūLa</term>. After each circuit, he placed the point against the left side of the <term>Bā'bakuaūLa</term> and then continued his circuit. After he had gone around him four times, he once more placed the lance against his left side and began to push it in. Apparently, the point entered the body, blood streamed out of his side, and as the point penetrated farther, the <term>Bā'bakuaūLa</term> appeared to collapse. Finally, the entire length of the lance had pierced the body and the point was seen emerging on the right side a little below the armpit.¹ He was lifted so that the people could see his body. Then the lance was slowly pulled out again. The shamans were called and they blew and sang over his body, while the singers continued their song. Then he was led behind the curtain. After this, cloths were distributed among the women; the singers beat time and cried "hū."

This was the last dance of the night. The <term>Koskimo</term> did not allow their guests to go home but invited them to stay for a feast. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> still remained sitting in front of the door, preventing anyone from going out. They continued to eat and to make speeches until 10 o'clock, when everybody went home to rest.

On the 26th of November everything was quiet, as the people were exhausted by the preceding festivals.

In the afternoon of the 27th, the <term>Kwakiutl</term> held a secret meeting to determine what to do. The <term>seal society</term> was still confined to the dancing house. <term>K·ēx·</term>, whose mask had broken a few days earlier during the dance, was going to initiate his son to atone for this mishap. His elder son had died a few years before, after he had been made a member of the <term>hā'mats'a</term> society. Referring to this, he spoke—

As soon as these blankets were distributed, a young bear dancer appeared from the corner of the house and scratched the ground while the people sang and the women danced for him. Then he disappeared again.

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the Kwakiutl winter ceremonial, transitioning from the appearances of bear and ha'mshamtsEs dancers to the dramatic performance of the t'ō'X'uît.</meta>

# REPORT OF THE NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

Singers stood in the rear of the house. A *t'ō'X'uît* woman appeared, wearing a head ring made of hemlock branches but no neck ring. She held her elbows to her sides and her hands forward with palms upward, raising and lowering them alternately. The song followed a three-part rhythm, and she walked with a limp—taking one step on the quarter mora of the rhythm and the second step on the half mora—while singing her secret song. After each line of her song, the chorus continued it. She sang: "Yā, yā, yē."

Now *Hō'LElitē* stepped up to her and spoke. She replied with the exclamation "up, up," pointing to her chest to signify that the people should split her open. Then she moved her hands along her neck in the same way, signifying that they should cut off her head. *Hō'LElitē* proposed throwing her into the fire, but after some discussion, this idea was abandoned. The people beat time again. She began to dance and caught her supernatural power between her palms. After she had done this twice, she said "up, up" again, touching her stomach with her palms several times, meaning "take out my intestines." Then she tried again to catch her supernatural power, while *Hō'LElitē* walked around her, shouting "up." Now she tried a fourth time to catch her supernatural power. At once, whistles were heard. A bird was seen flying down from the roof, and a *nō'nlemg·ila* figure rose from underground. On this fourth attempt, a feather—which represents the horn of the *sī'siuL*—emerged from underground and moved with a trembling motion along the rear of the house. She went toward it, and suddenly she began to disappear into the ground. One man grabbed her, trying to rescue her, but his hands and forearms disappeared into the ground up to his elbows. Several men took hold of him to pull him back. Then he was apparently dragged through the entire house by the *t'ō'X'uît*, who had disappeared underground. He moved in winding paths through the whole house, plowing up the dirt. Finally, he seemed to lose his grip on the woman and fell backward.<note>1</note>

After the *t'ō'X'uît* had disappeared into the ground, a second one began to dance. The dancing woman guided the underground movements of the first, attempting to bring her up again with the movements of her hands. This second *t'ō'X'uît* was followed by one man. Finally, she left the house, and blankets were distributed while *Hō'LElitē* delivered a speech. Now a song was heard on the beach outside—

---

<note>1 This performance had been prepared during the preceding days when the members of the seal society kept everyone else away from the house. A deep ditch had been dug in the rear of the house where the *t'ō'X'uît* disappeared. A shallow ditch had been dug throughout the house, and a heavy rope had been placed in this ditch and covered with loose dirt. The man who appeared to be holding the *t'ō'X'uît* was actually pulling himself along this rope. Unfortunately, the rope had been laid too near the fireplace and was burned through. Because of this, the man had to let go. The original plan was to pursue the *t'ō'X'uît* to the front right corner of the house, where she was supposed to reappear from another ditch connected to the one in the rear where she had first disappeared.</note>

They were about fifty in all, and as soon as they stepped out from behind the curtain, they turned around and began a procession around the fire. In front of the fire, they turned again and continued their circuit. They held their fists in front of their bodies with their thumbs turned upward. While they were walking, they cried "yōu, hōu." After they had gone around the fire, they disappeared again behind the left entrance of the curtain. <term>Lā'g·us</term> made a speech, and then they began a second circuit in the same manner as before. When they had completed their fourth circuit, they stopped before entering the partition again. They kneeled around the fire, resting on their fists and knees. Now <term>Nu'xnēmīs</term> began a song, which was accompanied by rhythmic motions. They made another circuit and disappeared behind the curtain (Plate 36).

## XI. CEREMONIALS OF THE OTHER TRIBES OF KWAKIUTL LINEAGE.

The winter dance of the <term>Koskimo</term> begins in the month of November. In the evening, before the ceremonies are to begin, a number of boys are sent out to gather kelp. They return during the night and enter the village at the south end, blowing on the tubes of kelp and producing a noise like that of large horns. At the same time, a drum is placed in the river so that the wooden frame is in the water while the skin is held just above the surface. Beating this drum produces a very loud sound. As soon as the young men have passed through the village, they stop blowing their kelp horns, and the drum stops at the same time. Then all the people in the houses begin to sing their secret songs and continue to sing until the morning, when they come out of the houses. Then the chiefs go from house to house and ask the people if they know what produced the noise of the preceding night. Some reply that they did not hear it; others that they heard it; and still others that they had seen one of their dead relatives, who told them that he and the other ghosts came to take away the son or the daughter of one of the inhabitants. The chiefs continue to go from house to house until they come to the home of the young man or young woman who is to be initiated during the following ceremonies. When they enter the room, they see that the person has disappeared. Only a shirt and blanket remain, and these are covered with blood. The chief seizes the garments, takes them out of the house, and calls all the people together, asking for the murderer of the youth. A great commotion follows, with everyone running about. At

At last, they begin to blacken their faces and take up their weapons, ready to fight among themselves.

Suddenly, a person is heard crying out from the point of land at the west end of the village, "*hamamamama*." The people immediately go to see who is there. Now the master of ceremonies of the <term>winter dance</term>, named <term>Amā'k</term>, rises and begins to call all the people by their winter names. The people are surprised that he does this and they object. However, he does not listen to them and merely warns them not to be bitten by the <term>Hā'maa</term>. Then he calls four men whose names are <term>Lōakwaxstaôk</term>, <term>Walkaltsumt</term>, <term>Ā'Labala</term>, and <term>Henā'wa</term>, and asks them to go in a canoe to the point of land where the sound was heard to find out what produced it. The four men rise and enter the house, where the <term>hā'mats'a</term> are gathering at the same time. Soon they come out again with their faces blackened, rings of red cedar bark around their heads and necks, and paddles in their hands. The people ask why they are dressed in this manner; they reply that it is a protection against the lurking danger at the point of land to which they are going. They go down to a canoe and paddle slowly to the point of land. As they approach it, the sound "*hamamamama*" is heard again. The men pretend to be frightened and paddle back to the beach. They ask some of the <term>lōlō'LalaL</term>, or ghost dancers, to go with them.

Then the master of ceremonies asks four of the <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> to accompany the four men. The <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> dress up and sit close together in the middle of the canoe while the four men paddle toward the point. As soon as they approach it, the same sound is heard. Then the men in the bow of the canoe paddle backward while the steersman paddles forward and brings the canoe up to the point of land. As soon as they touch the land, the four <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> jump ashore and run into the woods, where they stay for a few minutes. Then they come back to the canoe and sit down in the same place as before. The other four men appear to be frightened, but not a word is spoken. They paddle back to the village, and when they reach the shore, they inform the master of ceremonies that they will not go back again because they are too frightened. Upon being questioned by the master of ceremonies, they say that they did not see anything, but that the sound scared them. He compels them to return and investigate the cause of the noise. The <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> have remained in the canoe all this time, waiting for the other four men to return. They paddle back to the point of land, and the four <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> jump ashore again and run into the woods, staying there for a few minutes. They come back, sit down in the middle of the canoe, and the four men paddle back again to the village. Now the four <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> jump ashore and go into the house of the father of the young man who had disappeared. The four paddlers stand and say that they have seen the missing youth among the ghosts at the point. The people all enter the house of the master of ceremonies.

They go ashore and rescue the novice, who had disappeared, from among the ghosts. They bring him down to their canoe and paddle slowly back toward the village. Then all the people go to their houses and have their breakfast. In the evening, the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> invites the tribe to his house. As soon as they stop, the master of ceremonies addresses the people, saying that they will try to restore the youth who had been taken away by the ghosts. While he is talking, someone is heard to cry "hamamamama" outside the house. They look about as though they were frightened and ask each other what might be the cause of the noise. After a short while, he returns to the master of ceremonies and says that he has seen some of his dead relatives in a hole in the ground, and that the <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> were sitting around the hole and talking to the ghosts. This signifies that this office is hereditary. <term>Tsakstâ'laqoals</term> goes and brings the rope into the house. The latter pretends to tie the end of the rope around the waist of the new <term>lōlō'LalaL</term> in order to prevent him from being taken away by the ghosts.

Then one of the members of the rival clan jumps up. The chief returns with the rope and twenty blankets. He ties the two broken ends together with his rope and says that he will be able to bring the ghost out of the ground. He calls his clan to leave the door and come to the rear of the house. Now the *yē'wix·ila*'s clan take their seats near the door. The other clan goes through the same ceremony, and last of all the chief brings forty blankets, which cause the rope to break. This signifies that the clan whose rope did not break until forty blankets were attached to it is more powerful than the other. After the rope breaks, the whole tribe sings as follows:<note>Appendix, page 728.</note>

->Look up to our world, look up to our world! Chief! Procurer of wealth!<-

This song is repeated four times. The *yē'wix·ila* distributes more blankets among the people, who then go home. On the following day, the *lōlō'LalaL* are seen walking about the village with rough rings of cedar bark on their heads; these rings are covered with down, and their faces are blackened. About midnight of this day, a number of men secretly climb onto the roofs of the village houses and begin to whirl "whirring sticks"<note>These are used for the hā'mats'a, mā'maq·a, hai'alik·ala, t'ō'X'uit, and hā'wina-laL. The noise of these sticks is supposed to be the voice of *Hai'aLilaqas* or *Wīnā'lag·ilis*, who comes to take away another novice. This noise is repeated four times, each time for about ten minutes. Then the people must sing their secret songs in the houses. When the noise stops, a *hā'mats'a* is heard to shout in the bush, and on the next morning a blanket is found in front of one of the houses. The people gather around it and try to discover whose blanket it is. After they have identified the owner of the blanket, they say, "It was certainly him whom we heard in the woods," and his father adds that *Hai'aLilaqas* probably came and has taken his son to *BaxbakuālanuXsī'waē*. The people request that he clean his house and prepare for the return of the novice. The man goes into his house at once and cleans it, and as soon as he is ready, the people enter. He asks them to be ready for the return of the *hā'mats'a*, as he might come back unexpectedly. The master of ceremonies asks the singing master to sing the new songs for the *hā'mats'a*, of which there are four. After the singing master has sung these songs, the master of ceremonies requests the new *yē'wix·ila* to prepare a feast. The people take their places and begin to sing the four songs of the old *hā'mats'a*. After these are sung, the feast is spread. When the people have entered, the old *hā'mats'a* comes out of his room and drives them out of the house.

During these days, the second yē'wix·ila collects all the debts that are due to him, and on the following morning, the new hā'mats'a is seen on the same point of land where the first one was recovered. The people go to him, capture him, and bring him to the singing house (kekoalela'tsē). Then they all begin to sing the four new songs: the first two are accompanied by fast beating, and the last two by slow beating. After these songs, the hā'mats'a is led back into his bedroom. At approximately 8 o'clock in the evening, he leaves the house, returns to the woods, and stays there until his father has invited all the people to his house to sing for him. As soon as they are assembled, they begin to beat time. After they have done so for about five minutes, one man cries “yaū.” The people repeat this cry four times. They have hardly done so when the hā'mats'a enters and they begin to sing. The hā'mats'a dances around the fire and, at the end of the last song, disappears into his bedroom. This night, all the dances are shown in a festival similar to the k·ik·î'lnala of the Kwakiutl.<note>See page 595.</note>

On the following morning, the yē'wix·ila invites all the people to his house and gives a feast for the men, women, and children. At the end of the feast, everyone receives a blanket “to wipe the mouth with.” After this, the hā'mats'a is allowed to bite four times—once every fourth day. During this time, he is purified in a way similar to that of the hā'mats'a of the Kwakiutl.

After the last night of the winter dance, the yē'wix·ila calls all the people to his house and asks them who is willing to keep the red cedar bark until the next year. No one responds. Suddenly, the door is opened and about twenty men rush into the house. They are covered with balsam pine branches, and blood is dripping from their bodies. They are called the Wīnā'lag·ilīs or qumqu'mx·dē (land otters). They run around the fire and suddenly take the cedar bark rings from the heads of several men. They then leave the house again as suddenly as they entered. The men whose cedar bark rings they have taken will give a winter dance the following year. After this, the rest of the people take off their cedar bark ornaments, tie handkerchiefs around their heads, and begin to sing summer songs.

During a feast, the young man who is to be initiated suddenly faints. At once, a number of newly initiated shamans are called to investigate the cause of his sickness. They are unable to determine what is wrong with the young man and send for the older shamans. They feel all over the youth's body and finally declare that the spirit <term>Wīnā'lag·ilîs</term> has taken possession of him. Then a sail is stretched across the rear of the house, and the patient is placed behind it. The house is cleaned, and everyone is invited—men, women, and children. From then on, this house becomes the dancing house. The <term>q'ā'qanas</term>, who correspond to the <term>mē'êmqoat</term> of the Kwakiutl, must stay in this house after they have entered it until the end of the entire ceremony. The uninitiated are not allowed to pass in front of the house above the high-water mark.

The master of ceremonies asks the people to sing the following song, which is supposed to have the power of restoring the patient to life:

->Hayas âhōnō lalä ya honô hanä häu.<-
->*Do not cry, you will come back safely.*¹<-

An old shaman stands by the patient, feeling his body. The song has no effect upon the young man, and the master of ceremonies requests the people to try another means of restoring him to life. Boxes are placed in front of all the assembled people, and at a signal, they beat time rapidly with their batons, ending with a loud rap. This is repeated four times.

The song above belongs to the clan <term>Naa'nqaēnôx</term> (those who always stay at home), while the rhythmic beating belongs to the clan <term>La'lauiLEla</term>, who obtained it from the <term>Awī'k'·ēnôx</term>. The shaman says that the beating of time had the desired effect upon the patient. After this, the people assume their winter names and rearrange themselves into the groups listed on page 419.

On the same night, the festival called <term>qap'ē'k^u</term> is celebrated. In the morning of this day, a number of young men were sent out to collect alder bark and to prepare red cedar bark, which is distributed among the people in the evening. In payment for their services, they receive a special allotment of food. When the people assemble for the <term>qap'ē'k^u</term>, the highest <term>hā'mats'a</term> is first led to his seat. The other <term>hā'mats'as</term> are placed at his side. They are followed by the <term>ts'ē'kôis</term> and by the <term>hai'alik·alaL</term>. The <term>quē'qutsa</term> take their seats last. They sit on each side near the door. As many <term>quē'qutsa</term> as there are <term>hā'mats'as</term> are charged with making the head rings for the latter. These <term>quē'qutsa</term> all stand on the right-hand side of the door, each holding his ring. They have a leader whose office is hereditary. They walk around the fire four times while singing. Then they step in front of the <term>hā'mats'as</term>, and on a signal, they all put the neck rings around them. At a second signal, they put the head rings on the heads of the <term>hā'mats'as</term>, and finally, they strew their heads with down. Then the <term>hā'mats'a's</term> whistle is heard, and the people quickly distribute the red cedar bark

among the others. The <term>que'qutsa</term> blacken their faces. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> begins to get excited and bites the people. He must bite a certain man first, whose duty it is to offer himself to the <term>hā'mats'a</term> when he gets excited for the first time. This office or duty is hereditary. The <term>hā'mats'a</term> carries a stick and drives the people around the fire. During the resulting excitement, another novice disappears, leaving his blood-covered blanket behind. It is found, and under great excitement, inquiries are made as to who is missing, until finally the father exclaims that his child has disappeared. Then the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term> dances.

Sometimes the disappearance of the novice takes place in a different way. Four men go on the roof of the house during the night and, running about, cry "hm hm hm." This noise is understood by the people to signify the approach of <term>Wīnā'lag·ilis</term>. On the following morning, it is found that one of the young men has disappeared, leaving behind his blanket, which is covered with blood.

Still another way of beginning the <term>Lē'xalakᵘ</term> is the following: The <term>mā'maq'a</term> dances in his house and suddenly throws his magic stick, which is believed to fly through the walls of the house and hit the person who is to be initiated and who lives in another house. The youth falls down, and then the parents call the shaman to cure him. The ceremony continues as described above.

To return to the festival. After the <term>ha'mshamtsEs</term> has finished his dance and has bitten a person, the people begin eating. They do not feed the <term>hā'mats'a</term> first, as is done by the Kwakiutl. Then they sing the song of the <term>Naa'nqaēnôx</term> four times;¹ three times they sing the refrain only, and the fourth time they sing the words:

->Do not cry, you will come back safely.<-

This is the end of the ceremonies of the first night. On the second and third nights, the same songs are repeated. Every night the shaman visits the novice, who is hidden behind a curtain. He reports that the novice is feeling better, and on the third night, he says that he is shaking violently.

The fourth night, the same songs are repeated. The shaman visits the novice again, and when he returns, he says, "Listen; he is singing his secret song." Now nobody is allowed to speak or to cough. Then they hear, as though from a great distance, the sound of a new song, which grows louder and louder. The secret song is sung four times. The singing master must listen attentively, because after the fourth time, he must repeat it. Two new songs are heard that night. On the following night, the same ceremony is repeated, and two more songs are learned by the people. Twelve <term>que'qutsa</term> women dance this night. Their faces are blackened, and they wear red cedar bark. Their dance is accompanied by the beating of batons. One man and one woman are stationed at the entrance to the secret room in which the novice is lying in order to watch it. Their positions are hereditary.

<page-num>614</page-num>
<header>REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.</header>

When the twelve women are about to finish their dance, the novice is seen coming out of his secret room. He does not wear any ornaments made of red cedar bark.

He dances on the four following nights. On the following day, there is a break in the ceremonies. The next day, the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> invites all the people to his house and asks them to prepare for the purification of the novice, which will take place on the fourth day. He also requests three officers, whose positions are hereditary, to prepare themselves for this ceremony. These officers are the man who makes the tongs, named <term>Q'aqiâ's</term>; the one who uses the tongs, named <term>NE'msqEmg·ala</term>; and the one who calls the people to the washing ritual. Early in the morning of the fourth day, the last officer mentioned must go to every house and, beating the doors with his baton, he must cry, "Yau, yau, listen, listen. There is food for you from <term>Qoā'yukolax·ilis</term>, from <term>Lā'xus'EML</term>."¹ The first is the <term>q'ā'q'anas</term> name of the novice, and the second is his <term>quē'qutsa</term> name. In the evening, everyone assembles in the dancing house. Then the first of these men makes a pair of tongs, which are wound with red and white cedar bark and placed on the west side of the house. A ladder with only four steps is placed against one of the rafters on the left side of the fire (that is, to the left when facing the back of the house). The man who made the ladder climbs it and puts his head through the roof. When he comes down, the people beat the boards and the drum. At midnight, he climbs the ladder again. He goes up a third time between midnight and dawn, and a fourth time when the day begins to break. This is done to ensure good weather. Every time he returns, he sings:

> Ha, ha! You do not give me a favorable answer, you who are to bring the southeast wind by washing our novice.²

The officer who made the ladder is given a dish as payment for his work. The one who made the tongs receives a knife and a hammer. The one who carries the tongs receives a belt, and another belt is given to the officer who invited the people. Sometimes paddles, canoes, or blankets are given to them, but these are always called a "dish," "knife," or "belt," depending on the role.

After the man has come down the ladder the fourth time, <term>NE'msqEmg·ala</term> takes the tongs down and circles the fire four times, holding the tongs stretched forward. He calls a man to open the door and strikes the stick that spreads the tongs four times. On the fourth strike, he hits it so that it flies out the door. Then he takes two stones out of the fire, one after the other, repeating the motion three times in each case before actually picking them up. He throws them into the water in the same way, and also dips them up after repeating the motion

Then <term>NE'msqEMg·ala</term> places the tongs vertically into the fire, the open end downward. The cedar bark with which they are wound catches fire, and then he lets them go. It is expected that the wind will blow in whichever direction they fall. Then the officer who made the tongs makes head rings of red cedar bark for all the people, who put them on. The singing master makes a new song, and singing it they go around the fire and leave the house, led by the <term>yiai'atalaL</term>, who carries a small rattle. This office is also hereditary. They go through the whole village and inform the people that the purification of the novice has been performed that morning. The people put their masks in order and gather the property which they are going to give away at the festival which is to be held that evening. This night the people are not arranged according to the groups described above, but according to their clans. In the morning, a man is sent around to call the people. First the boys enter the house and begin to beat time. Then the various groups enter one after the other, each carrying the property which they are going to give away during the festival. ->I will listen to what is told about it.<-

After they have finished their songs, a man named <term>Wiyō'tsEM</term> is called up. He puts on a canoe sail like a blanket and goes around the fire dragging the sail behind him. This means that he is sweeping the house for the dancers, who will enter next. The first dancer to enter is the <term>wā'tanEm</term>. He is followed by the ghost dancer, the <term>ō'lala</term>, <term>hai'alik·auē</term>, <term>ts'e'koîs</term>, <term>wī'x·sâ hā'mats'a</term> (or <term>hamtsEtsōē</term>), and <term>hā'mats'a</term>.

While he is dancing, the <term>yē'wix·ila</term> distributes his presents among the people. On the following day, another man gives a feast in the house of the <term>yē'wix·ila</term>. After four days, another man gives a feast in the same house. When all have entered, the novice is called out of his secret room. He wears a smaller head ring now. Two more feasts are given in the same way at intervals of four days. Every time, the dancer wears a smaller head ring.

At the end of the last night, the <term>q'ā'q'anas</term>, who have stayed in the dancing house throughout the entire ceremony, are led home by their wives.

It will be noticed that in these ceremonies, the festival corresponding to the <term>k·ik·i'lnala</term> of the Kwakiutl is celebrated after the return of the novice. Among the <term>La'Lasiqoala</term>, when the novice has disappeared into the woods (being a <term>lā'xsâ</term>), his whistles are suddenly heard on the roof of the house or behind the houses. At night, while the people are assembled, he is heard on the roof of the house, but disappears again. On the following morning, he is seen on a point of land. Four canoes are lashed together and connected by planks. In this way, the people paddle up to him and bring him back. The same night, all the dances are performed.

The winter dance ceremonies of the <term>Ts'ā'watEēnôx</term> differ from those described previously. I have received detailed information from Mr. Hunt only in regard to the closing ceremonies, while the progress of the ceremony seems to be much like that of the Kwakiutl. The beginning is as follows:

The <term>yē'wix·ila</term> invites all the people to his house, where they sit down according to their clans. Then he asks his wife to bring food. While the food is being prepared, the people sing. In the middle of the third song, the whistles are heard on the roof of the house. The people stop singing. They group themselves at once according to their dances and societies. They burn the salmon because it was prepared before the beginning of the winter dance. That night, they begin their ceremonies.

The song is the same as the one which Qa'mtalaL used when taking off his cedar bark ornaments. As soon as they had finished their song, they changed their names. Now, the one whose name had been Xū'gamsila was called Ha'mts'it. Then NEg·e', whose name had been Pa'xalats'ē, spoke: "My tribe, now let someone rise who wants to take these red cedar bark ornaments for next winter."

Then Yā'qōLas arose and spoke: "I come, NEg·e', in answer to your speech. I will take this red cedar bark." Then he spread his blanket, the cedar bark ornaments were thrown into it, and he hid them in his bedroom. Then all the members of the T'Ena'xtax tribe tied handkerchiefs around their heads. They had finished their winter dance. Walas NEg·e' distributed blankets. They did not give to the <term>hā'mats'a</term> first, but to the head chief.

## XII. THE <term>LAŌ'LAXA</term>.

I noted earlier that the <term>La'Lasiqoala</term> group their dances into two classes: the <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term> and the <term>nō'nLEM</term>. The <term>nō'nLEM</term> dances are closely connected to the clans, and during their performance, the standard social system remains fully in effect. The <term>Kwakiutl</term> have only a few of these dances, which they call <term>Laō'laxa</term>—a name also sometimes used by the <term>La'Lasiqoala</term>. It is difficult to establish any fundamental difference between a <term>Laō'laxa</term> dance and a <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term> dance, as in both cases a hereditary spirit initiates the novice, and in both ceremonials, membership is obtained in the same way—through marriage or by killing a person who is entitled to the ceremony. The distinction is relatively clear among the <term>La'Lasiqoala</term> and their affiliated tribes. Only those dances originating from <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term> and his followers, or from <term>Wīna'lag·ilis</term>, are <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term>; all others are <term>nō'nLEM</term>. All the animals belong to this class, and we find that they are much more clearly clan deities than those in the former class. At the same time, it is distinctly stated that the entire ceremonial was introduced through marriage with the northern tribes, particularly the <term>Hē'iltsuq</term>. This awareness of an entirely foreign origin for all the <term>Laō'laxa</term> dances is even stronger among the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, while they have incorporated many dances into the <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term> that undoubtedly had the same origin.

The <term>La'Lasiqoala</term> use cormorant down instead of eagle down in the <term>nō'nLEM</term> ceremonial, white cedar bark instead of red cedar bark, and red paint instead of black paint. They sing both secular songs and <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term> songs. The celebration takes place in November and December.

Among the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, the <term>Laō'laxa</term> may be celebrated at any time of the year. The man who wishes to host the festival calls his clan or tribe to his house and informs them of his plans. I am indebted to Mr. <term>George Hunt</term> for the following description of such a meeting:

<term>Ots'ēstalīs</term>, a man whose mother was a <term>Hē'iltsuq</term>, was about to give a <term>Laō'laxa</term>. He invited his clan and spoke as follows:

> "Now come, my tribe; come <term>Ha'mts'it</term>, come <term>Yē'qawitē</term>, come <term>G·ē'so-yag·ilīs</term>, come <term>Lā'qoag·ila</term>, come <term>Tsō'palīs</term>; come to hear the words of our chief. Come <term>Guē'tEla</term>, come <term>Q'ō'moyuē</term>, <term>Walas Kwakiutl</term>, <term>Q'ō'mk·utīs</term>. Thank you, my tribe, for coming. I must tell you about my plans. I will perform the dance which came down from heaven, the <term>Laō'laxa</term>, this coming night. Pay attention, my tribe; pay attention, all of you second-class chiefs. I do not mean you, Chief <term>Ha'mts'it</term>. I mean <term>Mā'Xua</term> and <term>Wā'nuk<sup>u</sup></term> and <term>Ō'ts'ēstalīs</term> and <term>Mā'mXua</term> and <term>Lā'lak·uts'a</term> and you third-class young chiefs. Now pay attention; the supernatural power will come to live among the tribes assembled at our camp, great <term>Kwakiutl</term>! Now I will tell you what I hold in my hands. I will give away my <term>copper</term> <term>Wā'nung·ila</term> to the <term>Nā'q'oaqtôq</term>, <term>Koskimo</term>, <term>G·ō'p'ēnôx</term>,"

...and <term>L'a'sq'ēnôx</term>. Its price is 800 blankets. I think that will be enough for these eight tribes here, and my other copper, <term>Mā'mukoalila</term>, shall fall on the <term>Ma'malēlēqala</term>, <term>Qoē'xsōt'ēnôx</term>, and <term>Nimkish</term>, and the <term>Lau'itsīs</term> and <term>Matilpē</term> and <term>T'Enā'xtax</term> and <term>A'wa-iLala</term> and <term>Ts'ā'watEēnôx</term> and <term>Hā'xuamîs</term>. I think that is enough! The price for <term>Mā'mukoalila</term> is 6,000 blankets. This will be enough for the nine tribes, and I will sell my copper, <term>Māu'aga</term>, for food—for which I paid 2,400 blankets at the time when <term>Lalak·uts'a</term> wanted to sell it quickly at <term>Mē'mk·umlîs</term>. Otherwise, the tribe might say that they are starving in this great country. But this way, they can find no fault when they come." Sometimes one or the other of the old men said "yes, yes" during his speech, and he continued: "Furthermore, such is my pride that I will kill this copper of mine, <term>Dandalāyū</term>, which is groaning in my house, on this fire. You all know how much I paid for it. I bought it for 4,000 blankets. Now I will break it in order to vanquish our rival. I will make my house a place of competition for you, my tribe, wa. Now you know it all, my tribe; be happy, chiefs! For this is the first time that such a great invitation has been issued. There are 9,200 blankets, in addition to the 4,000 blankets for the copper that I am going to break. Now count all that the invitation will cost. It is 13,200 blankets, and in addition 250 button blankets, 270 silver bracelets, 7,000 brass bracelets, and 240 wash basins; and I am not even counting the spoons, abalone shells, the <term>Laō'laxa</term> head mask, and the numerous kettles which I am expecting from my wife. Now you know all my plans!"

Then <term>Wā'k·as</term> arose and spoke: "Wa, my tribe! Did you hear what our chief counted up? Are you not awed by the various kinds of property which he is expecting? Now long life to you, <term>O'ts'ēstalîs</term>, you who were made a chief by your fathers. Take care of our chief, my tribe. Take care, <term>Guē'tela</term>, <term>Q'ō'moyue</term>, <term>Walas Kwakiutl</term>, and <term>Q'ō'mk·utîs</term>. He is pouring out everything that he has in his mind. My tribe, are you not also glad for our chief? I think you are proud in your hearts. Thank you, <term>O'ts'ēstalîs</term>. Thank you from my heart, chief. I wish you long life. You will be the first of all the chiefs of all tribes. So I say, <term>Ts'ō'palîs</term>; thus I say, <term>Hä'masaqa</term>, <term>G·ēsoyag·ilîs</term>, <term>Ma'koayalisamē</term>, <term>Dā'dants'it</term>, <term>Lā'lakanx·it</term>, wa, wa. So we say, our whole tribe."

Then <term>Mā'mXua</term> arose: "That is your speech, Chief <term>O'ts'ēstalîs</term>; that is your speech, <term>Wā'k·as</term>. Thank you, chief. How handsome is my chief! Thank you, friend. Now my heart is revived, for I was afraid when I heard the news of our rival. Ho, ho, ho. Now I lift the heavy weight of your speech, chief. Thank you, brother. So I say for my whole tribe." Then <term>Ō'mx·it</term> arose and said: "Thank you for your speech, <term>O'ts'ēstalîs</term>. Long life to you for your speech. How well you stand on our earth. You will be the only post of our world. The chiefs of all the tribes will be jealous of you, you overhanging mountain, you chief who cannot be equaled. You do not need to fear anything. How..."

"Your name is great, chief. Now you have made my back strong. Take care, my tribe, and wish long life to our chiefs." Everyone applauded his speech. Then O'mx'it sat down.

Next, Hâ'mEsk·inîs stood up and spoke. He said: "My tribe, are you not ashamed before this young man? He will be your chief, Kwakiutl! I am half ashamed myself on account of the amounts counted. Go on, my son, be proud of what you said." Then he lifted his right hand and shouted: "Hide yourselves, tribes! Never has such an amount of property been seen as our chief has announced. Ya, ya, my tribe, do you not consider the great mountain of property belonging to Ō'ts'ēstalîs to be awe-inspiring? He is still a young man. Take care, my children, so that you may have two men who will give away blankets to the whole world. That is what I say to the chiefs of the Kwakiutl, wa, wa."

Now it was growing dark, and Ō'ts'ēstalîs stood up and spoke: "Look at me, my tribe! This young man is handsome; he is growing up well. Now I will sing the secret song and try to summon the spirit of my dance."

The people said: "Go on." And he sang his secret song, calling down the spirit of the <term>Laō'laxa</term>:

> 1. I am the greatest magician, O hihihi, i, the greatest magician.
> 2. I alone am full of magic, O hihihi, i, the greatest magic.
> 3. I am the only one who makes life short by means of his magic, the greatest magic.
> 4. I am the only one who knows how to call down the magical power, the greatest magic.
> Come now, magical power, O hihihi, i, greatest magic.

As soon as he had finished his song, the sound of whistles came down through the roof of the house. Then they called all the women and children. They came to the dancing house for the <term>Laō'laxa</term>. Ō'ts'ēstalîs stood up. He

He was glad that the people had come quickly and said: “Yes, my tribe, you have done right to come to this large house. Make yourselves comfortable. Do not be in a hurry to go home to your houses. Thus I say, Wa'k·as. Thus I say, Ōm’x’it, wā, wā.” Then the songmakers sang, and the people sat around them learning the dancer's songs. When everyone knew the song, Ō'ts'ēstalis stood up and sang:

He stopped singing and said: “Ho, ho, ho! Yes, my tribe. In this way, I lift the heavy weight of my wealth. Now we will call all the tribes so that they may come in the morning. Now go to sleep. As this festival was to be given to a number of tribes, all the Kwakiutl took part in this meeting. When only the Kwakiutl are to be present, the host announces his intention to his clan alone. Then, after the meeting is over, he sends word to the chiefs of all the clans, advising them that the Lāō'laxa whistles will be heard that night. Then all those who have celebrated a Lāō'laxa before may go to ask him what masks he intends to show, in order to make sure that he will not infringe upon their rights. In the evening, the whistles are heard to blow behind the house of the man who is going to give the Lāō'laxa. After about ten minutes they stop, and then blow again. This is repeated four times. For four nights, the whistles are heard in the woods behind the house. On the fourth night, after they have been blown in the woods three times, they are heard on the roof, and finally in the bedroom. Then the man begins to sing his secret song.

At the same time, he invites all the young men to come to his house and sing. Then the young men enter the house and sing, and some of them dance, one after another. When the grease has been eaten, the relative of the host who is to be initiated comes out of the bedroom where the whistles are sounding and begins to dance around the fire. He wears a beautiful carved headdress with a long ermine trail (Plate 47). All of a sudden, he throws his mask off and runs out. After a short while, a dancer wearing the <term>Laō'laxa</term> mask comes in. His arrival is announced by a relative of the host who is stationed at the door and who, as soon as the dancer approaches, shouts "wōî!" It is supposed that when the first dancer threw down his headdress, he became possessed by the spirit of the <term>Laō'laxa</term> and was transformed into the spirit personified by the mask. In reality, another dancer wears the mask. After one circuit of the fire, the mask disappears again, and the novice—for so we may call him—comes forward and continues the dance that was interrupted before. The people accompany the dance with the <term>Laō'laxa</term> song. After he has finished, a few women dance in honor of the new <term>Laō'laxa</term>. The host joins them, carrying a pole about six feet long on his shoulder. The pole indicates that on the next day he will give another feast, to which he invites the people after ending his dance.

In the evening, the whole tribe—men, women, and children—assemble in the host's house to witness the dance, and the morning performance is then repeated.

On the following morning, the messengers go out again, dressed up and with their faces painted red, to call the people to the second feast. The ceremony of the preceding day is repeated, but another <term>Laō'laxa</term> dance may be shown. This is repeated again in the evening, when the

A man standing next to him carries the blankets to those who are to receive them. As soon as the blankets intended for one clan are distributed, he calls, "Let us change!"

This is the end of the <term>Laō'laxa</term>.

## XIII. THE RELIGIOUS CEREMONIALS OF OTHER TRIBES OF THE NORTH PACIFIC COAST.

### THE NOOTKA.

The Nootka speak a dialect distantly related to the Kwakiutl. They have two ceremonials which are similar to the winter ceremonial of the Kwakiutl. Good descriptions of the customs connected with these ceremonials have been provided by Sproat, Swan, Jewitt, and Knipping. I will repeat here what I have stated on this subject elsewhere. <note>1. Report of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, 1890, page 47.</note> The name of the ceremonial among the Nootka is *Lō'koala*, a Kwakiutl word which designates the finding of a manitou <note>a guardian spirit</note>. The ceremonial corresponds very closely to the *Walas'axa'* and to the *Lō'koala* of the Kwakiutl (pp. 477, 478). Certain features are, however, embodied in it which correspond to other dances, mainly to the *mā'tEm* and the *hā'mats'a*. The *Lō'koala* are a secret society who celebrate their festivals only in winter. They have a chief whose name is *Yaqsyaqstē'itq*. Anyone who wishes to join the *Lō'koala* can do so, or the society may invite a man to become a member. Then the friends of this man make a collection on his behalf and turn over the property collected to the chief of the *Lō'koala*, who distributes it during a feast among the members. Those who are not *Lō'koala* are called *wīcta'k·ū*, that is, those who are not shamans. The *Lō'koala* is believed to have been established by the wolves, the tradition being that a chief's son was taken away by the wolves, who tried to kill him; however, being unsuccessful in their attempts, they became his friends and taught him the *Lō'koala*. They ordered him to teach his people the ceremonies on his return home. They carried the youth back to his village. They also asked him to leave some red cedar bark for their own *Lō'koala* behind whenever he moved from one place to another; a custom to which the Nootka tribes still adhere. Every new member of the *Lō'koala* must be initiated by the wolves. At night a pack of wolves—that is, Indians dressed in wolf skins and wearing wolf masks—make their appearance, seize the novice, and carry him into the woods. When the wolves are heard coming outside the village in order to fetch the novice.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Nootka Lō'koala initiation ceremony, specifically focusing on the symbolic death and revival of novices and the temporary restructuring of tribal society.</meta>

<page-num>633</page-num>
<header>THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.</header>

The members of the Lō'koala blacken their faces and sing the following song: <note>Appendix, page 731.</note>

> Among all the tribes there is great excitement because I am Lō'koala.

On the following day, the wolves return the novice as dead. Then the Lō'koala must revive him. The wolves are supposed to have put the magic stone *häina* <note>Xuē'la in Kwakiutl. The *x* of the Kwakiutl is always changed into *h* in the Ts'Eciā'ath dialect of the Nootka, from whom I obtained the word; *n* and *l* alternate constantly—for example, *lō'kualē* and *Lō'kuanē*.</note> into his body, which must be removed in order to restore him to life. The body is left outside the house, and two shamans go to remove the *häina*. This stone appears to be quartz. The concept is the same as that found among the Kwakiutl, where the Mā'tem is initiated by means of quartz, which is put into his body by the spirit of his dance. The returning novice is called *ū'cīnak*.

After the novices have been restored to life, they are painted red and black. Blood is seen streaming from their mouths, and they run at once down to the beach and jump into the water. Soon they are found drifting lifelessly on the water. A canoe is sent out and the bodies are gathered into it. As soon as the canoe lands, they all come back to life, go to the dance house, to which only the initiated are admitted, and stay there for four days. At night, dances are performed in the house, which the whole population is allowed to watch. After the four days are over, the novices leave the house, their heads being wrapped with wreaths of hemlock (?) branches. They go to the river, in which they swim, and after some time are brought back by a canoe. They are almost exhausted from the physical effort they have undergone during the previous days. Novices must eat only dried fish and dried berries.

Each Lō'koala lasts four days. It is only celebrated when some member of the tribe gives away a large amount of property to the Lō'koala, the most frequent occasion being the initiation of new members. Sometimes it is celebrated during the ceremonies practiced when a girl reaches maturity. The house of the man who pays for the Lō'koala seems to be the taboo house of the society. As soon as the Lō'koala begins, the ordinary social organization of the tribe is suspended, just as it is among the Kwakiutl. The people organize themselves into companies or societies, which bear the names of the various Nootka tribes, regardless of which tribe and clan the persons actually belong to. Each society has its own festivals, to which members of the other societies are not admitted, although they may be invited. These societies are called *ū'paL*. Each has a certain song, which is sung during their festivities. <note>Appendix, pages 731, 732.</note>

At night, when the whole tribe assembles in the taboo house, the societies still stay together. They are hostile to each other, and teasing between the various groups is continuously going on. It
