It appears that there are no separate societies for men and women, but a certain division must exist, as they seem to have separate feasts. When a man, during a <term>Lō'koala</term>, brings in any game and does not give half of it to the women, but instead keeps the whole amount for the use of the men, the women will attack him and take the share due to them from the men. In the same way, the women must share everything they get or cook with the men.

Originally, each dance belonged to one family and was passed down from generation to generation. Both the mother and father had the right to transfer their dances to their children. Thus, dances which belonged to one tribe were transmitted to others. The dance was given to the novice at the time of his or her initiation, and no more than one dance could be given at a time. At present, these restrictions are fading away. Whoever is wealthy enough to distribute a sufficient amount of property may take any dance he likes. I was even told that the chief of the <term>Lō'koala</term>, at the beginning of the dancing season, distributes the various dances among the members of the order, and that he may redistribute them at the beginning of the following season.

It is a unique feature of the Nootka dances that two masks of the same kind always dance together.

Among the dances belonging to the <term>Lō'koala</term>, I mention the <term>aai'Lqē</term> (feathers on head). It is supposed to be a being that lives in the woods. The dancer wears no mask, but rather a head ornament made of cedar bark dyed red, which is the badge of the <term>Lō'koala</term>. His badge consists of a ring from which four feathers, wrapped with red cedar bark, rise—three over the forehead and one in the back. The face of the dancer is smeared with tallow and then sprinkled with bird down. The ornaments of each <term>aai'Lqē</term> dancer, as well as all others, must be their personal property. They must not be loaned or borrowed. The song of the <term>aai'Lqē</term> can be found in the Appendix <note>Page 732.</note>.

Another dance is that of the <term>hî'nEmîx·</term>, a legendary bird-like being. The dancer wears the head mask shown in Plate 48. In the top of the mask, there is a hole in which a stick is fastened; this stick is greased and covered with down. When the dancer moves, the down becomes loose, and anyone in the audience who catches a feather receives a blanket from the chief of the <term>Lō'koala</term>. The song of the <term>hî'nEmîx·</term> is given in the Appendix <note>Page 732.</note>.

The <term>A'Lmaxkō</term> is a dance in which two men wearing human masks appear. The masks are called <term>A'Lmaxkō</term>. When they appear, the spectators sing:

<image-desc>A single line of musical notation consisting of five measures. The melody uses quarter and eighth notes. Below the staff are two lines of lyrics aligned with the notes.</image-desc>

->Kwai as kwai - as A'L - max-kō<-
->*That is*, "Back out, back out, A'Lmaxkō."<-

---

Then they leave the house and run around the village. The <term>A'Lmaxkō</term> is a being that lives in the woods. The first person to see him was a member of the <term>Netcumu'asath</term>, and ever since then, this clan has performed the <term>A'Lmaxkō</term> dance.

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.
<page-num>635</page-num>

The *sā'nEk* (panther) is very similar to the *nūLmaL* of the Kwakiutl. The dancer wears a large head mask, like that of the *hî'nEmîx·*, and a bearskin. He smashes everything, pours water into the fire, and tears dogs apart to devour them. Two canine teeth in the mask's mouth are its most distinctive feature. A rope is tied around his waist, by which he is led by several attendants.

The *hī'Ltaq* (self-torture) corresponds to the *hāwī'nalaL* of the Kwakiutl. The dancers rub their bodies with the juice of certain herbs and push small lances through the flesh of their arms, back, and sides.

Other dances include the *pu'kmîs* dance, in which the dancer is covered entirely with pipeclay; the *hu'Lmîs* dance—the *hu'Lmîs* is another being that lives in the woods and is constantly dancing—performed only by women, who wear ornaments of red cedar bark and bird down and who dance with one hand extended upward and the other hanging down; the *ā'yeq* dance, in which the dancer smashes and destroys household tools, canoes, and other types of property; and dances representing a wide variety of animals, particularly birds. The masks are all very similar in style (fig. 198). Head rings made of red cedar bark are worn in these dances.

<image-desc>Line drawing of a Nootka mask (Figure 198). The mask is shown in profile, elongated horizontally with a bird-like face featuring a large eye and a hooked beak. Carved patterns decorate the side, and two bundles of fibers hang from the bottom.</image-desc>
->Fig. 198.<-
->MASK OF THE NOOTKA.<-
->Neeah Bay.<-
->Cat. No. 23439, U. S. N. M. Collected by J. G. Swan.<-

Plate 49 shows an old bird mask and an old mask representing a human face. They are from the west coast of Vancouver Island and were likely made before the beginning of the nineteenth century. Plate 50 represents the type of rattle used by the Nootka. This specimen was likely collected during Cook's voyage around the world.

The tribes north of Barclay Sound have a dance in which the performer cuts long parallel gashes into his chest and arms. The *hā'mats'a* dance, which was acquired through intermarriage with the Kwakiutl, has spread as far south as Nutcā'lath. The killing of slaves, which has been described by Sproat <note>Sproat, "Scenes and Studies of Savage Life," page 155.</note> and Knipping, may belong to this part of the *Lō'koala*.

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of rituals among the Aht (Nuu-chah-nulth) tribes, shifting from descriptions of specific dance masks to a detailed account of a human sacrifice and the annual Klooh-quahn-nah festival ceremonies.</meta>

<header>REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.</header>
<page-num>636</page-num>

A celebration of a unique character, which was to last several days, and the murder of the woman undoubtedly formed a part of this celebration. The woman was stabbed to death by an old man in whose house she lived; he likely owned her as a slave and offered her as a victim. The body was then laid out, uncovered, by the waterside about 150 yards from the houses. There appeared to be no intention to bury the body, and it was only after the chief was strongly protested to that the poor victim’s remains were removed after being exposed for two days. I observed that, even after this removal, certain intense rites took place on the very spot where the body had been lying. The main feature of the celebration, apart from the murder, was a mock attack on the Indian settlement by wolves. These wolves were represented by Indians, while the rest of the population—painted, armed, and shouting fiercely—defended their houses from the attack. This horrific practice of sacrificing a victim is not an annual event but occurs either once every three years or, more likely, at irregular intervals. However, whenever it does happen, the sacrifice takes place during the *Klooh-quahn-nah* (*lō´koala*) season, which lasts from about the middle of November to the middle of January. 

The *Klooh-quahn-nah* or *Klooh-quel-lah* is a major festival observed annually by all the Aht tribes after they return from their fishing grounds to their winter encampment. It is generally a time of joy and feasting, during which tribal rank is granted and respect is shown to the chief through many rituals that have now lost their original meaning and cannot be explained by the natives themselves. I was not aware, until this murder was committed before our eyes, that human sacrifice was a part of the *Klooh-quahn-nah* celebration. I suspect that elderly, exhausted slaves are usually the victims. The Seshaht Indians at Alberni describe the practice as very ancient, and the fact that the other tribes of the Aht nation (about twenty in number) observe it supports this idea. Their legends differ slightly regarding this practice: some say that it was established by the creator of the world, while others say it originated when the sons of a chief from former times were actually seized by wolves.^1 To some extent, it is a secret institution, as the young children are not told about it until they are formally initiated. Many of them are very alarmed during the horrific rite; the display of ferocity, the firing of guns, and the shouting are calculated—and probably intended—to frighten them. Part of a day is dedicated to instructing the children who are to be initiated, and it is impressed upon them that the *Klooh-quahn-nah* must always be maintained, or evil will befall the tribe. 

Undoubtedly, the tendency and likely the intention of this human sacrifice and the entire celebration is to destroy natural human feelings against murder and to instill hardened and fierce hearts in the people generally, and especially in the younger generation. They say themselves that their “hearts are bad” as long as the ritual continues. In the accompanying ceremonies, children are taught to watch—without showing any emotion—savage preparations for war, strange dances performed in hideous masks accompanied by unearthly noises, and occasionally the cruel destruction of human life. Although I have no direct evidence, I believe that part of the training for those being initiated would involve viewing, howling over, and perhaps even handling or stabbing their knives into the victim's body without showing any sign of pity or horror.

^1 These Indians imitate animals and birds very well, such as wolves or crows. During this *Klooh-quahn-nah* celebration, they had their hair tied out from their heads to represent a wolf’s head and snout, and their blankets were arranged to look like a tail. They closely imitated the running motion of a wolf. Their acting as crows was even more extraordinary; they had large wooden beaks and blankets arranged so much like wings that, in the twilight, the Indians truly looked like large crows hopping around—especially when, in the manner of these birds, they went into shallow water, shook their wings, and “dabbed” with their long bills.

During the song and dance, which at first seemed to show nothing unusual, a well-known slave—one who was in a relatively independent position, however, being employed as a sailor on the steamer *Thames*—suddenly stopped dancing and fell to the ground, apparently in a dying state, with his face covered in blood. He did not move or speak; his head fell to one side, his limbs were drawn up, and he certainly presented a gruesome sight. While the dance continued wildly around the fallen man, the <term>medicine man</term>, along with several others, seized him and dragged him to the other side of the fire they were dancing around, placing his bare feet very close to the flames. After this, a pail of water was brought in, and the <term>medicine man</term>, who supported the dying man on his arm, washed the blood from his face. The people beat drums, danced, and sang, and suddenly the patient leaped to his feet and joined the dance, appearing no worse for his seemingly hopeless condition a moment earlier. While all this was happening, I asked the host of the feast whether it was real blood on the man's face and if he were truly wounded. He told me so seriously that it was real that I was at first tempted to believe him, until he began to explain that the blood coming from the nose and mouth was due to the spells of the <term>medicine man</term>, and that all the people would be very angry if he did not restore him afterward. I then remembered that earlier in the day, before the feast, I had seen the <term>medicine man</term> and the slave holding very friendly talks; and the former had used his influence to get a pass for the latter to attend the entertainment, to which he likely had no right to come.

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of the ceremonial rituals of the Northwest Coast tribes, shifting from eyewitness accounts of specific rites to a broader explanation of how these ceremonies are conceived through guardian spirits and the specific origin legend of the thunderbird ceremony.</meta>

REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

There are a great variety of these ceremonies, and they seem to take the place, to some extent, of theatrical performances or games during the season of the religious festivals. There are no persons especially set apart as priests for the performance of these ceremonies, although some, who seem more expert than others, are usually hired to give life to the scenes. However, these performers are quite as often found among the slaves or common people as among the chiefs, and except during the continuation of the festivities, they are not looked upon as being of any particular importance. On inquiring about the origin of these ceremonies, I was informed that they did not originate with the Indians, but were revelations from the guardian spirits, who made known what they wished to be performed. An Indian, for instance, who has been consulting with his guardian spirit—which is done by going through the washing and fasting process described before—will imagine or think he is called upon to represent the owl. He arranges in his mind the style of dress, the number of performers, the songs and dances or other movements, and, having the plan perfected, announces at a <term>tama'nawas</term> meeting that he has had a revelation which he will impart to a select few. These people are then taught and drilled in strict secrecy, and when they have perfected themselves, they will suddenly make their appearance and perform before the astonished tribe. Another Indian prepares the representation of the whale, others do the same for birds, and in fact for everything that they can think of. If any performance is a success, it is repeated and gradually comes to be looked upon as a regular part of the ceremonies; if it does not satisfy the audience, it is laid aside. Thus they have performances that have been handed down from remote ages, while others are of a more recent date.

->*  *  *<-

The ceremony of the great <term>Dukwally</term>, or the thunderbird, originated with the <term>Hesh-kwi-et</term> Indians, a band of <term>Nittinats</term> living near Barclay Sound, Vancouver Island, and is attributed to the following legend:

Two men had fallen in love with one woman, and as she would give neither the preference, they finally came to a quarrel. But one of them, who had better sense than the other, said: "Do not let us fight about that <term>squaw</term>; I will go out and see the chief of the wolves, and he will tell me what is to be done. But I cannot get to his lodge except by a trick. Since they know we are at odds, you should take me by the hair and drag me over these sharp rocks which are covered with barnacles; I shall bleed, and I will pretend to be dead, and the wolves will come and carry me away to their house." The other agreed and dragged him over the rocks until he was lacerated from head to foot, and then left him out of reach of the tide. The wolves came, and, supposing him dead, carried him to the lodge of their chief. But when they got ready to eat him, he jumped up and astonished them with his boldness. The chief wolf was so much pleased with his bravery that he shared with him all the mysteries of the thunderbird performance, and on his return home, he instructed his friends, and the <term>Dukwally</term> was the result. The laceration of the arms and legs among the <term>Makahs</term> during the performance to be described is intended to represent the laceration of the founder of the ceremony from being dragged over the sharp stones.

A person intending to give one of these performances first gathers together as much property as he can obtain—blankets, guns, brass kettles, beads, tin pans, and other articles intended as presents for his guests—and procures a sufficient quantity of food, which in recent years consists of flour, biscuit, rice, potatoes, molasses, dried fish, and roots. He keeps his intention a secret until he is nearly ready, and then shares it with a few of his friends, who, if necessary, assist him by adding to his stock of presents and food. The first indication the village has of the intended ceremonies is on the night before the first day’s performance. After the community has retired for the night, which is usually between 9 and 10 o’clock, the performers begin by hooting like owls, howling like wolves, and uttering a sharp whistling sound intended to represent the blowing and whistling of the wind. Guns are then fired, and all the initiated collect in the lodge where the ceremonies

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

...are to be performed, and they drum with their heels on boxes or boards, producing a sound like thunder. Torches of pitch wood are flashed through the roof of the house, and at each flash the thunder rolls; then the entire group whistles like the wind. As soon as the performers' noise begins, the uninitiated flee in terror and hide themselves. Their superstitious belief in the supernatural powers of the Dukwally is so great that they have frequently fled to my house for protection, knowing very well that the *<term>tama'nawas</term>* performers would not come near a white man. They then visit every house in the village and extend an invitation for everyone to attend the ceremonies. Once this has been done, the crowd retires to the lodge of ceremonies, where the drumming and singing are kept up until near daylight. They remain quiet for a short time and then begin again at sunrise. The first five days are usually devoted to secret ceremonies, such as initiating candidates and a variety of performances consisting chiefly of songs, choruses, and drumming to imitate thunder. They perform this part very well, and their imitation of thunder is quite equal to that produced in the best-equipped theater.

I have never learned what the ceremony of initiation entails. The initiation of the Clallams, which I have witnessed, consists of putting the initiates into a mesmeric sleep; however, if the Makahs use mesmerism or any similar influence, they do not keep the candidates under it for any great length of time, as I saw them every day during the ceremonies, walking out during the intervals. The first outdoor performance usually begins on the fifth day and consists of a procession of men and women whose legs, arms, and sometimes bodies have been scarified with knives, with every wound bleeding freely. The men are entirely naked, but the women wear a short petticoat. <insert>The wounds are made as follows:</insert> A bucket of water was placed in the center of the lodge, and the candidates, squatting around it, washed their arms and legs. The people who did the cutting—anyone who had sharp knives, though butcher knives were preferred—grasped them firmly in the right hand with the thumb placed along the blade so as to leave only an eighth or quarter of an inch of the edge bare. Then, taking hold of the arm or leg of the candidate, they made gashes five or six inches long, both across and parallel to the limb, with four or five gashes cut each way. Cuts were made in this manner on each arm above and below the elbow, on each thigh, and on the calves of the legs; some, though not all, were also cut on their backs. The wounds were then washed with water to make the blood run freely. When all was ready, the procession left the lodge and marched in single file down to the beach, their naked bodies streaming with blood, presenting a barbaric spectacle. A circle was formed at the water's edge, around which this bloody procession marched slowly, making gestures and uttering howling cries.

Five men then came out of the lodge carrying the principal performer. One held him by the hair, and the others by the arms and legs. He, too, was cut and bleeding profusely. They laid him down on the beach on the wet sand and left him while they marched off and visited every lodge in the village, making a circuit inside each one. At last, the man on the beach jumped up and, seizing a club, struck out violently, hitting everything in his way. He also went the same round as the others, and after every lodge had been visited, they all returned to the lodge they had started from, and the outdoor performances were closed for that day. Meanwhile, a delegation of fifteen or twenty men, with faces painted black and sprigs of evergreen in their hair, had been sent to the other villages with invitations for guests to come and receive presents. They went as a group to each lodge, and after a song and a chorus, the spokesman of the party loudly announced the purpose of their visit and called out the names of the invited persons. Anyone has a right to be present at the distribution, but only those specially invited will receive any presents.

Every evening during the ceremonies, except for the first few days, is devoted to masquerades and other amusements, when each lodge is visited and a

performance enacted. * * * The masks are made primarily by the Clyoquot and Nittinat Indians and sold to the Makahs, who paint them to suit their own preferences. They are made of alder, maple, and cottonwood; some are very cleverly made, having movable eyes and lower jaws. By means of a string, the performer can make the eyes roll around and the jaws clash together with a frightening noise. As these masks are kept strictly hidden until the time of the performances, and as they are generally presented at night, they are viewed with awe by the spectators. Certainly, the scene in one of these lodges—dimly lit by the fires that show the faces of the assembled spectators and light up the performers—presents a most strange and wild spectacle when the masked dancers emerge from behind a screen of mats and perform their wild pantomimes. The Indians themselves, even as accustomed as they are to these masks, feel very afraid of them, and a white man, viewing the scene for the first time, can only compare it to a carnival of demons.

Among the masquerade performances that I have seen was a representation of mice. This was performed by a dozen or more young men who were entirely naked. Their bodies, limbs, and faces were painted with stripes of red, blue, and black; red bark wreaths were twisted around their heads, and they held bows and arrows in their hands. They made a squealing noise, but otherwise, they did nothing that reminded me of mice in the least. Another group was composed of naked boys with bark fringes, like veils, covering their faces and armed with sticks having needles in one end; they made a buzzing noise and stuck the needles into any of the spectators who came in their way. This was a representation of hornets. These processions followed each other at intervals of half an hour, and each made a circuit around the lodge, performed some antics, sang some songs, shouted, and left. Another party then came in, composed of men with frightening masks, bearskins on their backs, and heads covered with bird down. They had clubs in their hands, and as they danced around a big fire blazing in the center of the lodge, they struck wildly with them, caring little whom or what they hit. One of their number was naked, with a rope around his waist, a knife in each hand, and letting out a terrifying howl. Two others held the end of the rope as if to keep him from doing any harm. This was the most ferocious exhibition I had seen, and the spectators got out of their reach as far as they could. They did no harm, however, except that one with his club knocked a hole through a brass kettle; after which they left and went to the other lodges, where I learned that they smashed boxes and did much mischief. After they had gone, the owner examined his kettle and dryly remarked that it was worth more to him than the pleasure he had experienced from their visit, and he would look to the man who broke it for compensation.

On a later evening, I was present at another performance. This consisted of dancing, jumping, firing guns, etc. A large fire was first built in the center of the lodge, and the performers—with painted faces, and many with masks resembling owls, wolves, and bears—crouched down with their arms clasped about their knees, their blankets trailing on the ground and fastened around the neck with a single pin. After forming in a circle with their faces toward the fire, they began jumping sideways around the blaze, their arms still around their knees. In this manner, they whirled around for several minutes, producing a most extraordinary appearance. These performers, who were male, were followed by about thirty women with blackened faces, their heads covered with bird down, and a belt around their blankets, drawing them in tight at the waist. These danced around the fire with a shuffling, awkward walk, singing a song as loud as they could scream, which was joined by everyone in the lodge, while beating time with sticks on boards placed before them for that purpose. When the dance was over, some five or six men with wreaths of seaweed around their heads, blackened faces, and bearskins over their shoulders rushed in and fired a volley of musket fire through the roof. One of them then made a speech, the gist of which was that the ceremonies had gone well so far; that their hearts had become strong, and that they felt ready to attack their

enemies or to repel any attack upon themselves. Meanwhile, their guns had been loaded, and another volley was fired, with the whole assembly shouting to show their approval. The daytime performances consisted of various reenactments on the beach. There was one representing a whaling scene. An Indian on all fours, covered with a bearskin, imitated the motion of a blowing whale. He was followed by a party of eight men armed with harpoons and lances, carrying all the tools of whaling. Two naked boys, their bodies rubbed with flour and white cloths around their heads, represented cold weather; others represented cranes moving slowly at the water’s edge and occasionally dipping their heads down as if seizing a fish. They wore masks resembling a bird’s beak, and bunches of eagle feathers were stuck in their hair. During all of these scenes, the spectators kept up a continual singing and drumming. Every day during these performances, feasts were given at different lodges for those Indians who had come from other villages. At these feasts, great quantities of food were eaten and many cords of wood were burned, as the host of the feast was very generous with his winter’s supply of food and fuel. The latter, however, is gathered quite easily from the forest and only requires a little extra labor to obtain enough.

The final exhibition of the ceremonies was the <term>T'hlūkloots</term> representation, after which the presents were distributed. The morning, from dawn until about 11 o’clock, was taken up by indoor performances consisting of singing, drumming, and occasional speeches. When these were over, some twenty performers—dressed in masks and feathers, some with naked bodies, others covered with bearskins, and accompanied by the whole assembly—went down to the beach and danced and howled in a most frightening manner. After making as much uproar as they could, they returned to the lodge, and shortly after everyone climbed onto the roofs of the houses to see the performance of the <term>T'hlūkloots</term>. First, a young girl came out upon the roof of a lodge, wearing a mask representing the head of the thunderbird, which was topped by a knot of cedar bark dyed red and filled with white feathers from eagles’ tails. Over her shoulders she wore a red blanket decorated with a profusion of white buttons, brass thimbles, and blue beads; her hair hung down her back, covered with white down. The upper half of her face was painted black, and the lower half red. Another girl, with a similar headdress, was naked except for a skirt around her hips. Her arms and legs had rings of blue beads, and she wore bracelets of brass wire around her wrists; her face was painted like the first girl’s. A smaller girl had a black mask to resemble the <term>ha-he'k-to-ak</term>. The masks did not cover the face but were on the forehead, from which they projected like horns. The last girl’s face was also painted black and red. From her ears hung large ornaments made of <term>haikwa</term> or <term>dentalium</term>, and blue and red beads, and around her neck was an immense necklace of blue beads. Her skirt was also covered with strings of beads, giving her quite a picturesque appearance. A little boy, with a black mask and a headband of red bark—the ends of which hung down over his shoulders—and eagle feathers in a topknot, was the remaining performer. They moved around in a slow and stately manner, occasionally spreading out their arms to represent flying and making a sound to imitate thunder, though it resembled the noise made by a nighthawk when swooping for its prey. Meanwhile, the spectators beat drums, pounded the roofs with sticks, and rattled shells. This show lasted half an hour, when everyone again went into the lodge to witness the distribution of presents and the grand finale. Once the group was arranged—the performers at one end of the lodge and the women, children, and spectators at the other—they began by extinguishing the fires and removing the burning logs and cinders. A quantity of feathers were scattered over the dirt floor of the lodge, and a dance and song began, with everyone joining in the latter, each person seemingly trying to make as much noise as possible. A large box, hanging by a rope from the roof, served as a bass drum. Other drums were improvised from the brass and sheet-iron kettles and tin pans belonging to the household furniture; meanwhile, those who had no kettles, pans, or boxes banged with their clubs on the roof and sides of the house until the noise was

mony also was borrowed from the winter ceremonial of the Kwakiutl. I obtained the following description of these ceremonies: The members of the <term>tsa'yēq</term> assemble and process through the whole village, walking in single file and in a circle, so that their left hand is on the inner side (counter-clockwise). Nobody is allowed to laugh while they are making their circuit. The <term>tsa'yēq</term> of the <term>Hopetcisā'th</term> and <term>Ts'ecā'ath</term> sing as follows during this circuit:

> Ha, hä, hä', he is not a shaman.<note>Appendix, page 733.</note>

When dancing, they hold the index fingers of both hands up, trembling violently. They enter all houses and take the patients and all the other people who desire to become members of the <term>tsa'yēq</term> along, two members of the society taking each novice between them and holding him by his hair, while they continue to shake their free hands. The novice must tilt his head forward and shake it while the

<columns>1</columns>
society continues its circuit. Thus they go from house to house, and all those who desire to become members of the society join the procession. Once the circuit is finished, they assemble in a house in which, during the following days, none but members of the <term>tsa'yēq</term> are allowed. They sing and dance for four days. After these days, the novice obtains his cedar bark ornament (fig. 199 and Plate 51). Small carvings representing the crest of his sept <note>A clan or tribal subdivision.</note> are attached to the front part of the head ring. The dress of the <term>uctā'qyū</term>, the shaman, who is the most important member of the society, is larger than that of the other members.

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

Swan<note>Swan, "The Indians of Cape Flattery," page 73.</note> has described the ceremony as follows:

> The other performance is called <term>Tsiahk</term>, and is a medicine performance, just as interesting but not as savage in its details. It is only performed occasionally, when some person—either a chief or a member of his family—is sick. The Makah believe in the existence of a supernatural being who is described as an Indian of dwarfish size, with long yellowish hair flowing down his back and covering his shoulders. From his head grow four perpendicular horns, two at the temples and two behind the ears. When people are sick with any chronic complaint and are very weakened, they imagine they see this being in the night, who promises relief if the ceremonies he prescribes are performed well. The principal performer is a doctor whose duties are to treat the patient, who is first initiated by secret rites into the mysteries of the ceremony. What these secret rites consist of I have not determined, but there is continual singing and drumming during the day and evening for three days before spectators are admitted. From the haggard and feeble appearance of some patients I have seen, I suspect the ordeal must have been severe. The uniqueness of this ceremony consists in the dress worn alike by patients, novices, and performers. Both men and women assist, but there are more women than men. On the head of the female performer is worn a sort of coronet made of bark, topped by four upright bunches or little pillars made of bark wound with the same material, and sometimes threads from red blankets to give a variety of color. From the top of each of the four pillars, which represent the horns of the <term>Tsiahk</term>, are bunches of eagle quills which have been notched and have had one side of the feather edge stripped off. In front is a band which is decorated in various ways, according to the taste of the wearer, with beads, brass buttons, or any trinkets they may have. From each side of this band, bunches of quills project, similar to those on the top of the head. The long hair of the <term>Tsiahk</term> is represented by a heavy and thick fringe of bark, which covers the back and shoulders to the elbow. Necklaces composed of many strings of beads of all sizes and colors, and strung in various forms, are also worn and serve to add to the effect of the costume. The face paint is red for the forehead and for the lower part, from the bridge of the nose to the ears; the portion between the forehead and the lower part is black, with two or three red marks on each cheek. The dress of the female novices is similar, with the exception of there being no feathers or ornaments on the bark headdress, and with the addition of black or blue stripes on the red paint covering the forehead and lower portion of the face. The headdress of the men consists of a circular band of bark and colored wool, from the back of which are two bunches of bark, like horses' tails. Two upright sticks are fastened to the band behind the ears, and on top of these sticks are two white feathers tipped with red; the quill portion is inserted into a piece of elder wood stick with the pith removed and then placed on the band sticks. These sockets give the feathers the charming effect of vibrating as the wearer moves his head. When dancing or moving in a procession, the hands are raised as high as the face and the fingers are spread out.
> 
> The doctor or principal performer wears a dress of plain bark on his head, similar to that of the female novice. He is naked except for a piece of blanket around his waist, and his body is covered with stripes of red paint. The outdoor performance consists of a procession that moves from the lodge to the beach; the principal actor or leader is at the head, followed by all the males in single file, with the doctor being the last one. Immediately behind the doctor, the patient follows, supported on each side by a female assistant. The women close the procession. All parties, male and female, have their hands raised as high as their faces, and the motion of the procession is a sort of shuffling dance. They move in a circle that gradually closes around the patient, who, along with the novice, is left seated on the ground in the center. Songs with choruses by all the spectators, drumming, shaking rattles, and the firing of guns conclude the performance, and everyone retires to the lodge, where

<summary>This page provides a detailed description by James G. Swan of the Makah Tsiahk ceremony, a healing ritual involving secret initiations, specific ceremonial costumes representing a horned supernatural being, and a public dancing procession.</summary>

<keywords>Tsiahk, Makah, medicine ceremony, ritual costume, cedar bark, shamanism, James G. Swan, Cape Flattery, healing rites</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of the Makah Tsiahk ceremony, specifically detailing the costumes of the participants and the legendary origins of their older ceremonial practices before transitioning to the secret societies of the Coast Salish.</meta>

Dancing and singing are kept up for several days. Finally, presents are distributed, a feast is held, and the friends retire. The patient and the initiates are required to wear their ceremonial dress for one month. It consists of a bark headdress that has two thin strips of wood instead of feathers; these are feather-shaped but painted differently. Those worn by the patient are red at each end and white in the center, with narrow horizontal blue bars. Those worn by the initiate have blue ends, and the center is left unpainted. The patient's face is painted red, with vertical blue marks on the forehead and the lower part of the face. The initiate's forehead and the lower portion of the face are painted with alternating red and blue stripes, while the rest of the face is blue; the headband is also wrapped with blue yarn and yellow bark. The patient's headband is wrapped with red. The bark tails of both headdresses are dyed red. The patient carries a staff that can be used for support while walking; this has red bark tied at each end and around the middle.

The <term>Dukwally</term> and <term>Tsiahk</term> are performed more frequently among the Makahs than any others, although they have several different ceremonies. The ancient <term>tamanawas</term> is called <term>Do-t'hlub</term> or <term>Do-t'hlum</term>,<note>This is clearly the Kwakiutl word <term>nō'nlem</term>.</note> and was formerly the favorite ceremony. However, after they learned the <term>T'hūlkoots</term> (or Thunderbird), they set aside the <term>Do-t'hlub</term>, as its performance involved so many ceremonies that it was too much trouble and expense. According to the Indians, the origin of the <term>Do-t'hlub</term> happened in this way: Many years ago, an Indian fishing for cod in deep water pulled up an immense <term>haliotis</term> shell on his hook. He had barely pulled it into his canoe when he fell into a trance that lasted a few minutes. Upon recovering, he began paddling home, but before reaching land, he had several more of these trances. When he reached the shore, his friends thought he was dead and carried him into his house, where he soon recovered. He stated that while in his stupor, he had a vision of <term>Do-t'hlub</term>, one of their mythological beings, and that he had to be dressed like <term>Do-t'hlub</term> to receive revelations. He described the appearance as he saw it in his vision, in which <term>Do-t'hlub</term> appeared with hands like deer's feet. He was naked down to his hips, around which was a petticoat of red-dyed cedar bark that reached to his knees. His body and arms were red; his face was painted red and black; his hair was tied in bunches with cedar twigs, with cedar twigs also hanging down his back. When his friends dressed him according to his instructions, he fell into another trance, in which he saw the dances that were to be performed, heard the songs that were to be sung, and learned all the secret ceremonies to be observed. It was also revealed that every performer must wear a piece of <term>haliotis</term> shell in their nose and ears. He taught the rites to some of his friends and then performed them before the tribe, who were so pleased that they adopted the ceremony as their <term>tamanawas</term> and continued to observe it for many years until it was replaced by the <term>Dukwally</term>. The custom of Makahs wearing <term>haliotis</term> shells in their noses originated from the <term>Do-t'hlub</term>. Other ceremonies are occasionally performed, but the description given above serves to illustrate all those observed by the Makahs. Different tribes have ceremonies unique to themselves, though their general character is the same. It can be seen that the public portions of these performances are more like amusements, similar to our theatrical pantomimes, than religious observances, though they are nonetheless observed religiously.

### THE LKU'ÑGEN.

My information regarding the ceremonies of the Coast Salish is very limited. I obtained the following information from the <term>Lku'ñgEn</term>, the tribe occupying the territory near Victoria, British Columbia. They have two secret societies: the <term>tcyiyī'wan</term> and the <term>xEnxanī'tEL</term> (dog howlers).

# THE KWAKIUTL INDIANS.

Any member of the tribe may join the <term>tcyiyi'wan</term>. When he wishes to do so, he retires into the woods and stays there for some time, bathing in ponds and washing his body with cedar branches. The intended novice is called <term>xausa'lokuL</term>. Finally, he dreams of the dance which he will perform and the song which he will sing. In his dream, his soul is led all over the world by the spirit who gives him his dance and his song. Then he returns to the village. According to what he has dreamed, he belongs to one of five societies which constitute the <term>tcyiyi'wan</term>: (1) The <term>sqe'iep</term>, who dance with elbows pressed close to the body, the arms extended forward and moving up and down; (2) the <term>nuxsoa'wēqa</term>, who jump about in wild movements; (3) the <term>sqä'qoaL</term>, who dance in slow movements; (4) the <term>sqôîē'lec</term>, whose dance is said to be similar to that of the <term>sqē'iep</term>, and (5) the <term>tcîlqTE'ñEñ</term> (derived from <term>tcâ'loq</term>, meaning woods). The general name of the dances of the <term>tcyiyi'wan</term> is <term>mē'iLa</term>, which word is borrowed from the <term>Kwakiutl</term>. When the novice returns from the woods, he teaches his song for two days to the members of the society to which he is to belong. Then the dance is performed, and henceforth he is a regular member of the society.

The <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term>, the second society, are also called <term>Lō'koala</term> and <term>nō'nLEm</term>, although the first name is the proper <term>Lku'ñgEn</term> term. The <term>Lku'ñgEn</term> state that they obtained the secrets of this society from the <term>Nootka</term>, and this is undoubtedly true. It appears that the secrets of these societies spread from the <term>Nootka</term> to the <term>Lku'ñgEn</term>, <term>Clallam</term>, and the tribes of Puget Sound. The <term>Tc'â'tELp</term>, a sept of the <term>Sanitch</term> tribe, also have the <term>nō'nLEm</term>, while the <term>Snanai'muX</term>, the <term>Cowichan</term>, and the tribes of <term>Fraser River</term> have hardly a trace of it. The <term>Comox</term> and <term>Pentlatch</term> obtained it through intermarriage with both the <term>Kwakiutl</term> and the <term>Nootka</term>.

The right to perform the <term>nō'nLEm</term> is jealously guarded by all tribes who possess it, and many a war has been waged against tribes who illegally performed the ceremonies of the society. Its mysteries were kept a profound secret, and if a man dared to speak about it, he was torn to pieces by the <term>quqq'ē'lEñ</term>, about whom I shall speak presently. Only rich people can become members of the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term>, as heavy payments are required at the initiation. If the father of the novice is not able to pay them, his relatives must contribute to the amount required. The initiation and the festivals of this society take place in winter only. When a young man is to be initiated, his father first invites the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term> to a feast, which lasts five days. During these days, mask dances are performed, which those who are not members of the society are also permitted to witness. They occupy one side of the house in which the festivities take place, while the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term> occupy the other. The latter wear head ornaments of cedar bark and have their hair strewn with down. The faces of all those who take part in the festival are blackened. At the end of three days, the father of the novice invites four men to bathe his son in the sea.

<summary>This page describes the initiation rituals and the five subgroups of the tcyiyi'wan society among the Lku'ñgEn, as well as the exclusive xEnxanī'tEl society. It details how these ceremonial practices and secrets were transferred between Northwest Coast tribes, particularly from the Nootka.</summary>
<keywords>tcyiyi'wan, xEnxanī'tEl, Lku'ñgEn, Nootka, secret societies, initiation rituals, mask dances, mē'iLa, Northwest Coast tribes</keywords>

--- Page 458 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term> society initiation rites among the <term>Lku'ñgEn</term> (Songhees) and introduces the social organization and mythic origins of the <term>Bî'lxula</term> (Bella Coola) societies.</meta>

One of them must wash his body, one must wash his head, and the two others hold him. In return they receive one or two blankets each. During this ceremony the <term>quqq'ē'lEñ</term>, who are described as wild men, dance around the novice. They have ropes tied around their waists, and are held by other members of the society by these ropes. Then the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term> lead the novice into the woods, where he remains for a long time, until he meets the spirit that initiates him. It seems that during this time he is secretly led to the house in which the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term> continue to celebrate festivals at the expense of the novice's father, and there he is taught the secrets of the society. During this time, until the return of the novice from the woods, the house is considered taboo. A watchman is stationed at the entrance, who keeps out uninitiated persons. During the absence of the novice, his mother prepares cedar bark ornaments and weaves mountain goat blankets for his use. One afternoon he returns, and then his father gives a feast to let the people know that his child has returned. The latter performs his first dance, in which he uses masks and cedar bark ornaments. This dance is called <term>nuxneä'mEñ</term>. On this day the father must distribute a great number of blankets among the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term>. The initiated are permitted to take part in the feast, and sit on one side of the house. The new member spends all his nights in the woods, where he bathes. In the spring the new member, if a man, is thrown into the sea, and after that is free from all regulations attending the initiation. One of the principal regulations regarding novices of the <term>xEnxanī'tEl</term> is that they must return from the woods in the direction in which the sun is moving, starting so that the sun is at their backs. Therefore they must sometimes go in roundabout ways. They must go backward through doors, which are <term>sLā'lEqam</term> (supernatural) against them. Frequently the <term>siō'ua</term> (a female shaman) is called to speak to the door on their behalf before they pass through it. Before their dance the <term>siō'ua</term> must also address the earth, as it is supposed that otherwise it might open and swallow up the dancer. It is also <term>sLā'lEqam</term> against the novice. The expression used is that the earth would “open its eyes” (<term>k'u'nalasEn</term>); that means, swallow the novice. In order to avert this danger, the <term>siō'ua</term> must “give a name to the earth,” and strew red paint and feathers over the place where the novice is to dance.

### THE BÎ'LXULA.

The social organization, festivals, and secret societies of the <term>Bî'lxula</term> are still more closely interrelated than they are among the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, and must be considered together. We have to describe here the <term>potlatch</term>, the <term>sisau'k·</term>, and the <term>kū'siut</term>. The <term>sisau'k·</term> corresponds to the <term>Laō'laxa</term> of the northern <term>Kwakiutl</term> tribes, the <term>kū'siut</term> to the <term>ts'ē'ts'aēqa</term>. The <term>Bî'lxula</term> believe that the <term>potlatch</term> has been instituted by ten deities, nine brothers and one sister, the foremost among whom is <term>Xē'mtsioa</term>, to whose care the sunrise is entrusted. He resides with the others in a beautiful house in the far east, and cries “ō, ō,”

...every morning when the sun rises. He takes care that he rises properly. The first six of these deities are grouped in pairs and are believed to paint their faces with designs representing the moon, stars, and rainbow. In the <term>kū'siut</term>, these deities make their appearance and are represented by masks. <term>Xē'mtsioa</term> and <term>Xēmxēmalâ'oLa</term> wear the design of the full moon. This is indicated on the mask of <term>Xē'mtsioa</term> by a double curved line in red and black—the black on the outside—passing over the forehead, cheeks, and upper lip. <term>Xēmxēmalâ'oLa</term> has a double curved line in red and black—the red on the outside—which passes over the forehead, cheeks, and chin. <term>Aiumkī'lik·a</term> and <term>Aiumalâ'oLa</term> wear the design of the crescent moon, drawn in red and black, with differences similar to those between the first and second masks. The fifth and sixth, <term>Q'ōmq'ōmkī'lik·a</term> and <term>Q'ō'mtsīoa</term>, have designs representing stars, and both wear the same style of mask. The seventh is <term>Qula'xawa</term>, whose face represents the blossom of a salmon-berry bush. The next in order, <term>Kulē'lias</term> (who wants to have blankets first), wears the design of the rainbow in black and blue. The ninth, <term>A'L'amā'k</term>, wears a mask on the head representing a kingfisher and is clothed in a bird-skin blanket. The last of the series is a woman called <term>L'ētsā'aplēLāna</term> (the eater), the sister of the others. Her face is painted with the design of a bladder filled with grease. She figures in several legends as stealing provisions and being pursued by the people whom she has robbed.

The <term>sisau'k·</term>, which is danced at potlatches and other festivals of the clans, is presided over by a being that lives in the sun. A man who had gone out hunting met the <term>sisau'k·</term> and was instructed by him in the secrets of the dance. When he returned, he asked the people to clean their houses and to strew them with clean sand before he consented to enter. Then he danced the <term>sisau'k·</term> and told the people what he had seen. He said that the being had commanded them to perform this dance and to adorn themselves when dancing with carved headdresses with trails of ermine skins, and to swing carved rattles. The man, later on, returned to the sun. Ever since that time, the <term>Bî'lxula</term> dance the <term>sisau'k·</term>. 

Besides this, it is stated that the raven gave each clan its secrets. Each clan has its peculiar carvings, which are used in the <term>sisau'k·</term> only and are otherwise kept a profound secret; that is to say, they are the sacred possessions of each clan. All clans, however, wear the beautiful carved headdresses and use the raven rattles, regardless of the carving they represent. Every time the sacred objects of a clan are shown to the people, a potlatch is given. The sacred objects, although the property of the various clans, must nevertheless be acquired by each individual—that is to say, every free person has the right to acquire a certain group of carvings and names, according to the clan to which he or she belongs. Slaves and the children of slaves, as well as illegitimate children, cannot become <term>sisau'k·</term>. A person cannot take a new carving but must wait until it is given to him by his relatives—father, mother, or elder brother. <term>Nusk'Elu'sta</term>, the Indian, to whom I

# REPORT OF NATIONAL MUSEUM, 1895.

I owe my information regarding the clans to a man who is a member of the <term>gens</term> <term>Ialō'stimōt</term> of the <term>Taliō'mx·</term>. He stated that he had received the raven when he gave his first <term>potlatch</term>. At his second <term>potlatch</term>, he received the eagle. He hoped that his mother would give him the whale at his next <term>potlatch</term> and would, at the same time, reveal to him the secrets connected with it. In time, he said, he might even receive others from his brother; however, if his brother's children should prove to be very capable and develop rapidly, his brother would probably give his secrets to his own children instead. At festivals, when a person acquires a new secret, he changes his name. Each person has two names: a <term>kū'siut</term> name, which remains throughout life, and a <term>Xē'mtsioa</term> name, which is changed at these festivals. Thus, <term>Nusk'Elu'sta's</term> (which is his <term>kū'siut</term> name) had the <term>Xē'mtsioa</term> name <term>Al'īLEmNE'lus'aix·</term>, but at his next <term>potlatch</term>, he intended to take the name <term>Kaliā'kis</term>. These names are also the property of the various clans, with each clan having its own specific names. When a man possesses several <term>sisau'k·</term> secrets, he will distribute them among his children. When a girl marries, her father or mother may—after a child has been born to her—give one or several of their <term>sisau'k·</term> secrets to her husband, as his children make him a member of her clan. When a person grows old, he gives away all his <term>sisau'k·</term> secrets. After any secret has been given away, the giver must not use it any longer. The crest and the <term>sisau'k·</term> carvings must not be lent to others; instead, each person must keep his own carvings. The only exceptions are the carved headdresses and the raven rattles, which are not the property of any particular clan.

The laws regarding the <term>potlatch</term> are similar to those of the <term>Kwakiutl</term>. The receiver of a gift becomes the debtor of the person who gave the <term>potlatch</term>. If the giver should die, the debts become due to his heirs. If the debtor should die, his heirs become responsible for the debt. Property is also destroyed at <term>potlatches</term>. This property is not returned and serves only to increase the social status of the individual who performed the act. It is not necessary for all the property given by a person in a <term>potlatch</term> to be owned by him personally. He may borrow part of it from his friends and must repay it with interest. I was told, for example, that a man borrowed a large copper plate and burned it at a <term>potlatch</term>. When doing so, he had to name the price he intended to pay the owner in its place. Since that feast, he has died, and his heirs are now responsible for the amount named at the <term>potlatch</term>.

The <term>kū'siut</term> is presided over by a female spirit called <term>Anaūlikuts'ai'x·</term>. Her home is a cave in the woods, which she keeps shut from February until October, remaining inside the entire time. In October, she opens the door of her cave and sits in front of it. A woman is said to have been the first to find her. <term>Anaūlikuts'ai'x·</term> invited her into her cave and taught her the secrets of the <term>kū'siut</term>. She wore ornaments of red cedar bark around her head, waist, and ankles; her face was blackened, and her hair was sprinkled with eagle down. She commanded the

woman to dance in the same way as she saw her dancing. The people should accompany her dance with songs, and, after she had finished, they should dance with masks. She said, “Whenever a person sees me, your people shall dance the <term>kū'siut</term>. If you do not do so, I shall punish you with death and sickness. In summer, while I am in my house, you must not dance the <term>kū'siut</term>.”

Ever since that time, the <term>Bī'lxula</term> dance the <term>kū'siut</term>. When a man has seen <term>Anaūlikuts'ai'x·</term> sitting in front of her cave, he will invite the people to a <term>kū'siut</term>. A ring made of red and white cedar bark is hung up in his house, and those who are not initiated are not allowed to enter it. Only in the evening, when dances are performed, may they look on while standing close to the door. As soon as the dances are over, they must leave the taboo house. Each <term>kū'siut</term> lasts three days.

The various dances performed by members of the <term>kū'siut</term> are also the property of the clans, and the right to perform them is restricted to members of the clan. They must not be given to a daughter's husband, as is the case with the <term>sisau'k·</term> dances, but instead belong to the members of the clan, who have a right to a particular dance but do not own it. Permission to use a mask or dance is obtained from the owner through payments. The owner may reclaim the dance, or the borrower may return it at any time. Membership in the <term>kū'siut</term> is obtained through an initiation. At this time, the novice is given his <term>kū'siut</term> name, which is inherited by young people from their parents or from other relatives. Thus, a young man who had the name of <term>Pō'pō</term> until he was about seventeen years old obtained the name of <term>L'akō'oL</term> at his initiation. I have not reached a very clear understanding of the details of the initiation; it seems that the dance is simply given to the novice in the same way as the <term>sisau'k·</term>, with this initiation being connected to a <term>potlatch</term>. However, it still seems possible that he must “dream” of the dance which he is to perform. Only those in the highest degrees of the <term>kū'siut</term> must pass through a religious ceremony of some importance. The highest degrees are the <term>Elaxō'La</term> (the <term>hā'mats'a</term> of the Kwakiutl), the <term>ō'lEx</term> (the <term>nū'LmaL</term> of the Kwakiutl), and the <term>dā'tia</term> (the <term>nō'ntsistalaL</term> of the Kwakiutl). These grades are also hereditary. A <term>kū'siut</term> novice may acquire them immediately at his first initiation.

When the <term>Elaxō'La</term> is initiated, he goes into the forest, where he encounters his guardian spirit. It is believed that he goes up to the sun, and formerly he had to take human flesh along for food. The chiefs held a council the night preceding the beginning of the ceremonies, and anyone who wanted to show his generosity offered one of his slaves to be killed in order to serve as food for the <term>Elaxō'La</term>. The offer was accepted, and a payment of ten to twenty blankets was made for the slave. The slave was killed, and the members of the <term>Elaxō'La</term> order devoured half of the body before the departure of the novice to the woods. There, the novice was tied up and left to fast. He may stay there for twenty or thirty days until the spirit appears

He has lost all his hair, which is believed to have been torn out by the strong wind blowing in the upper regions. He is completely naked and bites everyone he can catch. If he cannot catch anyone, he will bite his own arm. It is believed that he has lost his soul, which fled from his body when the spirit came to him. Therefore, the shamans must try for four days to recapture his soul. Some Elaxō'La do not bite people, but simply devour raw salmon or tear dogs to pieces and eat them. Those who bite people will also devour corpses. The Elaxō'La must observe a number of regulations. For four years after his initiation, he must not gamble. He must stay away from his wife for one year, though this period is now being reduced to one month. For two or three months, he must not leave his house.

The ō'lEx (the laugher) and the dā'tia (the thrower) do not go into the woods to be initiated; instead, both must fast for three days before their first dance. The ō'lEx "makes fun of everything" and scratches people with his nails. The dā'tia carries stones and sticks and breaks household goods and canoes. If he destroys an object during the day, he pays for it at night when he dances. The ō'lEx and the dā'tia, after they have danced, must stay in their houses for one month.

If a person breaks the laws of the kū'siut—for instance, if an Elaxō'La gambles, or if a man performs a dance to which he has no right, or if a person mocks the ceremonies or makes a mistake while dancing—his punishment is death. The chiefs assemble in council and the offender is called before the court. After his offense has been proved, he is asked whether he is willing to suffer the penalty of death. If he is unwilling and one of his relatives is willing to take the penalty upon himself, the guilty party is spared and the substitute is killed in his place. The execution of the judgment is entrusted to the shaman, who bewitches the condemned person by "throwing" disease into him or by poisoning him in some other (possibly supernatural) way. The object thrown by the shaman is a shell, bone, or finger nail, around

The masks (but not the whistles and other ornaments) used in the <term>kū'siut</term> are burned immediately at the close of each dancing season. Novices must wear a necklace of red cedar bark over their blankets for a whole year. The masks used in the dances represent mythical figures, and the dances are theatrical reenactments of myths. ### THE TSIMSHIAN, NÎSQA', HAIDA, AND TLINGIT.

The tribes of this group openly state that they learned the ceremonial from the Hē'iltsuq. Although I have not witnessed any part of their ceremonies, the descriptions I received clearly show their similarities to the winter ceremonial of the Kwakiutl. The ceremonies seem to be almost identical among all these tribes. They are most complete among the southwestern Tsimshian tribes, particularly the G·itxā'La, but they have been adopted by all the tribes of the coast. It is said that the ceremonial reached the Haida no more than a hundred years ago.

I will describe here what I learned from the Nîsqa'. They have six societies, which are ranked in the following order: the <term>sEmhalai't</term>, <term>mēila'</term>, <term>lŌLE'm</term>, <term>ōlala'</term>, <term>nanēstā't</term>, and <term>hōnana'L</term>, the last being the highest. The <term>sEmhalai't</term> is not actually confined to the winter ceremonial but is obtained when a person acquires the first guardian spirit of his clan and performs the ceremony associated with this event. The tradition regarding the origin of these ceremonies places the events at Bella Bella, and it

The Nisqa' state that with the ceremonies came the use of large whistles. I will give the Nisqa' tradition of the origin of the secret societies:

A Wutsda' (He'iltsuq), named Sāsaitlā'ben (a Nisqa' or Tsimshian name), went hunting. He saw a bear, which he pursued. He shot it several times, but was unable to kill it.

Finally the bear reached a steep cliff, which opened and let him in. When the rock opened, the hunter heard the voices of the ōlala' crying "hāp," and he fainted. Then his soul was taken into the house.

He told him: “You shall kill men, you shall eat them, and carry them to my house.” And he opened the door. The singers sang and beat time, and SaGaitlā'bEn flew away. He flew from town to town over the whole world, crying “hāp” all the time. He went from the country of the Wutsda' to the Skeena River, and then to the Nass River. Sometimes he was seen on high cliffs. He killed and devoured people whom he found in the woods.

After three years, he was seen near the village of the G·it'amā't. They attempted to catch him. They killed dogs and threw them into a hole, and a number of shamans hid under a canoe nearby. Soon he was heard to approach. He landed on the top of a dry cedar tree. He lay there on his stomach, and the point of the tree was seen to penetrate and pierce his body. But it did not kill him. When he saw the dead dogs, he flew down, and after he had eaten, the shamans rushed up to him, caught him, and took him up to the house. They tried to cure him, and the people sang *ōlala'* songs (all of which have a five-part rhythm). He tried to fly again, but was unable to get out of the house. Finally, he was tamed and became like other men. Then the G·it'amā't took him back to his friends and received in return many slaves, coppers, and canoes.

The ceremonies take place in the month called Lōk·s Em gunä'k (cold month, or December).

In his dances, the *ōlala'* of all the northern tribes use headdresses which represent a corpse (figs. 201–204). The whistles which are used to imitate the cries of the spirit are large and give a deep, hollow sound. They are all carved or painted with the design of the head of a corpse, either with hollow eye sockets or with closed eyes. Some of these whistles (figs. 205–207) are attached to bellows. They are carried under the arms, hidden by the blankets, and thus blown without being seen. The rattles which are carried by the companions of the dancer also show the same design.

Figure 215 (p. 660) shows another mask, which is used in a similar way. It represents the cold. The staring eyes and the chattering mouth express the extreme cold from which the wearer is suffering.

One dancer after another tries to bring back the novice. If he does not return by midnight of the first night, the ceremony is interrupted and continued the following night. On one occasion, a member of the <term>lōLE'm</term> was the last to try. He took his supernatural helper, a small, carved human figure, held it up, and asked it to bring back the novice. Then he poured a spoonful of grease into the fire and threw the carving after it. At once, the whistles of the novice were heard on the roof. All the <term>lōLE'm</term> rushed out of the house, but they soon returned, saying that they had seen him but lost him again. They cried, "ē" (drawn out very long). Then all the people left the house.

After the novice is lost in this manner, he is expected back on the following day. Early in the morning, a killer whale or some other animal is seen on the river, carrying the novice on its back. He is crying "mâ, mâ, mâ, mâ" the whole time, and the people go to see him. The <term>lōLE'm</term> take a canoe and paddle toward the novice while singing. When they have almost reached him, one of their number, who stays ashore dressed in a bearskin, drives all the people into the houses. The <term>lōLE'm</term> take the novice into their canoe and destroy the whale float that carried him, which is operated by means of ropes. Then he runs up and down the street like one gone wild, and the <term>ōlala'</term> follow him and bite any of the uninitiated who dare to leave the house. The novice catches a dog, tears it to pieces, and eats it while he is going from house to house.

When he returns in this way, he is completely naked. From the time he enters his house, it becomes taboo. A rope hung with red cedar bark is stretched from the door of the house to a pole erected on the beach, preventing people from passing in front of the house and forcing them to go behind it. A large ring of red cedar bark is fastened to the pole in front of the house. These remains on the house for a day after the novice’s return. On the following day, four men put on bearskins and place rings of red cedar bark on their heads. Dressed like this, they go from house to house, inviting the people to see the novice's dance and to learn his songs. When the people have gathered, the novice's uncle spreads blankets on the floor for the youth to dance on. Then his uncle pays the chiefs who tried to bring him back and also distributes blankets among the rest of the people. He holds a feast where two kinds of berries are served, each mixed with grease. Chiefs are given large spoons filled with grease. Their people help them eat the contents, as they must not leave any of the food they receive. After the ceremony, the novice is called Laamg·a't (a perfect man).

People who want to become members of the ōlala' must have been <term>shamans</term> first.

The following description of an ōlala' initiation was given by a man who had undergone the ceremony himself, though he is now a Christian. I wonder whether the grave ceremonies he described were actually performed, or if he was simply reflecting the dread in which the ōlala' were held.

During a festival where he was to be initiated, his friends pretended to start a quarrel. They drew knives and pretended to kill him. They made him disappear and cut off the head of a dummy that had been skillfully introduced. Then they laid the body down and covered it, and the women began to mourn and wail. His relatives gave a feast, distributed blankets, slaves, canoes, and coppers, and burned the body. In short, they held a standard funeral.

After his disappearance, the young man went to a grave. He took a body out of the grave and wrapped a blanket around both himself and the corpse. He lay with the corpse in this way for an entire night. The other ōlala' watched him from a distance. In the morning, he put the body back into the grave. He continued doing this for some time to build his courage. During all this time, and for a full year afterward, he was not seen by any member of the tribe except the ōlala'.

The G·ispawaduwE'da are brought back by a killer whale, as described above; the Laxk·ebō' by a bear, the Laxskī'yek on the back of an eagle which rises from underground, the Qanha'da on the back of a frog. This is accomplished by means of a raft which is covered with planks and weighed down so that it floats a short distance under the surface of the water. It is pulled by means of a rope by some of the other ōlala' while the novice is dancing on it, so that the impression is conveyed that he is approaching on the surface of the water. When he reaches the village, he eats of the body which he is carrying, and one or another of the chiefs kills a slave and throws the body to the ōlala', who devour it. It is said that before eating human flesh the ōlala' always use emetics, and that afterwards they tickle their throats with feathers to ensure vomiting.

During the dancing season a feast is given, and while the women are dancing, the <term>novice</term> is suddenly said to have disappeared. It is supposed that he goes to heaven. If he is a child, he stays away four days; youths remain about six days, and grown-up persons several months. Chiefs are supposed to stay in heaven during the fall and the entire winter. When this period has elapsed, they suddenly reappear

The chief goes first. The women sit down in one row, handsomely dressed in button blankets with their faces painted red. The chief wears the <term>*amhalait*</term>—a carving rising from the forehead, decorated with sea-lion bristles and a long drape of ermine skins (see Plate 47)—while the others wear the cedar bark rings of their societies. Then the women begin to dance. After a while, a prominent man rises to deliver a speech. He says: “All of you know that our novice went up to heaven; then he made a mistake and has been returned; now you will see him.” Then he begins the song; the curtain is drawn and masked dancers are seen surrounding the novice, representing the spirits which he encountered in heaven. At the same time, eagle down is blown into the air. After the dance is over, the presents which were strung on the rope are distributed among the members of the secret society.

The novice has a beautifully painted room set apart for his use. He remains naked during the dancing season. He must not look into the fire. He must abstain from food and drink and is only allowed to moisten his lips occasionally. He wears his head ring continually. After the ceremonies are all finished, the festival of “clothing the novice” is celebrated. He sits in his room quietly singing while the people assemble in the house. His song is heard to grow louder, and at last he makes his appearance. He has taken off his ring of red cedar bark. Then the people try to throw a bear skin over him, which they succeed in doing only after a severe struggle. All the societies take part in this feast, each sitting grouped together. The uninitiated stand at the door. This ends the ceremonies.

The initiations are repeated from time to time, and a person's rank becomes higher the more frequently he has gone through the ceremony; but nobody, except for chiefs, can be a member of more than one secret society. The <term>*sEmhalai't*</term> is a preparatory step to the societies, as everyone who wants to enter them must have acquired the <term>*sEmhalai't*</term> first. A member of one of the other societies, namely the <term>*mēiLa'*</term>, <term>*nōnLE'm*</term>, or <term>*ōlala'*</term>, cannot enter any other society, but remains in the society in which he has been initiated. Those who have passed twice through the <term>*sEmhalai't*</term> ceremonies are called <term>*ts'ē'ik*</term>.

## XIV. THE GROWTH OF THE SECRET SOCIETIES.

The secret societies of the Kwakiutl, as we know them nowadays, are undoubtedly a complex growth. We will endeavor to clarify, as far as possible, the history of their development by means of the material presented in the preceding paper.

A comparison of the ceremonials of the various tribes of the North Pacific Coast, which were briefly described in the last chapter, does

...does not leave any doubt that they are, in the main, derived from the same source. Not only are the ceremonies much alike, but even their names are identical. Among all the tribes, the badges of the ceremonies are made of cedar bark, which is dyed red in alder juice. Head rings, neck rings, and masks are worn by the dancers. The performances themselves are essentially the same from Alaska to Juan de Fuca Strait. But the most certain proof of their common origin lies in the identity of names among the various tribes. Among the Haida, Tlingit, and Tsimshian, we find the names <term>ōlala</term>, <term>mē'ila</term>, and <term>nō'nLEM</term>, which belong to the Kwakiutl ceremonies as well. Among the Biłxula, the names cannot be derived from the same words as among the other tribes, but there the ceremony itself is almost identical to that of the Kwakiutl. It certainly does not differ more from the ceremony described here than the ceremonies of other tribes of Kwakiutl lineage differ from the ceremonies of the Kwakiutl proper. In addition to this, the names of the dancers—if not those of their dances—are very often borrowed from the Kwakiutl. Turning to the south, we find the Nootka as well as the Salishan tribes who practice the ceremony, calling it by the two names <term>Lō'koala</term> and <term>nō'nLEM</term>, both of which are names used for portions of the Kwakiutl ceremonies.

As all the words which I have listed belonged originally to the Kwakiutl language, there can be no doubt that the ceremonies of the Kwakiutl have influenced those of the neighboring tribes to a very great extent. It does not necessarily follow that no secret societies existed before the Kwakiutl exerted their influence over the people of the coast. On the contrary, the wide distribution of secret societies and the general similarity of the underlying principle all over North America make it probable that such societies did exist. But there can be no doubt that their present character was attained among the Kwakiutl, from whom the societies in their present form spread over a vast territory.<note>It cannot be proved that any connection exists between the <term>hawī'nalaL</term> ceremonies described on page 495 and the sun-dance ceremonies of the Sioux and Blackfeet, but their similarity is quite striking.</note>

The question then arises: How did the societies acquire their unique characteristics among the Kwakiutl? At this point, I may be allowed to

I refer to what I previously stated (pp. 332, 336) regarding the growth of the <term>clan system</term> of the <term>Kwakiutl</term> tribes. I pointed out that this system probably reached its current development under the influence of the <term>clan system</term> of the northern tribes. The social distinction associated with possessing a clan legend provided enough inspiration for the Indian to turn his imagination in this direction, and the hereditary <term>manitou</term> probably became the <term>totem</term> of the clan.

The close similarity between the clan legends and those involving the acquisition of spirits presiding over <term>secret societies</term>—as well as the intimate relationship between these and the tribes' social organizations—allows us to apply the same argument to the growth of <term>secret societies</term>. This leads us to the conclusion that the same <term>psychological factor</term> that shaped the clans into their current form also shaped the <term>secret societies</term>.

If this argument is correct, we should expect the legends of the <term>secret societies</term> to show signs of foreign influence, even though they are among the tribes' most sacred myths, as these influences must have provided the material for the ideas that gave rise to the myths. I will not enter into a detailed discussion of these traditions here, as I have done so in another publication.<note>1. "*Indian Legends of the North Pacific Coast of America*," Berlin, 1895, p. 329.</note> I have shown that all legends in this region have complex origins and must have been carried over enormous distances from tribe to tribe. This is true for insignificant tales as well as the most important myths, such as creation legends and the legends regarding the origin of <term>secret societies</term>. To give only one or two examples: In the story of the origin of the <term>Hē'iltsuq</term> <term>cannibal society</term> (p. 401), it is said that a woman gave birth to a number of dogs who learned the secrets of the <term>cannibal society</term>. This tale is found throughout the entire northwestern part of North America—among all the <term>Athapascan</term> tribes, the <term>Eskimo</term>, and all along the <term>North Pacific Coast</term>. This is the only instance where it is connected to the origin of <term>secret societies</term>; therefore, I conclude that a foreign story has been incorporated into this myth.

While the foreign portion of the myth here forms only a loosely connected incident, foreign material is much more closely interwoven into the entire fabric of the most important of all the legends of <term>secret societies</term>, namely, the tale of <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>. When we compare this myth with the <term>Chinook</term> creation myth,<note>2. "*Chinook Texts*," Bulletin T 20 of the Bureau of Ethnology, Washington, 1894, p. 9.</note> we find a remarkable resemblance in certain parts of the legends. The grandmother of the <term>Chinook</term> deity was carried away by a monster when she was a child. Her child became the mother of the <term>culture hero</term>, and with her help, the monster was killed. Among the <term>Kwakiutl</term>, the cannibal spirit carries away a girl and is finally killed with her help. In one version, their child becomes the new cannibal spirit. There are several stories on the west coast of <term>Vancouver Island</term> which form
