These instances show that the myths referring to the ceremonial have complex origins.

I will point out another peculiarity of these traditions: When we compare the legends as told by the various tribes of the coast, we find that the ceremonial is derived from a variety of myths. Some men obtained it from <term>BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē</term>, others from the wolves, and still others brought it down from heaven. The legend of the <term>Tsimshian</term> tells that a hunter obtained it from a bear who took him into its lodge inside a rock (p. 652). Traditions that are entirely distinct in character and origin are brought forward to explain the origin of the same ceremonial.

What does this prove? We have seen that none of the tales referred to can be considered a product of the genius of any of these tribes uninfluenced by any foreign sources. All the traditions are full of foreign elements which can be traced, step by step, to distant regions. When we see, therefore, that the same ritual is explained by a variety of traditions, we must conclude that in this region at least the ritual is older than the tradition referring to the ritual; that the former must be considered primary, the latter secondary.

I believe the source of the ritual, as well as of the legends which are connected with it, must be sought in the advantages and the prerogatives that membership in <term>secret societies</term> provides. This must have caused a desire to possess such membership, which either led men to acquire memberships in existing societies, or, where these were not sufficient, for the people to invent new ones. Of course, I do not mean to say that the Indian invented traditions consciously and intentionally, but that the desire excited his imagination and his whole state of mind, and that in this manner, after appropriate fasting, the opportunity was given for hallucinations, the material for which was necessarily taken from the existing ideas, or from the ideas of neighboring tribes. These are the peculiar phenomena that were set forth by <term>Stoll</term> in his book on *Suggestion*, and I think in a deeper manner by <term>Tarde</term> in his book on the *Laws of Imitation*.

It is easy to understand how the exciting aspect of the ceremonial of the <term>cannibal society</term> caused a young man who had gone fasting to believe that he saw in his hallucinations the same spirit under new conditions, and to tell of his experience after his return. As the notion had become established that the spirit, after having been seen, had a tendency to reappear to the descendants, an opportunity was given for the formation of a new place in the secret society. ...therefore assume that the psychological explanation for the development of the complicated system of membership in secret societies lies in the combined action of the social system on the one hand and the method of acquiring <term>manitous</term> on the other.

While these considerations explain the variety of forms of the secret societies and prove that the myths on which the ritual is apparently founded are probably secondary in character, they do not give a clue to the origin of the secret societies and the peculiar customs connected with them. There are, however, indications that allow us to conclude that these customs had their origin in methods of warfare. First of all, the deity <term>Wīna'lag·ilis</term> is considered the bringer of the ceremonial. This name means "the one who makes war upon the whole world," and he rules the mind of man during times of war as well as during the period of activity of the secret societies. For this reason, also, the secret societies are active during times of war, in winter as well as in summer (see p. 429). All the oldest songs of these societies refer to war; the cannibal, the bear dancer, and the fool dancer are considered chief warriors and fall into ecstasies as soon as they have killed an enemy. All this seems to indicate that the origin of the secret societies is closely connected with warfare.

But one more thing must be considered. The customs we observe today are evidently a modern development of more ancient forms. The ceremonial of cannibalism, which today is the most important part of the entire ceremonial, is known to have been introduced among the various tribes recently, although its foundation—the idea of the existence of a spirit who kills people—is present among all the tribes. The <term>Kwakiutl</term> uniformly state that the custom of devouring men was introduced among their tribe about sixty years ago, and that it was derived from the <term>He'iltsuq</term>. We also have conclusive evidence that the custom was acquired by the <term>Tsimshian</term> no more than seventy years ago, and that they also obtained it from the <term>He'iltsuq</term>. Therefore, there is no doubt that the custom was originally confined to the small territory of the <term>He'iltsuq</term>. Among the southern tribes, the action of the cannibal was confined to his biting the heads of enemies that were cut off in war.

The form in which the ceremony of cannibalism of the <term>He'iltsuq</term> first appeared was as follows: A slave was killed by his owner and was then torn and eaten by the cannibals; or pieces of flesh were torn with the teeth from the arms or the chest of people; or, finally, corpses prepared in a particular manner were devoured by the cannibal. The first of these customs shows its close connection with warfare clearly. The slave is the booty of the cannibal or of his relatives, and by slaying him, the victory is once more brought before the eyes of his admiring friends. It is hardly possible to prove definitely that the secret societies developed exclusively from customs relating to warfare, but I believe my remarks have made clear the close connection between the two phenomena.

<vocab>Wīna'lag·ilis, Kwakiutl, He'iltsuq, Tsimshian, manitous, secret societies, cannibalism, warfare</vocab>

<summary>The author argues that the secret societies and their rituals, specifically cannibalism, originated from warfare practices and were recently adopted by the Kwakiutl and Tsimshian from the He'iltsuq tribe.</summary>
<keywords>Wīna'lag·ilis, Kwakiutl, He'iltsuq, Tsimshian, manitous, secret societies, cannibalism, warfare, ceremonial origins</keywords>

<image-desc>
A sheet music transcription with three lines of musical notation and lyrics in Kwak'wala.
- The first staff is in a treble clef with a key signature of three flats (E-flat major/C-minor). Below the staff is a rhythmic beating line indicated by eighth and sixteenth notes.
- The second staff introduces a 2/4 time signature after a double bar. The lyrics read: "ha - yē ya hâ . . . â . . .". Below the lyrics is a rhythmic line of eighth notes.
- The third staff features 2/4 time with triplet markings, transitioning into a 3/4 time signature. The lyrics read: "hâ - â - â â yē - hē | Mōtma nō - sa -". Below the staff, the rhythmic beating line changes to a 5/8 time signature. To the right of the staff are the notes "etc. as above." and "etc."
</image-desc>

The three-part beats are syncopated, with the sticks being raised at each quarter and therefore falling nearly on the second eighth note of the three-part bar. The four-part rhythm is syncopated in the same manner. The rhythm of the tune in the second line, *Lāts'ek·as g·anEmLē*, is not quite certain. I counted the F of the second bar as almost three eighth notes, and similarly in the seventh bar of this section; however, there seemed to be slight irregularities in the rhythm throughout the first seven bars of this part of the song, even though the beating is perfectly regular—five eighth notes against three of the melody. The text as sung by my informant differs slightly from the dictated text.

<summary>Nō'mas completes the ritual naming of the "Copper under rock" and takes on new ceremonial names after giving a feast. A new narrative begins with NEmō'guîs, who sets aside his supernatural bird mask to raise his son Ō'maxt'ā'laLē and begins building a cedar canoe for him.</summary>

L'ō'Lawas, the chief's younger brother, travels to numerous villages and river points to invite tribal leaders and their people to a great feast.</summary>

<summary>Chief NEmō'guîs hosts a large gathering of tribes, distributing seal meat and fur blankets according to strict rank and establishing tribal laws for future generations. His successor, Ō'maxt'ā'laLē, later departs to bathe and explore, where he hears the sound of adzing nearby.</summary>

<summary>This page concludes the story of the hō'xhok^u's death in the fire and introduces the legend of the Ghosts, where K·oā'La and his family descend from the upper world to the lower world using a copper post ladder and a magical growing mountain. K·oā'La remains behind, naming his children's tribe the Pēpā'wilēnōx and instructing them to return for his carvings.</summary>

<summary>A child who had died revives within his grave box and is taken by ghosts to their dancing house, where he is cautioned to learn their songs but refuse their food. He is eventually returned to the world of the living, where a shaman instructs the tribe to use urine for a purification ritual.</summary>

1. Wa! k·ik·a'lēqalag·ilak·asLē ts'aēqēwē'x·dēs BaxbakuālanuXsi'-
<gloss>Wa! Everyone is frightened by his winter mask, BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē.</gloss>
waē.
<gloss></gloss>
5 2. Wa! k·ik·a'lēqalag·ilak·asLē ha'msiwēx·dēs Qoā'qoaxuālanuXsi'-

waē.
<gloss></gloss>
3. WElwelq'ēqalag·ilak·asLē qalō'kwēx·dēs.
<gloss>His hooked beak causes real palpitations.</gloss>
4. WElwelq'ēqalag·ilak·asLē hau'xhokuēwēx·dēs.
<gloss>His hau'xhok mask causes real palpitation.</gloss>

<sup>1</sup>That is, from the nō'nLEM dancing house to that of the ts'ē'tsaēqa.

<summary>This page describes the ritual transition of Lē'laxa between ceremonial houses and provides the lyrics and musical score for the "Song of the Raven Mask." The verses emphasize the terror inspired by the masks of supernatural beings like BaxbakuālanuXsi'waē.</summary>
